repressing flhDC transcription and activating synthesis of colanic acid, a major component of biofilm matrix. As for RprA, the role of McaS in biofilm formation is not restricted to regulating csgD and flhDC, since McaS was found to increase biofilm formation in a pgaA-dependent manner. pgaA is required for the export of a polysaccharide adhesin called PGA (poly-β- 1,6 N-acetyl-D-glucosamine), another constituent of the biofilm matrix. Interestingly, while McaS regulates csgD and flhDC through base pairing, it activates pgaA indirectly through CsrA. Indeed, McaS is not only an Hfq-binding sRNA but also a CsrAbinding sRNA, and it therefore also affects biofilm formation by indirectly deregulating CsrA targets, among them pgaA, as well as flhDC and two genes for diguanylate cyclases (Figure 5.1.1) (Jorgensen et al., 2013). 

Despite this already extremely intricate network, sRNAs involved in biofilm formation or motility are not restricted to those mentioned so far. It is, for instance, likely that other known regulators of CsrA, such as CsrB or CsrC, could affect biofilm formation, even though it might not be true in all conditions (Jorgensen et al., 2013). Furthermore, GadY and MicA sRNAs were found to affect motility while ArcZ and SdsR upregulated biofilm formation (De Lay and Gottesman, 2012; Monteiro et al., 2012), via still-elusive mechanisms. It is also possible that, under specific conditions, regulators of RpoS, H-NS, or other TFs involved in the biofilm or motility pathway could have effects as well. 

These sRNAs can certainly allow the integration of environmental cues, in addition to the signals that are transduced by the multiple TF regulators of csgD and flhDC, to precisely control expression of these two key regulators. They also likely contribute to restrict induction of csgD or flhDC to very specific conditions, which might be beneficial by preventing the synthesis of curli or flagella when they are not required. These multiple sRNAs could also provide unique dynamic properties, in particular fast switch-like responses under both induction and deinduction conditions, and participate in the synchrony among the population (see Section 5.1.5). 

Importantly, direct control by sRNAs also applies to master regulators such as H-NS or Lrp, whose expression impacts hundreds of genes (Table 5.1.1; see also http://regulondb. ccg.unam.mx). 

## 5.1.4.3 Two-component systems

Several bacterial TFs are part of the so-called TCSs, in which their activity is regulated by phosphorylation. TCSs are widely used in bacteria as a way to sense and respond to the environment. They usually consist of a sensor histidine kinase (HK), located at the membrane, which autophosphorylates in response to a specific stimulus and can then transfer the phosphoryl group on a conserved aspartate residue of a cognate response regulator (RR). The RR is often a DNA-binding protein, whose phosphorylation leads to changes in transcription of target genes (see Chapter 3.1). There can be variations from this simplest scheme, for instance in phosphorelay systems (such as the Rcs pathway mentioned here) where additional phosphotransfer steps and additional components are involved (Laub and Goulian, 2007). In many cases, the genes for the cognate HK and RR are organized in an operon, allowing for a common regulation. As for other TFs, regulation of several TCSs has been shown to be mediated by regulatory RNAs through various mechanisms. 

Several sRNAs directly base-pair to mRNAs encoding TCSs and repress their expression. This is the case for two of the most thoroughly studied TCSs in enterobacteria, EnvZ–OmpR and PhoQ–PhoP, encoded respectively by the ompR–envZ and phoPQ operons. EnvZ–OmpR is involved in adaptation to changes in osmolarity (Pratt et al., 1996), and PhoQ–PhoP in magnesium homeostasis, LPS modifications, and bacterial virulence (Groisman et al., 2013). OmrA and OmrB, two seemingly redundant OmpR-activated sRNAs, repress OmpR synthesis (and presumably that of EnvZ as well), thereby creating a regulatory feedback circuit (Guillier and Gottesman, 2008). As for phoPQ mRNA, it is targeted by two unrelated sRNAs, MicA and GcvB, made in response to envelope stress and availability of amino acids, respectively (Coornaert et al., 2010, 2013). Surprisingly, however, regulation of these TCSs by sRNAs can have drastically different effects on the regulons of the TCSs. More precisely, OmrA/B does not change the level of OmpR-P, the phosphorylated form of OmpR, in agreement with the previously reported robustness of OmpR-P to changes in ompR or envZ expression (Batchelor and Goulian, 2003). Consequently, OmrA/B does not affect the transcription of robust OmpR targets such as ompC or ompF; nevertheless, OmrA/B can limit their own synthesis by repressing ompR (A. Brosse et al., unpublished data). In the case of PhoQ–PhoP, while both MicA and GcvB repress phoP translation and decrease phoPQ mRNA levels, only MicA has been found to indirectly repress PhoP targets (Coornaert et al., 2013). While the precise molecular mechanism underlying these observations is still unclear, these findings highlight the need to systematically study the effect of a regulatory RNA controlling a given TF on this TF’s regulon. 

Control of TCSs by RNAs is, however, not restricted to base pairing sRNAs. Recently, the study of the regulation of the ethanolamine (EA) utilization (eut) genes in two Gram-positive bacteria, Listeria monocytogenes and Enterococcus faecalis, unraveled an exquisite role for a riboswitch-controlled sRNA in binding an active response regulator. EA derives from mammalian and bacterial cell membranes and is prevalent in the gastrointestinal environment. Bacteria that possess the genes for EA catabolism can use it as a source of nitrogen and carbon, and EA utilization has been linked to bacterial virulence in several studies. In diverse bacteria, expression of the eut genes is induced in the presence of both EA and adenosylcobalamine (AdoCbl, one of the active forms of vitamin $\mathrm { B } _ { 1 2 } ) _ { : }$ , a cofactor required for EA utilization. In firmicutes such as L. monocytogenes or E. faecalis, a key component of this control is the EutWV TCS, which is activated in the presence of EA. EutV is an unusual RR that, in the phosphorylated form, binds to RNA (and not DNA) elements consisting of a dual hairpin structure (also called ANTAR elements) and promotes antitermination. Several ANTAR elements are found within the eut locus, including one downstream of an AdoCbl-responsive riboswitch, present toward the beginning of the locus (that comprises more than 15 genes in the two species). This riboswitch allows the production of a short transcript upon binding of AdoCbl, but in its absence, a longer transcript, that encompasses an ANTAR element, is produced. This long transcript can then sequester EutV-P, which prevents antitermination at the distal ANTAR sites. This ensures that, unless both EA and AdoCbl are present, expression of the eut genes is not induced (DebRoy et al., 2014; Mellin et al., 2014). 

## 5.1.5 Roles and properties of mixed regulatory circuits

The recognition that many regulatory circuits in bacteria are mixed – that is, composed of both protein regulators (that act at the transcriptional level) and regulatory RNAs (that, in many cases, act at the posttranscriptional level) – raises the question of the possible advantages and specific properties of such circuits. 

In general, having a regulator B in the regulon of a regulator A is expected to (i) expand the regulon of A, (ii) allow integration of multiple input signals to precisely control gene expression, (iii) allow the possibility to rewire an activator into a repressor and conversely (e.g., an activator A could indirectly repress gene expression through a repressor B), and (iv) connect different regulatory pathways. Furthermore, if A or B is a regulatory RNA, this might have other implications. 

## 5.1.5.1 Regulating gene expression with sRNAs

An advantage of using regulatory RNAs that is often proposed is a cheap and fast synthesis in comparison with protein regulators. Maybe more importantly, they act mostly at the posttranscriptional level (i.e., at a step that is closer to protein production than transcription). This allows for a faster response than transcriptional control (Shimoni et al., 2007), and, in the case of negative regulation, it can prevent expression of abundant and/or long-lived target mRNAs that, if regulation was exerted at the level of transcription, could be used in several rounds of translation (see Chapter 2.8). In this regard, it is striking that regulatory RNAs directly repress many mRNAs encoding OMPs (e.g., ompA, ompC, ompF, lpp, etc.) that have been reported to be both abundant and stable mRNAs (Bernstein et al., 2002). 

Possibly also contributing to the widespread occurrence of sRNAs in regulatory circuits is their ability to evolve quickly (Gottesman and Storz, 2011). For instance, many Hfq-binding sRNAs present in E. coli accumulate inside the Enterobacteriales order only (Peer and Margalit, 2014). Furthermore, these sRNAs can also rapidly acquire novel targets given the flexibility of sRNA–mRNA pairing, as exemplified by the fact that RybB controls the ompN gene in Salmonella but not in the closely related bacterium E. coli (Gogol et al., 2011). 

Another important aspect of regulatory RNAs is that they act through a noncatalytic (or stoichiometric) mechanism in many cases. In other words, they are used only once; this is true, for instance, for most base-pairing sRNAs because they are degraded along with their target mRNA, or because they form extremely stable sRNA–mRNA duplexes. This allows a threshold-linear mode of repression where, below a threshold of transcription, a target mRNA is tightly repressed, whereas above this threshold, repression decreases linearly with the difference between the transcription rate of the target mRNA and that of the sRNA (Levine et al., 2007). The threshold corresponds to the situation where transcription rates of the target mRNA and of the regulatory sRNA are similar; it is therefore a dynamic threshold dependent on conditions that will affect transcription of the sRNA and its target mRNA. This mode of response has important implications: at low transcription, a target mRNA can be tightly repressed by an sRNA, and this tight repression is expected to suppress fluctuations and decrease noise in gene expression (Levine et al., 2007). This can provide an important advantage for targets whose stochastic bursts of protein synthesis issued from noise in transcription can be deleterious. This can also sustain multistable genetic systems. For instance, positively autoregulated genes, such as genes for many TFs, can typically sustain two states of expression, high or low. And repression by a sRNA is expected to both maintain the bistability and increase the probability to remain in the low state over time, when compared to an autoregulated TF not controlled by a sRNA (Levine and Hwa, 2008). Interestingly, csgD was shown to display a bistable expression in Salmonella (Grantcharova et al., 2010), but whether the multiple sRNAs that control csgD expression have a role in this pattern remains to be determined. In this case, bistability could minimize the cost of making a biofilm as only the CsgD ON cells would produce the extracellular matrix, while maintaining the possibility for a fast development of a different phenotype with the CsgD OFF cells. 

An additional consequence of the threshold effect is the characteristic de-repression dynamics following the disappearance of the input signal for a repressor sRNA. Indeed, the switch from a repressed to nonrepressed state is predicted to be much more abrupt than with protein-mediated regulation (Levine and Hwa, 2008). It is also expected that stoichiometrically acting sRNAs filter transient signals while selectively responding to sustained stimuli (Legewie et al., 2008; Levine and Hwa, 2008; Mehta et al., 2008). 

At last, the very vast majority of sRNAs acting by imperfect base pairing have multiple targets, which will compete for sRNA binding. The regulation of any target will therefore depend on expression of the whole “targetome” of the sRNA, which itself is expected to vary with changing stimuli (e.g., Plumbridge et al., 2014). Furthermore, Hfq-binding sRNAs have been reported to compete for Hfq, and their abundance and activity will thus also depend on expression of all Hfq-binding sRNAs at a given time (Fender et al., 2010; Hussein and Lim, 2011; Moon and Gottesman, 2011). These two types of cross-talk, between targets and between sRNAs, are expected to set up unique patterns of regulation when conditions vary. 

## 5.1.5.2 sRNAs in mixed regulatory circuits

Network motifs that incorporate sRNAs have been extensively described previously (Beisel and Storz, 2010); we will focus more specifically on two of those: the feedback and the feedforward motifs (Figure 5.1.2). 

sRNAs commonly target genes for TFs or sigma factors in a feedback circuit (FC) (also called a feedback loop), in which the RNA controls expression of its own TF, and conversely. This can be mediated by direct regulatory interactions (as for the OmpR–OmrA/B FC) but also indirectly. For instance, the RpoEdependent sRNAs indirectly reduce RpoE activity by repressing expression of multiple or abundant OMPs. Many TFs are subject to negative autoregulation (i.e., they repress their own transcription), which has been shown to increase response time and decrease cell-to-cell variations (Alon, 2007b; Thieffry et al., 1998). However, examples of negative FCs based on two factors regulating each other are very rare in purely transcriptional networks, but are found in cases where the two arms of the loop act on different timescales (e.g., one arm of the loop engages in transcriptional regulation, and the other in protein–protein interaction). In such cases, a negative FC was reported to create oscillations or noise-driven excitable pulses, depending on the timescale of the two regulatory interactions (Figure 5.1.2) (Alon, 2007a; Thieffry, 2007). 

Whether this is true as well for those sRNA-containing FCs is still an open question. The possible roles of negative FCs mediated by sRNAs have been addressed experimentally in the Vibrio quorum-sensing pathway. Quorum sensing is the process by which bacteria communicate and switch between a singlecell behavior at low cell density (LCD) and a community behavior at high cell density (HCD). In Vibrio cholerae and Vibrio harveyi, this switch is governed by a mixed regulatory circuit, whose global architecture is similar between the two species, even though some important differences have been described (reviewed in Ng and Bassler, 2009; see Section 21). To summarize, multiple sRNAs called Qrr lie at the core of this pathway and control, in response to cell density and the phosphorylated LuxO RR, the expression of two TFs: HapR (in V. cholerae)–LuxR (in V. harveyi) and AphA, which are, respectively, the HCD and the LCD master regulators of quorum sensing. Multiple FCs have been described in this pathway, in particular mixed FCs between the Qrr and LuxO, the Qrr and LuxR–HapR (indirect in the case of HapR, as it indirectly activates Qrr synthesis), and the Qrr and AphA (Figure 5.1.2). These FCs provide specific dynamic properties (they delay entry in the HCD mode while accelerating the transition from HCD to LCD) and contribute, with the negative autoregulation of LuxO, LuxR–HapR, and AphA, to minimizing the fluctuations in the levels of the different components of the pathway. This allows a precise timing of the switch between LCD and HCD, with cells coordinately responding to a specific range of input signals (autoinducers), which is likely to be the key for a successful collective behavior (Ng and Bassler, 2009, and references therein; Rutherford et al., 2011; Tu et al., 2010). 

sRNAs also participate in positive FCs, where two repressors or two activators control themselves reciprocally: MicF inhibits synthesis of the Lrp master regulator in a double-negative FC (Corcoran et al., 2012; Holmqvist et al., 2012); and RyhB also forms a double-negative FC with the Fur TF, in this case through both a direct pairing and indirect control of Fur activity (Masse´ et al., 2005; Vecerek et al., 2007). A positive FC composed of two TFs has been reported to establish bistability, with both regulators being on or off (for double-positive FC) or, in contrast, with one regulator being on and the other off (for double-negative FC). In line with this, the MicF-Lrp FC was proposed to ensure that the levels of each regulator followed a reciprocal pattern with Lrp or MicF predominating in, respectively, nutrient-poor or nutrient-rich medium (Holmqvist et al., 2012). 

In several cases of mixed regulatory circuits, a TF controlled expression of genes both directly and indirectly through the control of a regulatory RNA, thereby creating a regulatory motif known as a feedforward motif (FFM; also called a feedforward loop). This is what is found, for instance, in the case of the multi-output FFM between CRP and Spot42 to control genes involved in sugar utilization, or in the control of ompC, ompF, or flhDC by OmpR, and by the OmpR-regulated MicC, MicF, and OmrA/B sRNAs, respectively (Figures 5.1.1 and 5.1.2). These are examples of coherent FFMs, where direct and indirect control both activate or repress gene expression. But regulatory RNAs are also found in incoherent FFMs, where two arms of the regulatory circuit have opposite effects: OmpR activates csgD transcription directly, while also promoting synthesis of OmrA/B, two sRNAs that repress csgD expression (Holmqvist et al., 2010). Similarly, PhoP activates transcription of the MgtC virulence factor in Salmonella, but also of an asRNA named AmgR, which in turn limits MgtC production (Figure 5.1.2) (Lee and Groisman, 2010). 

FFM properties have been studied in detail in purely transcriptional networks. Depending on the different interactions that can take place between the two regulators and the target, eight types of FFMs have been defined (four types of coherent FFMs and four types of incoherent ones). In general, coherent FFMs are expected to induce a delay in the (on or off) response and to filter transient (on or off) signals, whereas incoherent FFMs can increase response time and sometimes generate a pulse in gene expression (Figure 5.1.2) (Mangan and Alon, 2003). Interestingly, the mixed coherent FFMs that include transcriptional regulatory proteins and posttranscriptional repressor RNAs have been proposed to provide a tighter control of gene expression and a faster recovery following deactivation when compared to purely transcriptional FFMs (Shimoni et al., 2007). In the case of the CRP/Spot42-mediated FFM, the Spot42 sRNA was shown to further repress expression of the target genes, and to affect the dynamics of the regulation. More precisely, Spot42 delayed the response to loop activation (similar to what is expected for a similar TF-based FFM) (Figure 5.1.2), but also accelerated the response following loop deactivation (Beisel and Storz, 2011a). This last property has not been observed for purely transcriptional FFMs of the same type, and suggests that network properties could differ between mixed regulatory networks and purely transcriptional ones (Beisel and Storz, 2011b). 

## 5.1.6 Conclusions

Regulatory RNAs allow a rapid and dynamic response of bacteria to changes in their environment, and they are consistently widespread in stress responses. In many cases, they are part of mixed regulatory circuits that combine (i) transcriptional and posttranscriptional control, and (ii) protein and RNA regulators. Although the few examples studied in detail, such as those described in this chapter, suggested that regulatory RNAs can provide specific properties over proteins, the precise role of RNA in the very vast majority of mixed circuits remains to be precisely characterized. 

Furthermore, not only are many of those circuits certainly still incomplete, but also more connections between transcriptional regulators and sRNAs will undoubtedly be characterized in the future, in diverse bacteria. These findings should help answer important questions such as the role of those circuits in gene expression, the possible over- or underrepresentation of some motifs, and the conservation of circuits to control the same functions in distant bacteria where sRNAs themselves might not be conserved.

# Role of small RNAs in Pseudomonas aeruginosa virulence and adaptation

Hansi Kumari1, Deepak Balasubramanian2, and Kalai Mathee1 

1Department of Human and Molecular Genetics, Herbert Wertheim College of Medicine, Florida International University, Miami, Florida, USA 

2Department of Microbiology and Immunobiology, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts, USA 

## 5.2.1 Introduction

Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a highly adaptable and nutritionally versatile bacterium that can thrive in a wide variety of biotic and abiotic habitats. It is responsible for numerous nosocomial infections, especially in immunocompromised patients, and is the leading cause of persistent airway infections in cystic fibrosis (CF) patients (Gaspar et al., 2013; Papagheorghe, 2012; Salins et al., 2012). Moreover, acute infections by P. aeruginosa can transition into chronic, intractable infections at virtually any body site, spelling poor prognosis for the patient. P. aeruginosa possesses many unique traits that contribute to its success as an opportunistic pathogen. The primary determinants of its pathogenic potential are a high degree of intrinsic and acquired antibiotic resistance, and its multifactorial virulence factor production. It also has one of the largest genomes known among prokaryotes (Stover et al., 2000; Tummler et al., 2014). A complex and intricate gene regulatory network lies at the heart of the pathogenic and metabolic plasticity of P. aeruginosa (Balasubramanian et al., 2013b; Coggan and Wolfgang, 2012). The apparent discrepancy between the in silico (Balasubramanian et al., 2013a) and empirical (Balasubramanian et al., 2013b) gene regulatory networks highlights the fact that we are far from understanding the workings of this complex bacterium. 

Bacteria can respond to changing environmental conditions by modulating RNA levels, which can be achieved by transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation (see Section 4). Posttranscriptional regulation is mediated primarily by small RNAs (sRNAs), which control the rate of translation initiation by two major mechanisms (Papenfort and Vogel, 2009; Richards and Vanderpool, 2011; Waters and Storz, 2009). The first mechanism involves interaction of the sRNAs with the 5′ leader region of the messenger RNA (mRNA). This sRNA–mRNA interaction can either attenuate (by interfering with ribosome binding) or enhance (by relieving inhibitory secondary structures) mRNA translation (Storz et al., 2011). The Hfq protein functions as a RNA chaperone and stabilizes the sRNA–mRNA base pairing in Gram-negative bacteria (Bohn et al., 2007; Heidrich et al., 2006). The second mechanism of sRNA-mediated gene regulation involves sequestering of mRNA binding proteins, thus activating translation. Thus, sRNAs extend a quick and tight regulation of gene expression by either promoting or inhibiting translation of target mRNAs (Sonnleitner et al., 2012a). 

The sRNAs were originally discovered in prokaryotes and extensively studied in plasmid replication, transposition, phage development, and chromosomal gene expression (Green et al., 1986; Pestka, 1992; Simons, 1988; see Chapter 2.8). However, it gained wide popularity only after its effectiveness was demonstrated in eukaryotic gene regulation (Fire et al., 1991, 1998). Over the last 20 years, sRNAs have attracted an enormous amount of well-deserved attention as regulators of cellular responses, including pathogenesis and metabolism (Oliva et al., 2015; Zhou and Xie, 2011). Consequently, many studies have sought to explore sRNAs in P. aeruginosa, revealing over 500 thus far (Dotsch et al., 2012; Ferrara et al., 2012; Gomez-Lozano et al., 2012, 2014; Livny et al., 2006; Sonnleitner et al., 2008; Wurtzel et al., 2012). Characterization of these sRNAs is only beginning, but the established role of some sRNAs in important processes such as the acute–chronic infection switch, iron acquisition (see Section 19), and catabolite repression (see Section 7) suggests their yet unexplored, crucial role in P. aeruginosa pathogenesis and metabolism (Kay et al., 2006; Sonnleitner et al., 2009; Sonnleitner and Haas, 2011; Wilderman et al., 2004). Although numerous sRNAs are being identified in P. aeruginosa, there is a dearth of information on the regulation of their expression and assigning their targets. Owing to the difficulty in applying genetic and biochemical approaches to study sRNAs, comprehensive parallel efforts are needed to unravel their regulation and function. 

This chapter is an attempt to highlight the critical roles of sRNAs in the physiology and pathology of this important human pathogen. In order to distinguish the small RNAs from proteins, a newly established nomenclature has been followed, by which the small regulatory RNAs are referred to as rgRNA and the antisense RNAs as asRNA, as described in Balasubramanian et al. (2014, 2015) and Kumari et al. (2014b). However, standard three-letter nomenclature has been followed for the genes encoding sRNAs. The network of major regulatory interactions of the well-characterized sRNAs, connecting several important phenotypes in P. aeruginosa, is depicted in Figure 5.2.1. The role of sRNAs in each of the major processes is described in the remainder of this chapter. 

## 5.2.2 Acute chronic switch

The potential to transition from acute to chronic infection phenotypes is one of the defining features of P. aeruginosa infections. Free-living planktonic cells initiate the infection process by expression of structural features such as flagella and various pili that aid in attachment and surface motility (Lyczak et al., 2000; see Chapters 22.1 and 22.3). Establishment of an acute infection involves expression of a myriad of secreted virulence factors including elastases, other proteases, and toxins that cause localized tissue damage, targeted delivery of toxins into the host cells mediated by the Type III secretion system, expression of phenazines and other compounds that confer a survival advantage, among others (Gellatly and Hancock, 2013). In this mode of infection, P. aeruginosa is susceptible to antibiotic therapy, unless infection was established by a resistant strain. In response to triggers including the host immune responses such as oxidative stress and inflammation, antibiotic use, and other largely unidentified signals, the infection transitions to a chronic phase. This transition is characterized by drastic changes to the cell physiology (Hogardt and Heesemann, 2013; Li et al., 2014; Petrova and Sauer, 2009). Expression of most acute virulence factors is shut off, accompanied by accumulation of nichespecific adaptive mutations and diversification (Hoboth et al., 2009). These changes result in chronic infection traits such as biofilm formation, conversion to mucoidy, hypermutability, and enhanced resistance to antibiotics, resulting in a poor prognosis for the patient (Folkesson et al., 2012; Hogardt and Heesemann, 2013). 

At the heart of this acute–chronic switch is a network of transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulatory factors of the Gac–Rsm signal transduction pathway (Figure 5.2.1). The process starts with the sensor kinase GacS. GacS activation results in autophosphorylation and subsequent phosphotransfer to the response regulator, GacA (Ventre et al., 2006). The activated GacA protein binds to a GacA box in the promoters of the two sRNA genes encoding rgRsmY and rgRsmZ (Kay et al., 2006). The expression of the sRNA genes and, consequently, of the target genes increases with increasing cell densities, suggesting the existence of a positive feedback loop (Heurlier et al., 2004; Kay et al., 2006). The two sRNAs bind to and sequester the small RNA-binding protein RsmA (Heurlier et al., 2004; Kay et al., 2006). RsmA binds to GGA motifs in its target mRNAs, resulting in post-translational repression (Schubert et al., 2007). RsmA activity shifts the balance to favor acute infections by P. aeruginosa. RsmA targets include players and processes that are critical to the P. aeruginosa acute (Type 2 and Type 3 secretion systems (T3SS), and production of exotoxin ToxA and Type IV pili) and chronic (production of Pel and Psl polysaccharides, biofilm formation, T6SS, and hydrogen cyanide biosynthesis) infections (Brencic et al., 2009). By binding and nullifying the effects of RsmA, the two sRNAs, rgRsmY and rgRsmZ, play a crucial role in the transition between the two infection phenotypes (Kay et al., 2006).

As per the recently introduced nomenclature, regulatory RNAs are depicted as rgRNA, and antisense RNAs as asRNA.


Although the signals that activate the Gac–Rsm system remain largely unidentified, some progress has been made. Growth to high cell densities results in the production of signal molecules distinct from quoromones, which activate GacS (Dubuis and Haas, 2007). In addition, two hybrid sensor kinases RetS and LadS play a role in GacS phosphorylation. RetS inhibits GacS function by forming heterodimers, whereas LadS activates GacS by phosphorylation (Goodman et al., 2009). In addition, the sigma factor RpoN negatively regulates gacA expression (Heurlier et al., 2003). Given the importance of this regulatory cascade, there are additional points of control at the level of the expression of the sRNAs, rgRsmY and rgRsmZ. Expression of the ribonuclease CafA is activated by the BfiSR two-component system (TCS), which in turn targets rgRsmZ (Petrova and Sauer, 2010). Another mode of sRNA regulation involves the histidine phosphotransfer protein HptB. Phosphorylation of HptB is controlled by phosphotransfer from the hybrid sensor kinases PA2824, PA1611, PA1976, and RetS (Hsu et al., 2008). HptB in turn phosphorylates the response regulator PA3346, activating its Ser–Thr phosphatase activity (Lin et al., 2006). This results in dephosphorylation of an anti–antisigma factor PA3347 that indirectly regulates swarming and biofilm formation, and also represses rsmY expression (Bordi et al., 2010; Hsu et al., 2008). Moreover, the hybrid sensor kinase PA1611 can bypass the HptB–PA3346–PA3347 phosphorelay by interacting directly with RetS, thus allowing GacS to activate the Gac–Rsm pathway (Kong et al., 2013). Furthermore, members of the HNS family of global regulators, MvaT and MvaU, bind AT-rich regions upstream of the rsmZ gene, repressing its expression (Brencic et al., 2009). The transcriptional regulator AmpR negatively regulates expression of ladS and rgRsmZ, thus feeding into the acute–chronic transition (Balasubramanian et al., 2014, 2015). AmpR is a major regulator of antibiotic resistance and virulence in P. aeruginosa (Balasubramanian et al., 2012, 2014, 2015; Kong et al., 2005; Kumari et al., 2014a, 2014b). Under lowoxygen conditions, the major anaerobic regulator Anr activates NarL, which downregulates expression of rgRsmY and rgRsmZ (O’Callaghan et al., 2011). Given the significance of the acute-tochronic transition in bacterial survival and infection, the process is controlled by multiple, sometimes overlapping, gene regulatory mechanisms. 

## 5.2.3 Iron uptake

Iron, as a cofactor, is a crucial component of numerous enzymes that are involved in metabolism in all kingdoms of life, including bacteria. Most of the freely available iron is in the biologically unusable Fe3+ form, which is converted into the $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ form intracellularly. In addition, a high concentration of iron, such as under oxygen-rich conditions, is toxic to the cells due to generation of free radicals. Thus, a balance needs to be struck between iron starvation and toxicity. In P. aeruginosa, this iron homeostasis (see Section 19) is achieved by a network of transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation that allows the bacterium to maintain an optimal level of intracellular iron concentration, depending on the sensory inputs from the environment (Cornelis et al., 2009; Reinhart et al., 2015). During iron starvation, free iron from the environment is internalized by the secretion of siderophores, molecules that scavenge extracellular iron (Cornelis, 2010). The ferric-bound siderophores are then taken up via TonB-dependent receptors on the cell surface and reduced intracellularly to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ (Vasil, 2007). In contrast, under conditions approaching potentially toxic levels of intracellular iron, iron storage proteins such as bacterioferritin, and oxidative stress-neutralizing enzymes such as catalase and superoxide dismutase, are produced (Cornelis et al., 2009). These neutralize the toxic effects of excess iron, ensuring cell viability. 

The transcriptional regulator Fur, which is conserved in many Gram-negative bacteria, controls the process of iron uptake (Troxell and Hassan, 2013; see Chapters 19.1 and 19.2)). Under iron-replete conditions, the ferrated Fur protein binds DNA at a specific 19-bp consensus sequence (Fur box) upstream of target genes, typically functioning as a repressor (Prince et al., 1993). In addition, Fur also exerts indirect regulation by modulating expression of other transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulators, such as PchR, PvdS, TCS regulators, and the sRNAs asPrrF1 and asPrrF2 (Masse et al., 2007; Ochsner et al., 2002; Palma et al., 2003). 

Fur positively regulates expression of genes by repression of the sRNAs, asPrrF1 and asPrrF2, which form an integral part of iron acquisition, quorum sensing, and virulence in P. aeruginosa (Oglesby et al., 2008; Wilderman et al., 2004). Expression of asPrrF1 (116 nt) and asPrrF2 (114 nt) is repressed by Fur under high iron concentrations. The two sRNAs are >95% identical with redundant functions (Wilderman et al., 2004). Under conditions of iron starvation, Fur repression is relieved, allowing sRNA expression. Both asPrrF1 and asPrrF2 act by base pairing, typically in the promoter regions of target mRNAs. The asPrrF1 regulon includes over 50 target genes, especially those encoding iron metabolism and storage proteins (Oglesby et al., 2008; Wilderman et al., 2004). Thus, these two sRNAs play a critical role in determining iron storage and utilization under conditions of iron starvation in P. aeruginosa. 

The prrF sRNAs also play a role in the quorum-sensing (QS) process (see Section 21) by regulating anthranilate production (Oglesby et al., 2008). One of the two pathways of anthranilate biosynthesis is from chorismate by phnAB-encoded anthranilate synthetase (Essar et al., 1990). The phnAB operon is located just downstream of the Pseudomonas quinolone signal (PQS) biosynthetic operon (Winsor et al., 2011). The prrF sRNAs repress anthranilate degradation in iron-depleted environments, allowing for PQS biosynthesis (Oglesby et al., 2008). This allows for maximal PQS production in iron-limited environments (Nguyen et al., 2014). PQS, in addition to acting as a QS signaling molecule, functions as a redox partner with pyocyanin (Seviour et al., 2015). Given the role of phenazines in iron uptake (Price-Whelan et al., 2007; Wang et al., 2011), it is tempting to speculate that PQS has an indirect role in iron acquisition that is regulated by the prrF sRNAs. 

Another sRNA, rgPhrS, plays a role in PQS and pyocyanin expression (Sonnleitner et al., 2011). PqsR, a major QS regulator, is co-transcribed with a small open reading frame (ORF) called uof that overlaps with the pqsR ribosome binding site (RBS). By targeting the uof ORF, rgPhrS relieves the pqsR RBS, thereby allowing translation (Sonnleitner et al., 2011). The oxygen responsive regulator Anr controls the expression of rgPhrS, which is in turn regulated by the sRNA-binding protein Hfq (Moll et al., 2003; Sonnleitner et al., 2011). Thus, the sRNAs asPrrF1, asPrrF2, and rgPhrS together serve to link oxygen availability, QS, and iron acquisition in P. aeruginosa. 

At the same locus as asPrrF1 and asPrrF2 is a 325-nt sRNA, rgPrrH (Oglesby-Sherrouse and Vasil, 2010). rgPrrH is a hemeresponsive regulatory RNA whose coding region overlaps with the asPrrF1 and asPrrF2 ORFs. It is part of a heme-monitoring system that regulates heme biosynthesis, uptake, and degradation (Reinhart et al., 2015). Like the prrF sRNAs, rgPrrH is expressed maximally in the stationary phase and under conditions of iron starvation (Oglesby-Sherrouse and Vasil, 2010). The expression of rgPrrH is repressed by heme, in a process involving the two outer membrane heme receptors, PhuR and HasR (Smith and Wilks, 2015; Wilks and Burkhard, 2007). In addition to shared targets with the PrrF sRNAs (succinate dehydrogenase and aconitase operons), rgPrrH also represses nirL, encoding a protein that is involved in the biosynthesis of heme (Oglesby-Sherrouse and Vasil, 2010). Studies suggest that rgPrrH synthesis occurs due to antitermination at the asPrrF1 terminator, resulting in the hypothesis that heme regulates rgPrrH expression by antitermination of asPrrF1 transcription (Oglesby-Sherrouse and Vasil, 2010). However, the signals or the mechanisms involved in this process are as yet unidentified. 

## 5.2.4 Catabolite repression

The success of P. aeruginosa as a ubiquitously found opportunistic pathogen is partly due to its ability to adapt and thrive in diverse environments (Obritsch et al., 2004; Rahme et al., 1997; Rice et al., 2012). Its nutritional versatility is reliant on efficient use of available carbon sources driven by a process called catabolite repression. Catabolite repression is a general mechanism that enables bacteria to utilize preferential carbon sources to ensure the most efficient energy gain and growth (Gorke and Stulke, 2008; see Section 7). The process entails preventing transcription of genes required for the degradation of the less preferred substrates in the presence of the preferred substrate. In Gram-negative enteric bacteria such as E. coli, simple sugars such as glucose are preferentially utilized using two mechanisms, inducer exclusion and catabolite repression control (CRC) (Bruckner and Titgemeyer, 2002). Inducer exclusion involves lower uptake of less preferred substrate in the presence of the preferred substrate, and through CRC, transcription of less preferred substrate utilization genes is inhibited in the presence of preferred substrate by modulation of cyclic adenosine monophosphate (cAMP) levels (Crasnier, 1996; Saier, 1989). 

P. aeruginosa and other Pseudomonads, on the other hand, have a disparate concept of catabolite repression (Collier et al., 1996; Rojo, 2010). First, the hierarchy of carbon source utilization is reversed, with organic compounds and amino acids being preferred over sugars (Collier et al., 1996; Liu, 1952). This may have competitive advantage for P. aeruginosa in soil as they can use decomposing plant and animal tissue products, where the concentration of organic compounds typically exceed sugars. Another major difference is that carbon catabolite repression is controlled at the level of translation with no known role of cAMP (Rojo, 2010). The major post-transcriptional control of carbon catabolite repression in P. aeruginosa is through an RNAbinding protein called Crc (MacGregor et al., 1991). The Crc protein recognizes a CA motif (AACAACAA) region near the RBS of the mRNAs encoding enzymes required for metabolizing less preferred substrates, thereby inhibiting their translation (Sonnleitner et al., 2009). However, recent crystallization and purification studies on Crc showed no binding to its purported RNA targets (Milojevic et al., 2013). Hence, the exact mechanism of Crc-mediated translation repression remains unclear. 

Similar to RsmA–rgRsmY/rgRsmZ described in this chapter, a 407-nt sRNA rgCrcZ with five CA motifs regulates Crc activity by sequestration (Sonnleitner et al., 2009). The transcription of rgCrcZ is regulated by a TCS CbrA–CbrB located upstream of the crcZ gene (Sonnleitner et al., 2009; Sonnleitner and Haas, 2011). The sensor kinase CbrA senses the carbon source through an unknown mechanism and phosphorylates the response regulator CbrB, which regulates rgCrcZ expression (Nishijyo et al., 2001). The regulation of rgCrcZ by CbrB is also dependent on the sigma factor RpoN (Sonnleitner et al., 2009). In the presence of preferred substrates, such as succinate, the rgCrcZ levels are low, thus allowing catabolite repression through free Crc (Sonnleitner et al., 2009). The levels of rgCrcZ are moderate to high in the presence of intermediate and less preferred carbon sources such as glucose and mannitol, respectively. This allows titration of Crc levels, which unblocks the translation of metabolic genes, allowing gradual response to the changing growth conditions (Sonnleitner et al., 2009). Studies have demonstrated a wide-ranging regulatory effect of the CbrAB– Crc–rgCrcZ regulatory cascade, including a potential role in the establishment of chronic infections in the CF lung (Sonnleitner et al., 2012b; Yeung et al., 2011, 2014). This whole system bears close analogy to the RsmA–rgRsmY/Z system described earlier (Brencic et al., 2009), suggesting that similar strategies are used to regulate diverse phenotypes. 

For pathogens, the process of infection usually requires adapting physiology to new nutritional environments as well as mounting a virulent attack, in addition to dodging antibiotics. The Crc–rgCrcZ system appears to link the metabolic adaptation to virulence and resistance in P. aeruginosa (Linares et al., 2010). P. aeruginosa Crc is critical for resistance to various classes of antibiotics as well as manifestation of various virulence determinants such as porins, T3SS, motility, pyocyanin, and biofilm formation (Dong et al., 2013; Linares et al., 2010; O’Toole et al., 2000). Although, some of the proteins regulated by Crc harbor a Crc-binding region in their mRNAs, several of the observed effects are likely to be indirect. Recently, it has been demonstrated that rgCrcZ can sequester Hfq, negating Hfqmediated translational repression of catabolic genes (Sonnleitner and Blasi, 2014). These findings suggest that virulence and antibiotic resistance should not be seen as independent processes in the behavior of bacterial pathogens. 

## 5.2.5 Oxidative stress

Reactive oxygen intermediates (ROIs) include the products of $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ reduction, such as superoxide $\left( \mathbf { O } _ { 2 } ^ { - } \right)$ , hydrogen peroxides $\left( \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \right)$ , hydroxyl radicals (OH−), peroxynitrites (OONO−), and anhypochlorous acids (OONOH−), that are generated as part of the normal cellular metabolism. Most of these free radicals have the ability to nonspecifically damage cell membranes, DNA, and proteins (Imlay, 2008) (see Section 10). The mammalian immune system exploits this process as a defense against invading pathogens. During infections, host phagocytic cells produce ROS to prevent bacterial colonization. On the other hand, bacteria possess multiple antioxidant defense mechanisms to deal with the oxidative stress. In P. aeruginosa, intracellular $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ detoxification is achieved by the catalases (KatA, KatB, KatE, and KatG) (Lee et al., 2005; Panmanee and Hassett, 2009) and alkyl hydroperoxide reductases (AhpB, AhpCF, and Ohr) (Choi et al., 2007; Ochsner et al., 2001). Of these, KatA is the major catalase and is expressed in all stages of cell growth but is produced more in the stationary phase (Lee et al., 2005). KatA is a very stable enzyme, and is essential for virulence in a murine infection model (Lee et al., 2005; Shin et al., 2008). Furthermore, KatA is critical for P. aeruginosa survival at low cell densities, under aerobic conditions, in the absence of the oxidative stress regulator OxyR (Hassett et al., 2000). Expression of katA in P. aeruginosa is a complex process and is regulated by QS, iron levels, OxyR (Heo et al., 2010; Ochsner et al., 2000; Wei et al., 2012), iron sulfur cluster assembly regulator IscR (Kim et al., 2009), and the master anaerobic regulator ANR (Trunk et al., 2010). 

The complexity of regulation of the oxidative stress response is compounded by the discovery of a sRNA, rgRgsA, involved in this process. The rgRgsA (p16) was first identified in a bioinformatics screen (Livny et al., 2006), and later demonstrated empirically to be involved in $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ resistance (Gonzalez et al., 2008). Like KatA, rgRgsA is also expressed in the stationary phase, and rgsA mutants demonstrate decreased survival under oxidative stress (Gonzalez et al., 2008). The expression of rgsA was greatly reduced in gacA and rpoS mutants, suggesting that it is regulated by both GacA and the stationary phase sigma factor RpoS (Gonzalez et al., 2008). It has a typical RpoS-dependent promoter; however, it lacks the GacA binding motif, suggesting a direct regulation by RpoS and indirect regulation by GacA (Gonzalez et al., 2008). Although rgRgsA also contains a GGA motif, typical of RsmA-binding RNAs, it appears to be unable to bind RsmA in P. aeruginosa (Gonzalez et al., 2008). The mechanism of rgRgsA action and its target(s) remain to be identified. 

In P. aeruginosa, AmpR regulates the expression of both KatA and rgRgsA (Balasubramanian et al., 2014). The transcriptomic and real-time polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) data revealed the downregulation of katA and rgsA in PAOΔampR, indicating positive regulation (Balasubramanian et al., 2014). Whether AmpR regulation is direct or indirect and how it is intertwined with the GacA pathway remain to be seen. AmpR positively regulates RpoS, and so RpoS-mediated AmpR regulation of the oxidative stress pathway is a likely scenario. 

## 5.2.6 Heat shock

The heat shock response (HSR) is a universal cellular reaction to deal with misfolded proteins due to heat and other stresses (see Section 13). In E. coli and many proteobacteria, the HSR is controlled by two alternative sigma factors $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ and $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ (Arsene et al., 2000; Hughes and Mathee, 1998). The role of $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ HSR is well established as it drives transcription from promoters of approximately 40 heat shock protein (Hsp) genes (Yura et al., 1993). Many members of the Hsp system include chaperones that ensure proper folding of newly formed proteins and correct refolding of proteins damaged by the various cellular stresses. Although required for survival at high temperatures, the role of E. coli $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ is not well explored in HSR. 

P. aeruginosa codes for a $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ homolog RpoH, as well as two major chaperone systems, DnaK–DnaJ–GrpE (Hsp70) and GroEL (Hsp60)–GroES (Hsp10), that are involved in protecting cells from lethal damage from high temperatures (see Section 14). The DnaJ–DnaK–GrpE (PA4760–PA4762) chaperone is homologous to the Hsp70 system and prevents premature folding of nascent polypeptides. DnaK is the P. aeruginosa homolog of E. coli Hsp70, which regulates both the activity and amount of $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ (Winsor et al., 2011). Conversion between the adenosine triphosphate (ATP)- or adenosine diphosphate (ADP)-bound forms of DnaK is controlled by DnaJ and GrpE, which function as a co-chaperone and a nucleotide exchange factor, respectively (Harrison, 2003). GroEL (Hsp60) is another regulator of $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ , which together with Hsp70 forms the negative feedback loop to regulate the expression of $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ (Guisbert et al., 2008). The expression of HSR genes is subject to complex regulation to maintain the proper protein-folding environment of the cell, a process that is not completely understood. 

In P. aeruginosa, a sRNA P32 is the last gene of a three-gene operon with dnaJ and dapB (Winsor et al., 2011). Although sRNAs are usually not associated with regulation of HSR, translation of some small Hsps is regulated by cis-regulated RNA elements called RNA thermometers (RNATs) (Kortmann and Narberhaus, 2012). RNATs are present in the 5′ untranslated region (5′ -UTR) of mRNA and form complex structures to modulate translation efficiency in response to temperature fluctuations (Kortmann and Narberhaus, 2012). Under low-temperature conditions, RNATs form secondary structures occluding the RBS, inhibiting translation initiation. An increase in temperature destabilizes these structures, exposing the RBS and allowing translation initiation. In P. aeruginosa, the expression of a HSP IbpA displays dual control via RpoH and RNAT at the level of transcription and translation, respectively (Krajewski et al., 2013). However, P32 does not appear to be an RNAT as it is located at the 3′ end of the operon, suggesting yet another level of control through sRNAs.

The P. aeruginosa global regulator AmpR is involved in heat tolerance by regulating the expression of P32 as well as DnaJ– DnaK–GrpE genes (Balasubramanian et al., 2014). Since AmpR also positively regulates the stress sigma factor RpoS, the temperature sensitivity of PAOΔampR is more enhanced in the stationary phase compared to the log phase (Balasubramanian et al., 2014). Regulation of P32 and other hsp genes by AmpR is probably indirect as these genes lack an AmpR-binding site. The interaction of different elements and role and target of P32 needs further investigation.

Target identification is another major area of sRNA research. In spite of many in silico target prediction programs (CopraRNA, RNAPredator, TargetRNA2, and sTarpicker, among others), target identification is still a black box in this field. Recent approaches for targetome identification (Lalaouna et al., 2015) and structure–function analysis (Peterman et al., 2014) hold promise. The ideal approach, however, would be a combination of in silico and empirical techniques to identify and confirm sRNA targets under native conditions.

## C H A P T E R 5.3

# Physiological effects of posttranscriptional regulation by the small RNA SgrS during metabolic stress in Escherichia coli

Gregory R. Richards 

Biological Sciences Department, University of Wisconsin–Parkside, Kenosha, Wisconsin, USA 

## 5.3.1 Introduction

In the past 15 years, the field of small regulatory RNA (sRNA) research has witnessed a renaissance in regard to elucidation of the diverse array of molecular mechanisms by which bacterial sRNAs change gene expression in response to metabolic and environmental stresses (for reviews, see Bobrovskyy and Vanderpool, 2013; Richards and Vanderpool, 2011; Waters and Storz, 2009; see Section 5). While the physiological roles of some sRNA-mediated stress responses are known, for many others understanding of the biological functions has lagged behind that of regulatory mechanisms. This is due in part to the fact that, unlike many regulator proteins, deletion mutations of sRNA genes do not often yield obvious phenotypes. Nevertheless, in the last few years, new approaches to sRNA research have begun to improve our knowledge of the biology and physiology of these important cellular regulators and the stresses to which they respond. 

The Escherichia coli sRNA SgrS exemplifies this concept of utilizing complementary approaches to study both regulatory mechanisms and their physiological effects. SgrS regulates the response to glucose-phosphate stress, a type of growth inhibition resulting from intracellular accumulation of certain sugar-phosphates including glucose-6-phosphate (Englesberg et al., 1962; Kawamoto et al., 2006; Vanderpool and Gottesman, 2004). The molecular mechanisms of SgrS regulation are well characterized, but historically the cause of stress and the physiological role of the ensuing regulatory response have been uncertain. Recently, the dual methodologies of characterizing new regulatory targets of SgrS and identifying novel metabolic pathways and environmental conditions that affect this response have greatly advanced our understanding of glucose-phosphate stress. This chapter describes the mechanisms by which SgrS regulates the glucose-phosphate stress response as well as recent insights into the physiology of this model stress response. 

## 5.3.2 Physiology and regulation of gene expression by Hfq-binding sRNAs

SgrS belongs to perhaps the most prevalent and diverse class of bacterial sRNAs. Members of this class regulate expression of targets posttranscriptionally via direct, complementary base-pairing interactions with target messenger RNAs (mRNAs) (Bobrovskyy and Vanderpool, 2013; Waters and Storz, 2009). These sRNAs mediate the responses to a variety of metabolic and environmental stresses, including changes in nutrient availability, outer membrane disturbance, and virulence (Bobrovskyy and Vanderpool, 2013; Richards and Vanderpool, 2011; Waters and Storz, 2009). Base-pairing sRNAs like SgrS are referred to as trans-encoded because their genomic locus is not nearby that of the genes they regulate. Trans-encoded sRNAs also base pair with limited complementarity to their target mRNAs. In contrast, cis-encoded sRNAs exhibit identical complementarity to their mRNA target owing to the fact that the sRNA gene is located on the DNA strand directly opposite the target gene (Brantl, 2007; Waters and Storz, 2009). Trans-encoded sRNAs can exert negative and/or positive regulatory effects through an assortment of different mechanisms. For example, negative sRNA regulators typically prevent translation by binding to and blocking the ribosome binding site (RBS) of the target mRNA, while positive outcomes of sRNA–mRNA base pairing often enhance translation by preventing the mRNA from forming secondary structures that block the RBS (Storz et al., 2011; Waters and Storz, 2009). For optimal stability and pairing with target mRNAs, trans-encoded sRNAs also require the assistance of the RNA chaperone protein Hfq (Brennan and Link, 2007). 

While research on many trans-encoded sRNAs (including SgrS) has traditionally focused more on mechanism than physiology, there are some notable exceptions. Two of the best examples for which both regulation and function are well established are RyhB, which regulates E. coli iron homeostasis (see Section 19), and Spot 42, a global regulator of carbon and secondary metabolism. Insight into their physiological roles has been greatly assisted by phenotypes readily observed through genetic studies: E. coli ryhB mutants exhibit longer lag phase adjustments when introduced to iron-limited conditions (Masse and Gottesman, 2002), while Spot 42 overexpression results in numerous growth defects such as decreased colony size and difficulty adjusting to changes in nutrient availability (Rice and Dahlberg, 1982). The primary function of RyhB is to provide alternate sources of iron for essential cell functions when environmental supplies are scarce (Masse and Gottesman, 2002). RyhB accomplishes this task through multiple, distinct methods of regulation: it indirectly increases expression of genes involved in synthesizing iron-scavenging siderophores (Hantke, 1981; Salvail et al., 2010), while directly inhibiting synthesis of nonessential iron-containing enzymes like the sdhCDAB-encoded succinate dehydrogenase. Direct regulation of sdhCDAB and other targets typically occurs through RyhB base pairing and translational inhibition (Geissmann and Touati, 2004; Masse and Gottesman, 2002; Vecerek et al., 2003). Based on genomic analyses, RyhB likely exerts a broad regulatory effect on both direct and indirect targets, with one study finding 56 potential RyhB-regulated genes (Masse et al., 2005, 2007). 

The first characterized physiological role of Spot 42 was in regulating utilization of the sugar galactose. Spot 42 was found to inhibit translation via direct base paring with galK mRNA, which is a part of an operon that is required for galactose catabolism (Møller et al., 2002). Interestingly, Spot 42 discoordinately regulates the gal transcript, as it does not affect translation of operon members galE and galT (Møller et al., 2002). A metabolic function of this disparate regulation has been ascribed that involves the response to carbon source availability (Møller et al., 2002). When galactose is the sole carbon source, Spot 42 is not expressed and the entire gal catabolic operon is translated (Møller et al., 2002). In the presence of glucose, cells engage in catabolite repression, metabolizing the preferred carbon source (glucose) while inhibiting expression of genes required for catabolism of other carbon sources like galactose. Unlike most sugar catabolism enzymes, GalT and GalE (but not GalK) have a second important function in lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis (Adhya, 1987) and therefore must still be expressed even when glucose is present. Thus, Spot 42 serves to allow galE and galT mRNA translation in the presence of glucose while inhibiting the expression of unneeded galK (Adhya, 1987). As with RyhB, Spot 42’s initially described regulatory role has more recently been expanded by genomic analyses to include a greater diversity of metabolic effects, including redox metabolism, central metabolism, and alternative carbon source usage, with direct base pairing to several targets confirmed (Beisel and Storz, 2011). 

## 5.3.3 Regulatory mechanisms of the SgrS-mediated response to glucose-phosphate stress

In contrast to exceptions like RyhB and Spot 42, characterization of SgrS has been more typical of bacterial sRNAs: that is, research on regulatory mechanisms of SgrS has outpaced knowledge regarding the physiology of the glucose-phosphate stress response. Nevertheless, discovery of novel SgrS regulatory targets and mechanisms (in both E. coli and, to a lesser extent, Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium) has provided hints about the nature of glucose-phosphate stress and the metabolic function of the stress response. Regulation by SgrS has been well described for several targets. (See Table 5.3.1 for a complete list of known regulatory targets of the glucose-phosphate stress response.) Based on its known targets, the overarching modus operandi of SgrS is to mitigate stress by stopping transport and intracellular buildup of stress-inducing sugar-phosphates. 

Expression of sgrS itself is activated in response to stressor accumulation by the transcription factor SgrR, which works in concert with SgrS to alleviate stress (Horler and Vanderpool, 2009; Martinez-Hackert and Stock, 1997; Tam and Saier, 1993; Vanderpool and Gottesman, 2004, 2007). In E. coli, SgrR and SgrS are both absolutely required components of the glucosephosphate stress response, as deleting the sgrR or sgrS genes inhibits the ability to grow under stress conditions (Morita et al., 2006; Vanderpool and Gottesman, 2007). 

For targets described to date, SgrS employs several distinct posttranscriptional methods to either increase or decrease translation of mRNA transcripts. The first (and most crucial, in terms of the effect on sugar-phosphate accumulation) target to be identified is ptsG, which encodes EIICBGlc, a phosphoenolpyruvate phosphotransferase system (PTS) transporter. EIICBGlc is the major transporter responsible for the uptake and accompanying phosphorylation of glucose (Curtis and Epstein, 1975; Henderson et al., 1977). SgrS inhibits translation of the ptsG mRNA in the canonical trans-encoded sRNA manner: it directly base pairs with the ptsG transcript and occludes the RBS, thereby impeding transport of glucose-6-phosphate into the cell (Kawamoto et al., 2006; Morita et al., 2006; Vanderpool and Gottesman, 2004). While not required for inhibition of ptsG translation, the ptsG–SgrS duplex is also subsequently destroyed by the cellular RNase E degradosome (Kawamoto et al., 2006; Morita et al., 2005, 2006). 

The role of SgrS in the inhibition of sugar uptake extends to at least one other target, manXYZ. manXYZ encodes EIIABCDMan, the mannose PTS transporter that can also bring other sugars, including glucose, into the cell (Curtis and Epstein, 1975; Rephaeli and Saier, 1980). As with ptsG, SgrS inhibits manXYZ mRNA translation through direct base pairing, with subsequent RNase E degradosome-mediated degradation (Rice and Vanderpool, 2011). Unlike ptsG, in vitro RNA footprinting and mutational analyses demonstrated that SgrS does not bind to the manXYZ RBS region, but rather has two distinct binding sites within the coding region of the transcript (Rice and Vanderpool, 2011; Rice et al., 2012). The first SgrS binding site was found to be located in the manX coding sequence (Rice and Vanderpool, 2011), while a second, independent binding site is located in the intergenic region between manX and manY (Rice et al., 2012). The second site was also shown to be required for SgrS to completely prevent manY and manZ translation; in other words, SgrS binding to only the manX site is not sufficient to inhibit manYZ translation (Rice et al., 2012). Interestingly, SgrS must be bound to both sites in order for RNaseEmediated degradation of the SgrS–manXYZ complex to occur (Rice et al., 2012). Taken together, these results suggest that SgrS binds to two distinct sites on the manXYZ transcript in order to optimize regulation of the entire operon (Rice et al., 2012).
