The third SgrS target to be described, yigL, further expands the repertoire of SgrS regulatory mechanisms. YigL is a haloacid dehalogenase (HAD)-like sugar phosphatase (Koonin and Tatusov, 1994) with in vitro activity against a variety of sugarphosphates, including glucose-6-phosphate (Kuznetsova et al., 2006). In contrast to ptsG and manXYZ, binding of SgrS exerts a positive regulatory effect on yigL mRNA by blocking RNase E binding, thereby inhibiting degradation of yigL transcript and enhancing its translation (Papenfort et al., 2013). yigL mutants exhibit glucose-phosphate stress-specific growth defects, suggesting that yigL has functional relevance in the recovery from stress (Papenfort et al., 2013). Based on its in vitro function, it has been posited that yigL contributes to the stress response by “detoxifying” (dephosphorylating) stressor sugar-phosphates, which are subsequently excreted from cells (Papenfort et al., 2013). Indeed, yigL mutants also display a defect in their ability to export stressor sugars during stress (Papenfort et al., 2013). As with RyhB and Spot 42, genomic analyses (Balasubramanian, 

Bobrovskyy, Richards, and Vanderpool, unpublished data) imply that the SgrS regulon extends to a broader array of targets, and studies on the physiology of glucose-phosphate stress (described in the next sections) also support this notion. Indeed, another novel SgrS target, sopD, has been identified in S. Typhimurium (Papenfort et al., 2012). SopD is a secreted effector protein that contributes to the ability of Salmonella to cause disease in mice (Jiang et al., 2004). SgrS was shown to inhibit sopD translation in an extremely specific manner: it regulates mRNA transcripts of sopD but not of the highly similar effector gene sopD2 due to a single base pair difference in the SgrS binding region (Papenfort et al., 2012). 

While SgrS plays an important role in coordinating the response to accumulation of sugar-phosphates, other regulators extend the regulatory reach of this stress response, including SgrR and SgrT. SgrT is a small peptide encoded by SgrS in a region distinct from the sequence involved in base pairing (Wadler and Vanderpool, 2007). SgrT aids SgrS in regulating expression of ptsG by blocking EIICBGlc transport activity through an unknown mechanism, thereby preventing sugarphosphate uptake from existing transporters (Table 5.3.1) (Wadler and Vanderpool, 2007). SgrS is one of only a few bacterial sRNAs with dual base-pairing and protein-encoding functions (Vanderpool et al. 2011), and a recent study in S. Typhimurium suggests that the two functions have an established priority (in terms of both timing of expression and importance) during the stress response. Ectopic overexpression of either SgrT or the SgrS base-pairing function is sufficient to aid in cell recovery from stress (Balasubramanian and Vanderpool, 2013). However, when expressed from the native Salmonella chromosomal locus, only the base-pairing function, and not SgrT, is able to rescue cells from stress (Balasubramanian and Vanderpool, 2013). Thus, it appears that stopping ptsG mRNA translation is more important to stress rescue, with SgrT inhibition of EIICBGlc transport activity providing an additional, supportive level to the stringency of regulation. The key role of SgrS base pairing during stress is further supported by the fact that SgrS is expressed almost immediately after stress conditions are introduced (Balasubramanian and Vanderpool, 2013; Vanderpool and Gottesman, 2004), whereas SgrT is produced later in the response to stress (Balasubramanian and Vanderpool, 2013). 

SgrR, the third member of the glucose-phosphate regulatory response, regulates additional targets at the level of transcription (Sun and Vanderpool, 2011; Vanderpool and Gottesman, 2007). SgrR is one of a novel, broadly distributed class of bacterial transcription factors that possess both DNA- and small-moleculebinding domains (Horler and Vanderpool, 2009; Martinez-Hackert and Stock, 1997; Tam and Saier, 1993; Vanderpool and Gottesman, 2004, 2007). Activity of the SgrR protein itself is positively regulated by the binding of an unidentified small signal molecule related to glucose-phosphate stress (Horler and Vanderpool, 2009; Vanderpool and Gottesman, 2007). SgrR regulates at least four genes (Table 5.3.1), and as with SgrS, genomic analyses suggest that other uncharacterized targets likely exist (Richards and Vanderpool, unpublished data). SgrR has been demonstrated to act as a positive and negative regulator for different targets. In addition to activating sgrS, SgrR has been shown to repress its own transcription (Vanderpool and Gottesman, 2007), suggesting that limiting SgrR to optimal concentrations is important to its ability to function properly. The sgrR gene is divergently oriented from sgrS, and SgrR has been shown to bind the sgrS promoter in vitro within the intergenic region between sgrR and sgrS (Vanderpool and Gottesman, 2007). A 5 bp region with the sequence AAGGG was identified to be necessary for SgrR activation of sgrS in response to glucosephosphate stress, and other sequences within the promoter are also likely required for regulation (Vanderpool and Gottesman, 2004, 2007). A third target, setA, is also activated by SgrR and is co-transcribed with sgrS during stress (Sun and Vanderpool, 2011). SetA is part of the SET (sugar efflux transporter) family of transporters (Liu et al., 1999a) and is able to export various sugars, including glucose, from E. coli (Liu et al., 1999b). setA aids in recovery from glucose-phosphate stress, based on the fact that setA mutants are defective in growth under stress conditions (Sun and Vanderpool, 2011). While YigL dephosphorylates stressor sugar-phosphates, SetA has been hypothesized to contribute the complementary function of pumping the products of YigL from the cell (Sun and Vanderpool, 2011). However, because it was shown that SetA is not responsible for efflux of the specific sugar used to induce stress, SetA is instead thought to export other stress-related metabolites (Sun and Vanderpool, 2011). Transcription of the fourth characterized target, alaC (previously known as yfdZ), is activated by SgrR, and its promoter also has putative SgrR-binding elements (Vanderpool and Gottesman, 2007). Unlike most other SgrR and SgrS targets, AlaC has no obvious role in the glucose-phosphate stress response; it is a glutamate–pyruvate transaminase involved in the biosynthesis of alanine (Kim et al., 2010). However, AlaC can result in the formation of pyruvate (Kim et al., 2010), a product of glycolytic and other central metabolic pathways related to glucose-phosphate stress (described in more detail in Section 

5.3.4) (Richards et al., 2013; Vanderpool, 2007; Vanderpool and Gottesman, 2007). 

Beyond the targets of SgrST and SgrR, the implication of global regulators in glucose-phosphate stress has further expanded the regulatory network of the response. Both CRP (the cAMP (cyclic adenosine monophosphate) receptor protein, a global transcriptional regulator of, among other things, catabolite repression and preferential carbon source usage) and KdgR (which regulates transcription of genes involved in carbon transport and catabolism) (Murray and Conway, 2005; Pouyssegur and Stoeber, 1974) appear to operate upstream of SgrS and SgrR (Sun and Vanderpool, 2011). CRP and KdgR seem to have opposite regulatory effects on the glucose-phosphate stress response: a crp mutant exhibits decreased sgrS expression when grown during stress, whereas a kdgR mutant displays a moderate increase in sgrS expression (Sun and Vanderpool, 2011). However, both regulators appear to exert influence on sgrS transcription indirectly via SgrR, since ectopic expression of SgrR restores sgrS expression to wild-type levels in both the crp and kdgR mutants (Sun and Vanderpool, 2011). Although their exact mechanisms of regulation are unclear, the involvement of CRP and KdgR implies a broader input of signals related to carbon metabolism beyond the accumulation of sugar-phosphates. Given the role of CRP–cAMP in use of alternative carbon sources, its connection to stress involving sugar-phosphate accumulation is perhaps not surprising. Similarly, KdgR regulates expression of an aldolase that generates pyruvate as one of its products (Murray and Conway, 2005). Thus, like AlaC, KdgR could influence glycolytic and other central metabolic pathways related to glucose-phosphate stress. 

## 5.3.4 Recent advances in understanding the metabolic cause of glucose-phosphate stress

Despite the preponderance of information about regulatory mechanisms, the biological function of the glucose-phosphate stress response has remained elusive, in large part due to the fact that the cause of stress is unclear. Regulation by SgrST and SgrR, which prevents uptake and promotes degradation and efflux of sugar-phosphates, clearly suggests it is necessary to rid the cell of excessive sugar-phosphates. However, why their accumulation is a source of stress to begin with is not readily apparent and is the crux of understanding the physiology of glucose-phosphate stress. In recent years, multifaceted approaches have provided significant answers to questions about the physiological conditions and metabolic pathways and intermediates that contribute to glucose-phosphate stress. 

Although the cause is unknown, historically glucosephosphate stress was thought to be due to one of two causes: the inherent toxicity of accumulated sugar-phosphates (Morita et al., 2003, 2006), or depletion of intermediates in glycolysis or other associated metabolic pathways (Vanderpool, 2007). 

Indeed, the two means by which stress is induced experimentally not only result in accumulation of sugar-phosphates but also block the glycolytic pathway. In the first approach, cells are exposed to analogs of glucose such as α-methyl glucoside (αMG) and 2-deoxyglucose, which cannot be metabolized but are still recognized and brought into cells in their phosphorylated form by PTS transporters like $\mathrm { E I I C B } ^ { \mathrm { G l c } }$ and $\mathrm { E I I A B C D ^ { M a n } }$ (Amaral and Kornberg, 1975; Curtis and Epstein, 1975; Henderson et al., 1977; Rephaeli and Saier, 1980; Vanderpool and Gottesman, 2004). In the second approach, the glycolytic pathway is directly blocked by mutations in glycolytic genes $( \boldsymbol { \mathrm { e } } . \boldsymbol { \mathrm { g } } . , \ p \ g i ,$ encoding phosphoglucose isomerase), which results in sugar-phosphate accumulation when cells are exposed to glucose (Kimata et al., 2001; Morita et al., 2003). 

Recent research implicates depletion of metabolic intermediates related to glycolysis as the most likely cause of stress. Growth inhibition of an sgrS mutant induced by nonmetabolizable αMG can be relieved by addition of glycolytic intermediates downstream of the metabolic block (Richards et al., 2013). For example, the addition of glucose-6-phosphate or fructose-6- phosphate restores growth of the sgrS mutant to wild-type levels (Richards et al., 2013). Importantly, this rescue occurred despite the fact that αMG-6-phosphate was shown to be transported into cells, which strongly suggests that the presence of accumulated sugar-phosphates per se is not inherently toxic to cells (Richards et al., 2013). Similarly, when the glycolytic pathway is blocked by the alternate method of mutating glycolytic genes, stress is rescued by addition of downstream compounds. For example, when glucose-6-phosphate accumulates in $\mathit { p g i }$ mutants, stress can be relieved by addition of fructose-6-phosphate, which presumably restores glycolytic function (Kimata et al., 2001; Morita et al., 2003). Again, glucose-phosphate stress is relieved by introducing a second sugar-phosphate that bypasses the glycolytic block. This rescue is not exclusive to stress caused by glucose-6- phosphate. Rather, stress induced by accumulation of fructose-6-phosphate (by mutating pfk) or fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (by mutating fda) can also be ameliorated by introducing a downstream glycolytic intermediate (Kimata et al., 2001; Morita et al., 2003). Together, these studies demonstrate that stress is induced not by one particular sugar-phosphate but by a variety of stressor molecules, including glucose analogs and various glycolytic compounds. Moreover, as a whole, these results indicate that restoring glycolytic metabolism, and not necessarily preventing sugar-phosphate accumulation, is key to recovery from stress. 

If metabolic depletion is the key factor in glucose-phosphate stress, which depleted molecule might be responsible? Available evidence points to phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) as a likely candidate. PEP is positioned at the interface of sugar transport and metabolism. It is both one of the final intermediates in glycolysis and the initial phosphate donor that instigates the uptake of sugars via PTS transporters. Moreover, depletion of PEP has been shown to be responsible for one particular type of sugar-phosphate stress. When E. coli is grown with fructose as the only carbon source, 2-deoxyglucose inhibits growth by depleting PEP levels (Kornberg and Lambourne, 1994). Uptake of both 2-deoxyglucose and fructose utilizes available supplies of PEP via PTS transporter activity. However, since 2-deoxyglucose is incapable of being metabolized through glycolysis, PEP supplies cannot be replenished after 2-deoxyglucose uptake (Kornberg and Lambourne, 1994). Thus, increasing PEP levels by either expression of ppsA (which encodes the PEP synthetase that converts pyruvate to PEP) or addition of aspartate as the sole nitrogen source (which indirectly generates PEP via PEP carboxykinase) improves growth with 2-deoxyglucose (Kornberg and Lambourne, 1994). Additional evidence supporting the importance of PEP in other forms of glucose-phosphate stress comes from the effect of downstream glycolytic intermediates on stress caused by αMG. In striking contrast to upstream sugarphosphates, addition of pyruvate worsens stress, resulting in the death of an sgrS mutant during stress (Richards et al., 2013). The conversion of pyruvate to PEP though ectopic expression of PpsA prevents this lethality (Richards et al., 2013). If these results hold true for other forms of glucose-phosphate stress, growth inhibition during stress may be caused by depletion of PEP supplies through PTS sugar transport combined with the inability to operate glycolytic metabolism (Richards and Vanderpool, 2011; Vanderpool, 2007). Such a cause would underscore the need for the SgrR–SgrST response to block any further activity of the PTS. 

## 5.3.5 Novel environmental and metabolic connections expand the physiology of the glucose-phosphate stress response

## 5.3.5.1 Response of SgrS regulatory targets to different sources of glucose-phosphate stress

Studies examining the relative importance of SgrS regulatory targets in the response to different nutritional and environmental conditions have also yielded insight into glucose-phosphate stress. For example, the contribution of specific targets in responding to particular sources of stress suggests that the glucose-phosphate stress response may have broader biological roles than initially described. As mentioned, stress is induced by multiple sugar-phosphates besides glucose-6-phosphate, and regulation of at least two different PTS transporters aids in the ability of SgrS to deal with these diverse sources of stress. This flexibility of the stress response is reflected in the overlapping yet distinct specificities of the $\mathrm { E I I C B } ^ { \mathrm { G l c } }$ and $\mathrm { E I I A B C D ^ { M a n } }$ transporters for different stressor molecules. For example, although the ptsG-encoded $\mathrm { E I I C B ^ { G l c } }$ is the major glucose transporter, manXYZ-encoded $\mathrm { E I I A B C D ^ { M a n } }$ can also transport glucose. However, their affinity for other substrates varies: $\mathrm { E I I C B } ^ { \mathrm { G l c } }$ is a more efficient transporter of αMG than 2-deoxyglucose, whereas $\mathrm { E I I A B C D ^ { M a n } }$ can better transport 2-deoxyglucose than αMG (Amaral and Kornberg, 1975; Curtis and Epstein, 1975; Henderson et al., 1977; Rephaeli and Saier, 1980). Consistent with this, ptsG downregulation seems to be more important for recovery from stress induced by αMG-induced stress, whereas manXYZ regulation is required for recovery from 2- deoxyglucose-induced stress (Rice and Vanderpool, 2011). For stress caused by αMG, activation of the stress response (as measured by sgrS expression) can be greatly decreased by deleting the ptsG gene but not manXYZ. Conversely, when 2- deoxyglucose is the source of stress, the manXYZ mutation (but not ptsG) results in a large decrease in stress response activation (Rice and Vanderpool, 2011). Deleting both manXYZ and ptsG renders cells effectively impervious to stress caused by either substrate (Rice and Vanderpool, 2011). Another study suggests there may be diversity among strains of E. coli in the response to different sources of glucose-phosphate stress. E. coli B and K-12 strains were found to respond similarly to αMG by inducing sgrS expression and decreasing ptsG transcript levels (Negrete et al., 2010). However, the stress response of E. coli B but not K-12 also was induced by high levels of glucose in media (Negrete et al., 2010). Future analysis of the response of multiple E. coli strains to as-yet-untested sugar-phosphates, as well as assessing potential regulation of other sugar transporters, could provide information on the full extent of the glucose-phosphate regulatory response to various metabolic stressors. 

## 5.3.5.2 Effects of other environmental conditions on glucose-phosphate stress

Besides the source of sugar-phosphate stress, other studies have explored the role of stress response targets under different nutritional and environmental conditions. While glucose-phosphate stress-associated growth inhibition is more severe in minimal media than in rich media (Sun and Vanderpool, 2011, 2013), it was recently demonstrated that these different nutritional environments require particular targets to be regulated by SgrS. In rich media, preventing transport of sugar-phosphates by inhibiting ptsG or manXYZ translation was sufficient to help cells recover from stress (Sun and Vanderpool, 2013). In nutrientdeprived minimal media, regulation of additional SgrS targets, including yigL, was necessary to rescue cells from stress (Sun and Vanderpool, 2013). In minimal media, the presence of certain amino acids also mitigated the growth inhibition of an sgrS mutant, presumably because the availability of other carbon sources provides an alternate metabolic means for recovery (Sun and Vanderpool, 2013). These results suggest that target relevance can vary based on particular nutritional conditions, and that the SgrS response might be modular in order to adjust target regulation to specific nutritional environments during stress (Sun and Vanderpool, 2013). 

Exploration of other nutritional contexts has also expanded the connections of glucose-phosphate stress to branches of metabolism beyond sugar transport and glycolysis. For example, in an E. coli B strain, SgrS appears able to reduce stress caused by high levels of glucose in part by indirectly decreasing levels of acetate excretion into the surrounding medium (Negrete et al., 2011). (High levels of acetate are known to interfere with growth of E. coli.) In contrast, growth of K-12 strains, which do not express sgrS in response to high external glucose concentrations, was adversely affected by acetate excretion. Inhibition of glucose transport by ectopic overexpression of sgrS in K-12 strains prevented this acetate excretion (Negrete et al., 2011). Thus, glucose-phosphate stress affects carbon metabolism downstream of glycolysis in ways that have yet to be fully examined. 

Another recent study connected the glucose-phosphate stress response to phosphate metabolism in E. coli. This work demonstrated that mutation of pitA, which encodes a low-affinity phosphate transporter, can partially rescue the growth defect of sgrS and sgrR mutants during stress caused by αMG, although not to wild-type levels (Richards and Vanderpool, 2012). Deleting pitA also reduces stress levels in both wild-type and an sgrS mutant, as measured by lower levels of sgrS induction (Richards and Vanderpool, 2012). This rescue of sgr mutants from stress appears to be due to low-level induction of the phosphate starvation (Pho) regulon in the pitA mutants, and direct Pho induction in an sgrS mutant results in similar stress rescue (Richards and Vanderpool, 2012). Although the connections are not yet entirely understood, phosphate metabolism obviously impacts glucose-phosphate stress, perhaps by affecting sugar transporter activity through availability of phosphate (and, by extension, PEP) (Richards et al., 2013; Richards and Vanderpool, 2012). Indeed, the sgrS pitA mutant is resistant to the pyruvate-induced lethality observed in its sgrS parent. This resistance is likely due, at least in part, to increased PEP levels via PpsA activity: the sgrS pitA mutant exhibits increased expression of ppsA during stress compared to sgrS, and deletion of ppsA in the sgrS pitA background largely eliminates the resistance (Richards et al., 2013). 

In addition, work in related enteric pathogens suggests that biologically relevant conditions for the glucose-phosphate stress response may extend to the host environment and (in some cases) the ability to cause disease. As mentioned, the secreted effector protein SopD, regulated by SgrS in S. Typhimurium, is required for pathogenesis in mice (Jiang et al., 2004; Papenfort et al., 2012). Similarly, yigL is required for full virulence of Xenorhabdus nematophila, an enteric pathogen of insects (Richards et al., 2009). Interestingly, an X. nematophila yigL mutant is also defective in activity of an extracellular lipase, which is thought to have a role in acquisition of host nutrients (Richards and Goodrich-Blair, 2010; Richards et al., 2009). This phenotypic connection suggests that yigL could be a metabolic link between sugar and lipid catabolic pathways and/or contribute to signaling of carbon source availability. 

## 5.3.6 The glucose-phosphate stress response in other enteric bacteria

As demonstrated by studies described above from multiple E. coli strains and other related species, variations in the physiological (Negrete et al., 2010, 2011) and regulatory responses (Balasubramanian and Vanderpool, 2013; Papenfort et al., 2012; Wadler and Vanderpool, 2009) to glucose-phosphate stress undoubtedly exist. As evidenced by genomic and genetic studies, this diversity extends to SgrST–SgrR distribution and function across the Enterobacteriaceae. While relatively well conserved in some enterics, the presence and synteny of the three regulators of glucose-phosphate stress are by no means uniformly distributed among different species or E. coli strains (Horler and Vanderpool, 2009). Bioinformatics analyses show that both sgrS and sgrT are found in some enteric species (e.g., Klebsiella pneumoniae and S. Typhimurium), while only sgrS (lacking the sgrT-coding region) is found in other species (e.g., Photorhabdus luminescens and Yersinia pestis) (Horler and Vanderpool, 2009). Even some E. coli strains vary in this regard: while sgrS and sgrT homologs are observed in strains K-12 and CFT073, enterohemorrhagic E. coli strain O157:H7 is predicted to have only sgrS base-pairing functions (Horler and Vanderpool, 2009). Indeed, sequence comparisons among those species and strains with sgrS homologs indicate that base-pairing regions are most highly conserved, whereas sgrTcoding regions show the most variation (Horler and Vanderpool, 2009). A companion study revealed that at least some of these genomic differences translate to functionally relevant consequences. Ectopic expression of only the sgrT coding region of some sgrS homologs (e.g., those from K. pneumoniae and S. Typhimurium) is sufficient to restore growth of E. coli under stress conditions (Wadler and Vanderpool, 2009). For other homologs (e.g., those from E. coli and Y. pestis), the sgrS basepairing function has to be expressed in order to rescue growth (Wadler and Vanderpool, 2009). Additional studies like that in S. Typhimurium (Balasubramanian and Vanderpool, 2013) that further examine the distinct mechanistic roles of SgrS and SgrT in different enterics could help further illuminate the physiological reasons for these regulatory differences. 

## 5.3.7 Conclusion



Jiang X, Rossanese OW, Brown NF, Kujat-Choy S, Galan JE, et al. 2004. The related effector proteins SopD and SopD2 from Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium contribute to virulence during systemic infection of mice. Molecular Microbiology 54: 1186–1198. 





Storz G, Vogel J, Wassarman KM. 2011. Regulation by small RNAs in bacteria: expanding frontiers. Molecular Cell 43: 880–891. 



Bacterial sRNAs are now firmly positioned as central regulators in the response to environmental stress. The explosion in knowledge of sRNA-mediated regulatory mechanisms has not always been matched by corresponding investigations into biological function. Typical among many bacterial sRNAs, SgrS has a well-defined mechanism of regulation, whereas findings on the metabolic stress it responds to have been less forthcoming. Nevertheless, characterization of SgrS regulatory targets (Rice and Vanderpool, 2011; Sun and Vanderpool, 2013) has provided insights into metabolic and environmental cues related to glucose-phosphate stress. Conversely, recent advances identifying environmental conditions and physiological causes of stress (Richards et al., 2013; Richards and Vanderpool, 2012; Sun and Vanderpool, 2013) have likewise revealed more about the biological role of the regulatory response. Given these results, it is perhaps not surprising that two of the most informative sRNA studies to date, RyhB and Spot42, have combined analysis of molecular mechanisms with readily observable phenotypic and physiological effects. The blending of these two complementary approaches in other model sRNA systems will undoubtedly enhance our understanding of these important regulators in years to come.

# Three rpoS-activating small RNAs in pathways contributing to acid resistance of Escherichia coli∗

Geunu Bak1, Kook Han1, Daun Kim1, Kwang-sun Kim2, and Younghoon Lee1 

1Department of Chemistry, KAIST, Daejeon, Korea 

2Department of Chemistry and Chemistry Institute of Functional Materials, Pusan National University, Busan, Korea 

## 5.4.1 Introduction

Most pathogenic and nonpathogenic enteric bacteria are classified as neutrophilic, since they show optimal growth under neutral pH conditions (range, 5–9). However, enteric bacteria encounter many stress conditions during their passage through the digestive tract, including gastric acid in stomach where the pH range is 1.5–3.0, and weak acidic metabolites in intestine. A significantly lower dose of Escherichia coli is required for infection than other enteric bacteria (Peterson et al., 1989). Given that E. coli can survive under extreme acidic stress (pH <2.5) for up to several hours, the acid resistance (AR) systems of this pathogen have been extensively studied (Kanjee and Houry, 2013; Lin et al., 1996) (see also Chapters 16.2 and 16.3). 

Three main AR mechanisms have been defined in E. coli (Foster, 2004; Zhao and Houry, 2010). The first system, AR1, was initially observed in cells grown oxidatively in complex acidic medium without glucose to the stationary phase. The AR1 system does not require exogenous amino acids, and is controlled by the stationary-phase sigma factor (RpoS) and cyclic AMP (adenosine monophosphate) receptor protein (CRP) (Castanie-Cornet et al., 1999; Small et al., 1994). Amino acid–dependent AR2 and AR3 systems consume protons through amino acid decarboxylation, and they require glutamate and arginine, respectively, to function (Lin et al., 1995). Each amino acid– dependent AR system has a cytoplasmic decarboxylase and counter transporter that exchanges decarboxylation products for external amino acids as new substrates via an antiport mechanism. Activation of each AR system varies depending on the environmental conditions, such as growth or acid challenge media, growth phase, aerobic or anaerobic conditions, and pH. Recent studies have reported a novel type of AR involving glutamine deaminase (Lu et al., 2013) and adenosine deaminase systems (Sun et al., 2012), which release gaseous ammonia (NH ) to neutralize protons, yielding ammonium ion (NH +). In addition to these AR systems, genes located within the acid fitness island (Hommais et al., 2004; Masuda and Church, 2003) and the periplasmic protein repair chaperones, HdeA/B (Dahl et al., 2015; Hong et al., 2012), contribute to AR. 

In particular, the glutamate-dependent AR2 system provides major protection against extreme acidic conditions (pH <2.5) (Lin et al., 1996). The AR2 system consists of two homologous glutamate decarboxylases, GadA and GadB, and an antiporter, GadC, which exchange the decarboxylation product, γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), for extracellular glutamate (De Biase et al., 1999; Ma et al., 2012). Activation of the AR2 system is controlled by a complex network comprising local and global regulators. The key activator, GadE, stimulates expression of the gadA and gadBC operons (Castanie-Cornet et al., 2010; Ma et al., 2003a). 

The alternative subunit of RNA polymerase of the stationaryphase sigma factor, RpoS, is involved in regulation of the AR2 system through activation of the GadX regulator, which promotes gadE expression (Sayed and Foster, 2009; Sayed et al., 2007). The CRP affects the AR2 system by suppressing rpoS transcription (Ma et al., 2002, 2003b). Another global regulator, histone-like protein (H-NS), has also been shown to suppress gadAX and gadBC expression (Giangrossi et al., 2005; Waterman and Small, 2003). 

The two-component systems EvgAS (Ma et al., 2004), PhoPQ (Zwir et al., 2005), and TorSR (Bordi et al., 2003) are additionally involved in the AR2 regulatory network through gadE activation (see Chapter 16.3). Several noncoding small RNAs (sRNAs) are reported to confer AR to E. coli. GadY sRNA is encoded on the intergenic region on the opposite strand between gadX and gadW, and involved in the processing of gadXW transcripts by RNase III (Opdyke et al., 2004, 2011; Tramonti et al., 2008). DsrA sRNA, a regulator of rpoS translation and hns ∗This chapter was prepared by adapting data from Bak et al., 2014, MicrobiologyOpen 3(1): 15–28. 

mRNA stability (Lease and Belfort, 2000; Majdalani et al., 1998; Sledjeski and Gottesman, 1995; Sledjeski et al., 1996), induces AR-related genes, such as hdeAB, gadAX, and gadBC (Lease et al., 2004). GcvB sRNA, a regulator of genes within amino acid metabolic pathways (Pulvermacher et al., 2009a,b; Urbanowski et al., 2000), also enhances the AR system in an rpoS-dependent manner (Jin et al., 2009). ArrS sRNA is transcribed in the antisense direction from gadE and stabilizes gadE mRNA (Aiso, 2014). 

RpoS is a crucial factor regulating the overall response of E. coli to environmental stress conditions, including heat, high osmolarity, oxidative stress, and acidic pH (Battesti et al., 2011). Three Hfq-interacting sRNAs, ArcZ, DsrA, and RprA, have been shown to stimulate rpoS translation (Majdalani et al., 1998; Mandin and Gottesman, 2010; Sledjeski et al., 1996). Notably, superior acid tolerance attributable to simultaneous expression of DsrA, RprA, and ArcZ during active growth was recently reported (Gaida et al., 2013). Accordingly, it is speculated that increasing the RpoS level through the actions of these sRNAs may generate an effective response to acid stress. However, due to the complexity of the AR network, the specific roles of these sRNAs remain to be elucidated. 

In this chapter, we demonstrate that rpoS-activating sRNAs contribute to the acid tolerance acquisition pathway in E. coli. Acid tolerance depends on RpoS and, partially, GadX. DsrA and RprA act as mediator molecules for the acid stress response. Our findings improve current knowledge on the mechanisms underlying acquisition of AR through rpoS-activating sRNAs. 

## 5.4.2 Materials and methods

## 5.4.2.1 Strains and plasmids

A full list of strains, plasmids, and oligonucleotide sequences used in this study is provided in a previous report (Bak et al., 2014). MG1655 was used as the E. coli control wild-type strain, unless otherwise indicated. Mutant alleles of rpoS, hfq, arcB, gadX, and gadW were transferred into MG1655 via P1 transduction from deletion strains of the E. coli Keio strain collection (Baba et al., 2006). Knockout strains of sRNA genes were constructed using λRed-mediated recombination with the pKD46 plasmid, as described in Datsenko and Wanner (2000). Plasmid pKD13 was used as a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) template for generating amplified products containing kanamycin resistance cassettes flanked by regions homologous to the target genes. For the mutant strain of arcZ sRNA, only the -10 promoter mutation was introduced, since replacement of arcZ with the kanamycin cassette could trigger unexpected effects on expression of the overlapping arcB gene. To obtain a triple deletion mutant of all three rpos-activating sRNA genes, the kanamycin resistance cassette flanked by the Flp recognition target (FRT) from the first ΔdsrA deletion was removed using the pCP20 plasmid (Cherepanov and Wackernagel, 1995). P1 transduction was used to transfer the next ΔrprA mutation. The kanamycin cassette of the newly constructed double deletion strain was removed again using pCP20, and the resultant strain employed as a recipient for P1 transduction to introduce the arcZ promoter mutation. Desired expression of all genes in knockout strains was confirmed with the Northern blot assay. 

The multicopy ArcZ-expressing plasmid, pG-ArcZ, was constructed using a DNA fragment amplified from positions −107 to +208 relative to the transcription start site of ArcZ. Standard molecular biology techniques were used for preparation of plasmid DNA, restriction enzyme digestion, molecular cloning, and transformation. Isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG)-induced overexpression of each sRNA was accomplished using plasmid pHMB1 constructed based on pHM1 (Han et al., 2010). The AatII site of pHM1 was replaced with an XbaI site on pHMB1, and a modified rnpB terminator sequence (GAUUU to GGAGU mutations at the rne-dependent cleavage site) (Kim et al., 1996) introduced downstream of the XbaI site. ArcZ, DsrA, or RprA coding regions were amplified from E. coli genomic DNA, and cloned between the EcoRI and XbaI sites of pHMB1. The resulting plasmids, designated pArcZ, pDsrA, and pRprA, expressed sRNAs transcribed from their native transcription start sites and terminated at the native termination sites. 

## 5.4.2.2 Protein preparation and identification

E. coli MG1655 cells harboring the empty control vector, pGEM3 or pG-ArcZ, were cultured overnight, diluted 1:100 into fresh lysogeny broth (LB), and grown for 17 h at $3 7 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ Aliquots of culture were centrifuged at 10,000 g, resuspended in phosphate buffered saline (PBS) buffer, and sonicated. Subsequently, supernatant fractions were electrophoresed on a 10% sodium dodecyl sulfate–polyacrylamide gel (SDS-PAGE). Protein bands of interest were excised, digested in-gel with trypsin, and sequenced using electrospray hybrid quadrupole-time-offlight tandem mass spectrometry (Q-TOF2 MS/MS). Automatic searches against the Swiss-Prot and TrEMBL databases were performed using Mascot software. 

## 5.4.2.3 RNA extraction and Northern blot analysis

E. coli cells were cultured overnight in LB with 100 μg/mL ampicillin, where necessary. Overnight cultures were diluted 1:100 in fresh medium, and growth continued to the exponential phase $( \mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 } \sim 0 . 5 )$ . For overexpression of sRNA, IPTG was added to a final concentration of 1 mM. At the desired time points, cultures were directly extracted using the acidic hot phenol method (Kim et al., 1996) to obtain total cellular RNA. To examine the changes in sRNA expression following acid challenge, exponential phase cells were resuspended in LB with 100 mM MES (pH 5.0) or fresh LB (pH 7.0), and growth continued to the desired time points for total RNA extraction. 

Northern blot analysis was performed as follows: 10 μg total RNA was fractionated on a 7 M urea 5% PAGE and electrotransferred to a HybondTM-XL membrane (GE Healthcare, USA) 

using a TE70 ECL semi-dry transfer unit (GE Healthcare, USA) at 185 mA for 1 h. Membranes were hybridized with specific 32P-labeled DNA oligonucleotide probes in Rapid-Hyb buffer (GE Healthcare, USA) at $4 2 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ according to the manufacturer’s recommendations. Hybridization signals were assessed using Image Analyzer FLA7000 (Fuji, Japan). 

## 5.4.2.4 ??-galactosidase assay

Overnight cultures of three independent colonies of each strain were diluted 100-fold into fresh LB with 100 μg/mL ampicillin and 1 mM IPTG, where necessary. At the desired time points, a 20 μL aliquot was removed, and activation of the lacZ fusion reporter analyzed using the “Better Miller” assay as described in Zhang and Bremer (1995). At least three independent repeat experiments were performed. 

## 5.4.2.5 AR assay

Three colonies of each strain were pooled and cultured in LB overnight using a shaking incubator. The overnight culture was diluted 100-fold into fresh medium and grown at $3 7 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ with shaking. Cells at the exponential growth phase were removed from cultures grown for 2.5 h $\mathrm { ( O D } _ { 6 0 0 } \sim 1 . 0 )$ , and those at the stationary phase from cultures grown for 12 h $( \mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 } \sim 3 . 0 )$ . For strains containing plasmid, 100 μg/mL ampicillin was added to the culture and 1 mM IPTG used for overexpression of sRNA. 

AR was tested by diluting sample cells to ∼107 cells/mL with M9 minimal medium supplemented with 0.4% glucose and 1.5 mM glutamate, which was previously adjusted to pH 2.0 or 3.0 with concentrated HCl. Cells were incubated in 2 mL acid challenge medium within a 14 mL test tube with shaking at 250 rpm, $3 7 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ . No pH changes were detected during the 1 h acid challenge. After acid exposure, cells were serially diluted in LB, plated on LB agar, and incubated for 16 h at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ before colony counting. Control cultures without acid challenge were additionally serially diluted in LB medium and plated on LB agar. The survival rate was determined based on the ratio of colonyforming units (CFUs/mL) with and without acid exposure. The survival ratio is presented as the average of at least three independent experiments. In parallel, cultures exposed to acid conditions were 10-fold serially diluted in LB, and 10 μL of each dilution was spotted onto LB agar. 

## 5.4.3 Results and discussion

## 5.4.3.1 GadA accumulation upon overexpression of ArcZ in E. coli

ArcZ sRNA has been characterized as a negative regulator of multiple target mRNAs in Salmonella (Papenfort et al., 2009), and a positive regulator of rpoS as well as a negative regulator of arcB in E. coli (Mandin and Gottesman, 2010). ArcZ is widely conserved in various bacteria, and strongly associated with Hfq function (Sittka et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2003). 

To determine the physiological roles of ArcZ in E. coli, we compared the total protein profiles upon overexpression of ArcZ from a multicopy plasmid (Figure 5.4.1a). Two protein bands with significantly altered intensities were characterized using Q-TOF MS/MS. Expression of GadA/B, glutamate decarboxylase of the AR2 system, was highly induced, while TnaA, an alkaliinducible tryptophanase, was reduced upon overexpression of ArcZ. These changes in expression patterns were similar to those of GadY-overexpressing E. coli cells (Opdyke et al., 2004). GadY is reported as a cis-acting positive regulator of gadX and transcriptional activator of gadA and gadBC operons located on the opposite strand to GadY. 

## 5.4.3.2 Effects of ArcZ on AR

GadA and GadB, two homologous glutamate decarboxylases, are key enzymes of the AR2 system. Therefore, we further examined the effects of ArcZ on the AR of E. coli. The ArcZ encoding region was cloned into the IPTG-inducible RNA expression vector, pHMB1, to control ArcZ expression. Exponentially growing cells were exposed at pH 2.0 for 1 h in the presence of glutamate substrate, and the survival rates examined. The results showed increasing survival rates with IPTG concentrations, which increased up to ∼5000-fold at 1 mM IPTG (Figure 5.4.1b and 5.4.1d). Increased ArcZ expression was additionally observed with Northern blot (Figure 5.4.1c). Consistent with previous findings, arcB mRNA was negatively regulated by ArcZ (Mandin and Gottesman, 2010). However, the arcB mutant strain with ArcZ overexpression showed enhanced AR (Figure 5.4.1e), suggesting that arcB does not play a role in ArcZ-induced AR. 

## 5.4.3.3 Effects of rpoS-activating sRNAs on the AR2 system

Next, we focused on the sigma factor, RpoS, another regulatory target of ArcZ. The role of RpoS in general stress management, including AR systems, has been well characterized (Lin et al., 1996; Price et al., 2000). The AR1 and AR2 systems require RpoS, at least under specific conditions. While the mechanism underlying the AR1 system is poorly understood at present, many regulators in the AR2 system have been identified that function in different ways depending on the growth conditions. The glutamate decarboxylases GadA and GadB, key enzymes of the AR2 system, are induced via RpoS-dependent expression of GadX and, subsequently, GadX-dependent expression of GadE in stationary-phase cells grown in neutral-pH LB (Tramonti et al., 2002). 

In addition to ArcZ, DsrA and RprA are known to activate rpoS translation. Upon overexpression of DsrA and RprA in the exponential growth phase, survival rates under pH 2.0 challenge conditions were significantly increased (Figure 5.4.2a and 5.4.2c). We further examined whether AR enhancement upon overexpression of the three sRNAs occurs through the AR2 system (Figure 5.4.2g and 5.4.2h). Enhanced AR was dependent on the presence of 1.5 mM glutamate, supporting the involvement of the AR2 system.

The effects of sRNA overexpression on cells grown to the stationary phase were investigated. In contrast to the exponential phase, survival rates of stationary-phase cells after 1 h exposure at pH 2.0 were ∼100%, even in the absence of sRNA overexpression, suggesting that stationary cells have already acquired sufficient tolerance (Figure 5.4.2d and 5.4.2f). Two- to fourfold translational activation of rpoS by the three sRNAs was observed using a strain carrying the rpoS–lacZ translational fusion (Figure 5.4.2b and 5.4.2e). The finding that rpoS expression is increased by sRNAs at the stationary phase suggests that cells at this phase do not require further RpoS for AR, at least under these conditions. The acidresistant features of stationary-phase cells may be attributed to high-level RpoS induction by rpoS-activating sRNAs, since all three sRNAs are abundant during this period (Argaman et al., 2001). 

The issue of whether enhancement of AR by sRNAs is achieved through RpoS was investigated using rpoS mutant cells. Since the rpoS deletion strain did not survive during acid challenge at pH 2.0 (Figure 5.4.3c), cells were challenged at pH 3.0. Unlike wild-type cells, survival rates of rpoS mutant cells were not increased by the three sRNAs at both the exponential and stationary phases (Figure 5.4.3a and 5.4.3b), clearly indicating that promotion of AR by the three sRNAs is rpoS dependent. 

Moreover, overexpression of RpoS induced an increase in AR of exponentially growing cells to a similar level as that observed upon sRNA overexpression (Figure 5.4.3d). 

Activation of rpoS translation depends on Hfq, a global regulator of sRNA (Battesti et al., 2011). Moreover, Hfq appears to be essential for the wild-type level of AR (Figure 5.4.3c), and overexpression of sRNAs in hfq mutant cells does not increase AR (Bak and Lee, unpublished results). 

Extremely low AR of exponentially growing cells at pH 2.0 may be attributed to the lack of expression of GadA and GadB during this phase (Ma et al., 2002; Tramonti et al., 2002). However, overexpression of rpoS-activating sRNAs could confer AR to exponentially growing cells through the RpoS–GadX– GadA/B pathway, since direct overexpression of RpoS also promotes AR in E. coli. 

## 5.4.3.4 Role of GadX in promotion of AR

To identify the downstream components in the mechanism of sRNA-mediated AR, we examined the involvement of GadX in this process. GadX is a transcriptional activator of the gadE gene encoding the key activator of the AR2 system (Masuda and Church, 2003; Sayed and Foster, 2009; Sayed et al., 2007; Tramonti et al., 2006). Transcription of gadX is primarily induced by RpoS in neutral-rich medium at the stationary phase, and increased under acidic pH conditions (Ma et al., 2002, 2003b). Here, the survival rates of gadX mutant cells overexpressing sRNA were evaluated. Despite a significant decrease in AR in the absence of gadX, sRNAs conferred some residual AR to the mutant cells (Figure 5.4.4). This result is inconsistent with data obtained using rpoS mutant cells that showed no survival, regardless of sRNA expression (Figure 5.4.3a–c).

Overexpression of sRNA was induced with 1 mM IPTG. Average values from at least three experiments are shown. (b,e) Activation of rpoS-lacZ translational fusion upon sRNA overexpression measured based on β-galactosidase activity. (c,f,g) Ten-fold serial dilutions of cultures exposed to acid challenge were spotted on LB agar. The finding that ΔgadX cells overexpressing sRNAs show reduced AR, compared to wild type, but are more acid tolerant than cells lacking RpoS supports the existence of RpoSdependent, GadX-independent pathways for AR. Another AraC family regulator, GadW, is reported to affect GadX-dependent activation of GadE (Ma et al., 2002, 2003b). However, in our experiments, gadW mutation did not affect AR promotion by sRNAs (Figure 5.4.4), suggesting no direct involvement of this gene in sRNA-mediated AR. While the mechanisms involved in RpoS-dependent, GadX-independent pathways remain to be established, involvement of GadE is proposed, as overexpression of GadE induces acid resistance via expression of gadA and gadBC in gadX as well as rpoS mutant cells (Ma et al., 2003a). Accordingly, we conclude that enhancement of AR by rpoS-activating sRNAs is conferred via a GadX-dependent or-independent RpoS–GadE circuit in both exponentially growing and stationary-phase cells. 

## 5.4.3.5 AR in mutant cells lacking rpoS-activating sRNA

We used mutant strains lacking each rpoS-activating sRNA to examine the contribution of individual sRNAs to AR. Cells depleted of any one of the three sRNAs showed 3–5-fold reduced AR at the stationary phase, suggesting that all three sRNAs contribute to wild-type AR (Figure 5.4.5a and 5.4.5b). The survival rate of the triple mutant strain Δ3 lacking all three sRNAs was drastically reduced by nearly 1000-fold (Figure 5.4.5b). Therefore, maintenance of the appropriate cellular levels of these sRNAs appears essential for E. coli cells to acquire the wild-type level of AR. 

We further examined the effects of overexpression of individual rpoS-activating sRNAs on AR of Δ3 cells. Upon expression of each rpoS-activating sRNA, AR of Δ3 cells at the stationary phase recovered fully to the wild-type level. At the exponential phase, AR was further elevated to the level in wildtype cells expressing sRNA, regardless of the sRNA identity (Figure 5.4.5c), suggesting that all three sRNAs play the same role in promoting AR through RpoS-dependent activation of the AR2 system.

## 5.4.3.6 Induction of DsrA and RprA during acid challenge

Experiments were performed to determine whether all three sRNAs are induced during acid challenge. We subjected exponentially growing cells to pH 5.0 and examined alterations in expression levels under conditions of acid challenge. Moderate acid stress conditions were used, since more harsh conditions were liable to cause cell death. The shift to pH 5.0 not only induced DsrA and RprA expression but also activated translation of the rpoS–lacZ fusion (Figure 5.4.6a–c). Expression of ArcZ was slightly decreased, probably due to the reduced growth rate at pH 5.0. As acid exposure is reported to activate translation of rpoS in Salmonella (Battesti et al., 2011; Bearson et al., 1996), we further examined the expression patterns of DsrA and RprA under low pH in rpoS mutant cells. Our data revealed induction of these sRNAs in rpoS mutant cells (Figure 5.4.6a). Therefore, exposure to acidic conditions appears to induce rpoS expression through upregulation of DsrA and RprA expression. Moreover, induction of DsrA and RprA following acid challenge may occur via the two-component systems EvgAS (Eguchi and Utsumi, 2014; Johnson et al., 2014; Ma et al., 2004), PhoPQ (Zwir et al., 2005), and TorSR (Bordi et al., 2003).

## 5.4.4 Conclusions



De Biase D, Tramonti A, Bossa F, Visca P. 1999. The response to stationary-phase stress conditions in Escherichia coli: role and regulation of the glutamic acid decarboxylase system. Molecular Microbiology 32(6): 1198–1211. 





Opdyke JA, Fozo EM, Hemm MR, Storz G. 2011. RNase III participates in GadY-dependent cleavage of the gadX-gadW mRNA. Journal of Molecular Biology 406(1): 29–43. 



Results from this study showed that the three rpoS-activating sRNAs are important mediators of RpoS-dependent activation of the AR2 system, particularly in exponentially growing cells. On the basis of these findings, we have proposed a model of AR acquisition mediated by rpoS-activating sRNAs (Figure 5.4.7). 



Bordi C, Theraulaz L, Mejean V, Jourlin-Castelli C. 2003. Anticipating an alkaline stress through the Tor phosphorelay system in Escherichia coli. Molecular Microbiology 48(1): 211–223. 





Opdyke JA, Kang JG, Storz G. 2004. GadY, a small-RNA regulator of acid response genes in Escherichia coli. Journal of Bacteriolog y 186(20): 6698–6705. 



Different environmental signals trigger expression of individual rpoS-activating sRNAs. ArcZ is highly expressed under aerobic culture conditions (Mandin and Gottesman, 2010). Low temperature and osmotic stress induce DsrA expression (Majdalani et al., 2001; Sledjeski et al., 1996), and osmotic stress triggers RprA expression through the Rcs phosphorelay signal transduction system (Majdalani and Gottesman, 2005; Majdalani et al., 2002). Interestingly, a response regulator of the Rcs phosphorelay system, RcsB, is reported to be essential for gadA and gadB transcription at the stationary phase, and interact with GadE and act in cooperation with GadE in the AR2 system (Castanie-Cornet et al., 2010). 



Castanie-Cornet MP, Cam K, Bastiat B, Cros A, Bordes P, et al. 2010. Acid stress response in Escherichia coli: mechanism of regulation of gadA transcription by RcsB and GadE. Nucleic Acids Research 38(11): 3546–3554. 





Papenfort K, Said N, Welsink T, Lucchini S, Hinton JC, et al. 2009. Specific and pleiotropic patterns of mRNA regulation by ArcZ, a conserved, Hfq-dependent small RNA. Molecular Microbiology 74(1): 139–158. 



Finally, all three rpoS-activating sRNAs perform the same function in activating RpoS for AR in E. coli, since overexpression of individual sRNAs, regardless of origin, rescues loss of acid tolerance to the same extent in mutant cells lacking all three rpoS-activating sRNAs. 



Castanie-Cornet MP, Penfound TA, Smith D, Elliott JF, Foster JW. 1999. Control of acid resistance in Escherichia coli. Journal of Bacteriology 181(11): 3525–3535. 





Peterson WL, Mackowiak PA, Barnett CC, Marling-Cason M, Haley ML, et al. 1989. The human gastric bactericidal barrier: mechanisms of action, relative antibacterial activity, and dietary influences. The Journal of Infectious Diseases 159(5): 979–983.

# Thermal stress noncoding RNAs in prokaryotes and eukaryotes: a comparative approach

## Mercedes de la Fuente1 and Jose Luis Mart´ ´ınez-Guitarte2

1Departamento de Ciencias y Tecnicas Fisicoqu´ ´ımicas, Facultad de Ciencias, Universidad Nacional de Educacion a Distancia (UNED),´ Madrid, Spain 

2Grupo de Biolog´ıa y Toxicolog´ıa Ambiental, Facultad de Ciencias, Universidad Nacional de Educacion a Distancia (UNED), Madrid,´ Spain 

## 5.5.1 Introduction: strategies in thermal stress response involving noncoding RNAs

All living organisms must deal with their environment to maintain homeostasis and survive. Modulations in temperature that can be managed by each organism are related to the mechanisms activated to compensate the effects of the changes. All physiological and biochemical processes are highly dependent on the temperature, which affects the activity and the structure of the biological molecules that carry out the necessary tasks to stay alive. The molecular and cellular events that are activated to mitigate the damage under thermal stress include a wide variety of processes, which go from transcriptional activity changes to modification of the membrane viscosity (Cotto and Morimoto, 1999; Kultz, 2005; Verghese ¨ et al., 2012). A key step in the adaptation to temperature changes is regulation at the transcriptional and posttranscriptional levels (see Section 13). Besides a general decrease of transcription, an activation of the transcription of specific genes takes place, which depends on specific transcription factors. In prokaryotes, response to temperature changes involves the presence of different sigma factors, which are part of the bacterial RNA polymerase holoenzyme. The severity of the stress determines which sigma factor is used (Gruber and Gross, 2003; Kazmierczak et al., 2005; Osterberg ¨ et al., 2011), and each one of them can recognize specific promoter elements to regulate the transcription of the response genes (see Section 4; Chapter 2.4). Eukaryotic cells also have heat shock factors (HSFs) that bind to specific sequences. Although they have been named after heat shock, they can be activated during development and by several stimuli (Akerfelt et al., 2007; Fujimoto and Nakai, 2010; Pirkkala et al., 2001). 

In addition to these master regulators, thermoregulation also is mediated by other molecules, such as widely studied specific proteins and noncoding RNAs (ncRNAs) (de la Fuente et al., 2012). The discovery of ncRNAs as new actors in cellular physiology has changed our comprehension of cellular processes (see Chapter 2.8). These molecules have been implicated in several functions (Fatica and Bozzoni, 2014; Gomes et al., 2013), showing a relevant role in controlling gene expression in prokaryotes as well as eukaryotes. Importantly here, several ncRNAs have been involved in the cellular adaptation to temperature change. All of these mechanisms allow a great flexibility to manage the wide variety of changes that occur in the environment simultaneously (Repoila and Darfeuille, 2009). 

Here, we will cover some of these ncRNAs, specially focusing our attention on those that are involved in the bacterial response to thermal changes. A comparison with similar eukaryotic molecules implicated in heat shock response allows us to obtain a global perspective about the role that these ncRNAs could play in the cell to manage temperature changes. 

## 5.5.2 5′ -cis RNA regulatory elements: temperature-dependent alternative structural elements in messenger RNA (mRNA) regions control translation

One of the regulation methods identified as an extremely efficient modulator of the temperature-regulated response is the presence of 5′ -cis RNA regulatory elements. It has been demonstrated that a structured RNA rather than a particular RNA sequence is critical for thermosensing. Thus, different RNA secondary structure elements acting in heat shock response have been reported. These RNA thermometers, which may consist of more than a single stem loop, are able to block the access to the ribosome binding site (RBS) by masking the Shine–Dalgarno (SD) sequence and/or the AUG under normal conditions. When temperature increases, a conformational change may be produced by the melting of the secondary structure. This structural change allows ribosome access to the exposed RBS and, consequently, gives rise to translation initiation. Moreover, the folded RNA could display recognition motifs for cellular RNases, which eliminate the untranslatable transcripts (Johansson, 2009; Narberhaus, 2010; Narberhaus et al., 2006; Serganov and Patel, 2007). Several examples of these thermosensing RNA elements have been described in bacteria. The most widely distributed cis-acting RNA thermometers known to date are the repression of heat shock gene expression (ROSE) elements (Figure 5.5.1a), reported across more than 30 species of proteobacteria (Gardner et al., 2010; Gaubig et al., 2011; Narberhaus, 2010; Waldminghaus et al., 2009). These RNA elements are located upstream of the translation start codon of genes coding for heat shock proteins. They consist of 2–4 hairpins, extending from 60 to more than 100 nucleotides, with the SD site and the AUG start codon embedded in the last hairpin (Figure 5.5.1a) (Johansson, 2009; Narberhaus, 2010; Narberhaus et al., 2006).

Predicted secondary structures were calculated by means of RNAStructure 5.6 software with default parameters (Reuter and Mathews, 2010)


The most complex heat shock thermometer has been described in the 5′ -proximal regions to the coding sequence of rpoH (σ32) of Escherichia coli and other Gram-negative bacteria. These RNA thermosensors control the increase of $\sigma ^ { 3 2 }$ during the specific stress response (Hengge-Aronis, 2002; Morita et al., 1999; Narberhaus, 2010; Storz, 1999; Storz and Hengge-Aronis, 2000; Yura et al., 2000). 

On the other hand, the smallest natural RNA thermometer reported to date is found in the Synechocystis sp. heat shock gene hsp17 (Figure 5.5.1b). This RNA element consists of a single 44 nt stem loop structure, and it presents a UCCU motif pair of the AGGA nucleotides of the SD region (Kortmann et al., 2011; Narberhaus, 2010). Similarly, other RNA thermometers with four consecutive uridines (fourU), instead of the UCCU motif, have been found (Figure 5.5.1c). For instance, a fourU thermometer has been reported in the 5′ -UTR (untranslated region) of the Salmonella small heat shock gene agsA (Waldminghaus et al., 2007). 

5′ -cis RNA thermometers that increase gene expression due to cold shock have also been reported. This is the case of the temperature-dependent alternative structures described in the leader sequences of the E. coli cspA transcripts, which encode for one of the major, small, and evolutionarily conserved “cold shock proteins” that acts as an RNA chaperone (see Chapter 15.4). A pseudoknot has been noted as a possible key element of the global structural reorganization undertaken at lower temperature in the 5′ -UTR of this mRNA. Similar conformational changes have been predicted in the 5′ -UTR region of mRNAs for other cold shock proteins (Breaker, 2010; Giuliodori et al., 2010; Gualerzi et al., 2003; Mega et al., 2010).

Pathogens also use RNA thermometers to regulate the expression of virulence genes, such as the prfA gene in Listeria monocytogenes; the lcrF gene in Yersinia pestis, which is predicted to enclose a fourU-type RNA thermometer; and the cIII gene of bacteriophage λ, where a switch between two conformations and differences in the recognition of these two structures by RNase III have been identified as determining factors for translation efficiency (Altuvia et al., 1991; Bohme ¨ et al., 2012; de las Heras et al., 2011; Hoe and Goguen, 1993; Johansson, 2009; Johansson et al., 2002; Narberhaus, 2010; Waldminghaus et al., 2007). 

Concerning eukaryotic cells, RNA thermosensors have been postulated as important mechanisms for the translation control of some eukaryotic heat shock genes, such as the Hsp90 gene of Drosophila melanogaster (Figure 5.5.1d) and Hsp70 mRNA in human cells (Ahmed and Duncan, 2004; Duncan, 2008; Hernandez´ et al., 2004; Johansson, 2009; Narberhaus et al., 2006; Yueh and Schneider, 2000). The large ncRNA HSR-1 from human cells has also been defined as an RNA thermometer, although it is not a cis-regulatory element in a 5′ -UTR region. A temperature-dependent conformational change of this ncRNA provides the thermosensing capability that mediates the trimerization of the heat shock factor HSF-1 in eukaryotic cells during heat shock response. Subsequently, the transcription factor HSF-1 is activated for binding to the heat shock element (HSE), promoting activation of heat shock response genes. This thermosensor ability of the ncRNA HSR-1 has been related to the conformational change of $\mathfrak { c } ^ { 3 2 }$ mRNA in the bacterial heat shock response. Furthermore, comparative sequence analyses have led to proposing a bacterial origin for this ncRNA (Anckar and Sistonen, 2011; Kim et al., 2010; Shamovsky and Nudler, 2008). 

## 5.5.3 Trans-acting ncRNAs: DsrA ncRNA – regulation of general stress regulator translation, RpoS, or $\sigma ^ { \mathsf { S } }$ factor

The translation regulation by means of cis-regulatory RNA structural elements may require the assistance of additional factors that aid in the melting process of the implicated stem loop structures. In this regard, the existence of trans-acting ncRNAs that pair with 5′ -UTR regions to regulate the translation of selected genes has been reported. A classic instance of such ncRNAs is DsrA (Figure 5.5.2a), a trans-encoded ncRNA with 85 nucleotides fairly well conserved in Enterobacteriaceae; it interacts with the leader sequence of rpoS mRNA and increases its translation. The rpoS gene encodes the factors $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { s } }$ or $\sigma ^ { 3 8 }$ $( \sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } }$ in Gram-positive bacteria), and it is the master regulator of the general stress response. The existence of an inhibitory secondary structure element in the 5′ -UTR of its mRNA is a key feature in regulating translation. This structural element masks the SD sequence and the AUG codon, and it offers a cleavage site to RNAse III, leading to its degradation, under normal conditions (Figure 5.5.2b). It has been proposed that at high temperatures (heat shock), the melting of the hairpin should contribute to overcoming RNAse III action and inducing RpoS synthesis, likely without the assistance of an ncRNA. At low temperature, intramolecular pairing of the inhibitory stem is broken by means of DsrA–rpoS mRNA interaction and mediated by a protein called Hfq, a RNA chaperone protein that is homologous to the Sm and Sm-like proteins involved in a variety of RNA-processing events in eukaryotes, including splicing, telomere replication, and mRNA decay (Figure 5.5.2c). As a result, the inhibitory secondary structure is lost, rendering the SD accessible to ribosomes. In addition, it has been shown that DsrA ncRNA assists in overcoming the degradation of rpoS mRNA by one of the two major endoribonucleases, RNase E (Figure 5.5.2a), and eliminates the original cleavage site of the other one, RNase III. Furthermore, RNAse III seems to exert a positive effect on mRNA levels and the stability of rpoS mRNA. DsrA RNA also regulates the translation of the nucleoid-associated global repressor H-NS, an abundant histone-like protein that silences the expression of a variety of bacterial genes and affects recombination and transposition in a manner reminiscent of eukaryotic silencing. DsrA impedes the translation of hns mRNA. As a consequence, the cellular pool of the H-NS protein is reduced, and transcription is activated as this nucleoid-structuring protein overcomes transcriptional silencing. High DsrA levels are necessary for the downregulation of H-NS, whereas even low DsrA levels are sufficient to enhance RpoS translation. It has been suggested that DsrA acts as a riboregulator of gene expression at multiple loci since it also shows sequence complementarity with other genes involved in metabolic pathways such as argR, ilvIH, and rbsD (Arluison et al., 2007; Battesti et al., 2011; Brennan and Link, 2007; Freire et al., 2006; Guisbert et al., 2007; Hengge-Aronis, 2002; Lease and Belfort, 2000; Lease et al., 1998; Majdalani et al., 1998; McCullen et al., 2010; Møller et al., 2002; Repoila and Gottesman, 2001; Resch et al., 2008; Scofield and Lynch, 2008; Sledjeski et al., 2001, 1996; Sledjeski and Gottesman, 1995; Soper and Woodson, 2008; Storz et al., 2004; Updegrove and Wartell, 2011; Valentin-Hansen et al., 2004; Vecerek ˇ et al., 2010).

Figure 5.5.2 Trans-acting DsrA sRNA. (a) Enterobacter sp. 638 DsrA RNA (RFam: RF00014; GenBank: CP000653.1/2739273-2739189). The secondary structures were predicted from sequence by means of RNAStructure 5.6 software, default parameters, ΔG = −32 kcal mol−1 (Reuter and Mathews, 2010). Secondary structure of DsrA consists mainly of two clearly defined stem loops in the $5 ^ { \prime } \cdot$ - and ${ 3 ^ { \prime } } .$ -regions, named SL1 and SL3, and a more variable middle region with another hairpin element, SL2. SL1 is complementary and base pairs with the upstream leader portion of rpoS mRN, SL2 involves the hns mRNA interacting region, and SL3 is a transcription terminator for DsrA. (b) Inhibitory secondary structure in the 5′ -UTR of the rpoS gene by intramolecular pairing. In the presence of DsrA trans-acting sRNA and mediated by the Hfq protein, intramolecular pairing is broken, and the hairpin is open (c); the intermediate duplex DsrA–rpoS mRNA provides an alternative cleavage site for RNase III after the dissociation of Hfq. RNase III processing should provide a translationally competent rpoS mRNA prior to ribosome binding. Adapted from Vecerekˇ et al. (2010) and de la Fuente et al. (2012).


Other trans-acting ncRNAs involved in cellular response to high temperature also have been described: the MicF RNA, a regulator of the synthesis of the outer membrane porin OmpF, and the SdsR RNA, which downregulates the synthesis of the major Salmonella porin OmpD. Another two ncRNAs (i.e., MicA and RybB RNA) are transcribed under control of the $\sigma ^ { 2 4 } / \sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ factor, a second heat shock sigma factor activated at critical high temperatures (extreme heat stress, $4 5 \mathrm { - } 5 0 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } )$ . These four trans-acting ncRNAs are also dependent on the Hfq protein, and they impair translation and/or induce the RNase Edependent cleavage and degradation of their mRNA targets. Some of them interact with the 5′ -UTR region, preventing ribosome binding, whereas others, such as RybB or SdsR, bind the downstream translation initiation region (Andersen et al., 1989; Delihas and Forst, 2001; Frohlich ¨ et al., 2012; Gottesman and Storz, 2011; Johansen et al., 2006; Udekwu and Wagner, 2007; Valentin-Hansen et al., 2007; Vogel and Papenfort, 2006). 

Trans-encoded ncRNAs may be considered functional analogs to eukaryotic microRNAs as suggested by their ability to modulate the activity and stability of multiple mRNAs, in a comparable manner to the modulation of microRNAs. In addition, the effect of RNase III on their activity could rather resemble the generation of noncoding microRNAs and the RNA interference (RNAi) scenario in eukaryotic organisms. Finally, the growing number of trans-acting small RNAs (sRNAs) that are being described and characterized in bacteria indicate a sign of a successful mechanism selected (Gottesman and Storz, 2011; Kim et al., 2008; Resch et al., 2008; Waters and Storz, 2009). 

## 5.5.4 ncRNAs acting on proteins: sRNAs interacting with proteins in thermal stress response – 6S (or SsrS) RNA

Heat shock response is characterized by the activation of specific genes that allow the adaptation of the cells to the temperature changes. But it is not the only event that happens to cells. In eukaryotes, there exists also a general repression of the transcriptional activity and a reduction of the posttranscriptional processing (Allen et al., 2004; Biamonti and Vourc’h, 2010). In these organisms, it has been suggested that some ncRNAs work as sequestering RNA-processing factors and regulate their availability during heat shock response. SatIII transcripts from human and hsr-omega from Drosophila would be examples of these ncRNAs (Biamonti and Vourc’h, 2010; Jolly and Lakhotia, 2006; Lakhotia, 2011, 2012). 

It has also been reported that ncRNAs interact with eukaryotic RNA polymerase II to repress the transcription during heat shock (Allen et al., 2004). B2 and Alu RNAs, short interspersed elements (SINEs) transcribed by RNA polymerase III, are retrotransposons found in mouse and human that complex with RNA pol II at the promoters of several genes and repress their transcription upon heat shock (Mariner et al., 2008). They have also been implicated in other functions, acting like a boundary element for B2 or participating in alternative splicing for the Alu element (Ponicsan et al., 2010). Although both SINEs show a similar mechanism of RNA pol II repression, they seem to have no relation in sequence or overall secondary structure. B2 is a ∼180-nucleotide element whose secondary structure shows two regions: a long interrupted stem loop about 70 nt at the $5 ^ { \prime } { \mathrm { - e n d } }$ (related to transfer RNAs (tRNAs)) and three stem loops with intercalated single-strand sections at the 3′ -end. The binding to RNA pol II and the transcriptional repression are related to the $3 ^ { \prime } .$ -end region (Espinoza et al., 2007). On the other hand, Alu RNA is about 280 nt in length and shows two 7SL-derived arms linked by an A-rich region (Sinnett et al., 1991). The A-rich region and one of the arms are the repression domains, and each arm can bind one RNA pol II molecule (Mariner et al., 2008). In mouse, a similar ncRNA to human Alu has been described, named B1, which is transcribed during heat shock and can bind the RNA pol II, but is not capable of repressing transcription (Ponicsan et al., 2010). The mechanisms involved in the repression of RNA pol II by B2 and Alu ncRNAs are still not fully understood, but it has been proposed that probably they disrupt the critical contacts between this protein and DNA (Espinoza et al., 2007; Yakovchuk et al., 2009). Recently, it also has been proposed that Alu antisense transcripts could be involved in repression of transcriptional activity by a cis-antisense mechanism, so it is possible that Alu ncR-NAs could have multiple roles during heat shock (Pandey et al., 2011).

Figure 5.5.3 6S RNA secondary structure of Escherichia coli predicted from sequence (MFE), ΔG = −81.6 kcal mol−1 (RFam: RF00013; GenBank: X01238.1/1-184), by means of RNAStructure 5.6 software, default parameters (Reuter and Mathews, 2010); then it was constructed with a VARNA applet (Darty et al., 2009). The region complementary to the short transcript pRNA is highlighted (Panchapakesan and Unrau, 2012).


In bacteria, an ncRNA exists that can be considered the counterpart of B2 and Alu ncRNAs, the 6S RNA (Figure 5.5.3) (Mariner et al., 2008; Oyoshi and Kurokawa, 2012). Discovered in E. coli very early and sequenced as one of the first sRNAs, it is found in almost all phylogenetic branches of bacteria, and its function has remained elusive for three decades. Now, it is known that it causes global downregulation of many genes during starvation and other stress conditions. It is a highly structured ncRNA with a size of around 180 nt that is processed from a longer mRNA and emulates DNA promoter open structure. This RNA binds tightly and sequesters σ70-containing RNA polymerase II, downregulating the transcription of some $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ - promoters and upregulating the transcription of $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { S } }$ -dependent promoters (Battesti et al., 2011; Cavanagh et al., 2008; Decker and Hinton, 2009; Geißen et al., 2010; Gottesman and Storz, 

2011; Klocko and Wassarman, 2009; Wassarman, 2007a, 2007b). However, the σ factor specificity is not absolute since there are also some non-σ70-dependent genes that are under control of the 6S RNA (Neusser et al., 2010). Thus, this ncRNA seems to help $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { S } }$ to compete for the RNA polymerase II core (Battesti et al., 2011) because the affinity of this factor for the core is lower than that shown by $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ . The presence of 6S RNA in the active site of RNA polymerase II is evidenced when, in the presence of high levels of nucleotides, it is possible to use this sRNA as a template to transcribe a short transcript (14–20 nt), termed pRNA (Gottesman and Storz, 2011; Wassarman, 2007b). This pRNA forms a triple-helix hybrid with a 6S RNA hairpin, a complex that seems to destabilize the interaction between the 6S RNA and the RNA polymerase II and rescue the enzyme activity by releasing the ncRNA. The 6S–pRNA complex would later be degraded (Oyoshi and Kurokawa, 2012; Repoila and Darfeuille, 2009; Wassarman, 2007b; Waters and Storz, 2009). As happens with most ncRNAs, the sequence conservation of 6S RNA is very low, but the secondary structure shows a conserved doublestranded RNA hairpin and a single-stranded central region that is fairly open with asymmetric loops (Figure 5.5.3) (Panek´ et al., 2011; Wassarman, 2007b), which is the recognition region for $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ . Although it is not clear, it seems that RNA- and DNAbinding sites overlap, so there is a competition between the 6S RNA and the promoter DNA (Klocko and Wassarman, 2009). This ncRNA has been considered as a central regulator in stress and growth adaptation networks (Geißen et al., 2010), but there is still no direct evidence that relates the 6S RNA and the cellular response to temperature modulation. However, the inhibition mechanisms could work similarly to 6S RNA and Alu/B2 RNAs, although the bacterial RNA does not bind the promoter and the RNA pol at the same time (Espinoza et al., 2007). 



Waters LS, Storz G. 2009. Regulatory RNAs in bacteria. Cell 136: 615– 628. doi:10.1016/j.cell.2009.01.043 



In conclusion, the collected information on the mechanism underlying the thermal stress response of bacteria in relation to noncoding RNAs led us to identify three main strategies: (i) cis-regulatory elements based in secondary structure elements in the translation initiation region of mRNAs, (i) trans-coding sRNAs acting via RNA–RNA interactions, and (iii) sRNAs interacting with proteins. On the other hand, the eukaryotic cellular response to temperature changes involves a wide diversity of mechanisms across the different species, although some key features seem to be preserved throughout evolution. Thus, thermosensors have been described in eukaryotes, some of them acting as cis-regulatory elements and others acting on proteins; several microRNAs and iRNAs appear to be related to the thermal change response; and SINE-related ncRNAs are being characterized as repressing factors of RNA polymerase II in heat shock response. Thus, it is postulated that this perspective could help to place each of the apparently disparate solutions into a framework of the regulation of gene expression pathways.

## 6.1.1 Introduction: restriction modification systems in epigenetic adaptation

The most basic paradigm in current biology is the dual action of the genetic material or the genome. Its information content, written in the letters ATGC, is inherited through replication, while its expression is regulated in various ways. In multicellular organisms, the genome sequence is inherited by daughter cells, as well as by the next generation. In most unicellular microorganisms, the two levels of inheritance are identical. Diverse genome sequences are thought to represent the units of natural selection in adaptive evolution. 

Challenging this scheme is the concept of epigenetics in evolution. Epigenetics is defined here as the modification of a genome sequence that is heritable through replication. Although there are increasing lines of evidence regarding the importance of epigenetics in multicellular development and gene expression, epigenetics, as defined here, is not limited to multicellular organisms. In multicellular organisms, epigenetic information is reprogrammed in the next generation in some cases, but is heritable to the next generation in other cases. In most unicellular microorganisms, trans-generation epigenetic inheritance is, by definition, identical to the cell-to-cell inheritance and may be regarded as the norm. Numerous epigenetic states can be associated with a specific genome sequence. Such diverse epigenomes may be regarded as the true units of natural selection. 

Here, we develop these ideas by surveying recent studies on prokaryotic restriction modification (RM) systems. There have been many recent reviews of these systems, some from a historical point of view (Loenen et al., 2014a,b; Rao et al., 2014), as well as some by ourselves (Furuta and Kobayashi, 2012a, 2013; Mruk and Kobayashi, 2014). 

Most students with a biology-related major are familiar with restriction enzymes, the DNA cutters that aided the revolution in biology. However, few people are aware that the early history of RM systems ran counter to the prevailing paradigm of biology: adaptive evolution through natural selection among genome sequences a la Darwin. The relevant observation is that` microorganisms adapt to their host. This has been known for a long time to microbiologists and, even before the birth of modern microbiology, to those working with microorganisms. This concept is illustrated in Figure 6.1.1a. A microorganism that has been grown on one host (Host A) can grow well on the same host, but not on the other host (Host B). However, once some of them successfully replicate in Host B, they (and their descendants) can grow well in this host. This may be regarded as the inheritance of acquired traits, as the Lamarckian theory of evolution envisioned. 

The emergence of molecular biology revealed the molecular mechanisms underlying such adaptation for the case of bacteriophages (the best studied microorganisms) and their host bacteria, which turned out to be mediated by RM systems (Figure 6.1.1b) (Loenen et al., 2014a). In an RM system, a modification enzyme (DNA methyltransferase, or MTase) transfers a methyl group to a specific DNA sequence, while a cognate restriction enzyme (REase) cleaves a DNA with the recognition sequence unmethylated, thereby enabling the selfepigenome, which is methylated, to be distinguished from nonself-epigenomes, which are not. A microbial genome (such as a bacteriophage genome) that has already been modified by the RM system of Host A is not damaged and can multiply in its presence. When the bacteriophage genome enters Host B, which has a different RM system, it is destroyed. However, rare survivors are methylated by the RM system in Host B and can now multiply there. Thus, RM systems form a barrier against foreign DNA (Figure 6.1.1c). Thus, RM systems contribute to the maintenance of genetically discrete populations of bacteria and archaea.
