Figure 6.1.1 Restriction modification systems. (a) Host-controlled variation of microorganisms. A microorganism (bacteriophages, in particular) grown on a host organism (a bacterial strain, in particular) can grow well on the same host (Host A). It cannot grow well on a different host organism (Host B). However, rare microorganisms that have emerged can now grow in Host B. There is no difference between the DNA sequences of the two microorganisms. (b) Distinction between self and nonself by a restriction modification system. A modification enzyme (a methyltransferase) transfers a methyl group to a specific DNA sequence, whereas a paired restriction enzyme will damage DNA lacking this epigenetic modification. (c) Dual action of restriction modification systems. These systems prevent genetic flux between lineages and maintain genetically isolated lineages. By methylating many copies of a specific sequence throughout the genome, the restriction modification system defines a specific pattern of gene expression and, therefore, a unique set of properties. These two actions may contribute to the adaptive evolution of prokaryotic lineages in their ecological niches.


Each of the modification enzymes may methylate a specific sequence at many sites along the genome (Figure 6.1.1c). This will affect the expression of many genes, and it defines a specific transcription pattern (among other epigenetic effects) and, consequently, a specific set of phenotypes. These diverse methylomes, each with unique properties, may be regarded as the true targets of natural selection in adaptive evolution (Figure 6.1.1c). Before presenting evidence for these concepts and the epigenetics-driven adaptive evolution hypothesis, we will further explore the nature and expression of RM systems. 

## 6.1.2 Restriction modification systems: types, abundance, and mobility

RM systems were first noticed as a host line of defense against invasive DNAs, such as the genomes of bacteriophages (see Section 6.1.1). This is why they are considered to be the host’s innate immune system, which is in contrast, by analogy, to the adaptive immune system (defense with memory) operated by CRISPR (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat) systems. Recently, it has been shown that these two systems may cooperate to efficiently prevent bacteriophage infection (Dupuis et al., 2013). Nevertheless, RM systems’ diversity, in terms of their sequence specificity and prevalence, suggests that they have other important roles (Vasu and Nagaraja, 2013). They behave as selfish mobile elements, as we will detail in this chapter (Kobayashi, 2001). They may be a key cellular factor in the control of DNA uptake and gene flow between bacteria, thereby facilitating speciation (Jeltsch, 2003; Murray, 2002), as discussed in Section 6.1.1 (Figure 6.1.1c). The double-stranded breaks following REase digestion of incoming DNAs stimulates their homologous recombination, which promotes their repair and integration into the genome (Murray, 2002). In addition, the restriction activity may also participate in nonhomologous recombination (Kusano et al., 1997). These mechanisms indicate the impact of RM systems on shaping genomes and generating genome diversity (Kobayashi et al., 1999). 

RM systems are classified into Type I, Type II, Type III, and Type IV (Roberts et al., 2003). The classification criteria are being continually modified in adjustment with a nomenclature system (Roberts et al., 2003, 2014). These four distinguished types form subdivisions based on their structure, cofactor requirements, sequence specificity, and cleavage position. These subdivisions are not mutually exclusive. 

The greatest number of RM systems belong to Type II (Oliveira et al., 2014), whose restriction enzymes are used by almost all molecular biologists, as their sequence-specific DNA cleavage is an excellent tool for genetic engineering (Loenen et al., 2014b; Pingoud et al., 2014). A Type II RM system is composed of two separately active enzymes, an REase and an MTase, which are encoded by separate genes. A Type I RM system is composed of three subunits: S (hsdS, specificity), M (hsdM, modification), and R (hsdR, restriction). S and M form a complex with modification activity, whereas S, M, and R form a complex with restriction activity (Ishikawa et al., 2009; Loenen, 2003; Loenen et al., 2014a). Type III RM systems are composed of a Mod protein and a Res protein. The Mod protein has a sequence-specific modification activity, whereas the Res protein bound to the Mod protein has restriction activity (Raghavendra et al., 2012; Rao et al., 2014). Type IV restriction systems (in contrast to RM systems) consist of restriction enzymes (Type IV restriction enzymes) that cleave DNA, with some sequence specificity, which has been methylated or modified in some other way (Loenen and Raleigh, 2014). In addition, a single gene activity may be encountered in a genome, such as the presence of a solitary (orphan) MTase without a cognate REase gene. To a lesser extent, REase genes without adjacent MTase genes may be also found (Ershova et al., 2012). 

RM systems are almost ubiquitous in prokaryotic organisms (Roberts et al., 2014). They are highly abundant in the bacteria and archaea, with no clear correlation regarding their mode of life or genome size (Furuta and Kobayashi, 2013; Kobayashi, 2004b; Makarova et al., 2011, 2013; Vasu and Nagaraja, 2013). Specifically, Epsilonproteobacteria contain the highest number of RM systems per genome, and its member Helicobacter pylori carries around 12 on average. Similarly, Mycoplasma, which belong to the Tenericutes, are wall-less bacteria with small genomes that harbor many RM systems. On the other extreme, intracellular, host-associated organisms, such as Chlamydia, have fewer than one RM per mega base in their genome (Oliveira et al., 2014). In contrast, there is a clear correlation between a high abundance of RM systems and the ability of its host, such as H. pylori, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Neisseria meningititis, and Haemophilus influenza, to undergo natural transformation (Oliveira et al., 2014). This may indicate a strong impact of horizontal gene transfer on the evolution of RM systems (Table 6.1.1) (Jeltsch and Pingoud, 1996; Kobayashi et al., 1999; Makarova et al., 2009). Indeed, RM systems are found on plasmids, prophages, integrons, and transposons (Furuta and Kobayashi, 2013; Kobayashi, 2004b; Makarova et al., 2011). However, a close and systemic database examination showed that bacteriophages are rarely vectors of RM system transfer. Similarly, fewer than 20% of RM systems are found on plasmids, and their transmission is due to mobilization during conjugation, rather than by natural transformation (Oliveira et al., 2014). Although RM systems’ mobility is often associated with mobile genetic elements, some RM systems behave as mobile units per se, thereby generating extensive genome rearrangements (Furuta et al., 2010, 2011b; Furuta and Kobayashi, 2013). In some RM systems, the individual component genes also appear to be mobile (Furuta et al., 2010). 

## 6.1.3 Attack on the host bacterial genome by restriction modification systems in postsegregational killing

While RM systems may be advantageous to the bacterial host, they may also be a dangerous burden if not dealt with properly. REase activity may target the host genome and degrade it, leading to the death of the host. The potential toxicity of RM systems needs to be sufficiently counterbalanced by its cognate modification activity. RM systems carried on plasmid DNA are especially challenging during cell division. Cells that do not receive the RM plasmid are killed by the remaining REase because they lack a sufficient amount of protective MTase activity. The diminishing amounts of both enzymes favor REase toxicity (Figure 6.1.2a). 

This postsegregational host-killing or genetic addiction mechanism ensures the proper propagation of certain genetic modules, and it was first noticed as a mechanism for the stable maintenance of plasmids in microbial populations (Gerdes et al., 1986; Kobayashi, 2004a). The genetic addiction behavior is mediated by toxin–antitoxin (TA) modules (see Chapter 2.7 and other chapters in Section 6), although with slightly different courses of action (Gerdes et al., 2005; Hayes, 2003; Mruk and Kobayashi, 2014). In Type II TA systems, the loss of a TA module from a cell leads to preferential degradation of the antitoxin by a protease, which allows the toxin to kill the modulefree descendant cells (Figure 6.1.2b). In contrast, postsegregational killing by Type II RM systems operates even if there is no difference in stability between the MTase and the REase (Ichige and Kobayashi, 2005). After the loss of the RM gene, the modification enzyme is diluted by cell division, leading to the exposure of unprotected recognition sites on newly replicated chromosomes. REase cleavage of the genome triggers cell death if the DNA damage is not repaired (Naito et al., 1995). However, there is also a case where the instability of the modification enzyme strengthens postsegregational killing (discussed further in this chapter) (Ohno et al., 2008).

A game theory study demonstrated that postsegregational killing would help RM systems and TA systems in competitive exclusion in a structured habitat (Mochizuki et al., 2006). 

## 6.1.4 Regulation of expression of restriction modification genes

RM systems employ certain mechanisms that tightly regulate their gene expression to avoid host killing until necessary. The molecular bases of these processes are still enigmatic and understood only to some extent for Type II RM systems. RM system activity may be harmful for its host in a steady state, as well as during RM system transfer to a new host by means of horizontal gene transfer. Many of these mechanisms are similar for TA units, which also demand that toxicity be counterbalanced to avoid the postsegregational killing of the host (Hayes and Kedzierska, 2014; Hayes and Van Melderen, 2011; Mruk and Kobayashi, 2014). When an RM system enters a new host bacterial cell, its genome is unprotected. Thus, RM gene expression needs host-independent timing properties so that the MTase is expressed and protects the chromosome before the production of the toxic endonuclease occurs (Mruk and Blumenthal, 2008). This temporal basis of gene expression regulation is still unclear for many RM systems, and most studies have focused on the level of transcription (Table 6.1.1). It seems that temporal regulation requires fine-tuned transcriptional feedback circuits to keep the REase–MTase expression in balance (Bogdanova et al., 2008, 2009; Mruk and Blumenthal, 2009; Mruk et al., 2007; Nagornykh et al., 2011; Protsenko et al., 2009; Williams et al., 2013). Practically nothing is known about gene expression during postsegregational killing by RM systems. 

Thus far, three major players are involved in the regulation of Type II RMs (Figure 6.1.3 and Table 6.1.1): a specialized controlling C protein, the MTase itself, or antisense RNAs. Thus far, it seems that they form separate modes of control; however, the impact of shared, multilayered mechanisms is very likely. 

## 6.1.4.1 Transcription control proteins

The effect of a controlling C protein on RM system activity was first discovered for the PvuII RM system (Figure 6.1.3a) (Tao and Blumenthal, 1992; Tao et al., 1991). Since then, several other type II RM systems were reported to rely on C proteins to modulate their gene expression (Bogdanova et al., 2008, 2009; Cesnaviciene et al., 2003; Kita et al., 2002; Mruk et al., 2007; Semenova et al., 2005). C proteins are relatively small proteins (8– 11 kDa) that act on a specific DNA operator sequence called the C-box (Sorokin et al., 2009; Tao et al., 1991). Their helical structure, comprising helix-turn-helix (HTH) motifs, resembles that of the Xre family of transcription regulators, including the λ repressor, which suggests a common mechanism of transcriptional activation by direct contact with $\sigma ^ { 7 0 }$ RNA polymerase (McGeehan et al., 2005). 

The C gene and REase gene usually form a single bicistronic operon that is under the control of the promoter $\mathrm { { P } } _ { \mathrm { { C R } } } ,$ which is located upstream of the C gene (Figure 6.1.3a) (Knowle et al., 2005; Vijesurier et al., 2000). The C-box sequence

is located within the $\mathrm { P _ { C R } }$ promoter, and it comprises two palindromic binding sites (proximal and distal) for two C protein homodimers. The C protein cooperatively binds and distorts the C-box sequence with an affinity depending on the C protein concentration (McGeehan et al., 2006; Mruk and Blumenthal, 2009). The C protein has greater affinity for the proximal C-box sequence, which facilitates its interaction with RNA polymerase and promotes the activation step (ON) in transcription (Figure 6.1.3a). Further C protein accumulation leads to binding of both the proximal and distal sequences of the C-box and results in transcriptional repression (OF) (Bogdanova et al., 2008; Mruk and Blumenthal, 2009; Semenova et al., 2005). In one tested case, in addition to its typical site, a second C-box was detected upstream of the MTase gene. The effect of the C protein varies, as the C protein has a different binding affinity toward the two sequence variants of the C-box (Bogdanova et al., 2009). 

The logic of C protein–mediated temporal regulation requires a genetic switch for the toxic endonuclease activity. This switch operates from the ON status to the OFF status so that the host cells are viable, yet the toxin activity is high enough to protect the cell against invasive bacteriophages. In addition, during the establishment of an RM in a new host, the requirement for the C protein can delay the expression of the restriction enzyme, thereby enabling the MTase to complete the modification of the host genome (Mruk and Blumenthal, 2008; Nakayama and Kobayashi, 1998; Williams et al., 2013). Typically, if C proteins are inactivated or deleted, restriction activity is not detected (Tao et al., 1991); thus, these proteins are essential for postsegregational killing (Nakayama and Kobayashi, 1998; Tao et al., 1991). However, an exceptional case shows a high REase expression regardless of C gene presence (Rezulak et al., 2015). The changes in their transcription, if any, during postsegregational killing have not been examined. 

In some cases, C proteins are also involved in the translational control of a downstream R gene via a translational coupling mechanism, as in the Esp1396I RM system (Cesnaviciene et al., 2003). 

C proteins can have another role in the social interactions of RM systems. They can exclude another RM system of the same C specificity, but of different restriction and modification specificity, through apparent cell suicide (Nakayama and Kobayashi, 1998). 

## 6.1.4.2 Transcriptional regulation by methyltransferases

In the second type of transcriptional regulation in RM systems, a modification enzyme that is able to bind DNA plays a central role (Figure 6.1.3b). Only a small subset of MTases possess a two-domain structure, and M.EcoRII, M.SsoII, and M.Ecl18kI among them have been studied in some detail (Butler and Fitzgerald, 2001; Christensen and Josephsen, 2004; Fedotova et al., 2009; Karyagina et al., 1997; Som and Friedman, 1994, 1997). One large domain has typical Type II MTase enzyme properties and is joined via a flexible linker to a small, Nterminal domain containing a HTH motif (Konarev et al., 2014). These regulatory MTases and the C proteins show a high level of amino acid sequence similarity in the HTH-motif region, suggesting that they are evolutionarily related (Fedotova et al., 2009). The recognition site (RS) for the MTase is composed of 15-nt inverted repeats located in the intergenic region of the two divergently oriented genes encoding the MTase and REase (Figure 6.1.3b). The promoters for the REase and MTase genes $- \mathrm { P _ { R } }$ and $\mathrm { { P } } _ { \mathrm { { M } } } ,$ respectively – face each other (Protsenko et al., 2009). 

Two MTase molecules may interact with the regulatory region, thereby blocking access of RNA polymerase access to the $\mathrm { P _ { M } }$ promoter (Burenina et al., 2013; Riazanova et $a l .$ , 2010). Such suppression is exclusively based on the competition between MTase and RNA polymerase to bind to the same region (Burenina et al., 2013). 

This creates a negative feedback loop, in which the MTase acts as an autorepressor that sufficiently controls its own cellular level to ensure the modification of the genome. It seems that during entry of the RM system with such a regulatory MTase, the expression of the MTase is switched on first, as its promoter is much stronger than the $\mathrm { P _ { R } }$ promoter (Burenina et al., 2013). The accumulation of the MTase results in its occupation at the $\mathrm { P _ { M } }$ promoter, and this switches off its expression (Figure 6.1.3b). At this point, the indirect stimulation of REase transcription occurs as a result of the promoter competition mechanism (Protsenko et al., 2009). The RNA polymerase complex is prevented from initiating transcription from $\mathrm { P _ { M } }$ by MTase dimer occupation, thereby allowing the expression from $\mathrm { P _ { R } }$ to begin. It seems that once $\mathrm { P _ { R } }$ -initiated transcription occurs, the RNA polymerase complex is able to displace the MTase at the $\mathrm { P _ { M } }$ site (Burenina et al., 2013; Ryazanova et al., 2011). The above structure suggests the independent action of either domain, but this is not so. Changes in the HTH motif interfere with the ability of the MTase to methylate its substrate, while mutational inactivation of the methyltransferase activity can increase its DNA-binding affinity via the HTH motif. The basis and biological significance, if any, of such reverse dependence between the domains are not clear (Fedotova et al., 2009). A mutation in the N-terminal region of the EcoRII MTase makes the enzyme metabolically unstable and increases postsegregational killing (Ohno et al., 2008). This indicates a similarity between postsegregational killing by RM and TA systems (Figure 6.1.1b) (see above; see Chapter 2.7). 

In some cases, the coordinated expression of an RM system relies on the methylation status of the cognate recognition site(s) in the promoter of the modification gene (Beletskaya et al., 2000; Christensen and Josephsen, 2004). See the REBASE Genomes database for the location of the cognate recognition sites along RM genes (http://rebase.neb.com). 

## 6.1.4.3 Regulation by antisense RNAs

The third mode of regulation for Type II RM systems relies on antisense RNAs. The significance of these antisense RNAs in RM system biology is still poorly understood. However, the control of the expression of the toxin has been better studied in analogous TA systems, which share many features, including the regulation patterns involving RNAs, with antisense RNAs (Mruk and Kobayashi, 2014; see Chapter 2.7). Antisense RNAs have been found in two Type II RM systems, EcoRI and Eco29kI, in which two genes are organized in an operon, with the REase gene preceding the MTase gene (Mruk et al., 2011; Nagornykh et al., 2011). They share a common gene regulation pattern: the upstream promoter $\mathrm { P _ { R } }$ from the REase gene drives a long bicistronic mRNA, whereas the MTase can be separately expressed from the downstream $\mathrm { P _ { M } }$ promoter within the REase gene (Figure 6.1.3c). The EcoRI transcription unit is complex, comprising four identified promoter regions (twice as tandems) within the REase coding sequence. Two sense promoters $( \mathrm { P _ { R } }$ and $\mathrm { P _ { M } } )$ face the reverse promoters $( \mathrm { P _ { R E V 1 } } , 2$ and $\mathrm { P _ { R E V 0 } } )$ , which produce the antisense RNAs aRNA1 and Rna0, respectively (Figure 6.1.3c). The reverse promoters have a strong negative effect in cis on their upstream convergent promoters and vice versa (Liu et al., 2007; Liu and Kobayashi, 2007; Mruk et al., 2011). However, some connecting mechanisms between the two feedback loops must exist, as a complete knockout of the $\mathrm { P _ { R E V 0 } } \cdot$ -produced 88-nucleotide antisense RNA (Rna0) is lethal for cells. Instead, a slight reduction in $\mathrm { P _ { R E V 0 } }$ action increases REase expression, which is revealed by a greater restriction of incoming bacteriophages in the cell (Mruk et al., 2011). 

In addition to the in cis effect, the antisense RNA Rna0 may operate via an in trans effect by an undefined mechanism. Overexpression of Rna0 in cells with the RM system resulted in the weakening of the postsegregational killing (Mruk et al., 2011). Further experiments are needed to understand the molecular mechanisms underlying these observations, as well as their biological significance. 

## 6.1.5 Effects of restriction modification systems on global gene expression

In bacteria and archaea, the methylation marks come from DNA MTases of different types of RMs, as well as from solitary MTases, which together transfer methyl groups to their recognition sites within a genome. As a result, each genome possesses a unique set of epigenetic marks (specific epigenetic signatures), which defines a specific methylome that is dependent on the active MTase repertoire (Furuta et al., 2014; Krebes et al., 2013; Lluch-Senar et al., 2013). Changes in the methylome may enforce changes in the transcriptome, which may, in turn, lead to phenotypic variations (Figure 6.1.4) (Furuta and Kobayashi, 2012a). Under conditions of selection, such variants may become established during the process of adaptive evolution. 

DNA methylation affects gene expression in prokaryotes as it does in eukaryotes. In general, the basic mechanism of gene expression modulation occurs by directly affecting RNA polymerase binding, or by preventing or permitting binding of transcription regulators (Wion and Casadesus, 2006). If the methyl group is located within a gene promoter, it may directly affect gene expression (Shell et al., 2013). It may also prevent the gene regulatory region from binding transcription factors, although there are some known transcriptional repressors that bind DNA in a methylation-dependent manner (Broadbent et al., 2010; Camacho and Casadesus, 2005; Haagmans and van der Woude, 2000). Changes in the expression of certain gene clusters may reveal distinct phenotypes, which show differences in the stress response, fitness, or resistance to antimicrobial agents (Militello et al., 2013; Shell et al., 2013; Wion and Casadesus, 2006).

Changes in presence or absence, expression, and sequence specificity


![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/6c2e57f4-f177-4731-acc4-f560c6f82e69/dec2810199c8723e377d81ed1f600c2f7d78f90178700bc315f714c507d30992.jpg)



Figure 6.1.4 Epigenetics-driven adaptive evolution (a hypothesis). Each of the restriction modification systems changes their presence or absence, expression, and sequence specificity. As a result, various epigenomes (methylomes) are generated, each with a unique transcriptome, proteome, and phenome (a set of phenotypes). These epigenetic states, as opposed to the genome sequences, provide targets for natural selection.


Solitary DNA MTases (without linked REases), such as Dam (Escherichia coli) or CcrM (Caulobacter crescentus), have also been reported to affect gene expression at a global level (Collier, 2009; Gonzalez et al., 2014; Jeltsch, 2002; Kozdon et al., 2013; Marinus, 1987; Wion and Casadesus, 2006). Their roles are different: CcrM is cell cycle regulated, whereas Dam is active throughout the cell cycle (Collier, 2009). DNA adenine methylation by Dam $\left( 5 ^ { \prime } { \mathrm { - } } \mathrm { G } ^ { \mathrm { m } } { \mathrm { A T C } } \right)$ affects the expression of multiple genes (Jeltsch, 2002; Marinus, 1987; Wion and Casadesus, 2006), and is related to the virulence of Salmonella, Haemophilus, Yersinia, Klebsiella, Campylobacter, Vibrio, and pathogenic E. coli (Balbontin et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2008; Marinus and Casadesus, 2009; Mehling et al., 2007; Murphy et al., 2008; Robinson et al., 2005; Wion and Casadesus, 2006). It also acts to coordinate DNA replication and DNA mismatch repair. Inactivation of Dam reveals a strong host mutator phenotype (Marinus, 2010; Marinus and Casadesus, 2009). The CcrM DNA MTase $\left( 5 ^ { \prime } { \mathrm { - G } } ^ { \mathrm { m } } { \mathrm { A N T C } } \right)$ is essential for DNA metabolism and cell division. CcrM expression and degradation are strictly correlated with the host cell cycle. DNA methylation affects hundreds of gene promoters, including some master transcriptional regulators that govern the complex regulatory network of C. crescentus, as well as the progression of the cell cycle (Gonzalez et al., 2014). Methylation by Dcm $\left( 5 ^ { \prime } { - } \mathrm { C } ^ { \mathrm { m } } 5 \mathrm { C } ^ { \mathrm { A } } / _ { \mathrm { T } } \mathrm { G } \mathrm { G } \right)$ affects the expression of genes in the stationary phase of E. coli. Dcm-defective mutants show increased expression of the stress response sigma factor, RpoS, as well as many of its targets in the stationary phase (Kahramanoglou et al., 2012). 

The impact of Type II RM systems on global gene expression has also been studied (Asakura and Kobayashi, 2009; Vitoriano et al., 2013). Among the transcriptome changes during postsegregational killing, activation of SOS genes and the ${ \mathfrak { o } } ^ { \mathrm { E _ { - } } }$ regulon was noticeable at early time points. With time, more SOS genes, stress response genes (including $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { S } } .$ -regulon, osmotic-, oxidative-, and periplasmic-stress genes), biofilm-related genes, and many hitherto uncharacterized genes were induced. As expected from the activation of the $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ -regulon, cell death was accompanied by cell lysis and the release of cellular proteins. The transcriptome changes resembled those observed during the action of bactericidal antibiotics (Asakura and Kobayashi, 2009). 

## 6.1.6 Dynamics of restriction modification systems and the methylome

A type of methylation-mediated gene expression regulation occurs via a mechanism of the regulation of phase-variable regulons (phasevarions) (Figure 6.1.4). Such methylation-mediated expression was shown to be associated with the modification activities of Type III (Table 6.1.1) (Srikhanta et al., 2010, 2011) or Type I RMs (Dybvig et al., 1998; Manso et al., 2014). Phase variation may occur due to the high probability of frameshift changes within the simple repeat tracts of a Mod gene. As a result, inactive, truncated forms of the Mod protein are generated. This causes a genome-wide change in the methylation pattern. Consequently, this leads to a reversible switching ON or OFF of multiple genes, which, in turn, results in the establishment of distinct cell subpopulations manifesting variant phenotypes. This has been associated with the pathogenesis of Neisseria, Helicobacter, Haemophilus, and Moraxella (Blakeway et al., 2014; Gawthorne et al., 2012; Jen et al., 2014; Srikhanta et al., 2010, 2011). 

H. pylori has a large number of Type III RM genes. They switch their sequence specificity by replacing their target recognition domains via allelic recombination or by ectopic recombination involving distant loci (Furuta and Kobayashi, 2012b). 

Some of the target recognition domains spread throughout the bacterial world. 

Type I RM systems may undergo phase variation by different mechanisms using special genetic rearrangements that are facilitated by the presence of a series of repeats within the hsdS gene (the RM specificity subunit; discussed in this chapter). The Mycoplasma pulmonis chromosome has two hsd loci, both of which contain two hsdS genes, which form complex, sitespecific DNA inversion systems. Embedded within the coding region of each hsdS gene are a minimum of three sites at which DNA inversions occur that generate extensive amino acid sequence variations in the predicted S subunits. The polymorphic hsdS genes produced by the gene rearrangements encode a family of functional S subunits with different DNA sequence specificities (Dybvig et al., 1998).

## 6.1.7 Concluding remarks

The observations collected here lead us to a simple picture (Figure 6.1.4). RM systems change their presence or absence, their sequence specificity, and their own expression over various time scales. These changes result in changes to and diversification of the methylome, which, in turn, result in a greater diversity of gene expression and phenotypes, which may aid adaptation. The ever-changing methylomes or epigenomes, as opposed to the genome sequences, may be regarded as the real units of natural selection.

# Toxin–antitoxin systems as regulators of bacterial fitness and virulence

Brittany A. Fleming and Matthew A. Mulvey 

Division of Microbiology and Immunology, Pathology Department, University of Utah School of Medicine, Salt Lake City, Utah, USA 

## 6.2.1 Introduction

Toxin–antitoxin (TA) systems are encoded by small bipartite operons that each express a stable toxin paired with a more labile neutralizing antitoxin (Schuster and Bertram, 2013; Unterholzner et al., 2013; Yamaguchi et al., 2011; see also Chapter 2.7). Plasmid-borne and chromosomal TA loci are present in a wide variety of bacterial species. To date, five categories of TA systems have been defined based on the nature of the antitoxin molecules. Type I antitoxins are essentially small noncoding RNAs (sRNAs) that block translation of the toxin (Brantl, 2012; Fozo et al., 2010). The antitoxins encoded by types II and III TA loci are proteins and sRNAs, respectively, that complex with and inactivate their cognate protein toxins (Blower et al., 2011; Schuster and Bertram, 2013; Unterholzner et al., 2013; Yamaguchi et al., 2011). Type IV TA systems have antitoxin proteins that stabilize the target of the toxin rather than interacting with the toxin itself, creating some semantic debate as to whether or not these loci are bona fide TA systems (Masuda et al., 2012; Schuster and Bertram, 2013; Tan et al., 2011). For the most recently described type V TA systems, the antitoxins are endonucleases that degrade the messenger RNA (mRNA) transcripts of their toxic counterparts (Wang et al., 2012). The toxins produced by the various known TA systems have diverse activities, and when unhindered they can wreak havoc on numerous cellular processes including membrane potential (Figure 6.2.1) (Brantl, 2012; Schuster and Bertram, 2013), peptidoglycan synthesis (Mutschler et al., 2011), ribosome assembly (Zhang and Inouye, 2011), mRNA stability (Maisonneuve et al., 2011), and transfer RNA (tRNA) availability (Garcia-Contreras et al., 2008; see Chapter 2.7). 

TA systems were originally characterized as extrachromosomal loci that can promote the faithful partitioning of plasmids upon cellular division (Van Melderen and Saavedra De Bast, 2009). In this context, plasmid-borne TA systems act as addiction modules, ensuring their maintenance in a bacterial population by requiring daughter cells to continually replenish labile antitoxin molecules that keep the more stable toxins from triggering cell dormancy or death. Chromosomal TA systems may likewise promote their own inheritance and maintenance while providing no obvious fitness advantage to the bacterial cell at large. Such observations have fostered arguments that TA systems function primarily as selfish genetic elements, or that they are essentially junk DNA (Leplae et al., 2011; Magnuson, 2007). However, an increasing number of studies demonstrate that plasmid and chromosomal TA systems can affect a variety of cellular processes that may enhance the overall fitness and survival of bacterial populations, especially under stressful conditions in which antitoxin levels are oftentimes diminished (Hayes, 2003; Schuster and Bertram, 2013). Of particular interest is emerging work showing that TA systems can impact the fitness and virulence potential of bacterial pathogens. In this chapter, we examine how TA systems can affect pathogen behavior through five vignettes focusing on Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Salmonella, extraintestinal pathogenic Escherichia coli (ExPEC), Haemophilus influenzae, and Enterococcus species. For further information see other chapters of Section 6 and Chapter 2.7. 

## 6.2.2 A multitude of TA systems for Mycobacterium tuberculosis

Tuberculosis (TB), which is caused by the obligate human pathogen M. tuberculosis (Mtb) and a group of very closely related Gram-positive bacteria known as the Mtb complex (MTBC), typically affects the lungs and is transmitted personto-person via a respiratory route. Mtb is a major global health threat, causing about 9 million new TB cases and 1.5 million deaths every year (WHO, 2014). It is estimated that up to a third of the world’s population has tuberculosis, although Mtb in the majority of those infected exists in a latent state (Dye et al., 2005, 2013). Reactivation of latent Mtb reservoirs eventually occurs in approximately 5 to 10% of infected individuals (Gomez and 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/6c2e57f4-f177-4731-acc4-f560c6f82e69/61861040d033284d5baba62ee5a22ba54469f200fbf0cfcc855027df010b42f6.jpg)



Figure 6.2.1 Schematic representation of a type II TA system, listing potential targets of the toxins and downstream consequences for the bacterium.


McKinney, 2004; Stewart et al., 2003). Latent TB infections have been attributed in part to the formation of metabolically dormant bacterial cells called persisters (Keren et al., 2011). The persister cell state may develop both by stochastic events and by deterministic mechanisms in response to environmental stimuli (Keren et al., 2011; see Chapter 6.3). Though persister cells initially comprise only a small portion of the overall bacterial population within the host, their quiescent state makes them tolerant of many antibiotics and therefore more difficult to eradicate relative to their more metabolically active neighbors (Figure 6.2.2) (Warner and Mizrahi, 2006; Wood et al., 2013). It is hypothesized that persister cell populations are a primary reason that it is necessary to treat TB patients with long-term antibiotic therapies (Gomez and McKinney, 2004; Warner and Mizrahi, 2006; see Chapter 6.3). 

TA systems have long had a defined role in the production of bacterial persister cells, with numerous TA systems, including HipBA, MazEF, YefM–YoeB, and RelBE, linked to their formation (Wang and Wood, 2011; see Chapter 2.7). Mtb contains two homologs of the type II TA system RelBE and one homolog of YefM–YoeB (Miallau et al., 2013; Singh et al., 2010). Work in E. coli shows that the RelE and YoeB toxins both act as ribosome-dependent ribonucleases (Feng et al., 2013; Griffin et al., 2013). In response to amino acid starvation and elevated levels of the alarmone guanosine tetraphosphate (ppGpp), RelE induces toxicity in E. coli by binding with 30S and 70S ribosomal subunits and inhibiting translation through the indiscriminate cleavage of mRNA and transfer-messenger RNA (tmTNA) (Hayes, 2003; Pedersen et al., 2003). YoeB has similar effects, although it interacts with 50S rather than 30S ribosomal subunits (Christensen-Dalsgaard and Gerdes, 2008). In Mtb, YefM– YoeB and the two RelBE homologs are thought to function like their counterparts in E. coli, but they are each differentially regulated in response to environmental stresses (Singh et al., 2010). During the course of an infection, Mtb will face a number of environmental stresses, including nutrient limitations and exposure to reactive oxygen and nitrogen species. In vitro, both nitrosative and oxidative stresses increase the transcription of yefM–yoeB, whereas starvation has no effect (Singh et al., 2010). In contrast, both oxidative stress and starvation stimulate transcription of one relE homolog (relE2) while the other homolog (relE1) is unaffected. All three toxins (YoeB, RelE1, and RelE2) are induced within human macrophages and within the lungs of infected mice (Korch et al., 2009; Singh et al., 2010). Under these conditions, the associated antitoxins are upregulated as well, but at levels that are likely too low to effectively neutralize their cognate toxins. In broth culture-based assays, overexpression of the YoeB or RelE toxins can enhance the development of antibiotictolerant persister cells, whereas in complementary experiments only the deletion of either yoeB or the relE2 homolog significantly decreased persister cell formation (Singh et al., 2010). These findings suggest that the YoeB and RelE toxins may promote the development of persister cells (see Chapter 6.3) and the establishment of latent Mtb infections, with each TA pair responding to unique sets of environmental stresses. However, deletion of the relBE or yefM–yoeB loci individually had no impact on Mtb survival within macrophages or in mice (Singh et al., 2010). 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/6c2e57f4-f177-4731-acc4-f560c6f82e69/9bb5463617c5fec13044ef798364a00399f9c08b15a90b273cdcbb3f08a1ecea.jpg)



Figure 6.2.2 The development of persister cells mediated by TA systems can enable bacterial populations to better withstand harsh environmental stresses, including the administration of antibiotics that are typically ineffective against nonreplicating bacteria.


The lack of in vivo phenotypes associated with the relBE or yefM–yoeB mutants may reflect an inability of mouse models to fully recapitulate the disease processes that normally occur in the natural human host for Mtb. In addition, functional redundancy among the multiple TA systems that are encoded by Mtb may make it difficult to discern phenotypes using single-gene knockout mutants. For example, in laboratory E. coli strains, up to 10 type II TA systems work cooperatively to promote the development of persister cells, and appreciable defects in this process are not observed until five or more of the TA systems are deleted (Maisonneuve et al., 2011). Remarkably, Mtb encodes about 79 TA systems, the largest number discovered in any organism studied to date (Ramage et al., 2009; Sala et al., 2014). At least two of these systems are upregulated by Mtb within cultured macrophages in a fashion similar to the relBE and yefM–yoeB loci, and another two are induced under hypoxic conditions akin to those often encountered within host environments (Ramage et al., 2009). Evidence that TA systems can act in a redundant or synergistic manner to promote the fitness of Mtb within the host has recently been obtained by analysis of the nine mazEF TA homologs in Mtb (Tiwari et al., 2015). Concomitant deletion of three of the mazEF homologs markedly reduced the growth and virulence of Mtb in a guinea pig infection model, and also rendered the pathogen more sensitive in vitro to antibiotics, starvation, and oxidative stress. Virtually no defects were observed in mutants lacking only one or two of the mazEF systems. The toxins encoded by the various mazE homologs in Mtb act as ribonucleases that have varying RNA substrate specificities. It is speculated that the coordinated activation of these toxins causes increased expression of stress resistance genes with a simultaneous reduction in Mtb metabolic processes, driving the reversible formation of persister cells that are less sensitive to antibiotics and the various stresses that are encountered within the host (Ramage et al., 2009; Tiwari et al., 2015). 

The numerous TA systems that are encoded by Mtb are fairly well conserved among all members of the MTBC, but are largely absent from phylogenetically more distant Mycobacterium species like the saprophytic strain Mycobacterium smegmatis and the free-living opportunistic pathogen Mycobacterium marinum (Ramage et al., 2009; Sala et al., 2014). In fact, M. marinum has at most only two of the 79 TA systems that are present in Mtb. Many of the TA systems carried by Mtb and other MTBC members appear to have been acquired by horizontal gene transfer, a process that is thought to be a primary mediator of speciation for bacteria within the MTBC (Becq et al., 2007; Ramage et al., 2009). In total, these findings suggest that the acquisition of TA systems has significantly influenced the evolution and biology of the MTBC, perhaps by enabling the pathogens to better withstand diverse environmental stresses via the formation of persister cells. Defining the specific effects that TA loci have on Mtb and other MTBC bacteria within the host requires further analysis, including the use of approaches that can effectively disentangle overlapping input from the multitude of TA systems that are carried by these pathogens (see Chapters 2.7, 6.4, 6.5). 

## 6.2.3 TA-mediated dissemination of Salmonella within the host

Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (S. Typhimurium) can cause severe gastroenteritis and serious systemic infections (Majowicz et al., 2010). In the United States, S. Typhimurium is the leading cause of hospitalization and death due to a foodborne illness, and worldwide this pathogen is responsible for about 98.3 million infections and 115,000 deaths annually (Majowicz et al., 2010). S. Typhimurium is versatile in its ability to colonize diverse environments and can be found in various hosts ranging from amoebae to the gastrointestinal tracts of livestock, birds, reptiles, and other animals (Berge and Wierup, 2012; Bleasdale et al., 2009; Rabsch et al., 2002). Key to the pathogenesis of S. Typhimurium is its ability to invade and proliferate within macrophages and other host cells (Fields et al., 1986). To enter host cells and to avoid destruction within phagolysosomal compartments, S. Typhimurium employs two type 3 secretion systems and many secreted effector molecules that can modulate host cell signaling cascades, membrane trafficking, and inflammatory responses (Haraga et al., 2008). Recent studies indicate that the success of S. Typhimurium as a pathogen may also depend on multiple TA systems. 

S. Typhimurium is known to encode seven type I TA systems and 20 type II systems (Lobato-Marquez et al., 2015). A number of these are expressed within cultured host fibroblasts, epithelial cells, and/or macrophages (Helaine et al., 2014; Lobato-Marquez et al., 2015). Three of the type I TA systems (hok–sok, ldrA–rdlA, and tisB–istR) and two of the type II systems (ta4 and vapBC2) promote intracellular survival of S. Typhimurium within fibroblasts, but only vapBC2 enhanced pathogen survival within epithelial cells (Lobato-Marquez et al., 2015). These results indicate that S. Typhimurium may utilize distinct sets of TA systems when engaging different host cell types. Analogous to the situation with Mtb, toxin activation in S. Typhimurium may promote the development of nonreplicating persister cells that are more resistant to stresses encountered within the intracellular milieu. Indeed, the number of persister cells present within a population of S. Typhimurium grown in broth culture rapidly increases 100- to 1000-fold upon entering the hostile confines of a macrophage (Helaine et al., 2014). The formation of these macrophage-induced persister cells is mediated by the cumulative actions of at least 14 type II TA systems, and is stimulated by acidification of Salmonella-containing vacuoles within the phagocytes and by nutrient limitations. About 5% of the persister cells recovered from infected macrophages are able to invade and replicate within na¨ıve macrophages, suggesting that these bacteria may be a source for relapsing infections. This could be especially pertinent to Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi (S. Typhi), the causative agent of typhoid fever. This human-specific pathogen carries a repertoire of TA loci similar to those found in S. Typhimurium, and is prone to cause relapsing infections (Bhan et al., 2005; De la Cruz et al., 2013; Lobato-Marquez et al., 2015). 

Two type II TA systems, SehAB and ShpAB, have been shown to promote the survival of Salmonella in vivo using mouse infection models (De la Cruz et al., 2013; Helaine et al., 2014). In susceptible mice, S. Typhimurium can disseminate systemically and multiply intracellularly within the liver, spleen, Peyer’s patches, and mesenteric lymph nodes (MLNs), eliciting a typhoid-like disease that is similar to that caused by S. Typhi in humans. In this infection model, the SehAB system is expressed in a subpopulation (∼5%) of S. Typhimurium shortly after the pathogens cross the intestinal barrier and reach the MLNs. Relative to wild-type S. Typhimurium, an isogenic mutant that lacks the sehAB locus is markedly attenuated in its ability to colonize sites within the MLNs, spleen, and liver following oral inoculation of mice (De la Cruz et al., 2013). Interestingly, the SehAB system is dispensable if mice are infected with S. Typhimurium via an intraperitoneal route that bypasses the gastrointestinal tract. SehA is homologous to a toxin called HigB, which cleaves tmRNA and mRNA subsets in Mtb and K-12 E. coli strains (Schuessler et al., 2013). It is feasible that SehA acts similarly in S. Typhimurium, stimulating the formation of stress-resistant persister cells that are better able to survive the transition from the gut to nearby MLNs. In a separate study, deletion of the shpAB TA locus in S. Typhimurium also decreased bacterial colonization of the MLNs following oral inoculation, but in this case the mutant phenotype was not manifest unless the mice were subsequently treated with the antibiotic enrofloxacin (Helaine et al., 2014). Without antibiotic treatment, the shpAB mutant actually outcompeted the parent wild-type strain. 

In total, these in vitro and in vivo findings support the idea that individual TA systems are responsive to distinct environmental insults, and may help explain the presence of multiple TA systems within S. Typhimurium and other pathogens like Mtb. As is the case for Mtb and most of the other bacteria discussed in this chapter, the TA systems in Salmonella species are often associated with mobile genetic elements. Interestingly, 17 of the 27 TA systems present in S. Typhimurium and related pathogens are absent in the sequenced nonpathogenic species S. bongori (De la Cruz et al., 2013; Lobato-Marquez et al., 2015). This situation is similar to that seen within the genus Mycobacterium, in which pathogenic species encode many more TA systems than their nonpathogenic counterparts (Ramage et al., 2009; Sala et al., 2014). However, this trend is not observed with all bacterial pathogens, as will become apparent when we consider ExPEC. 

## 6.2.4 Discriminating ExPEC-associated TA systems

E. coli strains act as commensals, typically localized within the lower intestinal tracts of mammals, or as opportunistic pathogens that can cause either diarrheagenic diseases or extraintestinal infections (Wiles et al., 2008). There are at least eight genetically distinct E. coli lineages, or phylogroups, with the majority of isolates belonging to Groups A, B1, B2, or D (Clermont et al., 2013). B2 isolates often appear to encode more virulence determinants than E. coli strains within the other phylogroups (Chaudhuri and Henderson, 2012). Most strains of extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli (ExPEC) belong to the B2 or D phylogroups, though there are many exceptions to this categorization. ExPEC can effectively colonize the gastrointestinal tract without harming the host, but can also disseminate to extraintestinal sites where they may elicit a variety of disease responses (Wiles et al., 2008). These pathogens are the primary cause of bloodstream and urinary tract infections (UTIs), and an important cause of neonatal meningitis, surgical site infections, intra-abdominal and soft tissue infections, pneumonia, and osteomyelitis (Russo and Johnson, 2000; Smith et al., 2007). 

The prevalence of ExPEC as a pathogen is especially evident when considering UTIs. These are among the most common of bacterial infections, accounting for well over 10 million cases per year in the United States alone at a cost of more than $3.5 billion (Barber et al., 2013; Brown et al., 2005; Dielubanza and Schaeffer, 2011). ExPEC isolates that are associated with UTIs are referred to as uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC), and are responsible for the majority of community- and hospital-acquired bladder and kidney infections (Dielubanza and Schaeffer, 2011; Foxman et al., 2002). The enormous health burden of UTIs mainly falls on females. One in three women will develop a UTI by the age of 24, and half of all women will experience at least one of these infections during their lifetime (Dielubanza and Schaeffer, 2011). Further exacerbating the problem is the fact that recurrent or relapsing UTIs (rUTIs) are extremely common. One-fourth of all women who experience a UTI will have a second infection within 3–4 months after the cessation of the first (Franco, 2005). The high frequency of rUTIs may be in part attributable to the ability of UPEC strains to invade bladder tissues and form long-lived intracellular reservoirs that are protected from host defenses as well as most antibiotic treatments, including those that effectively sterilize the urine (Blango and Mulvey, 2010; Blango et al., 2014; Mulvey et al., 1998). The perseverance of UPEC between episodes of symptomatic UTIs may also be facilitated by the development of stress-resistant, antibiotic-tolerant persister cells driven by activation of one or more TA systems (Norton and Mulvey, 2012). 

TA systems have been studied extensively in nonpathogenic laboratory K-12 E. coli strains belonging to phylogroup A. However, these bacteria are quite different from UPEC, other wildtype ExPEC, and related phylogroup B2 isolates. Though ExPEC genomes are in general substantially larger than those of K-12 lab strains, ExPEC isolates within phylogroup B2 encode only a subset of the multiple type II TA systems that have been identified in K-12 strains and other bacteria within phylogroups A, B1, and D (Fiedoruk et al., 2014; Norton and Mulvey, 2012). For example, of the 16 type II TA loci present in the K-12 strain MG1655, only seven are encoded by the reference ExPEC isolate CFT073 (Norton and Mulvey, 2012). These findings are in contrast to those reported for Mtb, S. Typhimurium, and a number of other pathogens, which typically have smaller genomes and higher numbers of TA systems than related nonpathogenic strains (Georgiades and Raoult, 2011). It has been suggested that the reduced repertoire of TA systems in B2 E. coli strains is directly related to their lifestyles (Fiedoruk et al., 2014). Among phylogroup B2 strains are many human commensals that, like ExPEC, may be considered host-adapted specialists (Carlos et al., 2010; Clermont et al., 2008; Gordon and Cowling, 2003; Nowrouzian et al., 2005; White et al., 2011). In contrast, group A and B1 strains may be thought of as generalists that are potentially better suited to persist within assorted environments and in a broader range of hosts (Carlos et al., 2010; Gordon and Cowling, 2003; Walk et al., 2007). The variety of stresses encountered by these generalists may select for increased numbers of TA systems that enable E. coli populations to better survive within changing ecological niches by enhancing biofilm formation (see Section 22), persister cell development (see Chapter 6.3), and general stress resistance (Fiedoruk et al., 2014; Wang and Wood, 2011). Whether or not this is the case remains to be tested. 

To examine functional roles for TA loci within the B2 lineage, and in UPEC specifically, six of the seven type II TA systems in the reference UPEC isolate CFT073 were deleted individually and tested in a mouse UTI model (Norton and Mulvey, 2012). Deletion mutants lacking the TA loci higBA, hipBA, or sohA(prlF)–yhaV were each able to colonize the bladder and kidneys similar to the wild-type parent strain, whereas mutants lacking either the ybaJ–hha (aka tomB–hha) or the yefM–yoeB TA system were defective in bladder colonization. Like its homolog in Mtb, yoeB encodes a ribosomedependent ribonuclease that can work cooperatively with multiple other TA systems to promote persister cell development by K-12 E. coli strains (Maisonneuve et al., 2011). The hha gene product functions in an entirely different manner by binding rare codon tRNAs (Garcia-Contreras et al., 2008). In K-12 E. coli, Hha expression can stimulate the dispersal of biofilms as well as the translational repression of type 1 pili and the poreforming toxin alpha-hemolysin (HlyA) (Garcia-Contreras et al., 2008; Nieto et al., 2000). Type 1 pili are important to the ability of UPEC strains to bind and invade bladder epithelial cells, whereas HlyA can modulate host inflammatory responses, inactivate phagocytes, and stimulate tissue damage (Barber et al., 2013; Wiles and Mulvey, 2013). Deletion of either ybaJ–hha or yefM–yoeB had no apparent effects on persister cell development, biofilm formation, or the expression of either type 1 pili or HlyA by CFT073, leaving open the question of how these two TA systems independently promote bladder colonization by UPEC (Norton and Mulvey, 2012). 

The sixth type II TA system tested is encoded by the pasTI locus and was found to greatly enhance colonization of the kidneys by CFT073, but was superfluous within either the bladder or the intestinal tract at the time points examined (Norton and Mulvey, 2012). The PasTI system carried by CFT073 and other ExPEC isolates is nearly identical to the RatAB system in K-12 E. coli. In vitro assays indicate that the PasT homolog RatA binds 50S ribosomal subunits and inhibits translation (Zhang and Inouye, 2011). In CFT073 and other ExPEC isolates, the induced expression of PasT in the absence of the PasI antitoxin results in bacterial stasis, whereas deletion of the pasTI locus renders ExPEC more sensitive to nutrient limitations as well as oxidative and nitrosative stresses (Norton and Mulvey, 2012). Without the pasTI locus, CFT073 is also markedly defective in its ability to form antibiotic-tolerant persister cells. This is in striking contrast to results from K-12 strains in which five or more TA systems must be knocked out before defects in persister cell formation are observed (Maisonneuve et al., 2011; Norton and Mulvey, 2012). Genetic analysis, including the use of truncation mutants, indicated that the N-terminal 69 amino acids of PasT are sufficient to promote both persister cell formation and bacterial stasis, while sequences within the C-terminus of PasT provide protection against environmental stresses like reactive nitrogen species (Norton and Mulvey, 2012). PasT can therefore be considered a multifunctional protein with both toxic (bacteriostatic) and growth-promoting beneficial effects. These contrasting functions may be differentially regulated dependent on PasT expression levels, interactions with the PasI antitoxin, the bacterial strain background, and varying environmental stresses. These results highlight novel functions for a TA system, and indicate that TA loci can impact bacterial pathogenesis independent of effects on persister cell development. 

## 6.2.5 An earful about the TA systems of Haemophilus influenzae

H. influenzae normally resides as a benign commensal within the upper respiratory tract of humans, but can also cause a number of serious infections (Agrawal and Murphy, 2011). The encapsulated serotype b strain, known as Hib, can cause meningitis and other lethal invasive infections in infants and children. Highly effective vaccines against Hib that were first introduced in the late 1980s have substantially reduced the numbers of illnesses and deaths due to this pathogen. However, no vaccines are currently available for unencapsulated nontypable H. influenzae (NTHi), which remains an important cause of bronchitis, pneumonia, conjunctivitis, and otitis media (Agrawal and Murphy, 2011). Like UPEC, Mtb, and S. Typhimurium, NTHi is also prone to cause recurrent and chronic infections. For example, worldwide, NTHi causes up to 330 million cases of recurrent or chronic otitis media each year (Agrawal and Murphy, 2011; Leibovitz et al., 2004). Recurrent episodes of otitis media are often observed within 2 weeks after completion of antibiotic treatments, and are typically caused by the same NTHi strain that was responsible for the initial infection (Barenkamp et al., 1984). The chronic persistence of NTHi within the host may be linked with the ability of this pathogen to form biofilms (see Section 22) and to invade host cells, and may be further promoted by the development of stress-resistant, antibiotic-tolerant persister cells that are induced via activation of TA systems (Agrawal and Murphy, 2011; Barenkamp et al., 1984; Clementi and Murphy, 2011; Ren et al., 2012, 2014; see Chapter 6.3). 

Three type II TA loci (vapBC-1, vapXD, and toxAvapA) in NHTi have been analyzed for their contributions to virulence and pathogenesis. Deletion of any one of these TA systems significantly reduced the intracellular survival of NTHi in a 3D tissue model of the human upper respiratory tract (Ren et al., 2012, 2014). The deletion mutants were also impaired in their ability to colonize host tissues and cause inflammation in a chinchilla model of otitis media. The toxins encoded by these three NHTiassociated TA loci are ribonucleases, and may stimulate bacterial stasis and persister cell formation by causing the degradation of metabolism-related transcripts (Daines et al., 2007; Ren et al., 2012, 2014). Of note, the NTHi VapBC-1 TA system is related to the VapBC2 system that promotes the intracellular survival of S. Typhimurium within epithelial cells (Lobato-Marquez et al., 2015), while ToxAVapA is a HigBA homolog similar to the SehAB TA system that enhances the colonization of MLNs by S. Typhimurium (De la Cruz et al., 2013). These findings suggest that NTHi and S. Typhimurium may utilize similar TA systemdependent strategies to avoid eradication from the host. 

## 6.2.6 Virulence modulation by an enterococcal TA system

Although once considered to be only harmless commensals within the gut, the Gram-positive bacteria Enterococcus faecalis and Enterococcus faecium have emerged over recent decades as important causes of hospital-acquired bloodstream, urinary tract, skin, soft-tissue, and surgical site infections (Arias and Murray, 2012). These opportunistic pathogens can withstand harsh environmental conditions, and many strains are resistant to broad-spectrum antibiotics. Especially concerning is the spread of vancomycin-resistant strains of E. faecalis that are difficult to eliminate and are oftentimes more deadly than antibiotic-susceptible strains (Arias and Murray, 2008; Bearman and Wenzel, 2005). Annually in the United States, enterococci cause about 66,000 healthcare-associated infections, with approximately 20,000 of these being attributable to vancomycinresistant strains (CDC, 2013). Antibiotic-resistant genes in enterococci are often associated with plasmids and other mobile genetic elements, typically linked with TA systems. For example, in enterococcal strains the MazEF and Axe–Txe type II TA systems are frequently encoded by vancomycin- and multidrugresistant plasmids, while the PezAT TA system is found in association with a chromosomal integrative conjugative element (ICE) that also carries vancomycin-resistant genes (Bjorkeng et al., 2013; Grady and Hayes, 2003; Moritz and Hergenrother, 2007; Sadeghifard et al., 2014). It is generally assumed that these TA systems are acting primarily as addiction molecules, helping to insure the stable partitioning and maintenance of mobile genetic elements within enterococci. However, as in other pathogens, TA systems may also modulate the fitness and virulence potential of enterococci independent of their roles as addiction molecules. This supposition is supported by recent functional analysis of the par type I TA carried by E. faecalis. 

The par locus was originally identified as an addiction module associated with retention of the enterococcal plasmid pAD1 (Weaver, 2012; Weaver et al., 1993). Two RNA molecules are convergently transcribed from the par locus, with the first (RNAI) encoding a 33 amino acid toxin known as Fst and the second (RNAII) acting as a regulatory RNA that suppresses the translation of RNAI (Weaver, 2012). Fst is predicted to integrate into the bacterial plasma membrane, and when overexpressed in E. faecalis it can induce aberrant nucleoid condensation followed by cell elongation, increased membrane permeability, and chromosomal mis-segregation during bacterial division (Patel and Weaver, 2006; Weaver et al., 2003). The precise target and mode of action of Fst and other par family toxins remain undefined. E. faecalis contains three homologous par loci – two are located on plasmids, and one is present on the chromosome (Shioya et al., 2011). Interestingly, when the chromosomally encoded RNAII antitoxin is deleted, E. faecalis displays increased virulence in an infection model using Galleria mellanella (honeycomb moth) larvae and improved survival in a mouse UTI model and within murine macrophages (Michaux et al., 2014). Relative to the wild-type parent strain, the RNAII deletion mutant was also more resistant to serum, bile, high salt, and hydrogen peroxide. These results are surprising, as it might be expected that deletion of the RNAII antitoxin would increase Fst expression and subsequently decrease bacterial viability. Whether or not the phenotypes seen with the RNAII deletion mutant are attributable to the absence of RNAII, the misregulation of RNAI, or a combination of the two is not yet clear. Regardless, the data do suggest that the par TA system can temper the virulence potential of E. faecalis, possibly helping the bacteria to better balance its pathogenic and commensal behaviors. 

## 6.2.7 Conclusions

Considering the widespread distribution of TA systems, it is perhaps not surprising that they can impact the fitness and virulence of bacterial pathogens. While the ability of pathogenassociated TA systems to promote the development of persister cells is undoubtedly important, this is not necessarily the only mechanism by which TA systems enhance pathogen survival within host environments. For example, the analysis of systems like PasTI in ExPEC and the par locus in E. faecalis makes it clear that TA genes can profoundly influence the stress resistance and virulence potential of pathogens independent of effects on persister cell development (Michaux et al., 2014; Norton and Mulvey, 2012). In addition, TA loci are often encoded within mobile genetic elements, and may thereby indirectly impact the behavior and resilience of bacterial pathogens by facilitating the dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes and other fitness and virulence factors (Van Melderen and Saavedra De Bast, 2009). Emerging data indicate that some TA system–associated toxins can also affect host cell functions, suggesting additional means by which TA loci may benefit bacterial pathogens (Audoly et al., 2011; Pinel-Marie et al., 2014). 

Despite ongoing advances, we still have much to learn about how TA systems are regulated in pathogens during the course of an infection and how, specifically, these systems modulate stress resistance pathways and pathogenic cascades. There is a growing appreciation that some TA systems can interact with and modulate the transcription and/or function of noncognate toxins and antitoxins, further enriching, but also complicating, our understanding of the regulation and evolution of TA loci (Goeders and Van Melderen, 2014). By defining how TA loci and networks of TA systems affect bacterial virulence and persistence within host environments, it may be possible to develop improved therapeutics to combat bacterial pathogens, many of which are becoming increasingly resistant to available antibiotics. Efforts to interfere with TA systems and persister cell development pharmacologically are already underway and showing promise (Chan et al., 2015; Keren et al., 2012). The coming years should continue to provide new insight into the functionality of TA systems in pathogens and their utility as therapeutic targets.

# Mechanisms of stress-activated persister formation in Escherichia coli

Stephanie M. Amato and Mark P. Brynildsen 

Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey, USA 

## 6.3.1 Introduction

Persister cells are rare and transient phenotypic variants within isogenic bacterial populations that cannot readily be killed by antibiotics. They were first discovered in 1944 by Joseph Bigger, who failed to sterilize a culture of staphylococci with penicillin and showed that the surviving colonies upon re-inoculation exhibited the same sensitivity to the antibiotic (Bigger, 1944). The existence of persisters can be detected from the dynamics of antibiotic killing, where the first phase of rapid killing represents the death of normal cells, and a second phase with a significantly reduced rate of cell death indicates the presence of persisters (Figure 6.3.1) (Balaban et al., 2004; Lewis, 2010; Maisonneuve and Gerdes, 2014; Orman et al., 2015). When persisters, which are survivors from the second phase of killing, are propagated, they produce cultures that exhibit the same biphasic killing kinetics as the original culture (Keren et al., 2004b), thereby demonstrating that the phenomenon is phenotypic and not attributable to genetic mutations associated with resistance (Gefen and Balaban, 2009; Lewis, 2010; Maisonneuve and Gerdes, 2014). 

Persisters have been clinically linked to chronic and recurring infections, such as cystic fibrosis, tuberculosis, and oral thrush (Grant et al., 2012; LaFleur et al., 2006; Mulcahy et al., 2010), and they are believed to be responsible for recalcitrant biofilm infections, which account for the majority of hospital-treated infections, including those associated with medical implants, oral diseases, genitourinary infections, and respiratory infections (Lewis, 2010; Mah and O’Toole, 2001; Pace et al., 2005; Percival et al., 2011; see Chapters 2.7 and 6.2). Due to the clinical importance of persisters, a deeper understanding of how these cells form will facilitate the development of more effective therapies to combat them. 

In general, persister antibiotic tolerances have been attributed to a transient inhibition of cellular functions that are targeted by antibiotics. They have been shown to form stochastically, and environmental cues and cellular physiology can influence the rate at which normal cells switch into the persister state (Amato and Brynildsen, 2014; Amato et al., 2013; Balaban et al., 2004; Dorr et al., 2010; Keren et al., 2004a; Nguyen et al., 2011; Vega et al., 2012). Studies that have identified mechanisms underlying persister formation have demonstrated a pivotal role for stress responses and revealed the presence of diverse and complex pathways. In this review, we discuss the different formation mechanisms that have been identified for the model organism Escherichia coli and how this information can be used to guide therapeutic discovery. 

## 6.3.2 Stress-induced persister formation pathways

A persister formation pathway can be broken down into modules as depicted in Figure 6.3.2. First, bacteria sense a stress and activate response pathways. These responses and the mediators associated with them affect bistable systems that enable the majority of cells to continue along a normal cell trajectory, whereas a small fraction transition into a persister state. Persister states are typically characterized by dormancy, where the activities of essential processes have been reduced to prevent antibiotic-induced cell death. 

We refer to persistence as a collection of states rather than a single state because a growing body of evidence has demonstrated the existence of different types of persisters, where each can exhibit a distinct set of antibiotic tolerances (Allison et al., 2011; Kint et al., 2012; Zhang, 2014). Therefore, a critical element of persister formation pathways is how specific antibiotic targets are perturbed within different persister states to achieve tolerance. This heterogeneity, originating from the diverse paths by which persisters form, presents a significant therapeutic challenge to the eradication of persisters. A striking example of this diversity can be found when one considers that the E. coli chromosome harbors at least 33 toxin–antitoxin (TA) modules (Yamaguchi et al., 2011), the most common bistable systems associated with persistence. TA modules are composed of stable toxins and their neutralizing antitoxins (Yamaguchi et al.,

Figure 6.3.1 (a,b) Persister cells within bacterial populations. (a) Biphasic killing kinetics of an isogenic bacterial population upon antibiotic treatment (black solid line). Following a supralethal dose of antibiotic, normal cells are rapidly killed and the bulk population sharply decreases (red dashed line). In the second phase, at longer treatment times the killing rate declines, illuminating the presence of a subpopulation of cells with a higher degree of tolerance compared to the bulk of the population; these surviving cells are persisters (blue dashed line). (b) Persisters can be preexisting in a bacterial population at a low frequency (Balaban et al., 2004; Maisonneuve et al., 2013). Exposure to stress, such as nutrient transitions (Amato et al., 2013), starvation (Fung et al., 2010), high densities (Vega et al., 2012), and DNA damage (Dorr et al., 2009), stimulates persister formation. When the bacterial population is treated with antibiotic, normal cells are killed. Once antibiotic is removed, persisters exit their tolerant state and regrow to generate a bacterial population of identical antibiotic susceptibility as the original population (Balaban et al., 2004). Viable but nonculturable cells (VBNCs) are another cell type present in bacterial populations that fail to die from antibiotic treatment, but also fail to robustly regrow once the antibiotic has been removed (Orman and Brynildsen, 2013).

Figure 6.3.2 Structure of stress-induced persister formation pathways. Bacterial populations sense a stress and activate one or more response pathways. These responses transduce signals through their specific mediators to activate bistable systems, where some cells remain as normal cells and others switch to a persister state. Within this persister state, antibiotic tolerance is achieved through inhibition of antibiotic primary targets.
