Interestingly, different TA modules are activated by different suites of stresses (Christensen-Dalsgaard et al., 2010; Christensen et al., 2001; Dorr et al., 2010; Gerdes et al., 2005; Hong et al., 2012), and the antibiotic tolerances engendered by accumulation of different toxins vary (Christensen-Dalsgaard et al., 2010; Keren et al., 2004b; Shah et al., 2006; Tripathi et al., 2014). 

With this general structure as a guide, we will discuss different formation pathways that have been described for E. coli. To improve clarity, we have grouped pathways based on the source of the initial stress; namely, those that are activated by exogenous sources (e.g., chemical treatment) have been grouped and denoted as foreign stresses, and those that are self-imposed and experienced by bacteria during normal growth (e.g., nutrient limitation) have been grouped and denoted as native stresses (Amato et al., 2013). 

## 6.3.3 Persister formation mechanisms triggered by foreign stresses

Foreign stresses applied to an isogenic bacterial population have resulted in elevated persister levels. Dorr and colleagues iden-¨ tified the most complete persister formation pathway from a foreign stress to date, and it was in response to ciprofloxacin, a DNA-damaging fluoroquinolone antibiotic (Dorr et al., 2009; Dorr et al., 2010). In the first study describing this phenomenon, it was shown that the level of persisters to ciprofloxacin, but not to ampicillin or streptomycin, in the exponential phase was dependent on the DNA repair machinery and a functional SOS response (Dorr et al., 2009), suggesting that ciprofloxacin itself was participating in persister formation. Furthermore, the authors showed that pretreatment of exponentially growing cultures with concentrations of ciprofloxacin or mitomycin C, another DNA-damaging agent, below their minimum inhibitory concentrations (MICs) produced persisters to ciprofloxacin. In addition, with the use of a λ-phage-based SOS reporter, it was demonstrated that persisters comprised a subpopulation that hypo-activated the SOS response during ciprofloxacin treatment in comparison to cells that died (Dorr et al., 2009). In a subsequent study, Dorr and colleagues linked ciprofloxacin-triggered ¨ persister formation to the SOS-inducible type I TA system, tisB– istR, by showing that deletion of the toxin tisB resulted in decreased persisters upon treatment with ciprofloxacin (Dorr et al., 2010). In addition, overexpression of tisB during exponential growth was shown to elicit fluoroquinolone tolerance. The authors attributed this to the ability of TisB to decrease proton motive force and deplete ATP levels (Unoson and Wagner, 2008), which would depress topoisomerase activity, the primary target of ciprofloxacin (Dorr et al., 2010). 

In addition to ciprofloxacin-induced persister formation, treatment with paraquat to induce oxidative stress during exponential growth has been shown to increase persistence to several fluoroquinolones but not to ampicillin or kanamycin (Wu et al., 2012). Paraquat was shown to activate the $\mathrm { P } _ { s o x S } – g f p$ transcriptional reporter of SoxRS, an oxidative stress response regulon, as well as the $\mathrm { P } _ { t o l C } { - g f p }$ transcriptional reporter of the AcrAB– TolC multidrug efflux pump, which is also within the SoxRS regulon (Wu et al., 2012). Upon deletion of acrB, the protective effect of paraquat was significantly reduced, suggesting the AcrAB–TolC efflux pump is important for cells to induce fluoroquinolone persister formation when treated with paraquat. Tolerance was further linked to a functional SOS response since formation was reduced in a lexA3 mutant (Wu et al., 2012). Collectively, these studies demonstrate that exogenous stresses, including those imposed by antibiotics, have the capacity to form persisters. 

## 6.3.4 Persister formation mechanisms triggered by native stresses

The majority of persister formation in rich media has been shown to occur in the mid- to late-exponential phase (Keren et al., 2004a), a growth stage characterized by the emergence of nutrient transitions (Pruss et al., 1994) and high-density phenotypes (Surette and Bassler, 1998). Taking into account the complexity of this environment, each of these native stresses has the potential to signal a persister formation pathway, which, when taken collectively, can result in a vast number of mechanisms contributing to the generation of persisters. Several studies have been able to unravel various pathways associated with these native stresses. 

Strong evidence suggests that the nutritional environment of cells significantly influences persister formation (Amato and Brynildsen, 2014; Amato et al., 2013; Bernier et al., 2013; Fung et al., 2010). We have reconstructed a mechanistic persister formation pathway in response to carbon source transitions, which are nutritional perturbations commonly experienced during bacterial growth (Amato et al., 2013). Using minimal media with one or two carbon substrates (Monod, 1942; Roseman and Meadow, 1990), ofloxacin persisters were observed to form in response to diauxic transitions, where glucose was used as the primary carbon source. A pathway was elucidated from the source of stress, glucose exhaustion, to the activation of a unique bistable system, a metabolite–enzyme TA module. We demonstrated that the ppGpp biochemical network (see Chapter 7.1) can act as a novel metabolic TA module, where ppGpp is the metabolite toxin and SpoT is its enzymatic antitoxin, in contrast to classical TA systems that involve only protein and/or RNA components (Yamaguchi et al., 2011). Increasing ppGpp synthesis through RelA’ (Schreiber et al., 1991) overexpression resulted in growth arrest and increased persistence, which could be reverted by SpoT co-expression. Also, a mathematical model using physiologically relevant parameters showed that the ppGpp biochemical network (ppGpp, RelA, SpoT, DksA, and RNA polymerase) can exhibit bistability, where one subpopulation corresponds to normal cells (low ppGpp, elevated SpoT) and the other to persisters (high ppGpp, low SpoT). From the source of bistability, we sought to identify how ppGpp accumulation led to inhibition of DNA gyrase, the primary target of ofloxacin (Maxwell, 1997). DNA gyrase is responsible for (−) supercoiling of the chromosome, and we discovered that to form ofloxacin persisters, ppGpp required several nucleoidassociated proteins, SeqA, HU, IHF, and FIS, which modulate the supercoiled state of the chromosome (Amato et al., 2013). In a subsequent study of nutrient transitions in biofilms, this mechanism was found to be responsible for ofloxacin persister formation (Amato and Brynildsen, 2014). Interestingly, carbon source transitions have also been shown to trigger ampicillin persister formation; however, data suggest that separate mechanisms are present because the generation of ampicillin persisters is not observed in certain diauxic conditions where ofloxacin persister formation was found (Amato et al., 2013). This finding highlights that a single stress can produce heterogeneity in the persister population. 

Additional studies that focused on native stresses have also demonstrated the presence of heterogeneity in the antibiotic tolerances of persisters (Bernier et al., 2013; Fung et al., 2010). Fung and colleagues evaluated the effects of depletions in amino acids, glucose, ammonium, phosphate, and nucleobases on persistence to ampicillin, ofloxacin, and gentamicin and found complex trends where persister levels were dependent on the antibiotic (Fung et al., 2010). Further analysis revealed a link between activation of certain bacterial stress response networks during nutrient deprivation, including the stringent response (see Section 7) and SOS response (see Section 9), and the development of antibiotic tolerance. In addition, Bernier and colleagues reported that E. coli biofilms exhibited higher tolerance to ofloxacin or ticarcillin to varying degrees in response to specific nutrient depletions. Namely, biofilm-associated ofloxacin tolerance was attributed to a functional SOS response upon amino acid and glucose starvation and was partially dependent on the stringent response during leucine starvation (Bernier et al., 2013). 

Beyond nutrient transitions and deprivation, as bacterial cultures reach high densities, quorum sensing (see Section 21), the ability of bacteria to communicate with each other through chemical signaling (Surette and Bassler, 1998), has been shown to initiate persister formation. In E. coli, indole is a cell-to-cell communication molecule that possesses many roles in bacterial signaling, including activation of membrane and oxidative stress responses (see Section 10) (Garbe et al., 2000), motility (Bansal et al., 2007), biofilm formation (Lee et al., 2007; see Section 22), antibiotic resistance (Hirakawa et al., 2005), and virulence (Hirakawa et al., 2009). Vega and colleagues showed that higher concentrations of indole increased persisters to three different classes of antibiotics but to varying degrees, suggesting that this single stress can trigger formation pathways that yield persisters with variable antibiotic tolerances (Vega et al., 2012). Using an indole response transcriptional reporter, $\mathrm { P } _ { t n a C }  – g f p$ , fluorescence-activated cell sorting showed cells in the top 10% of reporter activity had significantly more ofloxacin persisters than those in the bottom 10%. Single-cell microfluidic analysis revealed that cells with a higher response to the indole reporter were more likely to survive than cells with a low response, thereby confirming the ability of indole to signal persister formation (Vega et al., 2012). Using transcriptome data and genetic deletions, it was found that OxyR, a major regulator of oxidative stress, and phage-shock pathways (PSPs) were required for indole-induced persister formation, although how OxyR and PSP networks lead to tolerance to ofloxacin, ampicillin, and kanamycin remains to be determined (Vega et al., 2012). In a subsequent study analyzing mixed-microbial communities, Vega and colleagues showed that indole, produced by E. coli, was able to signal persister formation in the pathogen Salmonella typhimurium in an OxyR- and PSP-dependent manner (Vega et al., 2013). These studies emphasize the ability of native stresses to signal persister formation and the potential for mechanistic information to illuminate targets that can form the basis of more effective treatments for persisters. 

## 6.3.5 ppGpp as a central regulator of persister formation

While diverse mechanisms of persister formation have been identified for various stresses, the metabolite ppGpp and the stringent response have emerged as prominent mediators of the persistence phenomenon (Amato and Brynildsen, 2014; Amato et al., 2013; Bokinsky et al., 2013; Germain et al., 2013; Hansen et al., 2008; Korch et al., 2003; Maisonneuve et al., 2013; Nguyen et al., 2011; see Section 7). In E. coli, amino acid limitation stimulates RelA to synthesize ppGpp, whereas various stress conditions, such as carbon (Xiao et al., 1991) and fatty acid starvation (Seyfzadeh et al., 1993), stimulate ppGpp synthesis from the cytoplasmic SpoT, which also encodes the sole ppGpp hydrolase. ppGpp interacts with RNA polymerase in conjunction with DksA to inhibit transcription from stable ribosomal RNA promoters, while simultaneously upregulating transcription of amino acid biosynthesis and stress response genes leading to a shutdown of cellular growth (Dalebroux and Swanson, 2012; Potrykus and Cashel, 2008). In addition to its transcriptional role, ppGpp has also been found to directly inhibit enzymes of several important cellular processes such as cell division, phospholipid synthesis, DNA replication, protein synthesis, and oxidative metabolism (Kanjee et al., 2012; Rodionov and Ishiguro, 1995). 

ppGpp was first shown to be involved in persister formation when Korch and colleagues observed significantly reduced ampicillin persister levels in ΔrelAΔspoT compared to wild type for exponentially growing cells (Korch et al., 2003). This study also elucidated the dependence of the hipA7 highpersistence mutant on ppGpp, where hipA7ΔrelAΔspoT had analogous ampicillin persister levels to wild type and significantly lower levels compared to hipA7. Further involvement of the HipA toxin in the stringent response was recently discovered where HipA, a Ser–Thr kinase (Correia et al., 2006), inactivated glutamyl-tRNA (transfer RNA) synthase (GtlX) by phosphorylation, which stimulated the accumulation of ppGpp leading to fluoroquinolone persistence (Germain et al., 2013; Kaspy et al., 2013). In a separate study, HipA toxin activity was linked to ppGpp synthesis via the activation of RelA, and evidence was shown that ppGpp inhibited DNA and RNA biosynthesis (Bokinsky et al., 2013). In addition, the stringent response was implicated in persistence in biofilms for E. coli as well as Pseudomonas aeruginosa through attenuation of oxidative stress (Nguyen et al., 2011). 

We expanded the stringent response’s role in persistence by demonstrating the importance of ppGpp and DksA, its transcriptional regulatory partner, in the formation of ofloxacin persisters in response to carbon source transitions (Amato and Brynildsen, 2014; Amato et al., 2013). We also demonstrated that the ppGpp biochemical network can act as a novel metabolic TA module, where ppGpp is the metabolite toxin and SpoT is its enzymatic antitoxin (Amato et al., 2013). 

Recently, Maisonneuve and colleagues have implicated ppGpp in persister formation through its indirect activation of the Lon protease (Maisonneuve et al., 2011, 2013). In their formation model, ppGpp stochastically accumulates to high levels, which increases polyphosphate (PolyP) levels through inhibition of exopolyphosphatase (Ppx). PolyP binds to Lon, which in turn degrades antitoxins, thereby enabling the accumulation of toxins. Strains with 10 different TA systems deleted (Δ10TA), Δlon, and ΔppkΔppx showed reduced persister levels to both ciprofloxacin and ampicillin, supporting this mechanism. The relationship between high ppGpp and ampicillin persistence was shown on the single-cell level using a ppGpp reporter based on activation of $\mathrm { P } _ { r p o s } \mathrm { - m C h e r r y }$ and fluorescence microscopy, where cells with high ppGpp survived ampicillin treatment and a portion of them regrew upon removal of the drug (Maisonneuve et al., 2013). These studies that implicate ppGpp highlight the prevalence of this metabolite as a signal for persister formation in response to multiple stresses and its role in the inhibition of antibiotic targets (Figure 6.3.3). 

## 6.3.6 Conclusions

Understanding the physiology of how bacterial persisters enter the transient, dormant state that renders them tolerant to antibiotics will aid treatment of recalcitrant infections (Amato et al., 2014; Kint et al., 2012; Maisonneuve and Gerdes, 2014; Zhang, 2014). Knowledge of persister formation mechanisms and how they inhibit the action of antibiotics suggests that multiple distinct signaling cascades underlie this phenomenon. Both foreign and native stresses have been shown to trigger persistence, and activation of response pathways and bistable systems appears to be a common theme in persister formation. Since many of these persister formation studies presented varied persister levels for different antibiotics or demonstrated that only a certain class of antibiotic is involved in the pathway, the importance of finding a link between key mediators and the antibiotic’s primary target cannot be overstated. The activation of the stringent response and the metabolite ppGpp has been extensively implicated in these formation cascades. Therefore, further development of stringent response inhibitors, such as relacin (Wexselblatt et al., 2012), has significant potential for antipersister therapies. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/6c2e57f4-f177-4731-acc4-f560c6f82e69/128d6f2999d9ebbed1a9a506b0b510db8f1db3b7830d4a35257d0b57c923241f.jpg)



Figure 6.3.3 ppGpp-mediated persister formation. Activation of RelA occurs in response to amino acid starvation (Potrykus and Cashel, 2008) and through the toxin HipA, which phosphorylates glutamyl-tRNA synthase (GltX) and inhibits charging of tRNAglu (Germain et al., 2013; Kaspy et al., 2013). A positive feedback loop exists where ppGpp activates transcription of relA (Shyp et al., 2012), which presents a potential source of bistability in the network. A diverse range of stresses activates SpoT and triggers synthesis of ppGpp (Kanjee et al., 2012; Potrykus and Cashel, 2008). The double negative feedback loop involving SpoT has been shown to confer bistability to the ppGpp biochemical network (Amato et al., 2013). ppGpp has the ability to inhibit many cellular processes. Through its interaction with DksA and RNA polymerase $( \mathrm { R N A P } ) , \mathrm { R N A P } _ { \mathrm { p p G p p , D k s A } }$ destabilizes open complex formation at stable RNA promoters, leading to inhibition of cellular growth (Potrykus and Cashel, 2008). ppGpp has been linked to various aspects of peptidoglycan metabolism, including inhibition of PlsB, regulation of autolysins, and alteration of murein composition (Goodell and Tomasz, 1980; Kanjee et al., 2012; Kusser and Ishiguro, 1985; Pisabarro et al., 1990; Ramey and Ishiguro, 1978). The stringent response has also been found to inhibit initiation of DNA replication in a Dam- and SeqA-dependent manner (Ferullo et al., 2009; Ferullo and Lovett, 2008). In addition, high levels of ppGpp lead to overall relaxation of the chromosome, which is indicative of altered topoisomerase activity (Ferullo and Lovett, 2008). Furthermore, ppGpp inhibits exopolyphosphotase (Ppx), which results in an accumulation of polyphosphate (PolyP). PolyP interacts with the Lon protease to activate degradation of antitoxins that results in free toxins, which inhibit translation and cellular growth (Maisonneuve et al., 2013).


In addition, recent evidence has illuminated a higher degree of complexity than first assumed, where persisters can no longer be viewed as exclusively multidrug tolerant, but rather persisters are viewed as heterogeneous, forming from different stresses and exhibiting varied tolerance to different antibiotics (Allison et al., 2011; Kint et al., 2012; Zhang, 2014). Persister heterogeneity diminishes the probability of finding a single magic bullet for treatment and adds considerable complexity to defining the molecular basis of the phenomenon. As more pathways are elucidated, we will gain a greater understanding of common nodes of persister formation, which will facilitate the discovery of broad-spectrum ways to eliminate this detrimental phenotype.

# Identification and characterization of type II toxin–antitoxin systems in the opportunistic pathogen Acinetobacter baumannii

Edita Suzied ˇ elien ˙ e, Milda Jur ˙ enait ˙ e, and Julija Armalyt ˙ e˙ 

Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, Vilnius University, Vilnius, Lithuania 

## 6.4.1 Introduction: A. baumannii – an emerging antibiotic-resistant opportunistic pathogen

The genus Acinetobacter (from Greek Acinetos for “nonmotile”), in the class of Gammaproteobacteria, presently comprises 35 species (www.bacterio.net/acinetobacter.html; LPSN, 2016). The establishment of taxonomy of the genus, and of A. baumannii in particular, underwent a complicated history during the 20th century (for a review, see Peleg et al., 2008); and until recently clinically important members of the genus – A. baumannii, A. pittii (formerly Acinetobacter genomic species 3), and A. nosocomialis (formerly Acinetobacter genomic species 13TU) – have been grouped into a single group, the so-called A. calcoaceticus complex, together with environmental A. calcoaceticus species due to high phenotypic similarity (Nemec et al., 2011). 

Acinetobacter species are Gram-negative, strictly aerobic, oxidase-positive, catalase-negative, non-fermenting, nonmotile (although able to produce pili responsible for conjugation and twitching motility) coccobacilli (Harding et al., 2013). They have been shown to utilize various organic compounds as carbon sources, often form capsules, and can be observed in pairs or clusters (Baumann, 1968). Many of the genus species can be found in different environmental sites, mostly in water and soil habitats (Baumann, 1968). They also have been observed in sewage (Vandewalle et al., 2012) and food products (Berlau et al., 1999; Lupo et al., 2014). The most clinically important member of the genus – A. baumannii – is generally found in hospital environments such as intensive care units, burn (trauma) wards, and field hospitals (Perilli et al., 2014; Sheppard et al., 2010), mostly on hospital workers and patients (Seifert et al., 1997). With the improvement of A. baumannii identification methods, it has become clear that this bacterium is not common in the environment or community sites, as previously thought (Seifert et al., 1997), and therefore its natural habitat is still debated. Interestingly, A. baumannii appears to have a long evolutionary history according to recent comparative genomic analysis of 133 genomes of the Acinetobacter genus, which revealed a large pan-genome of A. baumannii and suggested it could have arisen from an ancient population bottleneck, which was followed by the population expansion under purifying selection (Touchon et al., 2014). Another, more recent wave of A. baumannii population expansion is hyphothesized to have occurred after the beginning of the antibiotic era, and it resulted in the spread of several global multidrug-resistant clones (Antunes et al., 2014). 

The clinical importance of A. baumannii has begun to rise since the 1970s–1980s from being almost unknown to clinicians to becoming one of the most frequent opportunistic pathogens during the last two decades (for reviews, see Bergogne-Ber´ ezin ´ and Towner, 1996; Howard et al., 2012). The A. baumannii– associated nosocomial infections are prevalent in medical and surgical intensive care units (Munoz-Price et al., 2013; Zarrilli et al., 2009) and burn wards (Keen et al., 2010), and nosocomial pneumonia, in particular ventilator-associated pneumonia, is the most frequent infection (Peleg et al., 2008; Sandiumenge and Rello, 2012). Other cases such as A. baumannii–associated bacteremia (sepsis), surgical-site infections, urinary tract infections, secondary meningitis, infective endocarditis, osteomyelitis, and necrotizing fasciitis have also been reported (Charnot-Katsikas et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2013; Lahmer et al., 2014). The most susceptible to A. baumannii infections are immunocompromised and injured patients such as the elderly, premature newborns, oncology patients, and patients after organ transplantations, surgeries, and trauma (burn) (de Gouveaˆ et al., 2012; Eberle et al., 2010; Reddy et al., 2010; Runke et al., 2014). The A. baumannii infections are characterized by hospital outbreaks due to the long-term survival of A. baumannii in the hospital environment (on medical equipment, gloves, beds, curtains, ventilators, and hygiene items), the primary source being colonized or infected patients (Catalano et al., 1999; Rosa et al., 2014), from whom it can be transmitted into other hospital wards and other hospitals (Jawad et al., 1998; Thom et al., 2011; Weber et al., 2013). 

A. baumannii’s persistence and spread in the hospital environment are attributed to its developed stress responses, which are only beginning to be investigated, including the ability to colonize abiotic (plastic, metal, and glass) and biotic (human skin, mucous membranes, and host cells) surfaces, form biofilms (see Chapters 22.3 to 22.5) (Espinal et al., 2012; Gentile et. al., 2014; Longo et al., 2014; Mart´ı et al., 2011; McQueary and Actis, 2011), and respond to environmental and host stressors such as iron limitation (see Section 19; Eijkelkamp et al., 2011), components of the complement (Kim et al., 2009), disinfectants, (Nwugo et al., 2012), and antibiotics (Cardoso et al., 2010). 

In most cases, A. baumannii–associated infections are severe and difficult to treat; especially, A. baumannii–associated bacteremia is characterized by high mortality and morbidity rates (Reddy et al., 2010; Sunnenshine et al., 2007). The antibiotic therapy is limited due to resistance of A. baumannii to most antibiotic classes, which in the last decade have faced endemicity due to the spread of multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant (XDR) A. baumannii clones in clinical settings worldwide (Howard et al., 2012). Importantly, pandrugresistant (PDR) A. baumannii is being increasingly reported (Gottig ¨ et al., 2014). MDR A. baumannii is specified as being resistant to ≥1 agent in ≥3 antimicrobial categories, including the broad-spectrum antibiotics of the carbapenem class; XDR is defined as resistance to all but 1–2 antimicrobial categories; whereas PDR specifies resistance to all antimicrobial agents (Magiorakos et al., 2011). In parallel to innate resistance mechanisms (e.g., the presence of intrinsic class D OXA-51-type oxacillinases, AmpC cephalosporinases, and lowered membrane permeability), A. baumannii has the ability to acquire and/or overexpress antibiotic resistance determinants through horizontal gene transfer via integrons, mobilizable elements, and acquisition of insertional sequences (IS elements) (Imperi et al., 2011). Mechanisms of A. baumannii carbapenem resistance are represented by a variety of carbapenem-hydrolyzing beta-lactamases (carbepenemases), including serine oxacyllinases (Zarrilli et al., 2013) and metallo-beta-lactamases (MBLs) (Cornaglia et al., 2011), frequently harbored on plasmids (Bertini et al., 2010; Evans and Amyes, 2014). 

The genomic features of A. baumannii associated with its resistome and pathogenicity are beginning to be explored with increasing genomic data. A large pan-genome is a characteristic feature of the Acinetobacter genus, including A. baumannii, reflecting the capacity for horizontal gene transfer to acquire novel features toward environmental fitness (Imperi et al., 2011; Touchon et al., 2014). Toxin–antitoxin (TA) systems (see Chapter 2.7 and Section 6) are abundant genetic modules present in free-living bacteria and pathogens existing under variable conditions (Sevin and Barloy-Hubler, 2007). TAs have been shown to be involved in numerous functions from plasmid stabilization to regulation of cell growth and death under stressful conditions, mediation of bacterial persistence through generation of cells tolerant to antibiotics and other environmental changes, and biofilm formation (Hayes and Van Melderen, 2011). The mentioned features are crucial in the life of A. baumannii; therefore, understanding the role of TAs might bring novel insights into its pathogenicity. 

## 6.4.2 Approaches to detect A. baumannii TA systems

Until recently, TA systems have not been detected in A. baumannii despite several comprehensive genomic studies. Frequently, they are not annotated or are misannotated in A. baumannii sequences, and they are rarely mentioned in the literature. There are several approaches for detecting TA systems, the simplest being a search based on the currently known TA components from other organisms using BLAST tools. This method, depending on the initial database used as a query, can give different results and therefore is limited to currently described TAs. Another strategy is to use specific search tools that are based on typical constitutions and typical domains found in TA systems, such as RASTA or TADB (Sevin and Barloy-Hubler, 2007; Shao et al., 2011). Such tools give more possibilities to detect systems that have not been described yet, but their use requires more caution. For example, the adenosine triphosphate (ATP)-binding domain found in the Zeta toxin of the ω–ε–ζ TA system will give a number of false positives, as will DNA-binding domains typical to antitoxins that are also present in other transcriptional regulators. 

Both approaches mentioned here have been employed to detect TA systems in fully assembled genomes of Acinetobacter baumannii, and some of the most frequently found TA systems have been cloned and validated (Jurenait˙ e˙ et al., 2013). The tools mentioned are only convenient to search complete assembled A. baumannii sequences (to date, 19 chromosomes and 85 plasmids), and therefore BLAST searches can encompass a larger amount of data. BLAST searches of TA toxins, through all the sequences deposited under Acinetobacter baumannii (taxonomy ID: 470), have added several families that were not detected with the tools mentioned (Figure 6.4.1a). Despite these families not being present or being underrepresented in the complete genomes, they seem to be overall well spread – such as the HipA–HipB pair or Doc toxin, usually accompanied by a small hypothetical protein. Other rare occurrences detected by BLAST include a solitary MazF toxin homolog, a MazE–VapC pair, a RnlA–LsoB pair, and a YafO toxin preceeded by a hypothetical protein (Figure 6.4.1a,c). 

RelE family toxins constitute the most abundant TAs in A. baumannii, which is also the only family that contains a high variety of sequences that cannot be cross-detected by PSI-BLAST with 10E-05 value in this species. In the large RelE–ParEfold superfamily, toxins can share little sequence similarity and can only be compared by their structure (Anantharaman and Aravind, 2003; Makarova et al., 2009). A variety of subfamilies of distant RelE homologs also have been observed, such as the GP49 domain, DUF497 domain, and DUF1044 domain (Figure 6.4.1b,c). The first two, named HigB and SplT respectively, are the most common in bioinformatic searches and are found exclusively on the plasmids in clinical A. baumannii isolates (Table 6.4.1) (Jurenait˙ e˙ et al., 2013).

While the GP-49 and DUF497 domains were predicted to have RelE fold (Makarova et al., 2009) and validated to be translation inhibitors that cause mRNA degradation (Jurenait˙ e˙ et al., 2013), there is still no evidence of functionality of the DUF1044 domain, but its modeling by the PHYRE2 engine (Kelley and Sternberg, 2009) reveals structural similarity to RelE’s. 

## 6.4.3 Structural and functional features of A. baumannii type II TA modules

Except for the MazF toxin, all of the detected A. baumannii TAs constitute typical small operons consisting of toxin and antitoxin genes, where the toxin can be either the first or second open reading frame (ORF) and where ORFs overlap by as much as 38 bp $( \mathrm { R e l B E } _ { A b } )$ or are separated by 55 bp $( \operatorname { H i c A B } _ { A b } )$ (Figure 6.4.1c) or larger spaces (Jurenait˙ e˙ et al., 2013). While RelE family toxins are small (∼100 amino acid) proteins and HicA are typically even smaller proteins of ∼60 amino acids, some other families code for more elaborate toxins with larger enzymatic folds, such as HipA, Zeta, or RnlA, which stand out for their size (Figure 6.4.1c). However, all of the antitoxins are similar in size, being ∼100 amino acids in length (Figure 6.4.1c). 

Despite the genetic similarity to the described homologs in other bacteria, the functionality of TA systems observed using bioinformatic tools should be experimentally confirmed in bacterial cells by kill-rescue assay (Leplae et al., 2011). When cloned in separately controlled vectors, toxin and antitoxin should behave as follows: expression of toxin stops bacterial growth, whereas co-expression of antitoxin reconstitutes the growth. Using this approach, four out of six experimentally tested A. baumannii TA systems have been confirmed to be functional in E. coli: $r e l B E _ { A b } , h i c A B _ { A b } , h i g B A _ { A b } .$ , and splTA (Figure 6.4.1c). Interestingly, one A. baumannii gene pair, named cheTA, has behaved opposite than expected in the kill-rescue assay: CheA restored bacterial growth inhibited by the expression of CheT (Jurenait ˙ e˙ et al., 2013). Further research is needed to understand the real function of cheTA genes. Our recent study has revealed that HTH-domain and GNAT-domain proteins, named CheT and CheA respectively, do not interact in vivo and therefore cannot be considered as a classical type II TA system (J. Armalyte˙ et al., unpublished data).

Out of all functional A. baumannii toxins, all three RelE superfamily toxins – RelE, HigB, and SplT – and one HicA toxin have been shown to inhibit translation and cause mRNA degradation in vivo, albeit to different levels (Jurenait˙ e˙ et al., 2013). To further specify their activity, in vitro assays or primer extension mapping of cleavage sites would be required. 

To date, it is clear that A. baumannii is equipped with a spectrum of TAs, which, with the exception of the solitary MazF toxin, are found strictly on the plasmids (like $\mathrm { H i g B A } _ { A b } , \mathrm { S p l T A } ,$ and $\mathbf { Z e t a } _ { A b } )$ or both plasmids and chromosomes (Jurenait˙ e˙ et al., 2013). Several of those have been found to be repeated twice per chromosome in some cases. Two Rel $\mathrm { B E } _ { A b }$ (GIs: nt/385236512 and nt/385237910) TAs in the TDCD-AB0715 chromosome are located in a large ∼60 kb size identical reverse orientation sequence; and two HicA $\Omega _ { A b }$ (GIs: 322508802/322508803 and 322507734/322507733) TAs in the 1656-2 chromosome are located in similar, but not identical, smaller ∼20 kb inverse regions. These examples might also suggest the mobile nature of A. baumannii TAs. 

Surprisingly, no gyrase poisons (CcdB or ParE-like) were detected despite their strong plasmid addiction function (Hayes and Van Melderen, 2011). Zeta toxin, which is known to inhibit peptidoglycan synthesis (Mutschler et al., 2011), has been observed in A. baumannii plasmids; its toxicity has not been confirmed in E. coli (Jurenait˙ e˙ et al., 2013), but nevertheless the possibility of its functionality in the host remains. 

There are little data on the presence and functionality of TA systems in other Gram-negative opportunistic pathogens similar to A. baumannii, such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa or Klebsiella pneumoniae. It has been shown that P. aeruginosa isolates possess homologs of the relBE, higBA, and parDE systems and that these genes are expressed (Williams et al., 2011). A mixed type of effector–immunity pair first described as the Tse2–Tsi2 TA system is well studied in P. aeruginosa; however, it is associated with the type VI secretion system and most likely is utilized for competition rather than being a classical TA system (Li et al., 2012). RelE and Doc homologs have been reported in K. pneumoniae (Cherny and Gazit, 2004; Gerdes 2000), but the experimental data confirming their presence or functionality are lacking. Based on the TADB database (Shao et al., 2011), P. aeruginosa encodes several RelE and ParE homologs, and also VapC, whereas K. pneumoniae encodes several RelE, HipA, and Doc homologs and MazF and VapC homologs as well. In general, the proper experimental data are lacking on TA systems in opportunistic pathogens that would enable researchers to properly distinguish similarities or exceptions of this group in comparison to a TA spectrum in other bacteria. 

## 6.4.4 TA systems in A. baumannii plasmids

Recently identified A. baumannii SplTA and HigBA TA systems have been found to be located solely on plasmids (Jurenait˙ e˙ et al., 2013). Indeed, the database search using the 85 currently available A. baumannii plasmid sequences has detected SplTA and HigBA TAs on 17 and 20 sequences, respectively, which makes them to date the most common plasmid-associated A. baumannii TAs (Figure 6.4.2). Specific preferences toward plasmid size could be observed, namely, splTA was found present only on the small plasmids (up to 30 kb), whereas higBA did not possess such a preference. Although the A. baumannii Zeta TA system has not been confirmed as functional (Jurenait˙ e˙ et al., 2013), the database search restricted to plasmids showed its preference toward larger plasmids (60–80 kb; Figure 6.4.2). Interestingly, most of the largest A. baumannii plasmids (>100 kb) did not possess any predicted TA systems (data not shown). 

A. baumannii SplTA and HigBA TA systems were also the most prevalent plasmid-associated TA systems found in up to 75% of clinical A. baumannii isolates belonging to clonal lineages associated with carbapenem resistance, known as European clones I (ECI) and II (ECII) (Jurenait ˙ e˙ et al., 2013). Moreover, a SplTA-like TA system (named AbkA–AbkB) has been observed in a plasmid prevalent in a clinical setting in Spain (Mosqueda et al., 2014). These observations suggest plasmid-associated SplTA and HigBA TA systems are commonly carried in A. baumannii populations, which might indicate their role as plasmid stabilization modules, or stabilization modules of neighboring genes. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/6c2e57f4-f177-4731-acc4-f560c6f82e69/0ef7ecb279c8f5a493387eef6ac859e85b929be184b3ead65be1b96e6b0ee6ad.jpg)



Figure 6.4.2 Distribution of the most common SplTA, HigBA, and zeta TA systems in A. baumannii plasmids (n = 42). TA systems were detected using the RASTA tool and PSI-BLAST.


One typical example is a recently observed 10.9 kb plasmid pAB120, found to be present in 95% of carbapenem-resistant A. baumannii isolates belonging to the ECII clonal lineage (Povilonis et al., 2013). The plasmid has a rep gene homology group 2 (GR2) replicon and two copies of the $b l a _ { \mathrm { O X A - 7 2 } }$ gene encoding carbapenem-hydrolyzing class D OXA-24/40-like β- lactamase OXA-72 (Figure 6.4.3). pAB120 harbors genes coding for splTA and higBA TA systems located in close proximity to the two copies of $b l a _ { \mathrm { O X A - 7 2 } }$ genes. Both systems have been confirmed to be functional TA systems (Jurenait ˙ e˙ et al., 2013). Each of the $b l a _ { \mathrm { O X A - } 7 2 }$ genes are flanked by XerC–XerD-like binding sites (Figure 6.4.3), which are known to be involved in the separation of plasmids and chromosome dimers during replication and cell division (Carnoy and Roten, 2009). 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/6c2e57f4-f177-4731-acc4-f560c6f82e69/1cf7038b246b31641a65412d23d66af312634a0858896848a9497cdd021633fe.jpg)



Figure 6.4.3 A. baumannii pAB120 plasmid. The two genes coding for carbapenem-hydrolysing class D OXA-24/40-like β-lactamase OXA-72 are indicated in black, TA systems are indicated in gray, and XerC/XerD-like binding sites are shown as gray rectangles.


Genes coding for OXA 24/40 group carbapenemases have been reported to be flanked by XerC–XerD-like sites (D’Andrea et al., 2009; Merino et al., 2010; Wright et al., 2014), indicating their mobilization and possible spread via recombination between plasmids. Moreover, three additional XerC–XerD-like binding sites are present in pAB120 (Figure 6.4.3). The parts of the plasmid bracketed between XerC–XerD-like sites were observed to be highly similar to several different A. baumannii plasmids: the replicase coding genes are most similar to plasmids pAB0057 and p1ABTCDC0715; the region including the TonB receptor gene, splTA, and $b l a _ { \mathrm { O X A - 7 2 } }$ showed the highest homology to regions in plasmids pABVA01 and pMMCU3; and the region containing higBA genes was most similar to p3ABAYE and pMAC. XerC–XerD sites have been observed in a number of plasmids (pABVA01, p2ABAYE, pAB0057, pAB02, pAB2, pAV1, pABIR, and pMMA2 to date) and seem to represent the hotspots for plasmid recombination (see Table 6.4.1) (D’Andrea et al., 2009; Grosso et al., 2012; Merino et al., 2010; Povilonis et al., 2013). 

Plasmids of A. baumannii from clinical settings show signs of rearrangements with other plasmids and chromosomes (Acosta et al., 2011; Grosso et al., 2012; Povilonis et al., 2013; Wright et al., 2014), highlighting their role in mobilizing the genetic determinants between the strains. Mobile genetic elements play a major role in the acquisition and spread of multidrug resistance in A. baumannii, including mechanisms conferring resistance to carbapenems (Evans et al., 2013; Peleg et al., 2008; Poirel et al., 2011). Out of 85 analyzed sequenced A. baumannii plasmids found in clinical A. baumannii isolates from different countries, 21 encoded carbapenemase genes and the most common plasmid-associated TA modules by SplTA and HigBA (Table 6.4.1). 

Despite the increasing data on the presence of TA modules in A. baumannii plasmids, their role in plasmid maintenance is unknown. The SplTA TA system, widely spread in the A. baumannii plasmidome including carbapenem-resistant clinical isolates, can act as a plasmid maintenance mechanism, providing stability to genetic elements. We have constructed an unstable Acinetobacter plasmid pO1273 (J. Armalyte˙ et al., unpublished data), which is rapidly lost when bacteria are cultured under nonselective conditions (Figure 6.4.4). 

When the splTA TA module was cloned into pO1273, the plasmid retention was reconstituted to 100% during up to 80 h incubation in an Acinetobacter calcoaceticus host (Figure 6.4.4), thus confirming that the SplTA system is indeed a functional A. baumannii TA system required for stabilization and maintenance of mobile genetic elements. Such plasmid-encoded

Armalyte, personal˙ data).


TA systems could therefore be involved in a rapid accumulation and stabilization of genetic elements, responsible for antibiotic resistance in A. baumannii. 

## 6.4.5 Concluding remarks

A. baumannii is equipped with a spectrum of toxin–antitoxin systems, mostly existing on plasmids or both plasmids and chromosomes and belonging to type II TAs. All A. baumannii toxins tested so far inhibit translation through degradation of cellular mRNAs, albeit to different levels; however, their precise function in the host remains to be elucidated. The RelE family toxins represent the most abundant family of A. baumannii TAs, including the newly observed SplTA module, which together with the HigBA module is present exclusively on the plasmids, including a pool of plasmids harbouring carbapenem resistance genes from clinical A. baumannii isolates. The observed ability of A. baumannii SplTA to support plasmid maintenance suggests its role in the stabilisation of genetic elements, responsible for antibiotic resistance in A. baumannii. Increasing genome data along with functional analysis of TAs in the A. baumannii host would provide more answers regarding the role of these elements in the life of one of the most successful opportunistic pathogens today.

# Transcriptional control of toxin–antitoxin expression: keeping toxins under wraps until the time is right

Barbara Kedzierska1 and Finbarr Hayes2 

1Department of Molecular Biology, University of Gdansk, Gda ´ nsk, Poland ´ 

2Faculty of Life Sciences, The University of Manchester, Manchester, UK 

## 6.5.1 Introduction

Toxin–antitoxin (TA) systems are compact genetic modules generally composed of two genes encoding a toxin that hinders an essential cellular process and its specific antidote. An imbalance in the ratio between the toxic component and cognate antitoxin has dramatic consequences which trigger cell cycle arrest or death (Schuster and Bertram, 2013; Yamaguchi and Inouye, 2009; see Chapter 2.7). The vast majority of toxins interfere with the messenger RNA (mRNA) translation process. Other toxins target the DNA replication machinery or perturb the bacterial cell membrane or cell wall synthesis. 

TA modules are distributed widely in bacterial and archaeal plasmids and chromosomes, often in multiple copies (Fozo et al., 2010; Leplae et al., 2011; Pandey and Gerdes, 2005; Sberro et al., 2013; Yamaguchi et al., 2011; see Chapters 2.7 and Section 6). Depending on the genetic location, TA modules have been attributed distinct functions. Plasmid-encoded TA systems ensure faithful maintenance of these mobile elements after cell division. Daughter cells deprived of a plasmid are eliminated from the bacterial population by the action of liberated toxin. This phenomenon is named postsegregational killing or plasmid addiction and enables stable propagation of plasmids (Gerdes et al., 1986; Hayes, 2003). Particular chromosomal TA modules may fulfil a similar function in stabilization of exogenous DNA islands such as bacteriophages, transposons, and super-integrons (Szekeres et al., 2007). Moreover, certain TA cassettes have been implicated in the response to various stress conditions, in antibiotic persistence, and in biofilm formation (Gerdes and Maisonneuve, 2012; Schuster and Bertram, 2013; Wang and Wood, 2011; see Section 22). It also has been proposed that TAs may function as anti-addiction modules or may act principally as selfish genetic elements (Saavedra De Bast et al., 2008; Van Melderen, 2010; Van Melderen and Saavedra De Bast, 2009). 

The known TA systems are classified into five types based on the molecular nature of the antitoxin and the mechanism by which it inhibits the deleterious activity of the toxin (Hayes and Kedzierska, 2014; Schuster and Bertram, 2013; Unterholzner et al., 2013; see Chapter 2.7). The toxin universally is a protein, whereas the antitoxin is either a protein or a small regulatory RNA. The antitoxin in type I systems is an antisense RNA with sequence complementary to the toxin mRNA. Heteroduplex formation between these species blocks toxin translation either by preventing ribosome binding or by promoting transcript degradation by cellular RNases (Brantl, 2012). Both components are proteins in type II TA modules. Here, the toxin and antitoxin form a stable complex in which the active site of the toxin is masked by the antitoxin (Hayes and Van Melderen, 2011). In type III modules, the antidote is a small RNA with a characteristic secondary structure composed of pseudoknots which directly interacts with the toxin protein and thereby inhibits its activity (Blower et al., 2012; Short et al., 2013). Type IV cassettes differ from the other TA classes in the mechanism of antidote activity. Here, the antitoxin acts antagonistically to the toxin by directly binding and thereby protecting the latter’s intracellular target (Masuda et al., 2012). Finally, type V modules comprise a protein antitoxin which acts as a ribonuclease that specifically cleaves the toxin mRNA, thereby disabling its synthesis (Wang et al., 2012). 

This chapter focuses on type II modules which are the most abundant in the bacterial world and the best studied class of TA cassettes. Specifically, we provide current insights into the mechanisms that control expression and activation of these systems. The schematic molecular network of factors implicated in the action of a typical type II cassette is presented in Figure 6.5.1. The genes for the antitoxin and toxin are co-expressed from a common promoter. The proteins interact strongly and form a stable nontoxic complex. This complex binds an operator site that overlaps the promoter sequence and efficiently negatively autoregulates transcription. The Lon or Clp protease specifically degrades the antitoxin in response to certain environmental stimuli. The liberated toxin reaches its intracellular target to mediate bacterial growth inhibition or death. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/6c2e57f4-f177-4731-acc4-f560c6f82e69/40cd7a7b02b5a9c6aefb58b6cc9d23ff744b3f7b01d8b855e4029e10bf89a1ef.jpg)



Figure 6.5.1 Action of proteins which belong to a typical type II TA system. The antitoxin (blue) and toxin (red) genes are co-expressed in a single operon. The toxin-binding domain within the antidote remains unstructured until the TA complex is formed. The complex negatively regulates transcription from its own promoter (P) by binding specific palindromes within the operator region (O). In response to certain environmental conditions, the antitoxin is proteolytically cleaved by the Lon or Clp protease (green). The toxin is thereby released to act on its intracellular target (yellow) to induce cell cycle arrest or death.


## 6.5.2 Transcriptional autorepression of type II TA genes

The toxin protein in type II TA complexes is sequestered by binding of the cognate antitoxin protein as outlined above. However, conditions that inhibit translation or induce overproduction of cellular proteases (e.g., amino acid starvation) block replenishment of the antitoxin, which is proteolysed more rapidly than the toxin. The latter is liberated to disrupt a crucial cellular process. 

Importantly, type II toxin concentrations also are controlled tightly at the transcriptional level (Hayes and Kedzierska, 2014; Mruk and Kobayashi, 2014). The TA genes in typical type II complexes comprise an autorepressed operon (Figure 6.5.1). The antitoxin is a sequence-specific DNA-binding protein that recognizes an operator site that overlaps the TA operon promoter. Type II antitoxins usually are dimers in which each monomer consists of a folded N-terminal DNA-binding domain and a C-terminal module that is at least partially unstructured. The antitoxin is a weak transcriptional repressor of the operon. However, interaction with the toxin organizes and stabilizes the unfolded domain in the antitoxin. The TA complex consequently is a more efficient autorepressor than the antitoxin alone. There is significant variation in the details of TA-mediated autoregulation (Hayes and Kedzierska, 2014). 

The following sections illustrate examples of transcriptional repression in prototypical type II TA operons. 

## 6.5.3 Transcriptional autoregulation of mazE–mazF expression controls production of a sequence-specific endoribonuclease

The mazE–mazF operon is one of the most widely distributed and well-studied type II systems found on bacterial genomes. The MazF protein is a sequence-specific endoribonuclease that typifies a broad family of related toxins that cleave either free or ribosome-associated mRNA (Cook et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2003). The endoribonucleolytic activity of MazF normally is blocked by the MazE antitoxin. However, stressful conditions such as amino acid starvation or exposure to certain antibiotics that interfere with transcription and/or translation in bacteria inhibit the production of MazE. As the antitoxin is susceptible to degradation by the ClpP protease, MazF is liberated to induce toxicity (Aizenman et al., 1996). The role of MazF in bacterial physiology remains controversial. MazE–MazF may function as a primitive programmed cell death mechanism, or the activity of MazF may induce a temporary, reversible dormancy-like state (Tsilibaris et al., 2007). 

The expression of mazE–mazF in Escherichia coli is driven by a pair of promoters with different relative activities. The MazE antitoxin represses the promoters incompletely, but the MazE– MazF complex autoregulates expression more strongly. The promoter region contains three related repeat motifs that are bound by the complex (Figure 6.5.2). The extent of autorepression may be modulated by different occupation of these motifs by the MazE–MazF complex (Marianovsky et al., 2001). The MazE dimer possesses N-terminal swapped-hairpin β-strand structures which classifies the protein as a member of the Abr superfamily of DNA-binding proteins (Kamada et al., 2003). Recognition of the DNA repeat motifs likely involves residues in the N-terminal β-strands of MazE (Zorzini et al., 2015) as observed in a related VapB antitoxin (see Sections 6.5.7 and 6.5.8) (Figure 6.5.3e). Consistent with the type II TA paradigm, the Cterminal domain of MazE is intrinsically disordered but is stabilized by MazF which explains the higher affinity of the MazE– MazF complex for operator DNA (Kamada et al., 2003; Zorzini et al., 2015). 

## 6.5.4 The CcdA–CcdB complex autorepresses expression of a DNA gyrase poison

The CcdA–CcdB type II TA complex encoded by the F plasmid promotes the maintenance of this episome in E. coli (Ogura and Hiraga, 1983). The CcdA antitoxin neutralizes the CcdB toxin in plasmid-bearing cells. However, CcdA possesses a shorter halflife than CcdB and in addition cannot be replenished in any plasmid-free cells that emerge in the population. CcdB promotes postsegregational killing of these plasmidless cells by interfering with the action of DNA gyrase which is an essential type II topoisomerase in bacteria (Bernard and Couturier, 1992; De Jonge et al., 2009).

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/6c2e57f4-f177-4731-acc4-f560c6f82e69/6bd16d7a074d25e9f443fe428b526fe1bf5d73ae644b672edde8d9dc501839a3.jpg)


The ccdA–ccdB operon is autorepressed by the CcdA–CcdB complex. The N-terminal segments of dimeric CcdA assemble into a ribbon-helix-helix (RHH) fold that binds the operator site upstream of ccdA–ccdB by insertion of a pair of positively charged, antiparallel β-strands into the DNA major groove (Figure 6.5.3a) (Madl et al., 2006). In contrast, the Cterminal domain of CcdA is intrinsically disordered but is stabilized by interaction with CcdB (Drobnak et al., 2013). The CcdA–CcdB complex binds DNA and represses expression of the ccdA–ccdB promoter more effectively than CcdA alone (Afif et al., 2001). The principal binding site for CcdA on DNA is a 6-bp palindromic sequence situated downstream of the −10 box in the ccdA–ccdB promoter (Figure 6.5.2). This sequence may be a nucleation site for the assembly of additional CcdA–CcdB complexes into a repressive superstructure that includes ∼120 bp of DNA that stretches from the promoter-operator region into the 5’ end of the ccdA gene (Madl et al., 2006). 

## 6.5.5 Conditional cooperativity is a common theme in type II TA transcriptional regulation

Numerous examples have been described in which TA operon expression is modulated by the toxin–antitoxin ratio (Afif et al., 2001; Johnson et al., 1996; Madl et al., 2006; Magnuson and Yarmolinsky, 1998; Monti et al., 2007). For example, the postsegregational cell-killing toxin Doc encoded by plasmid P1 harbours low- and high-affinity binding sites for the cognate Phd antitoxin. The Phd–Doc complex is an efficient transcriptional repressor of the phd–doc genes when both binding sites on Doc are occupied by Phd, whereas Phd alone regulates expression less effectively (Garcia-Pino et al., 2010; Magnuson et al., 1996). However, the Phd antitoxin is sequestered preferentially by the high-affinity binding sites in the presence of excess Doc. The resulting structural changes in the Phd–Doc complex perturb the repressive state and inhibit operator site binding by the complex. Thus, the expression of the phd–doc genes is de-repressed specifically when toxin levels are increased. Derepression induces production of more Phd, which permits both capturing of excess Doc and re-establishment of transcriptional repression of phd–doc. This process in which the expression of TA genes is modulated by the toxin–antitoxin stoichiometry is denoted conditional cooperativity (Bøggild et al., 2012; Overgaard et al., 2008). Conditional cooperativity may fine-tune TA gene expression to minimize random toxin induction and to allow for capturing of excess toxin so that its deleterious effects can be reversed rapidly (Cataudella et al., 2012).

Like Phd–Doc, the RelB–RelE complex displays conditional cooperativity. RelB–RelE is one of the most abundant and wellcharacterized TA complexes (Goeders et al., 2013). The RelE toxin is an endoribonuclease, although with a different cleavage specificity on mRNA compared to MazF (Goeders et al., 2013). Furthermore, unlike MazF, mRNA cleavage by RelE is translation-dependent (Neubauer et al., 2009). The N-terminus of the RelB antitoxin forms a dimeric RHH fold connected to C-terminal extensions that bind a pair of RelE monomers. The complex is organized as an open V-shaped heterotetramer in which the RelB dimer is located at the apex (Bøggild et al., 2012; Li et al., 2008; Overgaard et al., 2009). This arrangement prevents access by the toxin to the ribosomal A site and causes structural transitions that disrupt the endoribonuclease catalytic pocket (Bøggild et al., 2012; Li et al., 2009). Transcription of the relB–relE module is autoregulated in E. coli. As is the general pattern with type II TA complexes (Hayes and Kedzierska, 2014), the RelB antitoxin represses expression partially, whereas RelE is a co-repressor (Gotfredsen and Gerdes, 1998). The operator bound by RelB–RelE consists of two tandem 12-bp inverted repeats, one of which overlaps the −10 promoter box for the relBE cassette (Figure 6.5.2). RelE enhances operator binding by RelB at subequimolar ratios but reduces binding at higher concentrations, thereby exhibiting conditional cooperativity (Overgaard et al., 2008). In this case, conditional cooperativity may be based on the differential occupation of the 12-bp operator repeats by RelB–RelE complexes with different toxin–antitoxin stoichiometries (Bøggild et al., 2012). 

The Kis–Kid complex encoded by the R1 plasmid specifies postsegregational killing in E. coli, and provides another pertinent example of conditional cooperativity among type II TA systems. Kid is a sequence-specific, translation-independent endoribonuclease toxin (Diago-Navarro et al., 2010). The protein is part of a wide group of structurally related toxins that encompasses MazF and CcdB (Blower at al., 2011), whereas Kis is related to the MazE antitoxin. The kis–kid operon is autorepressed at the transcriptional level. The antitoxin weakly regulates expression, whereas the Kis–Kid complex is a more effective repressor (Ruiz-Echevarria et al., 1991). Kis–Kid binds an operator that consists of two 18-bp inverted repeats that are separated by a 33-bp spacer in the promoter region upstream of the kis– kid module (Figure 6.5.2). The repeat which overlaps the −10 promoter motif is bound with higher affinity by Kis–Kid. The Kis antitoxin and Kid toxin form numerous complexes in vitro (Kamphuis et al., 2007). Equimolar or subequimolar Kis–Kid stoichiometries produce TA complexes that recognize the operator site most efficiently. In contrast, less stable complexes with the operator site are generated when the Kid toxin concentration exceeds that of Kis antitoxin, as is characteristic of conditional cooperativity. As a result, kis–kid expression will rebalance the Kis–Kid ratio away from toxin excess (Monti et al., 2007). 

## 6.5.6 Transcriptional control of hybrid TA complexes: YefM–YoeB and Axe–Txe homologues

The YoeB and Txe endoribonuclease toxins encoded by E. coli and Enterococcus faecium, respectively, are homologues of the RelE protein. In contrast, the cognate antitoxins, YefM and Axe, are related to Phd. Thus, YefM–YoeB and Axe–Txe are hybrid TA complexes in which the toxins are paired with non-canonical antitoxins (Grady and Hayes, 2003). These arrangements are reflective of shuffling of toxin and antitoxin genes during evolution (Hayes and Van Melderen, 2011). YefM–YoeB and Axe–Txe repress expression of the cognate TA genes (Boss et al., 2013; Kedzierska et al., 2007). However, despite protein and operator sequence homology between these modules, transcriptional control is specific (i.e., YefM–YoeB autoregulates the yefM–yoeB module and Axe–Txe represses axe–txe, but not vice versa). Moreover, the interactions between the toxins and antitoxins that form these complexes also are specific (Połom et al., 2013). Specificity is attributable in part to a single amino acid residue that differs in the C-terminal regions of the toxins (Połom et al., 2013). 

The YefM and Axe antitoxins partially repress expression of the cognate promoters, but the YefM–YoeB and Axe–Txe complexes are more effective autoregulators. Regulation is mediated by binding of the N-terminal domains of the antitoxins to pairs of palindromes that overlap the respective promoters (Figure 6.5.2) (Boss et al., 2013; Kedzierska et al., 2007). The sequences and spacing of these palindromes are vital for proper transcriptional repression (Bailey and Hayes, 2009). The homologous YefM, Axe, and Phd antitoxins lack canonical DNA-binding motifs, but a patch of positively charged residues, including a pair of key arginine residues, is involved in operator recognition (Arbing et al., 2010; Bailey and Hayes, 2009; Kamada and Hanaoka, 2005). 

In addition to transcription driven from a strong promoter upstream of the axe–txe module, an internal promoter within axe expresses the downstream txe toxin gene. Unlike the main promoter, the internal promoter is not repressed by the Axe– Txe complex (Boss et al., 2013). The activity of this internal promoter is crucial for the function of Axe–Txe in postsegregational killing, indicating that it plays a pivotal role in determining the Axe–Txe stoichiometry (Boss et al., 2013). Interestingly, the yefM–yoeB module of Streptococcus pneumoniae is expressed from a pair of upstream promoters, one of which is autoregulated and one of which is constitutive (Chan et al., 2011). Multilayered transcriptional regulation may be intrinsic for setting the toxin–antitoxin ratio of YefM–YoeB homologues, but also of TA complexes generally. 

## 6.5.7 Examples of atypical type II TA gene expression control

The majority of type II TA cassettes follow the general pattern of transcription regulation described in this chapter. However, some exceptions to this rule have been identified. One variation involves a tripartite TA module in which the first gene in the operon encodes a dedicated transcriptional repressor, followed by the antitoxin and toxin genes (Figure 6.5.4b). The polycistronic mRNA for the three proteins is initiated from a strong promoter located upstream of the additional gene. A second weak promoter preceding the antitoxin gene produces mRNA for the TA module (de la Hoz et al., 2000). A relevant example of this tripartite organization is the $\mathrm { \bf { \omega } } _ { \omega - \varepsilon - \zeta }$ operon specified by streptococcal plasmid pSM19035. Neither the ζ toxin nor ε antitoxin possesses DNA-binding activity. Instead, expression of the cassette is inhibited by the sole action of the ω RHH protein (de la Hoz et al., 2004). Moreover, the ω protein is a global negative regulator that also controls transcription of certain other genes required for accurate plasmid maintenance (de la Hoz et al., 2000). 

The chromosomal mazEF cassette of Staphylococcus aureus presents another example of a TA cassette in which expression is negatively controlled by a global regulator. However, in this case the role is executed by an alternative sigma factor, $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { B } } { } _ { ; }$ , which is not encoded by the TA operon (Donegan and Cheung, 2009). Thus, unlike repression of the mazE–mazF operon in E. coli described in this chapter, this TA module in S. aureus does not undergo autoregulation. Additionally, the mazEF promoter is positively regulated by SarA, another global regulator in S. aureus, which also is required for the expression of certain virulence genes (Figure 6.5.4c) (Cheung et al., 2008). 

Another variation on the theme of transcriptional regulation of TA genes is shown by the chromosomal mqsRA module of E. coli. First, this cassette has a reverse order of TA genes with the gene encoding the toxin preceding the antidote gene (Figure 6.5.4d). Second, the MqsA antitoxin protein possesses unique features. The protein binds zinc ions which help to maintain an ordered structure throughout its length (Figure 6.5.3b) (Brown et al., 2009). This contrasts with most known type II antitoxins, which possess a modular structure comprising a folded N-terminal DNA-binding domain linked to a C-terminal segment that acquires structure by interaction with the toxin. Moreover, the functions of the N-terminal and C-terminal domains in MqsA are swapped. The protein interacts with the operator site primarily via the C-terminal domain (Figure 6.5.3b). However, the N-terminal toxin-binding domain also makes a direct contact with DNA, thereby enhancing these connections (Brown et al., 2011). Interestingly, the MqsR toxin disrupts MqsA–DNA interactions, thus acting as a transcriptional activator of mqsRA expression, not as a co-repressor as in typical type II TAs (Brown et al., 2013). These clashes occur because the binding sites for DNA and MqsR partially overlap on MqsA. Furthermore, MqsA regulates certain genes associated with cellular physiology, including the mcbR, spy, and cspD loci (Kim et al., 2010). The protein also directly binds to an MqsRA-like palindrome located within the promoter of the rpoS gene and thereby represses transcription of a major regulator of stress, σS (Wang et al., 2011). Finally, MqsA also negatively regulates the expression of the CsgD protein. CsgD is a master controller of biofilm formation via pathways such as cellulose production and curli biogenesis (Soo and Wood, 2013).

Another exception to the canonical mechanism of TA regulation is shown by the vapBC-1 locus of nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae. Unlike other vapBC cassettes, the pattern of transcriptional regulation of vapBC-1 is distinct (Figure 6.5.4e). The module undergoes autorepression by the TA complex as is characteristic of homologous systems. However, DNA binding in this case is mediated by the VapC-1 toxin, whereas the antitoxin serves to target the TA complex to the operator site (Cline et al., 2012). Moreover, the Fis global regulator is implicated in modulation of expression: Fis upregulates vapBC-1 expression upon nutrient upshift, probably indirectly by altering the DNA topology. VapC-1 and Fis bind distinct sequences within the promoter-operator region (Cline et al., 2012). Fis also plays a role in regulation of the mazE–mazF operon in E. coli (Figure 6.5.2) (Marianovsky et al., 2001). 

It has become evident that TAs form part of the molecular network responsible for mediating the stress response in bacteria. The examples of atypical TA transcriptional regulation summarized here involve the action of diverse global regulators. Moreover, certain TA proteins regulate genes other than their own operons. The presence of multiple TA loci within bacterial genomes may allow the cell to respond to a specific stress or group of stresses via precisely regulated mechanisms that initiate programmed cell cycle arrest, persister cell production, or biofilm formation (Wang and Wood, 2011). 

## 6.5.8 Structures of TA complexes with DNA

The HipA–HipB complex is among the most well-documented TA systems that are involved in the persistence of bacteria to antibiotics (Gerdes and Maisonneuve, 2012). The HipA toxin is a eukaryote-like serine–threonine kinase that phosphorylates and thereby inhibits the aminoacylation activity of an aminoacyltRNA synthetase (Germain et al., 2013; Schumacher et al., 2009). The HipB antitoxin sequesters HipA. HipB represses hipBA expression by cooperative binding to four operator sites (consensus sequence $5 ^ { 3 } { \mathrm { - T A T C C N } } _ { 8 } { \mathrm { G G A T A } } { \mathrm { - } } 3 ^ { \mathrm { 3 } } )$ situated in the promoter region. HipA co-represses expression (Black et al., 1994). Dimeric HipB binds DNA via a helix-turn-helix motif that is related to those present in the Cro family of transcriptional repressors. The cooperative binding of HipB to multiple operator sites involves DNA bending that aligns the recognition helices in successive major grooves (Schumacher et al., 2009). The HipA–HipB–DNA co-structure comprises a HipB dimer sandwiched by HipA monomers that make asymmetric contacts with the antitoxin (Figure 6.5.3c). HipA alone does not bind DNA, but makes phosphate backbone contacts within the HipA–HipB–DNA complex (Schumacher et al., 2009). Interestingly, there may be considerable variation in the structural organization of HipA–HipB–DNA complexes in different bacterial species (Wen et al., 2014). Moreover, the consensus sequence for DNA binding by HipB is evident at multiple locations in promoter sequences on the E. coli genome. HipB binds and represses expression from a number of these promoters, suggesting that persistence may be modulated by a complex regulatory network (Lin et al., 2013). 

VapB–VapC complexes are among the most widely disseminated type II TAs in bacteria. Indeed, certain species possess tens of vapB–vapC loci. VapC toxins are part of the broader PIN domain family of endoribonucleases that are characterized by a cluster of three strictly conserved acidic amino acids that are required for sequence-specific RNA cleavage. VapB antitoxins bind to VapC and impair endoribonuclease function (Arcus et al., 2011). The VapB–VapC complex autoregulates expression at the transcriptional level (Robson et al., 2009). FitA–FitB is a VapB–VapC complex identified in Neisseria gonorrhoeae. The structure of the FitA–FitB–DNA heterotetramer complex comprises two FitA antitoxin dimers that are stabilized by binding to a pair of FitB PIN domain toxin monomers (Figure 6.5.3d). FitA interacts with DNA by a RHH fold analogous to the CcdA and RelB antitoxins (Mattison et al., 2006). Similarly, a VapB–VapC– DNA complex from Rickettsia felis, the causative agent of fleaborne spotted fever, consists of four VapC toxin molecules and four VapB antitoxin monomers that form a tetramer of heterodimers assembled on DNA (Figure 6.5.3e) (Mate´ et al., 2012). Whereas the VapC subunits possess a PIN domain architecture that is homologous to that of FitB, the VapB antitoxin contains a swapped-hairpin β-barrel fold, related to that detected in MazE (described in Section 6.5.3). Analogously, VapB interacts with DNA via the β-hairpins (Mate´ et al., 2012). The structural diversity in these FitA–FitB and VapB–VapC complexes again attests to the evolutionary “mixing-and-matching” that has occurred among TA modules (Anantharaman and Aravind, 2003; Hayes and Van Melderen, 2011; Leplae et al., 2011). 

## 6.5.9 New antibacterial drugs that interfere with transcriptional autoregulation and ignite toxin release

Infectious diseases are a leading cause of death worldwide (Bearman and Wenzel, 2005; Fauci et al., 2005). Moreover, the emergence and dissemination of multidrug resistant strains which have the ability to escape from currently available antimicrobial treatments highlight a pressing need for the development of novel antibacterial strategies (Boucher et al., 2009). TA modules play a pivotal role in both stable maintenance of mobile genetic elements that specify antibiotic resistance, as well as in bacterial persistence and virulence. TA loci are abundant on bacterial chromosomes and plasmids, including in pathogenic species, but are absent from the human genome, which contributes to their attractiveness as potential antibacterial targets. Therefore, there is considerable interest in natural and artificial molecules that trigger toxin activation to induce bacterial damage or death (Chan et al., 2015; Lioy et al., 2010; Shapiro, 2013; Unterholzner et al., 2013; Williams and Hergenrother, 2012). Developing molecules that alter TA transcription regulation directly is one possible approach. Sequence-specific DNA-binding ligands already function, for example, as anticancer therapies (Gniazdowski et al., 2003, 2005; Raskatov et al., 2012). Potential drugs that target TAs may alter interactions of the regulatory antitoxin proteins with DNA by a variety of different mechanisms. The main strategies, depicted in Figure 6.5.5, potentially include: (a) competition by drugs that interact with DNA for the operator sequences that are bound by the antitoxin; (b) competition by synthetic oligonucleotides or peptides for toxin or DNA-binding sites on the antitoxin; (c) ligands that alter the DNA architecture and prevent the antitoxin from binding the operator site; and (d) small interfering RNA (siRNA) or synthetic oligonucleotides that dampen expression of the antitoxin but not of the toxin. Thus, TA-based antibacterials may present an unusual opportunity to develop therapeutics against emerging infections caused by multidrug- or pan-drug-resistant pathogenic species when traditional drugs have failed.

## 6.5.10 Concluding remarks



Arbing MA, Handelman SK, Kuzin AP, Verdon G, Wang C, et al. 2010. Crystal structures of Phd-Doc, HigA, and YeeU establish multiple evolutionary links between microbial growth-regulating toxinantitoxin systems. Structure 18: 996–1010.

Pandey DP, Gerdes K. 2005. Toxin-antitoxin loci are highly abundant in free-living but lost from host-associated prokaryotes. Nucleic Acids Research 33: 966–976. 



TA complexes are present ubiquitously in bacteria and are involved in the response to nutritional deprivation and related stresses, in the maintenance of plasmids and other mobile elements, and in biofilm formation, among other functions. Moreover, an important role for TAs in bacterial persistence to antibiotics has emerged recently (Gerdes and Maisonneuve, 2012; Helaine et al., 2014). Certain TAs also are implicated in bacterial pathogenicity (Bukowski et al., 2013; De la Cruz et al., 2013; Tiwari et al., 2015). These multifarious roles of TAs in bacterial physiology and lifestyle necessitate the controlled production of toxin and antitoxin in a correct stoichiometry and the release of the toxin at key time points. Transcriptional autoregulation of TA genes is central to this control. Understanding how this regulation is mediated both illuminates the mechanisms of toxin activation and suggests strategies for artificial release of the toxin as a novel anti-infective therapy.
