## C H A P T E R 7.2

# Global Rsh-dependent transcription profile of Brucella suis during stringent response unravels adaptation to nutrient starvation and cross-talk with other stress responses

Stephan Kohler ¨ 1,2, Nabil Hanna1,2, Safia Ouahrani-Bettache1,2, Kenneth L. Drake3, L. Garry Adams4, and Alessandra Occhialini1,2 

1Universite Montpellier, Centre d’ ´ etudes d’agents Pathog ´ enes et Biotechnologies pour la Sant ` e (CPBS), Montpellier, France ´ 

2CNRS, FRE 3689, CPBS, Montpellier, France 

3Seralogix, Limited Liability Company, Austin, Texas, USA 

4Department of Veterinary Pathobiology, College of Veterinary Medicine and Biomedical Sciences, Texas A&M University, College Station, Texas, USA 

## 7.2.1 Introduction

The Gram-negative bacterial pathogen Brucella is responsible for brucellosis, a major zoonotic disease causing abortion and sterility in animals and “Malta fever” in humans (Franco et al., 2007). The intracellular survival and replication of Brucella, orchestrated by the type IV secretion system VirB, are critical for virulence (O’Callaghan et al., 1999), and comprise adaption to nutrient-poor conditions. Stringent response, a global regulatory network allowing rapid adaptation to several growthaffecting stress conditions, enables bacteria to cope with such conditions (Cashel and Gallant, 1969) and is mediated by the accumulation of the alarmone (p)ppGpp, resulting in downregulation of transcription (Toulokhonov et al., 2001; see Chapter 7.1). Adaptation to amino acid starvation (Murray and Bremer, 1996; Traxler et al., 2008), but also to carbon or nitrogen (Boutte and Crosson, 2011; Krol and Becker, 2011; Murray and Bremer, 1996; Xiao et al., 1991), iron (Vinella et al., 2005), and fatty acid starvation (Potrykus and Cashel, 2008), is mediated by the stringent response (see also Chapters 7.1; 7.3; 7.4). In Escherichia coli, RelA synthesizes the alarmone (p)ppGpp following activation by uncharged transfer RNAs (tRNAs), whereas the bifunctional enzyme SpoT is able to also hydrolyze (p)ppGpp (Murray and Bremer, 1996). In contrast, the α-Proteobacteria, such as brucellae, possess a single RelA–SpoT homolog named Rel or Rsh. RelA–SpoT homologs share both (p)ppGpp synthase and hydrolase activities and are bifunctional, as shown for Sinorhizobium meliloti and Rhizobium etli (Hogg et al., 2004; Krol and Becker, 2011; Mittenhuber, 2001; Vercruysse et al., 2011). 

Stringent response is required in many infectious processes (Dahl et al., 2003; Dalebroux et al., 2009; Kazmierczak et al., 2009; Primm et al., 2000): antibiotic tolerance and increased antioxidant defenses (see Section 10) have been observed in biofilms as a consequence of nutrient limitation (Nguyen et al., 2011; see Section 22). In symbiotic α-Proteobacteria such as S. meliloti and R. etli, the stringent response controls bacterial physiology critical to the establishment of symbiosis (Vercruysse et al., 2011; Wells and Long, 2002), and (p)ppGpp-dependent genes have been identified during the early exponential phase (Vercruysse et al., 2011). 

In Brucella, the unique rsh gene encodes a protein of 751 amino acids with conserved synthase and hydrolase residues, suggesting that Rsh is bifunctional. Previously, we provided evidence for the role of rsh for successful intracellular adaptation (Kohler¨ et al., 2002). Besides strong attenuation in various models of infection and lack of virB expression, the rsh null mutant showed altered morphology and reduced survival in minimal medium (Dozot et al., 2006). Similarly, a rsh mutant of Brucella abortus is strongly attenuated in the macrophage model and characterized by a lower general stress resistance (Kim et al., 2005). These observations justified a global gene expression study to elucidate the role of (p)ppGpp in the regulatory processes and networks implicated in adaptation of brucellae to their environment. We determined the transcription profiles of the wild type and a rsh mutant of Brucella suis, after stringent response induction in minimal medium, partially mimicking conditions encountered within the host cell, and resulting in the identification of the global rsh-dependent regulatory network in this pathogen. The stringent response controls $_ \mathrm { C u - Z n }$ superoxide dismutase, nitrate reductase, cbb3-type cytochrome c oxidase, and methionine biosynthesis. The large number of differentially regulated genes correlated with the pleiotropic effect of the stringent response. 

## 7.2.2 Materials and methods

Bacterial strains and media: The Brucella strain used in this study was B. suis bv. 1 1330 (ATCC 23444). E. coli DH5α was used for cloning. Brucella and E. coli were grown in tryptic soy (TS) and lysogeny broth (LB), respectively. For strains carrying resistance markers, antibiotics were used at 50 μg/ml. For the B. suis stringent response assays, a stationary-phase overnight culture in TS was washed once in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and diluted 1:5 in Gerhardt’s modified minimal medium (GMM) (Lestrate et al., 2003), followed by shaking at $3 7 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 4 h. Concentrations of live bacteria $\mathrm { m } \dot { 1 } ^ { - 1 }$ were determined after plating of serial dilutions onto TS agar. 

Growth assays: For the identification of amino acids essential for Δrsh growth in GMM, B. suis overnight cultures were harvested, washed twice with 9‰ NaCl, diluted 1:500, and used to inoculate 20 tubes containing 3 mL of GMM with glutamate replaced by ammonium sulfate, and all natural amino acids at 1 mM each (Sigma), except one. The method was applied to each of the 20 amino acids. 

Isolation and labeling of B. suis genomic DNA (gDNA): B. suis gDNA was isolated using a Qiagen DNeasy blood and tissue kit and labeled by direct incorporation of Cy-5-dCTP fluorescent dye (Amersham Biosciences) using the BioPrime DNA-labeling system kit (Invitrogen). For a 50 μL reaction mixture, 2 μg of gDNA template in 23 μL of sterile water was heated at $9 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 10 min, mixed with 20 μl of 2.5× random primers solution, heated at $9 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 5 min, and chilled on ice. 0.12 mM dATP, dGTP, and dTTP; 0.06 mM dCTP; 0.02 mM Cy5-dCTP; 1 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0); 0.1 mM EDTA; and 40 units of Klenow fragment were added. After incubation at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 2 h, the reaction was stopped with 45 mM EDTA (pH 8.0). The fluorescence-labeled DNA was purified using the CyScribe GFX purification kit (Amersham Biosciences) and eluted in 1 mM Tris, pH 8.0. 

Isolation of B. suis total RNA: Expression profiles of B. suis 1330 wild type and its isogenic Δrsh mutant were generated using 9 mL of bacteria incubated in GMM containing ammonium sulfate instead of glutamate at pH 7.0 for 4 h; this is known to induce expression of rsh-regulated genes (Dozot et al., 2006). For each strain, four independent RNA preparations from four independent cultures were processed with the RNeasy mini kit (Qiagen). 

After addition of ethanol–phenol solution (9:1) to inactivate the cultures, and their centrifugation, bacteria were suspended in TE buffer–lysozyme solution (Invitrogen). After 

5 min, the lysate was mixed with 10% sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) and proteinase K, and incubated for 10 min at $2 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ . Buffer RLT with beta-mercaptoethanol was added, followed by centrifugation. The RNA-containing supernatant was recovered and transferred to an RNeasy mini spin column. RNA samples were treated with RNAse-free DNase I (Ambion). RNA concentration and quality were determined at 260 nm using the NanoDrop ND-1000 and the Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer. 

Microarray construction: The whole-genome oligo arrays with 70-base nucleotides representing 3227 open reading frames (ORFs) plus unique sequences from B. abortus and B. suis were based on the Brucella melitensis genome (Rossetti et al., 2009). Oligonucleotides were suspended in 3× saline– sodium citrate (SSC) at a final concentration of 40 μM prior to robotic arraying in quadruplicates onto ultraGAPS-coated glass slides (Corning) using a spotarray 72 microarray printer (Perkin Elmer). Printed slides were steamed and UV crosslinked. 

Probe labeling and microarray slide hybridization: The RNAs were converted to complementary DNA (cDNA) and labeled with Cy3 fluorescent dyes (Amersham Biosciences) using the previously described two-step protocol (Hegde et al., 2000; Occhialini et al., 2005). Briefly, total RNA (30 μg) was first converted to cDNAs with incorporation of amino allyldUTP using Superscript III reverse transcriptase and random hexamers (Invitrogen), and then “post labeled” with the reactive forms of fluoroLink Cy3-NHS esters (Amersham Biosciences). The labeled cDNAs were combined with 0.5 μg of labeled gDNA to a final volume of 35 μL. After heating at $9 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 5 min, samples were kept at $4 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ until hybridization, when 35 μL of 2× formamide-based hybridization buffer (50% formamide; 10× SSC; 0.2% SDS) was added. Samples were applied to custom 3.2 K Brucella oligo-arrays, pretreated by washing in 0.2% SDS and 3× in distilled water, and immersed in pre-hybridization buffer (5x SSC, 0.1% SDS; 1% BSA (bovine serum albumin) in 100 ml of water) at $4 5 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for at least 45 min. Before hybridization, the slides were washed 4× in distilled water, dipped in 100% isopropanol for 10 s, and dried by centrifugation at 1000×g for 2 min. 

Per experimental conditions, four slides were hybridized at $4 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for ∼20 h in a dark, humid chamber and washed for 10 min at $4 5 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ with 1× SSC, 0.2% SDS, followed by two 5-min washes in 0.1× SSC, 0.2% SDS and 0.1× SSC at 22 ◦C with agitation. Slides were dried by centrifugation at 800×g for 2 min and immediately scanned. 

Data acquisition and microarray data analysis: Hybridized microarrays were scanned using a GenePix 4000A dualchannel confocal laser scanner (Axon Instruments), and representative genes were adjusted for background and normalized to internal controls using image analysis software (GenePixPro 4.0; Axon Instruments). Genes with signal values below background were disregarded in all analyses. 

Statistics were performed by Seralogix, employing their BioSignature Discovery System computational tools to determine significant gene modulations via a Bayesian z-score sliding window threshold technique and fold-change. Normalizations against gDNA were performed as previously described (Rossetti et al., 2009). The data were deposited in the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) database at the NCBI (Accession no. GSE44688). Significant differential gene expression was determined using an absolute value for the z-score cutoff of +/−1.96, equivalent to 95% confidence for the two-sided t-test, with all genes differentially expressed having a plain fold-change greater than 1.5. Description of the computational techniques employed by BioSignatureDS was previously published (Khare et al., 2012; Lawhon et al., 2011). 

Quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR) analysis: Expression of randomly selected genes from most of the different functional categories $( n = 1 9 )$ was analyzed by RT-qPCR. 800 ng from the same RNA samples used for microarray hybridization was reverse-transcribed using a 6-mer random primers mix (Occhialini et al., 2005), and RT-qPCR experiments were performed using the Light Cycler 480 with SYBR green chemistry to quantify the amplification rate (Roche). Primers were designed to produce an amplicon length between 150 and 250 bp. For each gene tested, the fold-change was calculated as published in Hanna et al. (2013). BR1035, characterized by constant expression in both strains, was used as a reference gene. For each primer pair, a negative control and an RNA sample without reverse transcriptase were included as controls. Array data were considered valid if the fold-change of each gene tested by RTqPCR was >1.5 and consistent with the microarray analysis. 

Nitrate reductase assay: Culture supernatants were assayed for nitrite accumulation by a spectrophotometric assay based on the Griess reaction (Loisel-Meyer et al., 2006). B. suis wild type and Δrsh were washed in PBS, and incubated in GMM pH 7.0 containing 10 mM of ${ \mathrm { N a N O } } _ { 3 }$ for 6 h at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ under vigorous shaking. Nitrite concentrations were measured as described (Hanna et al., 2013). 

Measurement of in vitro sensitivity to superoxide production: A previously described procedure was used to follow- up superoxide dismutase activity (Gee et al., 2005): Mid-logphase cultures of B. suis wild type, the Δrsh mutant, and the complemented mutant grown in TS broth were washed in PBS and adjusted to approximately $1 0 ^ { 6 }$ CFU/ml. Xanthine at the final concentration of 2 mM and 1 U/ml of xanthine oxidase were added along with 1000 U/ml of bovine liver catalase. The number of surviving bacteria in the cell suspension was determined at specific time points. The means from three independent platings of each bacterial cell suspension were expressed as log10 CFU/ml at each sampling time, ± standard deviations. 

Construction of rsh and methionine mutants of B. suis: The rsh null mutant has been described in Dozot et al. (2006). 

The mutants in methionine biosynthesis genes (metA, metZ, metH, and BR0793) containing a kanamycin resistance gene replacing an internal portion of the target gene, as well as the complemented ΔmetH mutant, were constructed as described (Hanna et al., 2013). 

Macrophage infection experiments with Brucella strains: Experiments were performed as described in Jimenez de ´ Bagu¨es´ et al. (2010): Murine J774A.1 macrophage-like cells were infected with early-stationary-phase B. suis for 45 min at a multiplicity of infection of 20 bacteria per cell. Cells were washed twice with PBS and incubated in RPMI 1640 with 10% fetal calf serum and gentamicin at 30 μg/ml at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and 5% $\mathrm { C O } _ { 2 }$ for at least 1 h. At various time points, cells were washed twice and lysed in 0.2% Triton X-100. The number of intracellular live bacteria was determined by plating on TS agar plates and incubation at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ Experiments were performed at least three times in triplicate. 

## 7.2.3 Results

## 7.2.3.1 Differential gene expression during stringent response in B. suis

Expression profiles of B. suis 1330 wild-type and the isogenic Δrsh mutant were generated by incubation for 4 h in minimal medium at pH 7.0, known to induce expression of rshdependent genes in Brucella spp. and necessitating the presence of Rsh for growth (Dozot et al., 2006). Prior to transcriptional analysis, the deletion of rsh in the Δrsh mutant was confirmed by PCR. Comparative transcriptional analysis between B. suis wild-type and the Δrsh mutant revealed the Rsh-dependent differential regulation of 380 genes, which represents 12% of the genome. 198 of these genes (52%) were upregulated and 182 genes (48%) were downregulated by Rsh (Figure 7.2.1) (Hanna et al., 2013). 

The differential expression varied between a 5.3-fold Rshdependent upregulation of a gene coding for a protein of unknown function (BR0629), and an 8.4-fold downregulation (ureB-1). Differentially expressed genes were grouped according to the COG nomenclature. Genes were relatively equally distributed over the different groups, except for a strong representation of genes encoding proteins with unknown functions. It appeared that in B. suis, Rsh controlled a variety of different metabolic pathways. Consistent with the link between stringent response and production of (p)ppGpp, 120 of the differentially expressed genes were involved in energy, nitrogen, amino acid, nucleic acid, fatty acid, protein, or sugar metabolism. 31% of these genes were upregulated and 69% were downregulated in the presence of a functional rsh gene. 

## 7.2.3.2 Genes upregulated during stringent response

198 (52%) of the differentially expressed genes were positively regulated by Rsh, characterized by a significantly higher

expression rate in the wild type than in the Δrsh strain (Hanna et al., 2013). Among the upregulated genes, only three (BR0793, BRA0338, and BRA0340) were homologous to genes encoding enzymes involved in amino acid metabolism: BR0793, encoding O-acetylhomoserine sulfhydrylase and participating in methionine biosynthesis; BRA0338, homologous to glutamate decarboxylase-encoding genes and possessing an authentic point mutation in B. suis; and BRA0340, encoding a glutaminase catalyzing the formation of glutamate from glutamine. Twelve genes were implicated in DNA–RNA metabolism, including himA (BR0778) encoding the integration host factor (IHF) alpha subunit. IHF participates in control of virB operon expression during the intracellular and vegetative growth in various media (Sieira et al., 2004). Twenty-two genes, including narG and narJ from the respiratory nitrate reductase operon, and ccoN and ccoP encoding 2 cbb3-type cytochrome c oxidase subunits, were involved in energy metabolism. The cbb -type cytochrome c oxidase is a high-oxygen-affinity oxidase allowing brucellae to adapt to low oxygen tension. It was identified to be strongly induced under microaerobic conditions in vitro and essential for chronic, B. suis–mediated murine infection (Jimenez de Bag´ u¨es´ et al., 2007; Loisel-Meyer et al., 2005). Six genes involved in nitrogen metabolism and belonging to the ure2 operon were upregulated. Two genes participating in fatty acid metabolism were also upregulated: BR1510 encoding an acyl-CoA hydrolase; and fadD (BR0289), which encodes an acyl-CoA synthase described to be required for infection by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Dunphy et al., 2010; Rindi et al., 2004). The gene sodC, encoding a Cu–Zn superoxide dismutase participating in detoxification of free oxygen radicals (Fee, 1991), was also upregulated. In addition, we observed Rshdependent upregulation of two ftsK genes encoding cell division proteins. This is consistent with the morphological abnormalities described in our and another previous study on B. abortus (Dozot et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2005). The stringent response also positively affected stress-related gene expression of a number of heat and cold shock genes and molecular chaperones (grpE, hdeA, csp, dnaJ, and usp; see Sections 13–15). Transcription of hdeA (BRA0341) was upregulated in the presence of rsh, and in B. abortus, HdeA contributes to acid resistance but is not required for virulence in vivo (Valderas et al., 2005). Several of the genes upregulated in a Rsh-dependent manner encode functions related to transcription, with the identification of 12 transcriptional regulators belonging to different families (GntR, RpiR, MerR, LysR, and Ros/MucR). GntR5 has been identified as HutC, which acts as a co-activator of transcription of the virB operon, and represses the hut genes of the histidine utilization pathway (Sieira et al., 2010). The regulator MucR is involved in virulence of B. melitensis and B. abortus in macrophage and murine models of infection (Caswell et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2006), and in lipid A-core and cyclic-β-glucan synthesis of B. melitensis (Mirabella et al., 2013).

Several other genes encoding factors associated with Brucella virulence were identified as being regulated by (p)ppGpp, which is in agreement with observations made in other bacterial pathogens (Aberg et al., 2006; Anderson et al., 2006; Dalebroux et al., 2009). These genes, upregulated in a Rshdependent manner and identified in independent virulence screens (Delrue et al., 2004), include those involved in cell envelope formation (amiC, lpsA, omp19, wbdA, and wbpL), in DNA and RNA metabolism (mutM and pyrB), in stress response (csp), and in transport and secretion systems (virB5 and dppA). The roles of the $c b b _ { 3 } – \mathrm { t y p e }$ cytochrome c oxidase (operon cco) and of the Cu–Zn superoxide dismutase (sodC) have been described elsewhere (Jimenez de Bag ´ u¨es´ et al., 2007; Loisel-Meyer et al., 2005). Table 7.2.1 lists these 15 genes that are positively regulated by (p)ppGpp and participate in Brucella virulence. 

## 7.2.3.3 Genes downregulated during the stringent response

In parallel, transcriptome analysis revealed 182 downregulated genes (Hanna et al., 2013). The gene most strongly downregulated in the presence of Rsh was ureB1 encoding the urease betasubunit, involved in nitrogen metabolism and part of the ure-1 operon. The other four genes belonging to the ure-1 operon (ureC, ureD1, ureE1, and ureG1) were also repressed. The hallmark of the stringent response is the downregulation of transcription of the genes encoding ribosomal proteins. In fact, in our transcriptome analysis, all the genes encoding ribosomal proteins identified in this transcriptome (n = 29) were downregulated. Among the genes coding for transcriptional regulators, we identified two genes (BR1187 and BR0872) belonging to the Cro/CI and ExoR families, respectively, as being downregulated. The latter has been described as repressing exopolysaccharide production. Interestingly, two genes of the flagella clusters, identified as flaF and fliG, were also affected. The biological function of flagella in Brucella remains unknown (Fretin et al., 2005). Fatty acid and glycerophospholipid biosynthesis were most likely reduced during stringent response, as we identified four genes involved in these processes being downregulated. Similarly, metabolism of sugars and glycolysis was apparently diminished, in agreement with a general reduction of metabolic activities. We also observed downregulation of glnE, responsible for adenylylation of glutamine synthetase (GS). Reduced adenylylation increases GS activity, and the synthetized glutamine plays a central role in the biosynthesis of amino acids, purines, and pyrimidines. 

## 7.2.3.4 Validation of the microarray expression data by RT-qPCR analysis

RT-qPCR was used to validate the expression trends of a total of 40 selected genes identified by microarray analysis. Using the same total RNA preparations as for the microarray hybridizations, expression of these genes was analyzed by RT-qPCR. Gene BR1035 of unknown function was used as internal reference for normalization, as its expression rate was constant for both strains. Thirty-one (78%) of the tested genes were differentially expressed using a cutoff value of plain fold-change >1.5 and were in agreement with the microarray analysis (Hanna et al., 2013). Correlation between the expression levels obtained by microarrays and those obtained by RT-qPCR was good, confirming that rsh-dependent differential gene expression evidenced by oligonucleotide microarray analysis could be reproduced by RT-qPCR. 

## 7.2.3.5 Nitrate reductase and superoxide dismutase of B. suis are under the positive control of (p)ppGpp

Induction of the nar operon by (p)ppGpp was confirmed biochemically by measurement of nitrate reductase. After a 4 h induction in GMM, the $\mathrm { N O } _ { 2 } { } ^ { - }$ production was measured in the bacterial culture supernatants. Significant production of $\mathrm { N O } _ { 2 } { } ^ { - }$ was observed in the B. suis wild-type strain with a mean nitrite concentration of $6 9 8 . 5 \pm 6 . 5 \mu \mathrm { M }$ , as compared to its Δrsh isogenic mutant with a strongly reduced nitrite concentration of only $4 0 . 2 \pm 6 . 4 \mu \mathrm { M }$ . This was consistent with the microarray and RT-qPCR results. Both microarray and RT-qPCR results also revealed induction of sodC, encoding Cu–Zn superoxide dismutase. Production of exogenous ${ \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } } ^ { - }$ was artificially induced by the xanthine oxydase reaction. The number of surviving bacteria in the cell suspension was determined at specific time points thereafter. A clear correlation between rsh expression and resistance to $\mathrm { O _ { 2 } } ^ { - }$ − radicals could be detected: The net difference in survival between the wild type and the Δrsh strain was 50-fold at 30 min and 500-fold at 1 h (Figure 7.2.2). Following complementation with the intact gene, the higher sensitivity of the rsh mutant to ${ \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } } ^ { - }$ was abolished, and survival was not significantly different from that of the wild type (Figure 7.2.2).

## 7.2.3.6 Methionine, present in the Brucella-containing vacuole of macrophages, is required for growth of a rsh null mutant in minimal medium

A Δrsh mutant lacks growth in GMM, which can be restored following complementation (Dozot et al., 2006). This led us to the characterization of the amino acid requirements of a Δrsh mutant under these conditions. Each of the 20 culture tubes per B. suis wild-type and Δrsh strain, respectively, contained all but one of the 20 amino acids. Control cultures in medium without amino acids and in medium containing all 20 amino acids (not shown), as well as a ΔmetH mutant and its complemented form, were also included. The ΔmetH mutant (BR0188) was unable to synthesize 5-methyltetrahydrofolatehomocysteine methyltransferase, the last enzyme in the methionine biosynthesis pathway. Results showed that the rsh mutant and, as expected, the ΔmetH mutant did not grow in medium lacking only methionine (Figure 7.2.3). Growth was restored upon addition of methionine, indicating that only methionine biosynthesis was affected in the Δrsh mutant (Figure 7.2.3). Addition of exogenous methionine to the wild type and to the complemented ΔmetH mutant favored rapider growth. 

Interestingly, the ΔmetH mutant was not attenuated in the J774 murine macrophage model of infection (not shown), leading to the conclusion that methionine was available in the Brucella-containing vacuoles and that the intracellular attenuation of the rsh mutant was not due to methionine starvation.

Microarrays and RT-qPCR data revealed that metA (BRA0486) was downregulated, and BR0793 was upregulated, in the presence of Rsh (Hanna et al., 2013). In agreement with the general methionine biosynthesis pathway, mutants respectively carrying the inactivated genes metA, metZ, or BR0793, encoding O-acetylhomoserine sulfhydrylase, grew less well in GMM. An eventual link between rsh and the expression of genes located further “upstream” on the methionine biosynthesis pathway was therefore systematically assessed by RT-qPCR (Figure 7.2.4). 

The transcripts encoding aspartate kinase (BR1871) and homoserine dehydrogenase (hom; BR1274) were significantly less abundant in the rsh mutant than in the wild type, indicating that Rsh was also involved in the regulation of these genes encoding proteins further upstream in the methionine biosynthesis pathway, between L-aspartate and the L-homoserine intermediate product (Figure 7.2.4).

## 7.2.4 Discussion

In bacteria, the stringent response affects a large number of structural and regulatory target genes and results in a pleiotropic phenotype. It mediates the adaptation of a bacterium to nutrient stress via a complex differential gene expression pattern. In this study, we investigated the global expression profile of the stringent response with the aim to decipher the (p)ppGpp-dependent regulatory network. 

The ability of the bacterium to resist to acid pH and nutrient deprivation within the macrophage host cells is a key element in the establishment of Brucella infection. Both signals are essential for a strong induction of the T4SS in B. suis, and, in accordance with previous work (Dozot et al., 2006), our transcriptome study showed that virB expression was Rsh dependent. On a fine-tuned level, a gene encoding integration host factor (IHF) and hutC, which both contribute to transcription of the virB operon, was also upregulated. The Rshdependent upregulation of IHF expression in Brucella confirmed that Brucella senses nutrient starvation via Rsh, resulting in (p)ppGpp production, which will then increase transcription of IHF, affecting the activity of the virB promoter, as suggested in Rambow-Larsen et al. (2009). Among transcriptional regulators participating in Brucella virulence, expression of MucR was shown to be Rsh dependent. In B. melitensis, MucR regulates genes involved in stress response and nitrogen metabolism (Arenas-Gamboa et al., 2011), as well as in cyclic-β- glucan and lipid A-core synthesis (Mirabella et al., 2013). Transcriptome analysis in the α-proteobacterium R. etli reported that Rsh positively controls expression of key regulators for survival during heat and oxidative stress (Vercruysse et al., 2011). 

Several consecutive genes, encoding glutamate decarboxylase A (BRA0338), glutaminase (BRA0340), and hdeA (BRA0341), all potentially involved in resistance to acid pH, were also Rsh induced. Glutamate decarboxylase, participating in resistance of Brucella microti and other newly described Brucella spp. to pH 2.5 (Damiano et al., 2015; Occhialini et al., 2012), is not functional in B. suis, but this gene potentially forms an operon with hdeA, playing a role in acid stress resistance in B. abortus (Valderas et al., 2005; see Section 16). These results suggest that Rsh may allow response to a possible acid stress subsequent to nutrient deficiency. 

One of the primary antimicrobial mechanisms is production of reactive oxygen intermediates (ROIs), and ROI formation has been described during macrophage infection by Brucella (Gee et al., 2004). We identified sodC, encoding the Cu–Zn superoxide dismutase, among the genes positively regulated by Rsh and contributing to virulence of Brucella. In B. abortus, a sodC mutant exhibited increased susceptibility to killing in a cell culture and in a murine model of infection (Gee et al., 2005). 

We suggest that the lack of upregulation of this protective gene might participate in the observed attenuation of Δrsh mutants of Brucella (Dozot et al., 2006; Kohler¨ et al., 2002). In biofilmforming P. aeruginosa, it has been reported that increasing production of active catalase and SOD against endogenous oxydant production resulted in higher antioxidant defenses by an active stringent response (Nguyen et al., 2011), indicating at least partial conservation of stringent response–dependent adaptation strategies of bacterial pathogens to various stress conditions encountered during chronic infection or biofilm formation. 

Downregulation of protein synthesis, together with induction of amino acid biosynthesis, is one of the hallmarks of the stringent response. In E. coli, repression of the translation machinery, including ribosomal proteins, is a major event of the stringent response (Durfee et al., 2008; Traxler et al., 2008). This was clearly confirmed by our study, as we identified 29 ribosomal proteins–encoding genes that were downregulated. In contrast to results obtained in E. coli, only methionine biosynthesis was controlled by (p)ppGpp in B. suis. Based on the observation of the attenuation of several Brucella mutants affected in amino acid and nucleotide biosynthesis pathways (Kim et al., 2004; Kohler ¨ et al., 2002), Rsh-dependent methionine synthesis might be crucial during infection. However, intracellular growth of the ΔmetH mutant was not impaired, indicating that methionine was available in the Brucella-containing vacuole and that the attenuation of the Δrsh mutant must have a different reason. Interestingly, (p)ppGpp-dependent upregulation of amino acid biosynthesis pathways was also not observed in R. etli (Vercruysse et al., 2011), indicating that induction of amino acid biosynthesis during the stringent response is not a key feature in α-proteobacteria. 

The nar operon, encoding the respiratory nitrate reductase, was also induced under stringent conditions in Brucella. Nar induction was shown by the Rsh-dependent control of the genes narG, narJ, and narK, involved in the first step of denitrification and in nitrite extrusion (Haine et al., 2006). This pathway may allow Brucella to survive under low oxygen tension, using nitrogen oxides as terminal electron acceptors (Al Dahouk et al., 2009). Denitrification can also be used by brucellae to detoxify NO produced during infection, and part of this denitrification island is important for virulence (Loisel-Meyer et al., 2006). Recent proteomic and genetic studies with B. suis have provided evidence for the induction of the nar operon under microaerobic conditions (Al Dahouk et al., 2009). In E. coli, expression of the narGHJI operon is induced by low oxygen tension and by the presence of nitrate (Showe and DeMoss, 1968). In M. tuberculosis, oxygen concentration–independent expression of nar has been described (Sohaskey and Wayne, 2003), and nitrate reductase component genes narH and narI have been identified as being under the positive control of Rel (Rsh) under comparable nutrient starvation conditions (Dahl et al., 2003). Therefore, nitrate reductase may be expressed in Brucella in a stringent response–dependent manner under aerobic conditions, and further induced under hypoxia. In analogy to these observations, genes encoding cbb3-type cytochrome c oxidase were also under the positive control of Rsh. We hypothesize that the stringent response therefore also acts as a first step of adaptation to gradual reduction of oxygen concentrations encountered by the pathogen in the host organism. 

The observation that flaF and fliG, belonging to flagellar loci I and loci III, respectively, were downregulated suggested that the flagellar apparatus of Brucella was repressed under stringent conditions. The E. coli transcription profile of the stringent response, where the expression of the flhDC flagella master regulator is rapidly downregulated (Lemke et al., 2009), is in agreement with our results. Hence, bacteria appear to shut down transcription of the flagella-encoding genes under starvation. Very recently, downregulation of these genes by the transcriptional regulator MucR has been described in B. melitensis (Mirabella et al., 2013). Our observation that MucR is positively regulated during the stringent response in B. suis, whereas genes encoding the flagellar apparatus are downregulated, confirms this link also in B. suis and, more generally, demonstrates that (p)ppGpp is located high up in the hierarchy of gene regulation in Brucella spp. 

Altogether, transcription analysis of the stringent response in the facultatively intracellular pathogen B. suis confirmed the pleiotropic character of the (p)ppGpp-mediated adaptation to starvation. Several of the genes identified as being under (p)ppGpp control have also been described previously as being essential for the virulence of the pathogen (Delrue et al., 2004), establishing a link between the stringent response and virulence. Five genes encode proteins involved in cell envelope biosynthesis, of which four are essential for intramacrophagic replication of Brucella (Delrue et al., 2004). Four outer membrane proteins (Omps), all under the positive control of (p)ppGpp during the stringent response, have also been identified previously as being upregulated in intramacrophagic B. suis (Al Dahouk et al., 2008), indicating the potential importance of these Omps. 

The function of 33% of the genes encoding Rsh-dependent transcripts remains unknown, illustrating the complexity of the processes involved in adaptation to starvation while bearing in mind that knowledge on the functions of a substantial part of the Brucella genome is still limited. Transcriptome analysis of the stringent response in B. suis resulted in the observation that the rsh mutant had a lower general stress resistance than the wild-type strain. This led us to the hypothesis that in Brucella, stringent response and adaptation to nutrient stress may trigger cross-talk with other general stress responses possibly encountered simultaneously or soon after. In the life cycle of B. suis within the host, intracellular starvation may be the first major stress encountered. According to the transcriptome data presented in this chapter, such cross-talk may take place between at least three stress responses playing a major role in Brucella adaptation to host: nutrient, oxidative, and low-oxygen stress.

# The stringent response and antioxidant defences in Pseudomonas aeruginosa

Gowthami Sampathkumar, Malika Khakimova, Tevy Chan, and Dao Nguyen 

Research Institute of the McGill University Health Centre, Montreal, Quebec, Canada 

## 7.3.1 Introduction

Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a metabolically versatile environmental organism that colonizes diverse habitats. Oxidative stress is ubiquitous in aerobic environments, as molecular oxygen causes cellular toxicity by generating reactive oxygen species (ROS) that react with macromolecules such as nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids (see also Section 10). Such ROS are formed spontaneously during bacterial respiration, by extracellular redox chemistry, or by UV-visible radiation (Imlay, 2003). Furthermore, P. aeruginosa is also an important opportunistic pathogen in different animal hosts, causing both acute and chronic infections in humans. Bacteria thus encounter oxidative stress generated by host phagocytic cells during infections. 

Antioxidant defences, which detoxify ROS and repair oxidative damage, are required for bacterial growth and survival in aerobic environments. Hydrogen peroxide $\left( \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \right)$ and superoxide anions (O2∙−) are the major ROS formed by partial reduction of oxygen, and enzymatic scavengers are the major bacterial defences that detoxify ROS. The genome of P. aeruginosa encodes several enzymatic ROS scavengers, namely, two superoxide dismutases (sodA and sodB), at least three functional catalases (katA, katB, and katC), and two alkyl hydroperoxide reductases (ahpB and ahpCF). Interestingly, antioxidant defences are induced by nutrient stress such as carbon, nitrogen, and phosphate starvation (Giard et al., 1996; Jenkins et al., 1988; Koga and Takumi, 1995; Seymour et al., 1996). Stationaryphase and biofilm bacteria are also nutrient-limited and exhibit high oxidant tolerance (Elkins et al., 1999; Hassett et al., 2000). Do nutrient stress responses provide cross-resistance to oxidative stress in P. aeruginosa? To investigate this, our studies have examined the role of the stringent response. 

The stringent response (SR), mediated by the alarmone (p)ppGpp, is a global response to different nutrient stress signals, including amino acid, carbon, phosphate, and iron limitation, as well as heat shock and osmotic stress (Dalebroux and 

Swanson, 2012; see Chapters 7.1, 7.2 and 7.4). It coordinates physiological changes to promote adaptation to, and survival under, stress. In Gram-negative bacteria such as P. aeruginosa and Escherichia coli, (p)ppGpp is synthesized by the synthetase RelA and the bifunctional synthase–hydrolase SpoT. The SR primarily modulates gene transcription to shut down biosynthesis of macromolecules and cell replication, while inducing protective mechanisms for stress survival (Braeken et al., 2006; Nystrom, 2004). So far, only a few studies have explored the link between the SR and control of antioxidant defences. For example, E. coli cells treated with $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ induced the accumulation of (p)ppGpp (Braeken et al., 2006). In addition, Enterococcus faecalis relA mutant cells were more susceptible to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ treatment (Yan et al., 2009). We have recently reported that inactivation of the SR in P. aeruginosa impairs catalase and superoxide dismutase activity (Nguyen et al., 2011). We here present a more comprehensive study of the role of the SR in regulation of antioxidant defences. 

## 7.3.2 Materials and methods

Bacterial strains and growth conditions: The ΔrelA ΔspoT mutant and the complemented strain for relA and spoT (named +SR) were constructed in the P. aeruginosa PAO1 strain background, as described in Nguyen et al. (2011). Bacteria were grown in lysogeny broth (LB) medium at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ , shaking at 250 rpm, for all experiments unless otherwise indicated. Overnight cultures were diluted in LB to $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 } = 0 . 0 5$ and incubated to the indicated times. To induce katB–lacZ expression with sub-lethal $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ,$ planktonic bacteria were grown to mid-log phase $( \mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 } = 0 . 5 )$ at $3 7 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and stimulated with 0.2 mM $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ pulses every 10 min for 60 min to a final concentration of 1.2 mM $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } )$ . To induce sodA– lacZ expression, bacteria were grown in iron-depleted LB medium supplemented with 0.5 mM 2,2-dipyridyl. Colony biofilm bacteria were grown on 0.4 μm pore size polycarbonate membrane filters (GE Osmotics) on 1.5% w/v agar plates with 25% w/v LB at $3 7 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 24 h, as described in Khakimova et al. (2013). Where appropriate for selection, antibiotics were used at the following concentrations: ampicillin 100 μg/mL (E. coli), and gentamicin 10 μg/mL (E. coli) or 50 μg/mL (P. aeruginosa). 

Oxidant killing assays: For killing of stationary-phase bacteria, cells were grown in LB with shaking at $3 7 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 16–18 h. Paraquat (PQ) (5 mM), tert-butyl-hydroperoxide (tBHP) (650 μM), and phenazine methosulfate (PMS) (50 μM) were added to stationary-phase cells, and the amended culture was incubated with shaking for 12 h at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ . For $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ killing of stationary-phase bacteria, overnight cultures were diluted in LB to $2 . 5 { \times } 1 0 ^ { 6 }$ cells/mL, and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ (3 mM) was added to cells and incubated for 2 h with shaking at $3 7 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ For $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ killing of logarithmic-phase bacteria, cells were grown in LB to $\mathrm { O D } _ { 6 0 0 } = 0 . 5$ , then $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ was added to cells at different concentrations and incubated with shaking for 1 h at $3 7 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } .$ . For $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ killing of biofilms, colony biofilms were immersed in 2 mL of 25% LB medium and challenged with 150 mM $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ pulses every 10 min for 30 min at $3 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ to a final concentration of 450 mM. After oxidant challenge, cells were washed and re-suspended in phosphate buffered saline (PBS), and plated for viable colony-forming units (CFUs) on LB agar using standard microdilution techniques. All results are the means from at least three independent replicates, and all experiments were performed at least three times. 

Catalase activity assay: Bacteria were grown in LB to late stationary phase (16–18 h), pelleted, washed, and lysed by sonication on ice. Total protein in the lysates was determined by the Bradford assay (BioRad). Catalase activity was measured spectrophotometrically at $\mathrm { O D } _ { 2 4 0 }$ using the method of Beers and Sizer (1952). Aliquots of 100 μL cell lysates containing 10 μg of protein were added to the assay solution, and 1 unit of catalase activity corresponded to 1 μmol of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ per min per mg of protein. Results are presented as relative catalase activity normalized to wild-type levels. 

Superoxide dismutase (SOD) assay: Cell lysates were prepared as carried out for the catalase assay. The SOD activity was measured using the method described by McCord and Fridovich (1969). Briefly, 10 μg of total protein was added to a mixture of 30 μM cytochrome c, 100 μM xanthine, and 0.0185 μM xanthine oxidase. The reduction of cytochrome c was measured spectrophotometrically as the change in $\mathrm { O D } _ { 5 5 0 }$ , and the SOD activity was calculated as the inhibition of cytochrome C reduction. One unit SOD activity inhibited by 50% the rate of reduction of cytochrome c per mg of protein. Results are presented as relative SOD activity normalized to wild-type levels. 

Promoter LacZ fusions and β-galactosidase assay: The katA and katB promoter–LacZ fusions were constructed as described in Khakimova et al. (2013). The sodA, sodB, and ahpC promoter–LacZ fusions were constructed using the 

MultiSite Gateway® Pro cloning system (Invitrogen). The putative promoter region upstream of the coding sequence of sodA (2348 bp), sodB (349 bp), and ahpC (261 bp), and lacZ coding sequences were amplified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and the PCR fragments were recombined into the pDONR221 P1-P5r and P5-P2 vectors, respectively, to generate pENTR entry clones as described in Khakimova et al. (2013). The LacZ reporter constructs were generated by recombination of the promoter and the lacZ pENTR plasmids with the destination vector pUC18miniTn7T-Gm-GW. A lacZ promoterless vector control was constructed by recombining upstream of the lacZ reporter a 100 bp sequence containing the multiple cloning site amplified from the mini-CTX2 vector (Hoang et al., 2000), as described in Khakimova et al. (2013). The recombinant vectors were integrated into the P. aeruginosa chromosome by electroporation, and integrants were selected on gentamicin 50 μg/mL, and confirmed by PCR as reported in Choi and Schweizer (2006). The β-galactosidase activity was assayed as described by Zhang and Bremer (1995). The background activity measured in the promoterless LacZ control strain was subtracted from all readings, and the normalized β-galactosidase activities were expressed as Miller units. All results are the means from at least three independent replicates, and all experiments were performed at least three times. 

Statistical analysis: Statistical differences between two means were determined with the Student t-tests using Prism version 5 software (Graphpad). 

## 7.3.3 Results

## 7.3.3.1 The stringent response is required for tolerance to multiple oxidants, including hydrogen peroxide

We have previously generated a (p)ppGpp-null mutant (ΔrelA ΔspoT mutant) where the relA and spoT genes are deleted (Nguyen et al., 2011). We examined the susceptibility of the ΔrelA ΔspoT to multiple oxidants, namely $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ,$ the O2∙− generating compounds PQ and PMS, and the organic peroxide tBHP. We first tested cells in the stationary phase because they are more tolerant to oxidative stress than log-phase cells, and observed that the ΔrelA ΔspoT mutant is significantly more susceptible to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } , \mathrm { P Q }$ PMS, and tBHP killing (Figure 7.3.1). Tolerance to all oxidants was restored upon complementation of the relA and spoT genes. Focusing on tolerance to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ,$ , we then tested bacteria at different growth phases and modes. The ΔrelA ΔspoT mutant was also more readily killed by $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ in planktonic bacteria growing in the exponential phase, as well as in biofilms (Figure 7.3.2). 

## 7.3.3.2 Inactivation of the stringent response reduces catalase and SOD activity

P. aeruginosa possesses multiple ROS scavengers; catalases and SODs are the primary enzymatic scavengers required to detoxify $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { O } 2 \bullet -$ . We found that total catalase and SOD activity are significantly reduced in the ΔrelA ΔspoT mutant by approximately 60 and 75%, respectively; complementation of the relA and spoT genes also restores both ROS scavenging activities (Figure 7.3.3). Using serine hydroxamate to cause serine starvation and induce the SR, we also found that (p)ppGpp accumulation led to increased catalase activity (Khakimova et al., 2013). Together, these results suggest that the stringent response controls basal catalase and SOD activities, and that nutrient starvation upregulates catalases through (p)ppGpp signalling.

## 7.3.3.3 Regulation of katA, katB, and ahpC expression by the SR

P. aeruginosa possesses catalases and alkylperoxidases for detoxification of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ,$ , namely, KatA, the primary constitutive catalase, and KatB, the OxyR-dependent inducible catalase expressed under conditions of exogenous $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ stress (Heo et al., 2010; see Section 10). Alkylperoxidases are involved in detoxifying $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ as well as organic hydroperoxides such as tBHP. We constructed katA, katB, and ahpC transcriptional LacZ reporters to measure the transcription of the katA, katB, and ahpCF genes. katA–lacZ activity was detected at the log and stationary phases during planktonic growth, with the highest levels during the early stationary phase (Figure 7.3.4a). expression is consistent with previous reports demonstrating that katA is regulated by the Las quorum-sensing system and stationary-phase sigma factor RpoS (Hassett et al., 1999; Suh et al., 1999). In contrast, katA–lacZ activity in the ΔrelA $\Delta s p o T$ mutant minimally increased, and was reduced to ∼35% of wild-type levels during the stationary phase. katB–lacZ in the wild-type strain activity was undetectable in the absence of exogenous $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ,$ and increased after $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ challenge in both planktonic and biofilm bacteria (Figure 7.3.4b). In contrast, both the non-induced and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ -induced katB–lacZ activities of the ΔrelA $\Delta s p o T$ mutant remained undetectable. These results revealed that the SR is involved in the transcriptional control of both growth-phase-dependent katA expression and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ -inducible katB expression. Using an ahpC–lacZ transcriptional reporter, we determined that the basal expression of ahpC is significantly reduced in the ΔrelA ΔspoT mutant, at less than 15% of wild-type levels throughout all growth phases in planktonic cultures (Figure 7.3.4c). 

## 7.3.3.4 Regulation of sodA and sodB expression by the SR

P. aeruginosa expresses two SOD enzymes: manganese (Mn) and iron (Fe)-cofactored, respectively, sodA and sodB, both of which mediate the dismutation of superoxide anion radicals to hydrogen peroxide (Hassett et al., 1993). The iron uptake regulator Fur represses sodA transcription when iron is replete. However, Fur is activated under iron limitation and no longer represses sodA transcription (Hassett et al., 1996). We thus examined the expression of sodA under iron-limited conditions and sodB under iron-replete conditions using, respectively, sodA–lacZ and sodB–lacZ transcriptional reporters. Under iron-depleted conditions using the iron chelator 2,2’-dipyridyl, sodA–lacZ activity is induced in stationary-phase wild-type strains. While this induction still occurs in the ΔrelA ΔspoT mutant, it is significantly reduced in magnitude, and is only at ∼50% of wild-type levels in late-stationary-phase cells (Figure 7.3.5a). We examined the sodB–lacZ activity in iron-replete conditions, and found that its expression is also induced during the stationary phase in both strains but is only at ∼50% of wildtype levels (Figure 7.3.5b) in the ΔrelA ΔspoT mutant. 

## 7.3.4 Discussion

Under aerobic conditions, bacteria are exposed to both intracellular and extracellular ROS formed by the partial reduction of oxygen. ROS are generated by the autoxidation of flavoproteins in the electron transport chain, by redox cycling agents such as phenazines, or extracellular redox reactions with metal (Korshunov and Imlay, 2010; Seaver and Imlay, 2004). Oxidative stress occurs when ROS levels overwhelm the cell’s ability to detoxify them and repair the incurred damage. Antioxidant defences are thus essential for bacterial growth and survival under aerobic steady-state conditions as well as under stress when ROS production increases (see Section 10). 

P. aeruginosa has several enzymes capable of degrading $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } { \mathrm { : } }$ KatA and KatB are both haem-containing monofunctional catalases that only accept hydrogen peroxide as a substrate. KatA is constitutively expressed, but this expression is under both lasR and rpoS control and is induced upon entry into the stationary phase (Hoang et al., 2000; Zhang and Bremer, 1995). The second catalase, KatB, is under the regulation of OxyR and is only induced under increased $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ stress conditions (Brown et al., 1995). P. aeruginosa also possesses KatC, a temperature-inducible catalase (Mossialos et al., 2006), and KatN, a non-haem catalase, but the functions of both are poorly characterized. Finally, P. aeruginosa has several peroxidases, including AhpCF, AhpB, and Ohr, and expression of both ahpB and ahpCF is OxyR dependent (Ochsner et al., 2000; Panmanee et al., 2006). In E. coli, AhpCF is the primary scavenger of low levels of endogenously produced $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ (Seaver and Imlay, 2001). While this may be the case in P. aeruginosa since AhpCF also has catalase activity, its function under a steady state still needs to be determined. Panmanee and Hassett report that this enzyme is most important to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ detoxification during biofilm growth (Panmanee and Hassett, 2009).

General stress responses can provide cross-resistance to a wide range of insults. Although the SR is involved in adaptation to various stresses, very few studies have examined its role in oxidative stress. For example, the relA mutant of E. faecalis is more susceptible to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ (Yan et al., 2009), and the relA mutant of Geobacter sulfurreducens exhibits impaired aerobic growth due to oxidative stress (DiDonato et al., 2006). (p)ppGpp accumulation has also been associated with oxidative stress tolerance in Streptococcus mutans (Seaton et al., 2011), and transcriptomic studies of (p)ppGpp-regulated genes in Rhizobium etli identified several genes involved in oxidative stress resistance (Vercruysse et al., 2011). Our group has recently examined the link between the SR and control of antioxidant defences. 

The ΔrelA ΔspoT mutant, which produces no (p)ppGpp, is highly susceptible to multiple oxidants and shows reduced catalase and SOD activity. In examining the expression of several key ROS scavengers such as katA, katB, sodA, sodB, and ahpCF in the ΔrelA ΔspoT mutant, we found that their basal transcription levels were significantly reduced compared to the wild-type strain. It should be noted that ahpC and ahpF are likely cotranscribed and the ahpC–lacZ activity reports on expression of both ahpC and ahpF. In the case of katB, its inducible expression was also abrogated. These results show that (p)ppGpp signalling is required for optimal expression of these major antioxidant defences (see Chapter 7.1). In addition, we also showed that inducing the SR with serine starvation also induced catalase activity (Khakimova et al., 2013), suggesting that starvation conditions can elicit cross-resistance to oxidative stress through (p)ppGpp-mediated upregulation of catalase activity. 

The SR likely controls antioxidant expression indirectly, and several of the regulators involved are integrated, in P. aeruginosa, into a complex network that allows it to respond to different environmental conditions. For example, the Las quorum sensing system regulates cell-density-dependent expression of the catalase katA and sodA, while sodB is under Rhl quorum sensing control (Hassett et al., 1999). Although both E. coli and P. aeruginosa possess stress response regulators such as RpoS, OxyR, and SoxR, there are notable differences between the two species. For example, RpoS and SoxR are prominent regulators of antioxidant defences in E. coli, but their role is more limited or unclear in P. aeruginosa (Palma et al., 2005). Until recently, SoxR was believed to be an O2∙− responsive transcriptional regulator required for protection against superoxide stress. However, recent data in P. aeruginosa suggest that SoxR may have a different and poorly understood function: SoxR activates a six-gene regulon, which includes genes encoding for multidrug efflux pump systems, and a probable monooxygenase but not SODs (Palma et al., 2005). OxyR is a redox sensor that is activated post-transcriptionally by $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ to induce transcription of genes such as ahpCF and katB under $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ stress (Ochsner et al., 2000). The reduced expression of ahpCF and katB in the ΔrelA ΔspoT mutant may thus be due to impaired OxyR activity or expression, but this remains to be determined. The alternative sigma factor RpoS is also required for optimal stationary-phase resistance to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ (Jorgensen et al., 1999) and catalase activities in P. aeruginosa (Cochran et al., 2000). Since (p)ppGpp also favours the binding of alternative sigma factors such as RpoS to RNA polymerase, this may enhance the transcription of RpoScontrolled antioxidant genes. Finally, (p)ppGpp is required for full expression of RpoS (Kohanski et al., 2008), as well as both Las and Rhl quorum sensing systems (Schafhauser et al., 2014); the indirect effects of the SR are therefore mediated, at least in part, by these pathways.

# Molecular basis of the stringent response in Vibrio cholerae

Shreya Dasgupta1, Bhabatosh Das2, Pallabi Basu1, and Rupak K. Bhadra1 

1Infectious Diseases and Immunology Division, CSIR-Indian Institute of Chemical Biology, Kolkata, West Bengal, India 

2Center for Human Microbial Ecology, Translational Health Science and Technology Institute, NCR-Biotech Science Cluster, Faridabad, Haryana, India 

## 7.4.1 Introduction

Environmental fitness and multiplication of microorganisms including pathogens are precisely tuned through the active contribution of transcriptional factors, which differentially regulate expression of single or multiple genes directly linked to metabolic pathways, including DNA replication, transcription, protein synthesis, amino acid biosynthesis, and proteolysis. Although substantial progress in the area of regulation has been made in recent times, particularly due to the availability of genome sequences of most known bacteria including pathogens, still our knowledge on the underlying mechanisms that precisely modulate bacterial multiplication, transmission, and subsistence in various environmental conditions is limited. In this respect, we will focus on the biology of Vibrio cholerae, the causative agent of cholera in humans, to study the regulation of gene expression, functions of modulatory proteins, and mechanistic insights of different proteins, which synchronize the optimal level of effector molecules linked to survival and growth of microorganisms. V. cholerae cells are basically autochthonous marine organisms, and their evolution as a devastating human pathogen is not clearly understood (Colwell, 2004; Kaper et al., 1995). V. cholerae has remarkable adaptive competence as evidenced by its prolonged survival in aquatic environments, which most likely helps the pathogen to spread across continents and evolve as epidemic strains. This is also supported by the fact that the organism, which is of a pandemic nature, has extraordinary fitness and can survive for a long time outside its host. This remarkable feature of the organism has probably aided in its evolution as a successful pathogen. Another important aspect of V. cholerae and other species of the genus Vibrio is the presence of two circular chromosomes, one large (∼2.9 Mb) and one small (∼1.1 Mb) (Heidelberg et al., 2000). It is interesting to note that not all V. cholerae strains are cholera causing. Only the strains belonging to the serogroups O1 and O139 can cause epidemic cholera. Both the O1 and O139 strains are infected with the filamentous phage CTXϕ, which carries the principal virulence factor genes ctxAB (Das et al., 2007; Faruque and Mekalanos, 2003; Khetawat et al., 1999; Maiti et al., 2006; Waldor and Mekalanos, 1996). The ctxAB operon encodes an enterotoxin called cholera toxin (CT). Apart from the CTX prophage, O1 and O139 also carry the tcp locus, which encodes the major colonization factor TcpA (Faruque and Mekalanos, 2003; Taylor et al., 1987). 

While living in the aquatic environment as well as within the human intestinal lumen, V. cholerae may face nutrient limitation, physicochemical stresses, and toxic secondary metabolites produced by other members of the environment. In fact, all microorganisms including pathogens have to face such stresses, which have profound roles in relation to their capabilities to evolve with myriads of gene regulatory circuits. Among such environmental stresses, nutrient deficiency appears to be a critical one for each and every organism. Nutritional starvation in bacteria evokes the stringent response, which is an adaptive response related to temporary management of cellular metabolism to sustain life under this negative growth condition (Cashel et al., 1996; Magnusson et al., 2005; Potrykus and Cashel, 2008; see also Chapters 7.1, 7.2 and 7.3). During the stringent response, metabolic adjustments at the levels of replication, transcription and translation, and protein degradation are crucial for existence (Figure 7.4.1) (Chatterji and Ojha, 2001; Maisonneuve et al., 2013; Srivatsan and Wang, 2008; Traxler et al., 2011). Since bacteria are the simplest form of life and the ribosome is the only cell organelle, it is therefore the obvious target for stringent control. The ribosome is composed of more than 50 highly specific proteins and three species of ribosomal RNAs (rRNAs) (23S, 16S, and 5S). Since enzymes are essential for syntheses of all cellular macromolecules and the ribosome is the site of protein synthesis, during the stringent response

Figure 7.4.1 Diagram showing involvement of (p)ppGpp in multiple regulatory processes in bacterial survival. (p)ppGpp is synthesized by RelA–SpoT–SAS enzymes under various stress-related signaling systems and degraded back to GTP or GDP by the (p)ppGpp hydrolase enzyme SpoT. Stress-mediated cellular accumulation of (p)ppGpp leads to simultaneous activation and repression of various intracellular processes to combat different stress situations as shown (see text for details). Arrowhead and inverse “T” indicate activation and inhibition, respectively.


ribosome synthesis is strongly inhibited by repressing transcription of rRNA genes (Figure 7.4.1). How is this quickly achievable? Bacteria have evolved with the adequacy of synthesis of alarmones – the small intracellular signaling molecules guanosine 5′ -triphosphate 3′ -diphosphate (pppGpp) and guanosine 3′ ,5′ -bisdiphosphate (ppGpp), together called (p)ppGpp – to reconcile cellular physiology by rapidly sensing adverse environmental stimuli including nutrient scarcity (see Chapter 7.1). As shown in Figure 7.4.1, (p)ppGpp allows increased persistence of the bacterial cells through activation of the intracellular Lon protease, which degrades proteins to enhance the intracellular amino acid pool (Maisonneuve et al., 2013). On the other hand, (p)ppGpp inhibits intracellular exopolyphosphatase activity, leading to a significant increase in polyphosphate (polyP) accumulation in the cells (Kuroda et al., 1997, 2001). (p)ppGpp also activates the SlyA regulon, which possibly plays a role in antimicrobial resistance in Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (Zhao et al., 2008). Furthermore, (p)ppGpp is involved in the regulation of glycogen synthesis through repression of the major regulatory gene csrA (Edwards et al., 2011). Natori et al. (2009) have shown that (p)ppGpp inhibits the activity of IMP dehydrogenase, the first enzyme of the guanosine triphosphate (GTP) biosynthesis pathway, which in turn decreases the intracellular GTP pool. Metabolic pathways and signals, which have crucial impacts on (p)ppGpp metabolism, are reported across bacterial phyla including proteobacteria, bacteroidetes, firmicutes, and actinobacteria (Atkinson et al., 2011). However, precise mechanistic insights related to (p)ppGpp synthesis and the effect of the suboptimal or elevated level of (p)ppGpp on survival, multiplication, and expression of genes directly linked to virulence and disease development by pathogens are not well characterized for all organisms. In this chapter, we will focus on the molecular details of the stringent response in V. cholerae, followed by a description of its probable role in pathogenesis including the formation of biofilm and expression of virulence factors.

## 7.4.2 Canonical stringent response genes in V. cholerae

In Gram-negative γ-proteobacteria (e.g., Escherichia coli), the intracellular level of (p)ppGpp is tightly regulated by the activity of two GTP-pyrophosphokinases, RelA and SpoT, which are encoded by the relA and spoT genes, respectively (Atkinson et al., 2011; Cashel et al., 1996; Mittenhuber, 2001; Potrykus and Cashel, 2008; see Chapter 7.1). Whereas RelA has only (p)ppGpp synthetic activity, SpoT is a bifunctional enzyme with both (p)ppGpp hydrolase and synthetase activities (Gentry and Cashel, 1996; Murray and Bremer, 1996; Xiao et al., 1991). In contrast, Gram-positive bacteria usually code for a single bifunctional enzyme Rel, which has strong (p)ppGpp synthetase and hydrolase activities (Avarbock et al., 2005; Hogg et al., 2004; Mechold et al., 2002; Mittenhuber, 

2001). Like in E. coli, the genome of the Gram-negative bacterium V. cholerae carries the relA (JCVI annotation no. VC2451) and spoT (JCVI annotation no. VC2710) genes. Our laboratory (Haralalka et al., 2003) first-time functionally characterized the stringent response gene relA of V. cholerae. It has been reported that in the presence of functional RelA, V. cholerae accumulates elevated levels of (p)ppGpp upon sensing amino acid limitation in the environment. Several studies have identified four distinct domains of RelA, which are called (i) hydrolase (HD); (ii) synthetase or RelA SpoT, RSD, or SYNTH; (iii) TGS (named after threonyl–tRNA (transfer RNA) synthetase, GTPases, and SpoT proteins where TGS domains are conserved); and (iv) ACT (named after acetolactate synthetase, chorismate mutase, and TyrR proteins where ACT domains are conserved) (Aravind and Koonin, 1998). The HD domain (named due to the presence of highly conserved histidine (H) 

and aspartic acid (D) residues in this domain) is essential for the (p)ppGpp hydrolase function of SpoT and Rel proteins. Sajish et al. (2007) have proposed a further extension of the HD domain, and they show that SpoT–Rel-like bifunctional enzymes carry the HDXXED motif (Figure 7.4.2a). We also found that in SpoT proteins of vibrios, including V. cholerae, the HDXXED motif is highly conserved (Figure 7.4.2a). On the other hand, in RelA the entire HDXXED motif is replaced by different amino acid residues (Figure 7.4.2b). Interestingly, in enteric bacteria and pathogens, we found that HD residues are replaced with FP (i.e., phenylalanine and proline, respectively), as shown in Figure 7.4.2b. The next domain of HD (i.e., RSD in RelA–SpoT–Rel proteins) is highly conserved, and it is involved in catalyzing the transfer of pyrophosphate group from an adenosine triphosphate (ATP) molecule to the 3′ OH group of GTP–GDP, leading to the synthesis of pppGpp–ppGpp (Cashel et al., 1996; Gentry and Cashel, 1996; Mechold et al., 2002; Potrykus and Cashel, 2008; Xiao et al., 1991). Note that RelA proteins need $\mathrm { M g ^ { 2 + } }$ for their synthetase activity (Hogg et al., 2004; Sajish et al., 2007). It is thus expected that the synthetase function of the bifunctional SpoT–Rel proteins will also need $\mathrm { M g } ^ { 2 + }$ . However, it has been experimentally shown that high $\mathrm { M g ^ { 2 + } }$ actually inhibits the synthetase activity of the Rel proteins of Mycobacterium tuberculosis $\left( \mathrm { R e l } _ { \mathrm { M t b } } \right)$ and Streptococcus dysgalactiae subsp. equisimilis $( \mathrm { R e l } _ { \mathrm { S e q } } )$ . In contrast, purified E. coli RelA enzyme, which is monofunctional in nature, is not inhibited by the use of higher $\mathrm { M g } ^ { 2 + }$ concentrations (Avarbock et al., 2000; Mechold et al., 2002; Sajish et al., 2007, 2009). Sajish et al. (2007) have solved this issue by showing that the RSD regions of monofunctional RelA proteins of different bacteria, including V. cholerae and other vibrios, carry the EXDD motif (Figure 7.4.2b). In bifunctional enzymes, this motif is replaced by the RXKD motif (Figure 7.4.2a), which is also true for SpoT proteins of vibrios. Sajish et al. (2007) suggested that this type of charge reversal of the RXKD motif of bifunctional enzymes to EXDD in monofunctional RelA proteins most likely helps in creating additional metal-binding sites in latter enzymes. Thus, it is conceivable that the N-terminal half of RelA–SpoT–Rel is solely responsible for hydrolysis and synthesis of (p)ppGpp. 

Compared to the N-terminal region, the exact function of the C-terminal half containing the TGS and ACT domains of the RelA–Rel protein is not clear. Studies conducted on the roles of the C-terminal half of the monofunctional RelA protein of E. coli $( \mathrm { R e l A _ { E c h } } )$ or the bifunctional Rel protein of M. smegmatis $( \mathrm { R e l _ { M s m } } )$ or $\mathrm { R e l _ { M t b } }$ or $\mathrm { R e l } _ { \mathrm { S e q } }$ indicate that it might play a critical role in the regulation of activities of these enzymes. For example, Gropp et al. (2001) reported that the C-terminal portion of the canonical (p)ppGpp synthetase Rel $\mathrm { A _ { E c h } }$ enzyme is involved in RelA–RelA interactions, and two cysteines (at positions 612 and 638) and one aspartate (at position 637) residues are needed for full enzymatic function. Note that these amino acid residues are also conserved in V. cholerae RelA $( \mathrm { R e l A } _ { \mathrm { V c h } } ) ,$ suggesting that they most likely play similar roles. Mechold et al. (2002) have found that the deletion of the C-terminal region of $\mathrm { R e l } _ { \mathrm { S e q } }$ leads to a moderate increase in (p)ppGpp synthetase activity and a substantial decrease in hydrolase function, which is probably needed to favor synthetase activity. Avarbock et al. (2005) have reported increased synthetase activity of $\mathrm { R e l _ { M t b } }$ after substitution of the C-terminal cysteine and aspartic acid residues. Similarly, Jain et al. (2006) observed that mutagenesis of the conserved C-terminal cysteine residues in $\mathrm { R e l } _ { \mathrm { M s m } }$ led to monomerization and increased (p)ppGpp synthetase activity of the protein. More recently, Battesti and Bouveret (2006) have shown that during fatty acid starvation $( { \mathrm { p } } ) { \mathrm { p p G p p } }$ synthetase activity of E. coli SpoT is regulated through an interaction with the Cterminal TGS domain of the enzyme with the acyl carrier protein (ACP), a central co-factor in fatty acid biosynthesis. 

Several studies conducted in recent years on the stringent response of different bacterial pathogens indicate that (p)ppGpp along with other related regulatory factors may play critical roles in the regulation of expression of virulence genes (Abranches et al., 2009; Dahl et al., 2003; Dalebroux et al., 2009, 2010; Gaca et al., 2012; Geiger et al., 2014; Haralalka et al., 2003; Pal et al., 2011, 2012; Primm et al., 2000; Sun et al., 2009; Vogt et al., 2011; Wu and Xie, 2009). Previously, mutational analysis of the relA gene of V. cholerae has indicated that the stringent response molecule (p)ppGpp may modulate expression of major virulence genes in the strain used (Haralalka et al., 2003). This is one of the initial reports indicating that hampering (p)ppGpp metabolism may influence the virulence gene regulatory cascade of a pathogen. Currently, the concept is becoming established that (p)ppGpp indeed plays important roles in bacterial pathogenesis. This is conceptually probably correct since (p)ppGpp regulates several genes both positively and negatively in bacterial cells, and the slightest imbalance in concentration of this critical signaling molecule may alter the overall metabolism of a pathogen, including its virulence gene expression. 

While $\mathrm { R e l A } _ { \mathrm { E c h } }$ is responsible for (p)ppGpp synthesis under amino acid starvation conditions, SpoT synthesizes (p)ppGpp during carbon (glucose), fatty acid, phosphate, and iron starvation conditions (Battesti and Bouvaret, 2006; Cashel et al., 1996; Seyfzadeh et al., 1993; Spira et al., 1995; Vinella et al., 2005; Wendrich et al., 2002; Xiao et al., 1991). Functional characterization of the spoT gene of V. cholerae has been reported earlier from this laboratory (Das and Bhadra, 2008; Das et al., 2009). It has been found that V. cholerae relA deleted cells are able to synthesize (p)ppGpp under glucose or fatty acid starvation, indicating that, like in E. coli, V. cholerae RelA and SpoT enzymes have evolved with similar functions. Furthermore, it has been found that the spoT gene is essential in a relA+ background (Das and Bhadra, 2008), which is also true for E. coli. However, Das and Bhadra (2008) have found that, unlike E. coli, V. cholerae ΔrelA–ΔspoT mutant cells can synthesize a significant amount of (p)ppGpp under glucose or fatty acid starvation, which strongly suggests the existence of a novel gene coding for a (p)ppGpp synthesizing enzyme. In fact, Das et al. (2009) later on discovered the relV gene, which codes for a (p)ppGpp synthetase as predicted earlier by Das and Bhadra (2008) and discussed in further details here. Das et al. (2009) also tried to understand the role of the ACT domain in the hydrolase activity by deletion analysis, and they found that the ACT domain is indeed essential for (p)ppGpp hydrolase activity of the SpoT enzyme of V. cholerae. 

As further evidence of RelA- and/or SpoT-mediated (p)ppGpp accumulation in wild-type (Wt) and mutant V. cholerae cells under different starvation conditions, Das and Bhadra (2008) have shown differential regulation of intracellular rRNA concentration. High intracellular (p)ppGpp levels strongly inhibit rRNA transcription by affecting the stability of the RNA polymerase–promoter complex (Barker et al., 2001; Haugen et al., 2006; Srivatsan and Wang, 2008; Zhou and Jin, 1998). Das and Bhadra (2008) reported a significant decrease in intracellular rRNA level in Wt V. cholerae cells compared to ΔrelA and ΔrelA–ΔspoT strains upon amino acid–starved condition. This is to be expected since ribosome-bound RelA is activated by amino acid starvation, leading to rapid (p)ppGpp synthesis for quick downregulation of rRNA synthesis and ultimately inhibition of ribosome biogenesis followed by translational blockage. For this reason, deletion of relA usually imparts a “relaxed” phenotype (i.e., excess rRNA accumulation due to uncontrolled regulation of rRNA transcription in bacterial cells). On the other hand, our knowledge regarding glucose starvation and rRNA transcription in bacteria is limited. In V. cholerae, glucose starvation leads to significant reductions of cellular levels of rRNA in the Wt, ΔrelA, and ΔrelA–ΔspoT strains. These results suggest that SpoT is activated at least in the Wt and ΔrelA strains under glucose starvation, leading to an increase in cellular levels of (p)ppGpp, followed by repression of rRNA transcription. Interestingly, decrease of rRNA in the ΔrelA–ΔspoT strain is unusual and further suggests that there could be another source of (p)ppGpp in V. cholerae, which is activated under glucose starvation; this is discussed in detail in this chapter. 

## 7.4.3 Novel (p)ppGpp synthetase RelV of V. cholerae

In 2009, Das et al. first reported the existence of a small alarmone synthetase in γ-Proteobacteria, a GTPpyrophosphokinase with (p)ppGpp-synthesizing activity. The study was carried out on V. cholerae strain N16961, whose genome has been sequenced (Heidelberg et al., 2000), and the gene was named relV (JCVI annotation no. VC1224). However, similar genes coding for small alarmone synthetase (SAS) were also reported in two other members of firmicutes, Bacillus subtilis and Streptococcus mutans (Lemos et al., 2007; Nanamiya et al., 2008). Nanamiya et al. (2008) identified yjbM and ywaC in B. subtilis, and Lemos et al. (2007) identified relP and relQ in S. mutans, and all these gene products have similar (p)ppGpp synthetase activity to RelV. Recently, a SAS-like protein, called MS RHII-RSD, has been identified in Mycobacterium smegmatis (Murdeshwar and Chatterji, 2012). However, the size of this MS RHII-RSD is ∼56 kDa, which is much greater than the other functional SAS proteins, which are usually within the range of 30 kDa. Interestingly, MS RHII-RSD has been found to be evolved with dual functions: an RNase HII-like activity in its N-terminal region, and (p)ppGpp synthetase activity in its C-terminal region (Murdeshwar and Chatterji, 2012). 

To date, V. cholerae relV is the only SAS gene that has been identified and characterized from a Gram-negative bacterium. Since this relA-like gene is conserved in different Vibrio species, it was designated relV. Conservation of the relV gene in vibrios suggests its importance in this group of organisms. Comparison of the chromosomal organizations of the relV regions of other vibrios is shown in Figure 7.4.3. Note that the relV open reading frame (ORF) of the V. cholerae El Tor strain N16961 shares a 91 bp overlap with its downstream ORF VC1223, a hypothetical gene of unknown function, indicating that these genes are co-transcribed (Figure 7.4.3) and might be functionally related.
