Figure 7.4.3 Schematic representation (not drawn to scale) of genetic organizations of V. cholerae relV gene and its homologs in genomes of different Vibrio spp. as indicated in the left margin. Arrowheads indicate direction of transcription of genes, and KEGG (www.genome.jp/kegg/) annotation numbers are given above each gene. Black arrows represent relV and its homologs, and patterned arrows indicate the flanking genes VC1226 (codes for thiopurine S-methyltransferase) or VC1222 (codes for α subunit of integration host factor) and their homologs. Black line denotes chromosomal DNA. In V. cholerae N16961 strain, relV and VC1223 (dotted arrow) represent a bicistronic operon. In V. fischeri, flanking genes of relV are not conserved and replaced with different genes (www.genome.jp/kegg/).


Interestingly, the hypothetical gene VC1223 of unknown function appears to be present only in V. cholerae (Figure 7.4.3), and further research is needed to establish its functional relationship, if any, with relV. The 780-bp-long relV ORF encodes a 259-amino-acid-long enzyme RelV, which has only a single RSD region (http://www.kegg.jp/dbget-bin/www bget?vch:VC1224). Thus, it appears that the RelV regulon is quite unique compared to the canonical RelA–SpoT–Rel proteins, and it evolved to work independently without the control or assistance of the accessory domains TGS and/or ACT. 

Das et al. (2009) have reported that RelV is a significant source of (p)ppGpp in V. cholerae cells, since ΔrelA–ΔspoT mutant can accumulate substantial amounts of (p)ppGpp under glucose and fatty acid starvation conditions. This is further supported by the analysis of a ΔrelA–ΔspoT–ΔrelV triple mutant, which failed to accumulate (p)ppGpp upon depletion of glucose or fatty acid; the triple-mutant strain behaved like $( \mathrm { p } ) \mathrm { p p G p p } ^ { 0 }$ cells. It is noteworthy that RelV is also unique for its activation by the low glucose and fatty acid signalling system. In contrast, the other functional SAS genes so far characterized are activated through amino acid starvation signals like that of RelA (Gaca et al., 2012; Lemos et al., 2007; Nanamiya et al., 2008). The regulation of relV gene function is fascinating because ΔrelA– ΔspoT V. cholerae cells that are relV+ are viable. As discussed in this chapter, spoT is essential in the presence of functional relA, which is believed to be due to accumulation of (p)ppGpp to toxic levels in the absence of SpoT hydrolase activity (Das and Bhadra, 2008). Note, however, that the V. cholerae ΔrelA–ΔspoT–relV+ cells exhibit an extended lag period when grown in rich medium (Das and Bhadra, 2008; Das et al., 2009; He et al., 2012). Nevertheless, it may be hypothesized that the viability of V. cholerae ΔrelA–ΔspoT cells in the presence of functional RelV could be due to below-toxic-level (p)ppGpp accumulation through tight control of the RelV function, or there is a cryptic source of (p)ppGpp hydrolase or modifying enzymes in V. cholerae that modulates the optimal level of (p)ppGpp in the absence of the canonical SpoT. Interestingly, apart from the V. cholerae ΔrelA– ΔspoT mutant, other combinations of mutations (i.e., ΔrelA, ΔrelA–ΔrelV, ΔrelV, or ΔrelA–ΔspoT–ΔrelV) did not show any such defect in their growth in rich medium (Das and Bhadra, 2008; Das et al., 2009; He et al., 2012). However, further research is needed to unveil this mystery of relV biology. 

Recently, through extensive deletion analysis, Dasgupta et al. (2014) have identified the exact boundaries of the minimal (p)ppGpp synthesizing region of the V. cholerae RelV enzyme. Although bioinformatics analysis using KEGG (http://www.kegg.jp/dbget-bin/www bget?vch:VC1224) predicted that the RSD of RelV consists of a stretch of only 94 amino acid residues, it has been experimentally shown that the minimal functional region of RelV comprises 189 amino acids, which includes the predicted RSD region of 94 amino acids (Dasgupta et al., 2014). We believe that similar analysis of other SAS proteins will allow us to understand more clearly the boundaries of the minimal functional region of these enzymes. 

Nevertheless, the flanking residues apart from the conserved core region appear to be crucial in maintaining the catalytic activity of RelV. 

Extensive site-directed mutagenesis has also allowed us to determine the essentiality of the amino acids lysine, aspartate, arginine, leucine, or glutamate at positions 107, 129, 132, 150, or 188 (K107, D129, R132, L150, and E188, respectively) in the RSD region of RelV for (p)ppGpp synthetase activity (Dasgupta et al., 2014). The functional roles played by these amino acids in determining the synthetase function of RelV could be extrapolated from the crystal structure analysis of $\mathrm { R e l } _ { \mathrm { S e q } }$ with which RelV shares significant conservation of amino acid residues within the RSD region. Due to this conservation, RelV most likely maintains a similar structural fold of its RSD region as the corresponding region of the $\mathrm { R e l } _ { \mathrm { S e q } }$ protein (S. Dasgupta and R.K. Bhadra, unpublished observation). Amino acids K107, D129, and E188 of RelV correspond to the K243, D264, and E323 amino acids of the $\mathrm { R e l } _ { \mathrm { S e q } }$ protein. Hogg et al. (2004) predicted that K243 of $\mathrm { R e l } _ { \mathrm { S e q } }$ coordinates the β and γ phosphates of the donor ATP molecule during (p)ppGpp synthesis, whereas D264 and E323 residues bind the cofactor $\mathrm { M g } ^ { 2 + }$ ion. It thus appears that K107, D129, and E188 residues of the RelV protein most likely play similar functions as $\mathrm { R e l } _ { \mathrm { S e q } } .$ However, the availability of a crystal structure of any SAS protein may help in further understanding of their functional aspects. 

At present, evolution of relV and other SAS genes with respect to bacterial physiology is not clear; however, recent studies conducted on these genes may shed some light on this aspect. For example, very recently it has been shown that RelV plays important roles in regulating virulence-related traits of V. cholerae, including biofilm formation and CT production (He et al., 2012; Oh et al., 2014). He et al. (2012) reported that RelV is required for transcriptional activation of the biofilm regulators VpsR and VpsT. Oh et al. (2014) have shown that an artificially created anaerobic growth condition using trimethylamine N-oxide (TMAO) as an alternative electron acceptor highly induces CT production by V. cholerae cells, and TMAO treatment leads to elevation of intracellular (p)ppGpp levels. They have shown further that the RelV-mediated stringent response plays a crucial role in CT production by V. cholerae cells grown under TMAOinduced anaerobic respiration. According to Oh et al. (2014), TMAO treatment of V. cholerae cells may cause the generation of intracellular reactive oxygen species or an increase in pH, which in turn possibly induces the stringent response. Studies on other SAS proteins also indicate that different environmental cues may activate them in regulating various physiological processes. For example, alkaline stress condition or treatment of cells with antibiotics activates the SAS gene ywaC of B. subtilis, followed by increased (p)ppGpp production (D’Elia et al., 2009; Nanamiya et al., 2008). In contrast, the SAS gene products YjbM and YwaC of B. subtilis are found to be involved in motility and chaining of cells (Ababneh and Herman, 2015). Similarly, RelQ of Enterococcus faecalis has also been found to accumulate (p)ppGpp in response to alkaline shock, heat shock, vancomycin treatment, and modulation of virulence of this organism along with the canonical relA gene (Abranches et al., 2009). Recently, Geiger et al. (2014) reported that the relP and relQ genes of Staphylococcus aureus are activated under cell envelope stress upon treatment with ampicillin or vancomycin. Thus, it appears that the SAS gene products of different organisms have evolved specialized functions to modulate different physiological processes apart from mounting the stringent response under different environmental cues. However, at present, our knowledge about activation signals or mechanisms needed for SAS gene expression or SAS protein activity is limited. It is possible that SAS gene products are needed for nichespecific adaptation. Furthermore, currently we have no idea about the cellular location of any SAS protein, including RelV, although it is well established that the major (p)ppGpp synthetase RelA is a ribosomally attached enzyme and synthesizes (p)ppGpp in the presence of the L11 protein when uncharged tRNAs occupy ribosomal A sites under amino acid starvation conditions (Wendrich et al., 2002). Thus, research is warranted to understand the exact roles of RelV and other SAS proteins in bacterial physiology and their adaptation to various niches, including biofilm formation and maintenance of virulence phenotypes within the host environments. 

## 7.4.4 Stringent response regulatory protein DksA and V. cholerae

It has already been discussed here that (p)ppGpp has strong effects on the transcriptions of rRNA and amino acid biosynthesis operons under in vivo conditions. However, when studies were conducted under in vitro transcription assay conditions, such magnitudes of effects of (p)ppGpp were not observed, suggesting the existence of unknown cofactors that modulate (p)ppGpp activity under in vivo conditions. Several studies conducted in this direction suggest that DksA may be such a modulator (Magnusson et al., 2005; Paul et al., 2004; Perederina et al., 2004). First, in E. coli ΔdksA auxotrophy is suppressed by an rpoB mutation (ΔT563P), which in turn suppresses the auxotrophy of the $( \mathrm { p } ) \mathrm { p p G p p } ^ { 0 }$ cells (Murphy and Cashel, 2003). Second, the effects of dksA deletion on rpoS induction roughly parallel those of the $( \mathrm { p } ) \mathrm { p p G p p } ^ { 0 }$ condition (Brown et al., 2002; Hirsch and Elliott, 2002). Finally, it has been shown convincingly that DksA is indeed needed for the regulation of transcriptions of rRNA and amino acid biosynthetic genes along with (p)ppGpp under in vivo conditions. Furthermore, when DksA is added in in vitro assays, it greatly amplifies the inhibition of rRNA promoters and activates amino acid biosynthetic gene promoters via (p)ppGpp (Paul et al., 2004, 2005; Perederina et al., 2004). DksA was discovered as a dose-dependent suppressor of a dnaK deletion mutant by Kang and Craig (1990). DksA is a highly conserved small protein encoded by the gene dksA. Analysis of several microbial genomes reveals that dksA ORFs are also present in important human pathogens such as V. cholerae and Yersinia enterocolitica, the extremophiles Aquifex aeolicus and Psychrobacter sp., and the endosymbiont Blochmannia floridans (Perederina et al., 2004). High conservation of dksA in microbial genomes suggests that it most likely plays an important role in bacterial physiology. 

Unlike other transcriptional regulators, DksA does not bind to the regulatory part of a gene; rather, it binds to the secondary channel of RNA polymerase. The crystal structure of E. coli DksA has been elucidated, and it consists of a globular domain, and a coiled coil structure with a C4-type zinc finger motif (Paul et al., 2004; Perederina et al., 2004). Two highly conserved aspartic acid residues at positions 71 (D71) and 74 (D74), present at the tip of the coiled-coil domain of E. coli DksA protein, help in stabilizing the $\mathrm { ( p ) p p G p p { - } M g ^ { 2 + } { - } R N A P }$ complex (Perederina et al. 2004). In V. cholerae DksA, these residues are conserved at positions 68 and 71, respectively (Pal et al., 2011). 

Pal et al. (2012) first characterized the function of DksA of V. cholerae and showed that the protein is needed for the stringent response. Interestingly, the same study also revealed that DksA positively regulates different virulence-related traits of V. cholerae, which are motility, expression of the major secretory hemagglutinin protease (HAP), and production of CT (Pal et al., 2012). The positive regulation of motility is most likely mediated by the upregulation of expression of the motility control– related specific sigma factor FliA $( \sigma ^ { 2 8 } )$ . Expression of HAP in V. cholerae is under the strong positive control of the quorumsensing master regulator HapR (Jobling and Holmes, 1997; Lenz et al., 2004). Since the V. cholerae ΔdksA mutant produces less HAP, it could be possible that DksA positively controls HapR. Alternatively, DksA may directly control the expression of HAP, which needs further investigation. Pal et al. (2012) also found that deletion of dksA of V. cholerae leads to reduced CT production under in vitro conditions. Recently, Oh et al. (2014) have shown that DksA is absolutely needed for CT production by V. cholerae cells treated with TMAO, which induces anaerobic respiration. Note that, apart from V. cholerae, DksA has been shown to be involved in regulation of virulence in several other pathogens (Dalebroux et al., 2009; Holley et al., 2014; Jude et al., 2003; Nakanishi et al., 2006; Sharma and Payne, 2006; Turner et al., 1998; Webb et al., 1999; Yun et al., 2008), although the genetic circuits involved in these processes are not clear. Therefore, more studies are warranted to unravel the mechanisms of action of the mysterious protein DksA. 

## 7.4.5 Conclusion

To survive and grow, bacterial cells have evolved different gene regulatory circuits to adjust and respond swiftly to a myriad of environmental stresses, such as temperature, osmolarity, and nutritional availability. Among these environmental onslaughts, nutritional stress is critical and faced by all organisms, including pathogens. V. cholerae is able to manage aquatic environmental stresses and is also capable of handling adverse conditions in the human intestine. Perhaps in both these conditions, V. cholerae confronts nutritional starvation. During the past 40 years or so of research in the laboratory on artificial deprivation of bacteria with amino acids, carbon (glucose) or fatty acid has been shown to lead to the generation of tremendous knowledge about crucial genes and regulatory circuits involved in survival management under nutritional stresses. The issue was solved by the discovery of the intracellular signaling molecule (p)ppGpp (Cashel et al., 1996; Potrykus and Cashel, 2008; see Chapter 7.1). Analysis of available genomic sequences of diverse bacteria also indicates the ubiquitous presence of genes responsible for (p)ppGpp synthesis and leaves no doubt about the fundamental role of this cellular alarmone in controlling gene expression under nutritional stresses. In fact, during this post-genome-sequencing era, it has become easy to study stringent response–related genes of any bacteria, particularly of pathogens, to understand the role of (p)ppGpp in controlling virulence gene expression. We and others have found that the stringent response regulon, in fact, is involved in regulation of virulence in various pathogens. However, our knowledge about how (p)ppGpp and stringent response–related other regulators modulate bacterial virulence is in a rudimentary stage, but, considering how research is progressing in this direction, it is expected to be unraveled very soon. When this knowledge will be available, perhaps we will be better equipped to design specific therapeutic interventions, which is currently in great demand due to rapid development of resistance against commonly used antibiotics. In this respect, it is important to note that in Gram-negative Wt bacteria, spoT is an essential gene. Therefore, it could be targeted to develop new therapeutics. Similarly, recent research indicates that relacin, a novel (p)ppGpp analog with anti-Rel properties, interferes with bacterial persistence, biofilm formation, and so on (Wexselblatt et al., 2012). Thus, the future of bacterial stringent response– related work is challenging and appears to be bright.

## Responses to UV irradiation

# UV stress-responsive genes associated with enterobacterial integrative conjugative elements of the ICE SXT/R391 group

Patricia Armshaw and J. Tony Pembroke 

Molecular and Structural Biochemistry Laboratory, Materials and Surface Science Institute, Department of Chemical and Environmental Sciences, University of Limerick, Limerick, Ireland 

## 8.1.1 Integrative conjugative elements (ICEs) – an introduction

Many mobile genetic elements (MGEs) are known to respond to UV irradiation exposure (see Chapter 2.10). Generally, this response is of a beneficial nature to the host cell, enhancing the UV resistance of the organism in some manner (Lawrence et al., 1996; Little et al., 1991; Walker, 1977). ICEs of the SXT/R391 family are an unusual set of MGEs as exposure induces both beneficial and detrimental ICE-encoded functions (Pembroke and Stevens, 1984). These functions include enhancement of mutagenic DNA repair and recombination for survival and adaptation of the host organism. In addition, UV exposure causes an increase in ICE transfer rates to recipient cells and, unexpectedly for an MGE, a decrease in host cell survival rates post UV exposure (Armshaw and Pembroke, 2013a). This unusual array of UV-inducible, ICE-encoded phenotypes have generated significant interest in the examination of this particular group of MGEs. 

MGEs have played an important role in the generation of the enormous genetic diversity found within bacterial species. It is predicted that up to 32.6% of each microbial genome is composed of non-native DNA that has been acquired by horizontal gene transfer (Koonin et al., 2001; Sakharkar and Chow, 2008). With the recent increase in the availability of genome sequences, more MGEs or remnants of their presence are being discovered with features that identify them as being related to classical MGE groups but with deviating features (Smalla and Sobecky, 2002). These newly defined MGE classes include genomic islands, integrons, conjugative transposons, and ICEs (see Chapter 2.10). 

ICEs are one of the more interesting classes of the newly defined MGEs. Uniquely, ICEs exhibit both plasmid and phagelike characteristics. They can mediate their own integration and excision within a host genome and, when required, their transfer from one host to another (Michael et al., 2012; Taviani et al., 2009). ICEs self-encode all features necessary for their own mobility, integrating and replication similarly to temperate bacteriophage while utilising type IV conjugative transfer systems for inter-host transfer (Pembroke et al., 2002). These mosaic MGEs are theorised to have originally formed from a combinatorial event between chromosome, plasmid and phage DNA. However, it is also possible that ICEs predate other MGEs and are in fact an ancestral precursor of the more classically known groups (Rice et al., 2010; Seth-Smith and Croucher, 2009; te Poele et al., 2008; Wozniak and Waldor, 2009). 

Similar to other MGEs, ICEs generally maintain a core set of genes for basic functionality along with a large variety of accessory DNA that can significantly influence the characteristics of the host cell (Brochet et al., 2008; te Poele et al., 2008). This accessory DNA can encode many beneficial functions, including assisting host adaption to new environmental conditions and niches, with resistance and fitness genes (antibiotic, heavy metal, or phage resistance genes), metabolic-related genes (sucrose utilisation), general fitness advantage genes (bacteriocin synthesis, nitrogen fixation, and biofilm formation), or DNA repair genes (umuC/D homologues and exo/bet homologues) (Boltner et al., 2002; Bordeleau et al., 2010; Drenkard and Ausubel, 2002; Michael et al., 2012; Rice, 1998; Sullivan and Ronson, 1998). ICEs have also been known to increase strain pathogenicity by providing virulence determinants (Heather et al., 2008; Seth-Smith et al., 2012) or support genome variability and evolution by transferring large blocks of genes between unrelated bacteria either by self-transfer or by promoting the mobilisation of other mobile elements such as genomic islands (Daccord et al., 2010; Hochhut et al., 2000). Much of the accessory DNA of sequenced ICEs has not yet even been characterised and as such is of unknown function. These unidentified genes could potentially encode many other advantageous functions not described to date (Taviani et al., 2009; Toussaint et al., 2003). 

## 8.1.2 The SXT/R391 family of ICEs

Over 460 ICEs thus far have been identified in a variety of Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacterial genomes (Bi et al., 2012; Ryan et al., 2009; Van Houdt et al., 2011). With the advent of rapid genome sequencing, this number is ever increasing, allowing extensive bioinformatic comparative analysis of ICEs and leading to the subgrouping of ICEs into families. These ICE families are categorised based on the similarity of the ICE integrase gene and the specific integration site utilised within the host genome. One of the largest known families is the SXT/R391 group with 89 assigned ICEs (Bi et al., 2012). SXT/R391-like ICEs integrate within the prfC gene of Gramnegative bacteria (McGrath and Pembroke, 2004). They have been documented to exhibit several interesting features, including an unusual UV-associated sensitisation phenotype (Pembroke and Stevens, 1984) and an association with pathogenic Vibrio cholerae strains (Beaber et al., 2002b). This has generated a significant interest in the analysis of SXT/R391-like ICEs and is perhaps what led to the large level of detection and characterisation of ICEs of this family to date. 

## 8.1.3 SXT/R391-like ICEs – the core structure

Similar to other ICE families and as described in Figure 8.1.1, SXT/R391 ICEs have a modular structure containing a “core” set of genes that are required for basic functionality: maintenance within the host genome, integration and excision in and out of the genome, and transfer between donor and recipient cells (Burrus et al., 2002; Pembroke et al., 2002; Roberts and Mullany, 2009). 

In total, SXT/R391-like ICEs have 49 core genes that are present in all fully sequenced and functional elements. Twentynine of these genes have been characterised, with the majority (19) involved in ICE conjugation between donor and recipient cells, allowing the ICE to transfer between cells via a type IV conjugative pilus. ICEs encode all the conjugative transfer genes necessary for the preparation of the ICE DNA for transfer and synthesis of the pilus required (Bacic et al., 2005; Burrus and Waldor, 2004; Guglielmini et al., 2011; Ramsay et al., 2006; Wozniak and Waldor, 2010). 

Two more core genes, int and xis, are responsible for ICE integration and excision into and out of the host genome (see Figure 8.1.2) (O’Halloran et al., 2007). SXT/R391-like ICEs are maintained and replicated along with the host genome within the prfC gene, the specific integration site of the SXT/R391 ICE family, until induced to excise and transfer to a new host. Remarkably, SXT/R391-like ICEs have been found to provide a replacement 5′ end to replace the truncated prfC gene which occurs on integration and thus generate a hybrid prfC gene such that function is unaffected upon integration (McGrath and Pembroke, 2004). 

Twenty of the core genes of SXT/R391-like ICEs are of unknown function. A number have been hypothesised to encode host-beneficial functions which are unrelated to basic ICE functionality (e.g., rumB, rumA, bet, and exo) but may have host benefit on occasions such as enhancement of mutagenesis and recombination for survival and adaptation. The core structure of all SXT/R391-like ICEs is interrupted in similar locations by a variable amount of diverse accessory DNA in each individual ICE (see Figure 8.1.3) (Wozniak et al., 2009). The size range of these insertion regions varies widely between different ICEs. Amongst the fully sequenced SXT/R391 ICEs, between 1 and 46 hypothetical genes have been found in the same hotspot within different ICEs. The functionality of these variable regions remains unknown with only one notable exception: the kanamycin resistance gene (aph) of ICE R391 in hotspot 1 (Boltner et al., 2002). 

## 8.1.4 The SXT/R391 family of ICEs – a phenotypical history

SXT/R931 family ICEs were first identified due to the antibiotic resistance genes they carry. SXT-like ICEs have a resistance cluster that integrates into the ICE core rumB gene (Figure 8.1.1.). This cluster can vary and has been shown to encode for resistance to chloramphenicol, sulfamethoxazole, trimethoprim, streptomycin, and occasionally tetracycline in some SXT variants (Beaber et al., 2002b). The second prototype, ICE R391, encodes kanamycin and mercury resistance (Boltner et al., 2002). Initially, these ICEs were mistakenly assumed to be plasmids and miscategorised as transferable antibiotic resistance determinants. The prototype member, ICE R391, isolated in 1967 from a human faeces sample in Pretoria, South Africa, from a kanamycin-resistant Proteus rettgeri showed low transfer frequency and was assigned to a new plasmid incompatibility group, IncJ, as the prototype member (Coetzee et al., 1972). Later, after further analysis, the IncJ group members were reclassified as the SXT/R391 family of ICEs. In general, SXT/R391 ICEs carry a variety of antibiotic resistance genes, and this was the basis for the initial surge of interest in these elements, especially as discovery of these ICEs had an association with pandemic V. cholerae strains (Waldor and Mekalanos, 1994; Waldor et al., 1996).

## 8.1.4.1 The UV sensitising phenotype of SXT/R391-like ICEs

While characterising phenotypes associated with SXT/R391- like ICEs, a unique UV-inducible cell-sensitising phenotype was discovered (Pembroke and Stevens 1984). Many SXT/R391- like ICEs were found to confer a significantly reduced post– UV irradiation survival rate on their host (see Figure 8.1.4) (McGrath et al., 2006; Pembroke and Stevens, 1984; Upton and Pinney, 1983). This was unusual as MGEs previously found to be involved in post–UV irradiation survival mechanisms were usually beneficial (e.g., pKM101) and not detrimental to host survival (Little et al., 1991; Walker, 1977). This unique phenotype was extensively characterised in the prototype ICE R391. ICE R391 was completely sequenced (Boltner et al., 2002), and several candidate ICE R391 genes were suspected to be involved. As the phenotype was found to be preserved across numerous SXT/R391-like ICEs, it was presumed that a core ICE gene (or genes) of unknown function was (or were) responsible for the sensitising phenotype. Previously, the usually beneficial effect of plasmids on UV survival had been linked to homologues of umuCD genes in the IncN plasmid pKM101 (Walker, 1977) involved in mutagenic DNA repair (Montibragadin et al., 1976; Walker and Dobson, 1979). The ICE R391 rumAB genes are functional homologues of umuCD which encode a polIV-like, Y-family, error-prone DNA polymerase that promotes a high level of mutagenesis during its repair action (Mead et al., 2007; Szekeres et al., 1996). Biochemical analysis has demonstrated that rumA and rumB are functional in ICE R391 but interrupted by inserts in SXT-like elements (Mead et al., 2007). The DNA polIV-like Y-family polymerase polV encoded by the rumAB genes of ICE R391 when cloned and expressed have been shown to induce higher levels of spontaneous mutagenesis in E. coli than its related umuCD-encoded counterpart, indicating that its hypothesised function in increasing bacterial diversity is likely (Ho et al., 1993; Mead et al., 2007). It was initially thought that rumAB might interfere with UV survival through blocking of DNA repair pathways (Ho et al., 1993; Kulaeva et al., 1995; Pembroke and Stevens, 1984; Strike and Lodwick, 1987; Upton and Pinney, 1983). However, knockouts of the rumAB genes do not abolish the UV sensitising effect (Armshaw and Pembroke, 2013a). Therefore, SXT/R391-like ICEs possess both apparently beneficial and detrimental functions that are UV-inducible. It is possible that these various phenotypes are induced by different levels of UV irradiation exposure for dissimilar unknown purposes.

## 8.1.4.2 Other SXT/R391 ICE UV-associated phenotypes

Interestingly, several other UV-inducible, ICE, and hostbeneficial phenotypes have been found associated with the SXT/R391 family of ICEs. The conjugative transfer rate of SXT/R391 family members to recipient cells is increased by preexposure to UV irradiation with enhancement of transfer from $1 0 ^ { - 5 }$ to $1 0 ^ { - 3 }$ per donor. This transfer enhancement has been linked to the upregulation of the ICE xis gene, which is UVinducible (McGrath et al., 2005; O’Halloran et al., 2007). For ICE R391, it has been shown that the upregulation of jef (xis) transcription causes an increase in the excised circular transfer form of ICE R391 (O’Halloran et al., 2007), making more circular forms available for conjugation. In addition, it was found that deletion of jef had no effect on cell sensitisation, suggesting that UV exposure stimulated multiple SXT/R391 ICE functions and that there may be a complex recA-mediated stress inducible pathway involved. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/6c2e57f4-f177-4731-acc4-f560c6f82e69/0c84759185a57396e5d895565eff875a8c43c4a29b3a94f7dc55b475e3b7f05a.jpg)


Another set of ICE-related, UV-associated genes are bet and exo. These genes are annotated as homologues of the bet and exo genes from E. coli λ phage and are known to function in homologous DNA recombination (Radding, 1970; Signer et al., 1968). The SXT Exo and Bet proteins have been examined (Chen et al., 2011), and the Exo protein has been shown to function in double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) and single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) degradation. The Bet protein functions in the stimulation of this activity (Chen et al., 2011). Co-expression of both has been shown to promote homologous recombination between PCR fragments and the chromosome (Chen et al., 2011). The SXT/R391 ICE family exo and bet homologues are unusual as they are the only non-phage-associated homologues found to date. It is possible that these genes are encoded on SXT/R391

The function of these genes has been suggestively linked to UV irradiation in multiple ways, and indeed the rate of homologous recombination activity is increased upon damage in ICE R391– containing hosts (Pembroke and Stevens, 1984). In addition, UV damage has been shown to provide suitable recombination substrates in the form of dsDNA breaks and increases the expression of these genes. However, the mechanism by which UV irradiation induces these genes is currently unknown (Garris et al., 2009). 

## 8.1.5 Identification of the sensitising genes of ICE R391

The sequencing of the complete genome of ICE R391 (Boltner et al., 2002) eventually led to the identification of the specific ICE-associated genes involved in UV sensitisation (Armshaw and Pembroke, 2013a). Based on the nucleotide sequence, a detailed ICE R391 gene deletion library (Armshaw and Pembroke, 2013a) was generated specifically to screen for the reversal of the cell-sensitising phenotype and identify the genes involved. This library identified the specific ICE R391 genes involved in sensitisation as orfs90/91 and orf43 (a traV homologue) (Armshaw and Pembroke, 2013a). This result was unexpected as these core ICE genes already had putative functions. orf90 and orf91 were hypothesised to encode a transcriptional enhancer complex that stimulates the expression of ICE-encoded genes such as jef (xis) and int (Beaber et al., 2004; O’Halloran et al., 2007). Orf43 was bioinformatically predicted as a structural homologue of TraV, a protein involved in type IV conjugative pilus formation. Further characterisation of these genes found that deletion of orf43 also abolished conjugative transfer (Armshaw and Pembroke, 2013b), suggesting that the gene may encode a protein with dual function. It was also determined that the product of orfs90/91, the putative transcriptional enhancer, increased the expression level of orf43 within the host cell (Armshaw and Pembroke, 2013a) such that its function might be to provide increased levels of Orf43 upon damage-induced stress. Cloning and expression analysis of both orf90/91 and orf43 determined that the expression of orf43 alone was sufficient for causation of the cell-sensitising phenotype (Armshaw and Pembroke, 2013b). However, the exact nature by which orf43 expression could be cytotoxic has yet to be characterised.

## 8.1.7 Conclusion



Hochhut B, Marrero J, Waldor MK. 2000. Mobilization of plasmids and chromosomal DNA mediated by the SXT element, a constin found in Vibrio cholerae O139. Journal of Bacteriology 182(7): 2043–2047. 





Van Houdt R, Toussaint A, Ryan MP, Pembroke JT, Mergeay M, et al. 2011. Tn4731 ICE family of bacterial mobile genetic elements. In Bacterial integrative mobile genetic elements (ed. Roberts AP, Mullany P). Austin, TX: Landes BioSciences, pp. 1–22. 



ICEs of the SXT/R391 family encode multiple UV-inducible genes. These genes express functions that can be either beneficial or apparently detrimental to the host and/or the ICE itself. These functions include bacterial diversity promotion through homologous recombination which may be beneficial to both the host cell and the ICE, mutagenic DNA repair which may aid in rapid recovery from damaging agents or rapid adaptive evolution by promoting mutagenesis, and unusually host sensitisation through the expression of a type IV conjugative gene. It is likely that this apparently detrimental sensitising phenotype is beneficial to either the host cell or the ICE encoding it in some manner. This would explain why the orf43 gene is one of the most highly conserved (≥98% at the nucleotide level) core ICE genes (Armshaw and Pembroke, 2013a). The pathway known to induce orf43 also induces the expression of the int and xis genes. Possibly, the interaction of these three ICE genes may have some manner of host–ICE beneficial effect.

# Altered outer membrane proteins in response to UVC radiation in Vibrio parahaemolyticus and Vibrio alginolyticus

Fethi Ben Abdallah 

Laboratory of Genetic, Biodiversity and Bio-resources Valorization, Higher Institute of Biotechnology, Monastir, Tunisia Department of Biology, College of Sciences, Taif University, KSA 

## 8.2.1 Introduction

Bacteria can sense and respond to changes in their external environment (Ben Abdallah et al., 2009). The ability of Vibrio spp. to sense and respond effectively to changes in the environment is crucial for their survival (Morita, 1997). Bacteria in nature have cellular physiological systems to protect cells from various stresses such as ultraviolet (UV) irradiation (Friedberg, 2008). Marine bacteria, such as Vibrio alginolyticus and Vibrio parahaemolyticus, are exposed to solar UV radiation daily. The response of marine bacteria to ultraviolet-A (UVA) irradiation is considered important because approximately 95% of UV radiation is UVA (320–400 nm). However, bacteria are also exposed to ultraviolet-C (UVC) (254 nm) radiation, which is used as a disinfection method to kill bacteria and prevent food poisoning in humans (Ben Said et al., 2010). 

UVC radiation has been suggested as one of the successful disinfection practices for water treatment. Therefore, UV sterilization has become a practical solution for safe disinfection of water (Ben Said et al., 2010). The effectiveness of UV radiation in biological inactivation arises primarily from the fact that DNA molecules absorb UV photons between 200 and 300 nm, with peak absorption at 254 nm (Jeffrey et al., 1990). This absorption creates damage in the DNA by altering the nucleotide base pairing, thereby creating new linkages between adjacent nucleotides on the same DNA strand (Sabri et al., 2000). Several investigators have determined the effects of UV radiation on the inhibition of growth (Zabala et al., 2009) and damage of outer membrane proteins (OMPs) for Vibrio (Ben Abdallah et al., 2012). Many vibrios are pathogenic for humans and/or marine vertebrates and invertebrates (Zhang and Austin, 2005). OMPs, whose production is often regulated by environmental cues, play important roles in bacterial pathogenesis by enhancing the adaptability of the pathogens to various environments. Thus, OMPs contribute to the virulence of bacteria and play essential roles in bacterial adaptation to host niches, which are usually hostile to invading pathogens (Lin et al., 2002). 

## 8.2.2 Bacterial OMP functions

In Gram-negative pathogenic bacteria, the outer membrane plays an important role in the infection and pathogenicity to the host (Tsolis, 2002). In the outer membrane, proteins have crucial roles during many cellular and physiological processes (Qian et al., 2008). OMPs play a key role in the adaptation to changes in external environments, due to their location at the outermost area of the cell (Xu et al., 2005). OmpX is synthesized in large amounts in stress situations, and it is probably used as a defensive weapon, binding to and thus interfering with foreign proteins (Vogt and Schulz, 1999). In contrast to OmpX, the long external loops of OmpA are highly mobile and for the most part not visible in the respective electron density map (Schulz, 2002). In vivo, the mobile loops are rather resistant to proteolytic attack, presumably because they bind to the surrounding lipopolysaccharides. Obviously, the mobile loops fulfill essential functions in bacterial life (Morona et al., 1984). 

The outer membrane enzyme OmpT is a special protease that has been implicated in the pathogenicity of bacteria. It is monomeric, with the active center pointing to the outside (Vandeputte-Rutten et al., 2001). A further enzyme, the phospholipase A OmpLA, produces holes in the outer membrane when it is activated. 

The general porins contain pores with sizes allowing the permeation of molecules with molecular masses up to about 600 Da (Nikaido, 1994). Porins OmpF, PhoE, and OmpC from Escherichia (Cowan et al., 1992) show permeation properties adjusted to different environmental conditions. PhoE allows an efficient uptake of phosphate. OmpC from E. coli and its homolog OmpK36 from Klebsiella pneumoniae (Dutzler et al., 1999) are osmoporins that are expressed at high osmotic pressures usually caused by high salt concentrations. 

## 8.2.3 Identification of altered OMPs under UVC radiation

Generally, bacteria such as V. alginolyticus and V. parahaemolyticus respond to stress by modifying the rate of synthesis of certain proteins (Ben Abdallah et al., 2009). Until now, few investigations have explored the effects of UVC radiation on the OMPs. Indeed, Ben Abdallah and collaborators (2012) have identified UVC-altered OMPs in Vibrio alginolyticus and V. parahaemolyticus using mass spectrometry (MS) and tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) (Table 8.2.1). First, a variable interspecies and intraspecies response has been noted. Thereby, each strain responds differently to UVC radiation. 

Alterations in the OMPs’ profiles of UVC-irradiated V. alginolyticus and V. parahaemolyticus are manifested by the appearance of several OMPs (Table 8.2.1) such as OmpW, OmpA, long-chain fatty acid transport protein, outer membrane receptor protein, putative uncharacterized protein VP0167, maltoporin, polar flagellin B/D, agglutination protein peptidoglycan-associated lipoprotein, and MltA-interacting protein (MipA). Thus, they can be considered as UVC stress proteins in some vibrio species. In addition, OMP, putative OMP, putative outer membrane porin protein, and putative OMP OmpA are induced under UVC radiation. These proteins can be regarded as UVC-inducible proteins. Furthermore, Nicholson et al. (1987) have demonstrated that UV radiation induces the synthesis of several proteins in Phormidium zaminosum. In addition, the RecA protein is induced in UV-irradiated E. coli (Bockrath and Hanawalt, 1980) 

The new and induced OMPs can protect V. alginolyticus and V. parahaemolyticus against UVC radiation. After the beginning of an adverse effect, such as irradiation, the synthesis of proteins is inhibited and cell division is interrupted. In parallel, the expression of several proteins increases; these are the socalled stress proteins (Kustos et al., 2007). OMPs are probably produced to stimulate the bacterial cells to enter an exponential growth phase in a shorter time and grow at a faster rate; this mechanism is important for a bacterial population to survive under UV radiation. 

UVC radiation can also reduce the level of expression of the vitamin $\mathrm { B } _ { 1 2 }$ receptor and maltoporin in V. alginolyticus and V. parahaemolyticus. According to Miller et al. (1999), UV radiation can cause indirect damage to DNA by generating reactive oxygen species that then damage bases, break strands, and cross-link DNA and proteins. Degradation of bacterial OMPs under UVC radiation could be due to any of the mechanisms proposed for protein inactivation by UV radiation (Mody et al., 1991). These include (i) splitting of disulfide bonds of cystine or photooxidation of tyrosine, thereby changing the tertiary structure of proteins; or (ii) ring cleavage in the aromatic part of the proteins. 

Comparative studies of the effects of starvation, gamma irradiation, and UVC irradiation on the OMPs of V. alginolyticus and V. parahaemolyticus have been carried out (Ben Abdallah et al., 2010, 2012). Under gamma irradiation, the authors have not observed gamma-induced proteins, since the expression level of all altered OMPs identified is reduced, whereas MipA appears; therefore, the latter may be involved in a gammairradiation stress response of vibrio. This is contrary to starvation conditions, in which the alterations of OMPs are less accentuated, but they are more accentuated compared to UVC irradiation conditions. 

Changes in environmental conditions influence the expression of ${ \mathrm { O M P s } } ,$ and a rise in temperature may induce significant changes in the OMP expression of E. coli (Molloy et al., 2000) and Borrelia burgdorferi (Obonyo et al., 2002). Acidic pH induced the expression of new proteins on the surface of Yersinia pestis (Feodorova and Devdariani, 2001), and OMP expression in B. burgdorferi is also altered at different pH values (Carroll et al., 1999). 

Modifications observed in the OMP patterns of UVCirradiated V. alginolyticus and V. parahaemolyticus may indicate the existence of certain modifications of resistance toward some antibiotics. Indeed, Mushtaq et al. (2004) have described the loss of the OprD protein from the OMPs of Pseudomonas aeruginosa strains, which causes increased resistance against carbapenems. Chen and Livermore (1993) have demonstrated the resistance to β-lactam antibiotics owing to the lack of OmpC and OmpF in the OMPs of Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae. The various alterations observed in the OMP profiles of UVC-irradiated V. alginolyticus and V. parahaemolyticus reflect the stability of these virulence factors under stress conditions. In addition, these alterations are variable inter- and intraspecies. This can be related to the genomic plasticity of the tested strains. 

## 8.2.4 Conclusions

In summary, V. alginolyticus and V. parahaemolyticus are able to adapt and respond to UVC radiation by changing their OMPs’ profiles. These modifications are manifested by the appearance of proteins as well as by a decrease and/or increase in the expression level of certain proteins. In addition, certain OMPs appear. This allows us to define UVC stress proteins capable of protecting these bacteria against UV radiation.

# Ultraviolet-B radiation effects on the community, physiology, and mineralization of magnetotactic bacteria

## Yingzhao Wang1,2 and Yongxin Pan1,2

1Biogeomagnetism Group, PGL, Key Laboratory of Earth and Planetary Physics, Institute of Geology and Geophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China 

2France-China Bio-Mineralization and Nano-Structures Laboratory, Institute of Geology and Geophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China 

## 8.3.1 Introduction

Solar radiation reaching the Earth can be divided into solar particle flux and electromagnetic waves (Iqbal, 1983). The Earth’s magnetic field shields most charged particles, but solar electromagnetic radiation can partially penetrate the Earth’s atmosphere and thus impact life on Earth (Cox et al., 1964; Crain, 1971; Glassmeier et al., 2009; Hays, 1971). Although it contributes only ∼8% to the whole solar electromagnetic spectrum, ultraviolet radiation (UVR) – which has wavelengths between 200 and 400 nm and is composed of ultraviolet-A (UVA; 320– 400 nm), ultraviolet-B (UVB; 290–320 nm), and ultraviolet-C (UVC; 200–290 nm) – can induce a variety of biological damages, such as damage to DNA, proteins, enzymes, and lipids (Cockell, 2000; Garcia-Pichel, 1998; Hader and Sinha, 2005; Jag- ¨ ger, 1985; Singh et al., 2010). Therefore, studies of UVR’s effects on life are of fundamental importance for understanding the origin and evolution of the biosphere on Earth and searching for extraterrestrial life. 

The oxidative state of Earth can be roughly divided into the anoxic period and oxic period corresponding to, respectively, before and after the great oxygenic event (GOE) at ∼2.5 Ga (Figure 8.3.1) (Bekker et al., 2004; Berner et al., 2003; Carver, 1981; Kasting, 1993; Kasting and Donahue, 1980; Kump, 2008). During the early stage, the biological effects of UVR were estimated to be about threefold higher in magnitude than in the present time, and the short-wavelength UVR has been known to be lethal for cells and a strong DNA mutagenic agent (Cockell, 1998). With the later formation of a natural UVR filter (i.e., the stratospheric ozone layer), UVR flux on the Earth’s surface could be significantly reduced in the Earth’s oxic period. 

However, the ozone layer protection is somehow unstable. For example, the instability of the ozone layer may be partially attributed to the variation of the geomagnetic field, which is an important shelter for life on Earth but changes over geological time (Glassmeier et al., 2009; Guyodo and Valet, 1999; Juarez et al., 1998; Pan and Zhu, 2011). During geomagnetic field reversal or excursion, the field is tilting, and its dipolar field strength drops to about 10–20% of the value of the present-day field (e.g., Cox et al., 1964; Glassmeier and Vogt, 2010; Mochizuki et al., 2011; Zhu et al., 2000). In this case, high-energy particles can penetrate into the middle atmosphere and photocatalyze nitrogen and oxygen into nitric oxide (a ozone depletion agent), thus depleting the ozone layer (Kerr and McElroy, 1993; Ma and Guicherit, 1997; Solomon, 1999). Numerical models also have been proposed that a decrease in the geomagnetic field results in an enhancement of UVR reaching the Earth’s surface (Glassmeier et al., 2009; Laˇstovicka, 2003; Lee and Kodama, 2009;ˇ Sinnhuber et al., 2003; Winkler et al., 2008). 

Microbes might have existed on Earth for at least ∼3.5 Ga and thus have coevolved with the Earth’s surface environments (Abrevaya et al., 2013; Cockell and Raven, 2007; Ehling-Schulz and Scherer, 1999; Glikson, 2014; Mojzsis et al., 1996; Sagan, 1973; Schopf, 2006, 2012). To avoid deleterious or lethal UVR, microbes have developed multiple strategies to mitigate its harmful effects, such as possessing a fast escape ability, DNA damage repair systems (see Chapters 8.2, 8.4), reactive oxygen species (ROS)-scavenging enzymes (see Section 10), and synthesis of UV-absorbing chemical compounds or protecting sheaths (Ehling-Schulz and Scherer, 1999; Gao and Garcia-Pichel, 2011; Goosen and Moolenaar, 2008; Hader¨ et al., 1998; Phoenix and Konhauser, 2008; Sinha and Hader, 2002a,b, 2008). For¨ examples, pigments have been formed by some cyanobacteria, acting as a passive sunscreen in protection against UVR (Dillon and Castenholz, 1999; Grant and Louda, 2013; Leavitt et al., 1997; Soule et al., 2009; Squier et al., 2004). The iron–silica biomineral-containing, filamentous cyanobacterium Calothrix exhibits a much stronger resistance to UVR than the same bacterium without a mineral sheath (Phoenix et al., 2001, 2006). Other microbes that possess the ability to calcify or synthesize iron–oxide sheaths are also supposed to shade harmful UVR (Emerson et al., 2010; Hedrich et al., 2011; Merz and Zankl, 1993; Merz-Preiß, 2000). In this scenario, UVR can shape the structures of microorganism communities because the sensitivity of microbes to UVR is highly variable and species specific (Langenheder et al., 2006; Nunez et al., 2006; Pajares et al., 2012; Roux et al., 2002; Winter et al., 2001). Previous artificial UVR simulations have shown that increased radiation input results in reduced diversity, with dominance by a few resistant bacteria species (Santos et al., 2011a,b, 2012b,c). Studies on benthic diatom mats also demonstrate increased UV screening compounds synthesis and a significant decrease in cell abundance under enhanced UVB radiation (Underwood et al., 2002).

Magnetotactic bacteria (MTB) are a group of prokaryotes that can synthesize intracellular magnetite $( \mathrm { F e } _ { 3 } \mathrm { O } _ { 4 } )$ or/and greigite $( \mathrm { F e } _ { 3 } \mathrm { S } _ { 4 } )$ particles (Bazylinski et al., 2013; Faivre and Schuler,¨ 2008; Komeili, 2012). These particles, called magnetosomes and usually arranged in one or multiple chains within a cell, help MTB navigate along the magnetic field (Lin et al., 2013a; Pan et al., 2009). Owing to the formation of iron-rich magnetosome crystals within the bacteria and their ubiquitous distribution in aquatic environments, MTBs are considered to play a vital role in the global iron cycle through biological and geochemical processes (Chen et al., 2014a,b; Lin et al., 2013b; Lins et al., 2007; Moisescu et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2013a). The magnetosome crystals can also be preserved as fossil biominerals (i.e., magnetofossils) after MTB die and are buried (Jimenez-Lopez et al., 2010; Li et al., 2013; Pan et al., 2005). They are potential geological records for paleoenvironmental and paleomagnetic information, as well as biosignatures for searching early life on Earth and even life on other habitable planets, such as Mars (Kim et al., 2005; Kopp et al., 2006, 2007; Liu et al., 2015; McKay et al., 1996; Moskowitz et al., 1993; Paterson et al., 2013). The MTB communities and magnetosome biomineralization have been found to be influenced by several environmental factors, such as oxygen, salinity, temperature, and strength of the geomagnetic field (Chen et al., 2014a,b; Faivre et al., 2008; Li and Pan, 2012; Lin et al., 2011, 2012, 2013a; Lins et al., 2007; Moisescu et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2013a). Our recent studies indicate that UVB irradiation could cause cell growth delay and enhance the magnetosome synthesis within Magnetospirillum magneticum AMB-1 under defined UVB irradiation conditions (Wang et al., 2013b). Yet, how UVB radiation affects MTB diversity and synthesis of intracellular magnetosomes remains poorly understood. In the present study, we investigated the various effects of UVB irradiation on natural uncultured MTB abundance and community, and the physiology and magnetite biomineralization of a newly isolated MTB strain, Magnetospirillum sp. XM-1. ROS effects on irradiated MTBs are also discussed, and a hypothetic model is proposed. 

## 8.3.2 Materials and experimental methods

Field sampling: Surface sediment samples (∼10 cm depth) were collected from a site $( 3 4 ^ { \circ } 1 5 ^ { \prime } 1 0 . 0 0 ^ { \prime \prime } \mathrm { N } .$ , 108◦55′ 13.41′′E) in the city moat of Xi’an, China. Information on the sampling site has been elaborated in Wang et al. (2013a). Specifically, the temperature and oxygen concentration of the sampling layer were $2 3 . 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and 0.27 mg/L, respectively. The water pH ranged from 7.1 to 7.5, and salinity was less than 0.34 ppt. The city moat was slightly eutrophicated, and it contained nearly 50 mg/L $\mathrm { N H _ { 4 } } ^ { + }$ , 250 mg/L ${ \mathrm { S O } } _ { 4 } ^ { 2 - }$ −, and $4 \mathrm { m g / L } \mathrm { P O } _ { 4 } { } ^ { 3 - }$ − when sampled in late autumn (October) 2012. The collected samples were transported to the lab at room temperature and incubated for a few weeks until the MTB community reached a stable state. Light microscopic and transmission electron microscope (TEM) observations revealed that the sediment used in this study was dominated by magnetotactic cocci (Figure 8.3.2).

Figure 8.3.2 Transmission electron microscope (TEM) micrographs of natural magnetotactic cocci collected from a city moat in Xi’an, China. Scale bar = 500 nm.


UVB irradiation experimental setup: Microcosm experiments were conducted using 50 mm sterilized plastic culture dishes. Each microcosm was prepared by gently adding 2 mL of thoroughly homogenized, live MTB–containing sediments and 3 mL of lake water into the dishes. Four different irradiation simulation conditions designated as the control (darkness), the predicted Archean condition (10.8 W/m2), calculated geomagnetic field reversal period levels (4.1 W/m2), and the present-day (2.6 W/m2) UVB strength analog levels were established (Cockell, 1998; Glassmeier et al., 2009). The UVB intensities were finely adjusted by adding a number of UVB lamps (USHIO, Japan) and measured using a double-channel UVB radiometer with a detective range between 275 and 330 nm (Beijing Normal University, China). Three samples were carefully put into each irradiation chamber and irradiated for 7 days before collection and analyses. 

Cell counting and TEM observation: MTB cells were counted using the hanging-drop method under the light microscope (Flies et al., 2005; Lin et al., 2012). For each microcosm, sediment and water were thoroughly mixed, and three positions with 10 μL of specimen from each dish were randomly chosen for counting. Average accumulated living MTB number per liter was considered as the abundance of each microcosm. The sediment and water of each microcosm were transferred into clean sterilized 10 ml tubes, and MTB were magnetically enriched through a capillary racetrack method for 6 h (Li et al., 2010; Wolfe et al., 1987). Five capillaries were used for each microcosm. The collected cells were stored in 1.5 ml Eppendorf tubes for further tests. For TEM analysis, 10 μL of the samples was dropped onto carbon-coated TEM copper grids. After 2 h, the excess water was removed by filter paper and washed twice with pure water. Specimens were air-dried and analyzed by a JEM-1400 microscope with an acceleration voltage of 80 kV (JEOL Corporation, Japan). 

16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene phylogenetic analysis: Two microliters of each enriched bacterial sample were used for 16S rRNA gene amplification by bacterial universal primers 27F (5′ -AGAGTTTGATCCTGGCTCAG-3′ ) and 1492R (5′ - GGTTACCTTGTTACGACTT-3′ ). The detailed PCR program was described previously in Wang et al. (2013a). All PCR products were purified and ligated into the pMD19- T vector (TaKaRa, China). DH5α competent cells (Tiangen, China) were used as the vector host, and after 15 h incubation at ${ } ^ { 3 7 } \ { } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$ 20 clones of each microcosm were randomly selected and sequenced at the Beijing Genomics Institute in Beijing, China. Low-quality sequences were manually removed, and chimeras were checked using the Greengenes chimera-check tool (Bellerophon server). Two hundred and thirty-seven nearly complete 16S rRNA gene sequences were blasted against the Nucleotide database on the US National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) website (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/nuccore). In total, 192 high-quality sequences were similar to known MTB and were considered in the present study. Complete linkage clustering of each microcosm was performed on RDPipeline (Cole et al., 2013). The phylogenetic distances between MTB communities from each microcosm were determined using the unweighted UniFrac algorithm (Lozupone and Knight, 2005). 

Magnetospirillum sp. XM-1 cultivation and experimental layout: In order to further examine how UVB irradiation influences biomineralization, the cultivated Magnetospirillum sp. XM-1 that was recently isolated from the Xi’an city moat was investigated (Wang et al., 2015). Strain XM-1 was cultivated in XM- ${ \bf \cdot C _ { B } }$ medium, which contains 5 ml Wolfe mineral solution, 5 mM potassium phosphate, 2 mM sodium nitrate, 5 mM sodium succinate, and 100 μM ferric citrate. After 2 days of incubation at 28 ◦C within sealed bottles, cells were transferred to high-purity quartz bottles with the same growth medium and cultivated for approximately 24 h until the cells reached the exponential growth phase, corresponding to the magnetosome synthesizing period. The irradiation system used in this study was described previously in Wang et al. (2013b). The UVB intensity was $2 . 7 ~ \mathrm { W / m } ^ { 2 }$ , similar to the above-described present-day UVB strength. In order to ensure the evenness of irradiation, we agitated the cells with a magnetic stirrer to prevent cell sedimentation and ensure vertical and horizontal mixing of cell suspension with 162 $\mathrm { J } / \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 }$ UVB doses. Irradiated bacteria and the dark control were quickly concentrated at 6000 rpm at $4 ~ { } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ and transferred into sealed fresh ${ \mathrm { X M - C } } _ { \mathrm { B } }$ medium with a series of initial oxygen concentrations (<0.01, 0.39, 0.62, 1.72, 2.34, 4.65, 8.34, 9.94, 14.21, 21.67, and >25 mg/L) to evaluate the biomineralization processes. 

Reactive oxygen species (ROS) analysis: The ROS contents in the XM-1 cells of the control and irradiation groups were analyzed by using the $2 ^ { \prime } , 7 ^ { \prime }$ -dichlorofluorescin diacetate (DCFH-DA) method described by He and Hader (2002a,b).¨ DCFH-DA is hydrolyzed to DCFH after transfer into the cell. Then, DCFH trapped within cell membranes and intracellular ROS can oxidize nonfluorescent DCFH into highly fluorescent DCF. In the present study, ROS content of XM-1 cells was measured at 0 h and 12 h, corresponding to immediately after the irradiation time point and empirical magnetosome synthesizing period, respectively. For each test, 2 mM 10 μL DCFH-DA was added to 200 μL of the concentrated control and irradiated samples, and the samples were incubated at $3 7 ~ ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ for 45 min in the dark. Cells were centrifuged, washed, and resuspended into 96-well plates. The fluorescence of the samples was measured by a spectrofluorometer (Synergy TMH4, BioTek, USA) with an excitation wavelength of 488 nm and emission wavelength at 525 nm, with 9 nm excitation and 15 nm emission wavelength widths, respectively. The fluorescence intensities, normalized to the optical density at 600 nm and the initial ROS value, were used to determine the relative ROS contents. 

Rock magnetic measurements: The synthesis of magnetosomes in XM-1 cell was examined by magnetic measurements. For room temperature rock magnetic measurements, cells that were grown in different media with initial oxygen concentration (MIOC) of both irradiated and control samples were collected by centrifugation at 8000 rpm for 10 min at $4 ~ { } ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$ after 72 h of cultivation, and the cell pellets were transferred into a COY anaerobic chamber (COY-7000220A, USA) and immediately loaded into nonmagnetic gelatin capsules and dried overnight. Room temperature magnetic parameters were tested using a vibrating sample magnetometer Model 3900 (Princeton Measurements Corporation, USA, sensitivity $5 . 0 { \times } 1 0 ^ { - 1 0 } \mathrm { A m } ^ { 2 } )$ . Hysteresis loops were measured between $\pm 3 0 0$ mT with an average time of 200 ms. After paramagnetic correction, saturation magnetization $( M _ { s } )$ , saturation remanence $( M _ { r s } ) _ { \ast }$ , and coercivity $( \boldsymbol { B } _ { c } )$ of each sample were determined. First-order reversal curves (FORCs) were measured following the instruction described by Egli et al. (2010). 

## 8.3.3 Results

## 8.3.3.1 Effects of UVB irradiation on cell abundance and community of uncultured MTB

After 7 days of UVB irradiation treatments, the cell number per liter of nonirradiated (control) and UVB radiation strength analogs of the present day, the geomagnetic field reversal period, and the Archean age displayed a gradually decreased pattern, suggesting the intensity-dependent deleterious effects on uncultured MTB growth (Figure 8.3.3), although there were little morphological differences in all of those cell samples. The control samples showed little change of cell numbers within a week of treatment, with cell density of approximately $1 . 4 5 \times 1 0 ^ { 4 }$ cells/mL. However, the total average cell numbers of simulation of the present-day $\left( 2 . 6 \mathrm { \ W } / \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } \right)$ , geomagnetic field reversal period (4.1 W/m2), and Archean age $\left( 1 0 . 8 \mathrm { W } / \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } \right)$ UVB irradiation analogs were reduced to 8.4×103 cell/mL, 6.7×103 cell/mL, and $3 . 2 \times 1 0 ^ { 3 }$ cell/mL, respectively. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/6c2e57f4-f177-4731-acc4-f560c6f82e69/8645b32b85722acbd2e321507b7c9484beb56e69d490025faf6be56e2dc16e67.jpg)



Figure 8.3.3 Cell abundances after 1 week under dark (red; control group) and UVB irradiation treatments with irradiation analogs of the present day (blue), the calculated geomagnetic field reversal period (green), and the predicted Archean (purple) UVB intensities.


Phylogenetic analysis based on 16S rRNA gene sequence showed that all MTB in the studied samples were closest to the genus Magnetococcus. The relationships between the 12 libraries were further statistically compared using the unweighted UniFrac program to test the influence of estimated UVB radiation on the phylogenetic composition of magnetotactic cocci. Principal coordinates analysis (PCoA) was carried out to examine the phylogenetic similarity between all samples. The results clearly showed that the dark control samples displayed phylogenetically distinct composition compared with those in the period of geomagnetic field reversal and the Archean UVB intensities samples, where PCoA axis 1 explained 12.68% of the variation (Figure 8.3.4). 

## 8.3.3.2 UVB irradiation effects on physiology and magnetite magnetosome biomineralization of Magnetospirillum sp. XM-1

After UVB irradiation treatments, ROS (see Chapter 10) within XM-1 cells significantly increased compared to that of non-irradiated samples (Figure 8.3.5a, points b and a), which is consistent with previous observations on strain AMB-1 after UVB irradiation. This indicates that the UVB irradiation stimulates the production of ROS within MTB cells. Then, the ROS contents of the XM-1 cells (both with and without UVB irradiation treatments, and grown in different oxygen gradients from <0.01 to >25 mg/L) were measured at 12 h (Figure 8.3.5a), a period of the empirical magnetosome synthesis stage, whereas the coercivity and saturation magnetization were tested at 72 h (Figure 8.3.5b and 8.3.5c), the time at which magnetosomes have matured completely. In Figure 8.3.5a, the averaged ROS values of UVB radiation–treated cells at a low oxygen level (<14.21 mg/L) dropped significantly after 12 h of incubation, suggesting that the cells possessed an efficient free radical– scavenging system. In the control group, the ROS within the cell decreased with the increase of initial oxygen concentrations in media, whereas at the higher oxygen level (>14.21 mg/L), the ROS within the cell started to increase rapidly with the increase of oxygen contents in growth media. The irradiated group showed a similar trend, yet the ROS accumulation started to increase in culture medium containing an initial oxygen concentration of 4.65 mg/L. However, when compared with dark control samples, the UVB irradiation effects on MTB under various oxygen stresses could be evaluated at the same time. The results showed that when oxygen contents were less than 4.65 mg/L, the ROS of the irradiated samples within specific initial oxygen concentrations were lower than in the dark control, whereas ROS values were higher than these control samples when oxygen levels were higher than 8.34 mg/L. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/6c2e57f4-f177-4731-acc4-f560c6f82e69/ba2f22d647103d268b4de9b222038cdad05fcd7907ef12ff520ed4caf16dea02.jpg)



Figure 8.3.4 PCoA analysis based on the matrix of pairwise distances between communities generated using the unweighted UniFrac. A, B, C, and D represent the MTB communities of the dark control, the present day, the calculated geomagnetic field reversal period, and the predicted Archean UVB intensities, respectively.


Magnetic results showed that after irradiation, cultures containing less oxygen (<4.65 mg/L) benefited the synthesis of magnetosome, whereas higher oxygen contents negatively influenced the biomineralization process compared with the dark control, regarding coercivity (Figure 8.3.5b), saturation magnetization (Figure 8.3.5c), FORC coercivity (Figure 8.3.5d), and average magnetosome size (Figure 8.3.5e). TEM micrographs of magnetosomes from the irradiated bacteria with <0.01 mg/L and 1.72 mg/L oxygen concentration were roughly 5–10 nm larger than their dark control; however, magnetosomes of UVB-treated cells with an oxygen content of 8.34 mg/L and 14.21 mg/L were 1–5 nm smaller (Figure 8.3.6). Notably, for both control and UVB-treated samples, their saturation magnetization and coercivity dropped to undetectable levels as they barely grew in high-oxygen-level (>21.67 mg/L) medium, suggesting that high-oxygen environments inhibit magnetosome biomineralization. 

FORCs diagrams also showed similar changes. Irradiated samples grown in media with less oxygen (<0.01 mg/L and 1.72 mg/L) showed on average 8 mT coercivity right shifts of the contour diagrams, suggesting that the magnetite magnetic particles within the samples were on average larger than those of the control samples (Figure 8.3.7). A previous study on Magnetospirillum magneticum AMB-1 using magnetic spirillum growth medium under different UVB irradiation doses in an anaerobic chamber also showed enhanced magnetosome biomineralization processes; whereas, in cultures with higher initial oxygen (8.34 mg/L and 14.21 mg/L), the results were opposite (Figure 8.3.7). FORCs contour diagrams of the irradiated samples displayed on average 4–5 mT coercivity left shifts and lower signal intensities, partially indicating that the samples contain fewer and smaller magnetite magnetosomes.

## 8.3.4 Discussion

Solar radiation of UVB usually generates deleterious effects similar to those of both the UVA and UVC ranges, such as induction of intercellular ROS and DNA strand breaks, and can partially penetrate into the atmosphere, reaching the Earth’s surface. UVB radiation also induces cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers (CPDs), pyrimidine (6-4) pyrimidone photoproducts (6-4 PPs), and several other photoproducts. Most of the photoproducts are lethal since they can block the transcription and translation process of prokaryotes (Goosen and Moolenaar, 2008; Hader¨ and Sinha, 2005; Hader¨ et al., 2015; Sinha and Hader, 2002a,b).¨ During the Archean time, ancient MTB, if they existed, may have lived in the upper layer in anaerobic aquatic environments, and, without an ozone layer, they might have suffered from higher intensities of UVB radiation. After the ozone layer built up, when the Earth had gone through solar particle events during the geomagnetic field reversal periods, the UVB intensity would increase more than 20%, even to 40%, depending on different times and latitudes (Cockell, 1998; Valet and Valladas, 2010; Vogt et al., 2007; Winkler et al., 2008). Studies on narrowband-wavelength electron magnetic wave radiation (e.g., UVB radiation) could give us knowledge of specific effects in order to understand the comprehensive consequences of natural UV radiation on microorganisms. Results of the present study experimentally demonstrate that UVB irradiation could influence the abundance and community, physiology, and biomineralization process of MTB evolutionarily. 

We observed that after 1 week of radiation treatment, cell numbers of natural MTB under the simulated Archean, geomagnetic reversal period, and present-day UVB intensities dropped compared with the initial samples. MTB communities based on 16S rRNA gene sequences were also changed by the 1 week UVB radiation treatments. As revealed by unweighted Unifrac PCoA results, the P1 separates the dark control and the estimated Archean, geomagnetic reversal, and present-day UVB intensity simulations. The changes of MTB abundance and community indicate that the UVB radiation is an important environmental factor for microbes, including MTBs, probably due to the deleterious effects of UVB on cells. The UVB radiation generates DNA lesions and intercellular ROS in microbes, which would stop cell division and even lead to death of UVB-sensitive bacterial species (Langenheder et al., 2006; Pajares et al., 2012; Santos et al., 2011b, 2012a, 2013). As seen in both previous and current studies, Magnetospirillum magneticum AMB-1 and Magnetospirillum sp. XM-1 cells were severely affected by UVB irradiation, which showed increase of the CPD formation and ROS accumulation and delayed cell growth as radiation intensity increased (Figure 8.3.5) (Wang et al., 2013b). Moreover, UVB irradiation can influence the living environments of aquatic bacteria by oxidizing certain chemical compounds, breaking down large organic acids, and altering the redox status (Cockell and Airo, 2002; Davidson, 1998; Hader ¨ et al., 1998, 2015; Helbling and Zagarese, 2003; Sinha and Hader, 2002ab; Sommaruga, ¨ 2001; Williamson, 1995). These changed surroundings would vary the dominant bacterial population achieved by specific metabolism adaptions (Davidson and Belbin, 2002; Santos et al., 2012b,c; Vinegla ˜ et al., 2006; Winter et al., 2001). 

It was noted that the UVB irradiation and generated ROS within the cells might influence the biomineralization process of the cultured MTB Magnetospirillum sp. strain XM-1. Although intracellular ROS (which usually causes cellular damage yet can be efficiently removed by antioxidant enzymes such as peroxidase) increased directly after the UVB irradiation, it then dropped during the cultivation process to levels lower than the dark control in cells that were incubated in culture medium with an initial oxygen concentration less than 4.65 mg/L, but higher when oxygen content was higher than 8.34 mg/L. The changes of ROS values were also reflected in the magnetic results of MTB. Irradiated cells containing less ROS showed better biomineralization such as larger magnetosome grain size and number per cell, whereas in oxygen concentrations higher than 14.21 mg/L, the magnetosome synthesis processes of both the control and UVB-irradiated groups were inhibited, and the growth of irradiated cells was lower than that of the dark control, probably due to the intrinsic damage after UVB radiation plus the negative effects of high environmental oxygen. In the control and irradiated groups, bacteria with higher ROS content (e.g., at oxygen concentration >14.21 mg/L) tended to have a worse magnetite crystallization, which also agreed with the study of oxygen effects on MTB strains AMB-1 and MSR-1 (Heyen and Schuler, ¨ 2003; Li and Pan, 2012; Matsunaga et al., 1991). 

The processes of magnetite magnetosome biomineralization have been studied in detail, taking advantage of molecular microbiology (Bazylinski et al., 2013; Faivre and Schuler, 2008;¨ Komeili, 2012; Posfai and Dunin-Borkowski, 2009). All MTB´ contains one or two genomic islands with several gene clusters such as mamAB, mamCDEF, mamXY, and mms6 have been proven to have specific functions during biomineralization of magnetite magnetosomes. They include magnetosome membrane vesicles formation on actin-like skeletons, iron transport, and crystallization (Komeili, 2012). Recently, the synthesis of magnetite magnetosome was also suggested to be closely related to oxygen regulation. Genes associated with intracellular ROS and redox control were found to be up- or downregulated during the synthesis of magnetosome (Ge et al., 2011; Guo et al., 2012; Qi et al., 2012; Rong et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2013b). The low oxygen concentration benefits magnetite synthesis while this process, which involves large ferrous and ferric transport and transformation, would largely generate Fenton reactions. The increased ROS is harmful for biomineralization yet can be eliminated by magnetosome and redox-related enzymes (Guo et al., 2012). However, after appropriate UVB irradiation in a low-oxygen condition, some genes related to redox balancing (e.g., oxyR, katG, and sodB) are likely upregulated to scavenge intercellular ROS, which creates favorable redox environments within the cell for biomineralization of magnetosomes. Previous transcriptome analyses of both the radiation-resistant bacterial Deinococcus spp. and a facultative anaerobic Gammaproteobacteria Shewanella oneidensis MR-1 demonstrated that intracellular redox gene regulation significantly increased after UV irradiation (Qiu et al., 2005; Yuan et al., 2012). This would explain the enhanced magnetosome formation in this study. A hypothetical model is presented in Figure 8.3.8 to illustrate the scenario. However, at high oxygen levels, the formation of magnetosomes was prohibited, regardless of UVB radiation, compared with the control.

Figure 8.3.8 Hypothetical model of how UVB radiation would influence magnetite magnetosome synthesis in Magnetospirillum sp. XM-1. The arrow refers to the putative stimulation process; the short line means inhibition.


Apart from oxygen, metabolisms of nitrate and iron would also influence the mineralization of magnetite magnetosome, as previously demonstrated in strains AMB-1 and MSR-1 (Li et al., 2012, 2013; Qi et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2013b). In other bacteria, nitrate reduction genes such as nap and nos genes and genes related to iron sequestering (dps and hemH) upregulated after UV irradiation (Qiu et al., 2005; Yuan et al., 2012). Magnetosome biomineralization would be influenced by UVB radiation, probably through some similar specific metabolism or regulation network. Nevertheless, further investigations on the gene expression pattern of the irradiated MTB XM-1 cells are needed to reveal the detailed mechanisms that are still unresolved.
