# Nucleotide excision repair system and gene expression in Mycobacterium smegmatis

Angelina Cordone 

Department of Biology, University Federico II of Naples, Naples, Italy 

## 8.4.1 Introduction

Mycobacteria include more than a hundred species, and they are diverse in terms of pathogenicity and environmental distribution (Shinnick and Good, 1994). Among them, Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB), the etiological agent of human tuberculosis, is considered one of the most powerful human pathogens, and it is ranked as the second leading cause of death from a single infectious agent, after the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) (WHO, 2014). 

MTB enters lungs through aerosol droplets and is internalized by alveolar macrophages, which have the task to destroy any invading microbe. One of the leading mechanisms used by macrophages to kill pathogens is the generation of mutagenic and genotoxic agents, such as reactive oxygen and nitrogen intermediates (ROIs and RNIs), which can easily pass the bacterial cell wall, thus causing serious damage to biomolecules including DNA (Kurthkoti and Varshney, 2012; Nathan and Shilon, 2000; Warner and Mizrahi, 2006). 

The major types of DNA damage resulting from the actions of such substances are (i) the formation of oxidized bases, among them 7,8-dihydro-8-oxoguanine; (ii) the formation of apurinic sites; and (iii) the deamination of cytosine, which results in uracil incorporation in DNA (Davis et al., 2007; Demple and Harrison, 1994; Neeley and Essigmann, 2006). Importantly, mycobacteria have genomes with a high GC content; this implies that their genomes are more susceptible to the action of oxidizing substances than other bacteria (O’Sullivan et al., 2005). 

One of the hallmarks of human tuberculosis is the ability of the pathogen to persist in a poorly understood, non-replicating, latent-state inside granuloma, a fibrotic mass surrounding bacteria formed by the host to contain the pathogen. 

It has been hypothesized that mycobacterial latency occurs in response to immune system injuries such as oxygen and nutritional limitations and the generation of ROIs and RNIs (Gomez and McKinney, 2004; Honer zu Bentrup and Russel, 2001; Manabe and Bishai, 2000). 

Latency is a common behaviour to both pathogenic and non-pathogenic mycobacteria in vitro; this allows the study of pathogenic species using non-pathogenic mycobacteria as model systems. 

The fast-growing Mycobacterium smegmatis is a useful and attractive model to study the adaptive response of human pathogens during infection. Similarly to MTB, M. smegmatis is able to adapt and persist under conditions that mimic the hostile environment encountered by the pathogen during infection (Gupta and Chatterji, 2005; Smuelders et al., 1999). Several studies, using M. smegmatis as a model system, have revealed the importance of mycobacterial DNA repair machineries to minimize and counteract the deleterious effects of genotoxic agents, like ROIs and RNIs, during either active replication or a latent-induced state (Cordone et al., 2011; Kurthkoti et al., 2008; Kurthkoti and Varshney, 2010; Venkatesh et al., 2003). 

This chapter refers to recent discoveries in this research area, focusing attention on the role played by the nucleotide excision repair (NER) system in M. smegmatis. 

## 8.4.2 Mycobacterial infection

MTB is an intracellular pathogen that enters human lungs and is quickly phagocytized by alveolar macrophages. This process is mediated by the Pattern Recognition Receptors (PRRs), localized on the macrophage surface, and specific MTB cell envelope molecules (mannosylated lipoarabinomannan, trehalose dimycolate and N-glycolyl muramyl dipeptide). As a result, the pathogen is internalized inside a cytosolic vacuole. The first strategy used by the infected macrophages to kill the pathogen is to transfer the vacuole-containing bacteria to the destructive environment of lysosomes (Handzel, 2013). 

MTB is able to block this process and to reside inside the infected macrophages. If the host immune system is weak, mycobacteria are able to infect nearby cells and to disseminate to other organs, causing the active disease (Houben et al., 

2006). In order to cause the disease, mycobacteria, which are continuously subjected to the genotoxic actions of ROIs and RNIs, have to keep their genomes safe. This is probably due to the presence of highly efficient and functional DNA repair systems. 

In most cases, the host immune system is able to contain the infection, recruiting other cells to the site of infection, which form a structure, the granuloma, inside which mycobacteria remain viable in a latent form (Cooper and Torrado, 2012; Gupta et al., 2012; Ramakrishnan, 2012). MTB remains confined inside the granuloma in a dormant form for long periods of time. As the host immune system decreases, latent bacilli can exit latency, giving rise to the active form of infection (Parrish et al., 1998; Tiruviluamala and Reichman, 2002). Hypoxia, the condition under which latent mycobacteria persist inside granuloma, generates DNA damage in humans (Grishko et al., 2001; Moller et al., 2001). Although the direct link between hypoxia and DNA damage in bacteria is not well documented, it is possible to speculate that, similarly to humans, hypoxia is harmful also for bacterial DNA. This implies that latent mycobacteria have to provide a greater protection to preserve their genome integrity and be able to reactivate infection. 

## 8.4.3 DNA repair systems during infection

In silico analysis of mycobacterial genomes has revealed the presence of genes encoding enzymes required for NER, base excision repair (BER), homologous recombination (HR), and non homologous end joining (NHEJ) repair systems. In general, DNA lesions following oxidation, deamination, and alkylation of bases are repaired by the BER system; more bulky lesions, as pyrimidine dimers, are corrected by the NER system; and the double-strand break lesions are resolved by HR and NHEJ. The main aspects of the mycobacterial DNA repair system have been discussed elsewhere (Davis and Forse, 2009; Dos Vultos et al., 2009; Kurthkoti and Varshney, 2011). 

Importantly, mycobacteria lack all genes encoding proteins required for the mismatch repair (MMR) system, a system highly conserved throughout evolution which contributes to safeguard genome integrity. This task is achieved due to the ability to correct errors resulting from nucleotide misincorporation and polymerase slippage during replication (Springer et al., 2004). 

In spite of the lack of an important post-replicative repair system, the mutational rate of mycobacterial genomes is similar to that of other bacteria (Hiriyanna and Ramakrishnan, 1986). 

A recent whole-genome-sequencing analysis has compared the mutational events occurring in MTB genomes isolated in a non-human animal model with active, latent, and reactivated disease. This study has shown that the mycobacterial genome mutational rate is the same across all states of infection and that it is similar to that observed during in vitro bacterial growth. In addition, the authors reported that the major source of DNA damage during infection is oxidative stress, highlighting the importance of genes required to repair such errors (Ford et al., 2011). 

The lack of a functional MMR system together with the high GC content have led several authors to propose that mycobacteria exploit their existing DNA repair machineries in an alternative or compensating way to safeguard their genomic integrity with respect to other bacteria (Machowski et al., 2007; Springer et al., 2004; Wanner et al., 2008). 

An MTB gene expression profile has been analysed during the active phase of infection in human and murine macrophages, and has revealed that genes belonging to BER, NER, and HR systems are upregulated (Dubnau et al., 2002; Fontan et al., 2008; Gorna et al., 2010; Schnappinger et al., 2003), suggesting an active role for these systems during infection. The same trend of expression has been observed in vitro in response to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ (Boshoff et al., 2003). 

The relevance of BER and NER pathways in mycobacteria has been demonstrated through the construction and analysis of MTB mutant strains. In particular, it has been reported that the Ung protein, the uracil DNA glycosylase of the BER system that corrects uracil misincorporation in the genome, is required for MTB survival in a mouse model of infection (Sassetti and Rubin, 2003). Moreover, deletion of the adaA and alkA genes, other important players of the BER machinery required to repair alkylation errors, increases MTB susceptibility towards RNIs in vitro but does not attenuate its virulence in mice (Durbach et al., 2003). The importance of the NER system during MTB infection has been evaluated in a similar way. It has been previously reported that an MTB NER-deficient strain, mutated in uvrB, is markedly attenuated in its virulence in mice and that the UvrB protein is an important player to counteract the effects of RNIs in vitro. A similar behaviour was recently observed using an MTB UvrA-deficient strain (Rossi et al., 2011). 

Taken together, these results clearly underline the linkage between mycobacterial survival, virulence, and alteration of DNA repair systems, particularly of the NER and BER systems, during the active state of infection, and they suggest that some components of these repair systems can be considered as molecular targets for a future tuberculosis treatment. 

Although there is still no clear evidence which demonstrates that the activities of DNA repair systems influence the latent state of infection and subsequent pathogen reactivation, several studies, performed by using M. smegmatis as a model system, highlighted a critical role for the NER system during mycobacterial dormancy. These recent findings are summarized here. 

## 8.4.4 The NER system: gene expression and role during the in vitro dormancy induced in M. smegmatis

The NER system has been well characterized in E. coli, where it is mainly involved in repairing UV-light-induced DNA lesions, such as pyrimidine dimers (Goosen et al., 1998; Van Hounten et al., 2005). It is highly conserved among bacteria and acts as a multi-enzymatic complex composed of four proteins: UvrA, UvrB, UvrC, and UvrD (Kisker et al., 2013). 

UvrA, the initial DNA damage sensor of the system, belongs to the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) superfamily of ATPases. Structural studies of UvrA proteins from several bacteria have identified a multidomain organization of this protein, which is characterized by a nucleotide-binding domain (NBD), a UvrBbinding domain (UvrB-BD), and the insertion domain (ID) (Pakotiprapha et al., 2008; Timmins et al., 2009). The same architecture has been recently reported for the MTB UvrA protein (Rossi et al., 2011). UvrA acts as a dimer and binds to UvrB, forming a complex which plays a key role in the recognition of DNA distortions. 

UvrB belongs to the superfamily 2 DEAD-box family helicases (Theis et al., 2000). This protein contains five specific domains which reflect its function. In particular, Domains 1A and 3 are involved in ATP binding, Domain 1B provides interaction with DNA, whereas Domains 2 and 4 interact with UvrA and UvrC proteins, respectively. When encountering a damaged site, UvrA leaves the complex and, subsequently, UvrC drives UvrB to the damaged site. 

UvrC is a small protein which contains two catalytic sites that are responsible for the single-strand incision at both sides of the lesion (Skorvaga et al., 2002). A DNA fragment of 12–13 residues is then removed by the action of UvrD helicase. The action of this enzyme generates a gap which is then resolved by the combined action of a DNA polymerase I and a DNA ligase (Runyon et al., 1990; Yang, 2010). In E. coli, the uvrA and uvrB genes are members of the SOS regulon, a group of more than 40 genes whose expression is induced following DNA damage (Radman, 1974). The SOS regulatory elements are twofold: the activator protein RecA and the repressor protein LexA. Briefly, under normal conditions, LexA binds to a specific sequence, known as the SOS-box (Erill et al., 2003), localized upstream of the genes it negatively regulates. Following DNA damage, RecA protein is activated and is able to bind to single-strand DNA. Once activated, RecA stimulates the autocatalytic cleavage of LexA, which is no longer able to bind the SOS-box (Harmon et al., 1996). As a result, there is an increased transcription of SOS genes. Although the key regulatory elements of the SOS response have been identified in MTB (Durbach et al., 1997), only a few DNA repair genes are under their control. In particular, it has been reported that, in MTB, the upstream region of the uvrA gene lacks a specific LexA-binding site and that its expression, following DNA damage, is RecA independent (Brooks et al., 2001). Further studies are needed to clarify the alternative mechanism used by mycobacteria for the NER genes regulation in response to DNA damage. 

Although the mycobacterial NER system is still not well characterized, several authors have suggested a central role of such a system in mycobacterial survival during latency. The in vivo condition in which latent mycobacteria persist is oxygen limitation (Timm et al., 2003; Tsai et al., 2006). During recent years, several in vitro dormancy systems, using oxygen as a limiting factor, have been developed. Among them, the Wayne method has been used extensively to induce latency in mycobacteria (Wayne and Hayes, 1996). The method is performed by incubating mycobacterial cultures inside stirred sealed tubes, thus resulting in a gradual oxygen depletion at which bacilli seem to adapt. Given the difficulty to work with MTB, mainly due to its pathogenicity and its slow growth, several studies have been performed adapting the in vitro dormancy system to M. smegmatis. 

Using the Wayne method, Kurtkoty and colleagues have shown that a M. smegmatis NER-deficient strain, mutated in the uvrB gene, is markedly more sensitive to hypoxia and that its survival is highly compromised during the recovery phase compared to wild-type and BER-deficient strains (Kurthkoty et al., 2008). These results show that the NER system is one of the most important pathways in mycobacteria. 

Another study used an in vitro plate-based dormancy system (Lim and Dick, 2001) to screen a M. smegmatis mutant library for mutants unable to enter or exit dormancy. This system, based on growing mycobacteria on agar plates under hypoxic conditions generated by using anaerobic jars, has allowed the isolation of a M. smegmatis uvrA mutant with an impaired dormancy behaviour (Cordone et al., 2011). In the same study, it was also demonstrated that the UvrA protein is needed for cells to neutralize oxyradical-induced damage, highlighting that the mycobacterial NER system is able to correct a wider range of DNA damages than the corresponding E. coli system, as previously reported (Darwin and Nathan, 2005; Guthlein et al., 2009). Interestingly, a real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) analysis revealed that the uvrA gene expression is downregulated during the in vitro dormancy condition of growth and that this expression level increases upon exiting dormancy (A. Cordone, unpublished data). A similar trend of expression was previously reported for other genes involved in DNA repair systems (Kurthkoti and Varshney, 2010). This downregulation can be explained as a direct effect of the general slowed-down metabolic processes during latency. As results, the mycobacterial genomes accumulate DNA errors which are not corrected during this state of growth. It is possible to speculate that these lesions are not detrimental for their survival during latency because the mycobacteria are viable in a non-active replicating state. The increased expression levels of genes involved in several DNA repair systems, among them the NER system, observed during the recovery phase is probably due to the mycobacterial need to correct and preserve their genome integrity, a critical condition for the subsequent active phase of infection. 

## 8.4.5 Conclusions

Although the mycobacterial NER system is still not well characterized with respect to other species, the experimental evidence summarized in this chapter indicates that it is an important player for mycobacterial adaptation to hostile conditions of growth, and suggests that the NER system can be considered a good candidate as a target in a future antitubercular therapy.

## SOS and double stranded repair systems and stress

## Darja Zgur Bertok ˇ

Department of Biology, Biotechnical Faculty, University of Ljubljana, Ljubljana, Slovenia 

## 9.1.1 Introduction

The SOS response is an inducible pathway governing DNA repair. It is also one of the most significant bacterial transcriptional responses to stress. Two proteins control the SOS response, LexA (a repressor) and RecA (an activator). Upon DNA damage and/or stalled replication forks, RecA is activated (RecA∗) by binding to exposed single-stranded DNA (ssDNA). RecA∗ then stimulates autocleavage of LexA de-repressing genes involved in nucleotide excision repair, recombinational repair, DNA damage tolerance, and virulence (Butala et al., 2009). The lexA gene is present in almost all eubacterial groups examined; however, the lexA regulon is variable with regard to gene number and gene type. Thus, among diverse bacteria, the SOS system may exhibit a variety of roles due to adaptation to different ecological niches. The evolutionary core set of the SOS regulon seems to be genes lexA, dnaE2 (the error-prone α subunit of DNA polymerase III essential to DNA damage–induced mutagenesis), imuA, and imuB (umuDC in E. coli) for an SOS error-prone polymerase (Baharoglu and Mazel, 2014; Erill et al., 2007). 

The SOS response is provoked by exogenous and endogenous factors that damage DNA or interrupt DNA replication. Exogenous triggers are UV irradiation, oxidative compounds, organic mutagens, acids, high pressure, as well as some antibiotics (e.g., fluoroquinolones, ß lactam, trimethoprim, and in some species aminoglycosides) (Baharoglu et al., 2013; Baharoglu and Mazel, 2011). Endogenous triggers are stalled replication forks, defects following recombination or chromosome segregation, as well as metabolic by-products including reactive oxygen species (ROS) (see Section 10). The latter are generated as by-products of aerobic metabolism. In addition, ROS and reactive nitrogen species (RNS; see Section 17) are also produced by phagocytic cells of the innate immune system as a response to invading microorganisms. Further exposure to bile and acid in the gastrointestinal tract can result in DNA damage (Jeong et al., 2008; Merritt and Donaldson, 2009; Prieto et al., 2006). At the molecular level, the SOS response is activated by formation of intracellular ssDNA upon replication arrest or stalling, repair at double-strand breaks, or horizontal gene transfer, namely conjugation and transformation. In addition, a recent investigation revealed that in Vibrio cholerae, transcription blocking at DNA lesions plays a significant role in SOS induction (Baharoglu et al., 2014). 

Besides DNA damage repair, the SOS response has the capacity to generate genetic diversity, including antibiotic resistance, via translesion DNA synthesis performed by the SOS errorprone polymerases that may be highly mutagenic. Additionally, bacterial species produce persisters, transiently dormant cells that are antibiotic tolerant and therefore play a significant role in chronic bacterial infections (see Chapter 6.3). Persister formation was shown to require SOS induction and, in E. coli, the TisB toxin of the toxin–antitoxin system tisB–istR1. TisB shuts down cell metabolism by decreasing the proton motive force and adenosine triphosphate (ATP) levels (Dorr¨ et al., 2010). SOS induction of other toxin–antitoxin systems has been described, indicating that other toxins might be involved in persister formation (Singletary et al., 2009). 

This review focuses on the significance of the SOS response for bacterial pathogenesis. In addition to inducing repair and tolerance of DNA damage suffered within the host, the SOS response may directly induce virulence factor production, enhance dissemination of virulence and antibiotic resistance genes, induce translocation of virulence factors, trigger interand intraspecies bacterial competition, as well as induce biofilm formation. 

## 9.1.2 Activation of the SOS response promotes bacterial pathogen survival and virulence

Bacterial pathogens generally produce virulence factors, such as adhesins, capsules, iron uptake systems, and toxins, to overcome host defense mechanisms and to survive and multiply within the host. Specialized bacterial secretion systems deliver virulence factors or effectors into host cells. The expression of virulence factor genes and that of their delivery systems are tightly regulated and coordinated by environmental or metabolic cues. 

Pathogens are exposed to numerous factors that activate the SOS response. Thus, products of normal metabolism, host defense systems, bacterial interference mechanisms, as well as classical antibiotics have been shown to regulate the expression of virulence factor genes and their dissemination. During aerobic metabolism, ROS such as the superoxide radical $( \mathrm O _ { 2 } ^ { - } ) _ { : }$ , hydrogen peroxide $\mathrm { ( H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ) .$ and the hydroxyl radical (. OH) are generated continuously. ROS damage DNA by inflicting singleand double-strand breaks, as well as damage RNA, proteins, and lipids. ROS and RNS, such as nitric oxide (NO), that also damage DNA are generated by cells of the innate immune system, neutrophils, and macrophages to destroy invading microorganisms. Furthermore, intestinal epithelial cells express the inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) to produce NO as a response to infection (Mysorekar et al., 2002). 

SOS induction plays a significant role in pathogenesis of a wide spectrum of pathogens, including the versatile E. coli pathogenic strains, facultative intracellular pathogens that may replicate within macrophages, as well as among opportunists that may cause severe, even life-threatening, infections. 

## 9.1.2.1 Escherichia coli – a versatile pathogen

E. coli is a commensal in the gut; however, particular strains that produce virulence factors provoke a variety of intestinal and extraintestinal infections. Among the intestinal pathogenic strains, the enteropathogenic E. coli (EPEC) causes severe, acute watery diarrhea primarily in infants. EPEC is characterized by enterocyte attachment and effacement (EAE) provoked by injection of specific protein effectors, via a type 3 secretion system (T3SS), into host intestinal epithelial cells. The T3SS and effector proteins are encoded by the locus of enterocyte effacement (LEE) (Clarke et al., 2003). DNA damage and the SOS response have been shown to induce the T3SS (Mellies et al., 2007). Furthermore, the T3SS has been implicated in evasion of the innate immune system as it was shown to inhibit phagocytosis by murine macrophages (Quitard et al., 2006). The enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC), which includes the E. coli foodborne pathogen O157:H7, also provokes the EAE phenomenon. However, EHEC additionally produces Shiga-like toxins (SLTs) encoded by a bacteriophage. Due to production of SLTs, EHEC has the potential to cause acute kidney failure and hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). Induction of the SOS response induces expression of prophage genes via RecA∗-induced autocleavage of the phage repressor as well as expression of SLTs (Kimmitt et al., 2000). 

Additionally, in 2011, a large outbreak caused by an enteroaggregative E. coli, serotype O104:H4 expressing a bacteriophage encoded Slt-2, occured in northern Germany and France. A total of 3816 cases and 54 deaths were reported in Germany. The outbreak included the highest number of HUS cases (22%) in an outbreak of SLTs producing E. coli, with some patients additionally suffering severe neurological disorders (Frank et al., 2011). 

SOS induction thus induces effector protein injection, toxin production, and dissemination of the toxin genes via bacteriophage replication. Treatment with SOS-inducing antibiotics, such as fluoroquinolones, may thus aggravate the disease. 

On the other hand, the most frequent extraintestinal infections provoked by E. coli are urinary tract infections (UTIs). Uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC) causes approximately 80% of UTIs, including cystitis in the bladder and pyelonephritis in the kidney (Foxman, 2010). A recent study has shown attenuation of a RecA-deficient strain during murine UTI, indicating that the SOS response is required for UPEC virulence (Li et al., 2010). To provoke lower UTIs, UPEC undergoes a complex intracellular cycle (Justice et al., 2004). UPEC initially adheres to uroplaktin proteins on the luminal surfaces of the bladder uroepitelium. Following attachment, bacteria invade and replicate intracellularly, forming large biofilm-like colonies (IBCs) (see Section 22). In response to UTIs, the iNOS in bladder epithelium cells produces NO that attacks DNA and proteins activating the SOS response (Mysorekar et al., 2002). Subsequently, bacteria flux out, with a subpopulation exhibiting filamentation due to cell division inhibition provoked by the SOS-regulated SulA protein. Transient inhibition and delay of cell division generally provide time to repair damaged DNA. The released bacteria repeat the infectious cycle, whilst neutrophils are recruited to the site of infection. SulA has been shown to be essential for UPEC pathogenesis in immunocompetent hosts, and filamentation presumably provides the extracellular UPEC a selective advantage for evasion of phagocytosis (Horvath et al., 2011; Justice et al., 2006). Activation of the SOS response is also essential for UPEC DNA damage repair and DNA damage tolerance (Li et al., 2010). 

In addition, the SOS response has been shown to play a significant role in the pathogenesis of other uropathogens. Thus, in urine samples of patients with UTIs, filamentous UPEC, Klebsiella pneumonia, Proteus mirabilis, and Enterobacter aerogenes have been observed (Rosen et al., 2007). Furthermore, in a murine cystitis model, K. pneumonia also formed IBC and exhibited filamentous morphology (Rosen et al., 2008). 

## 9.1.2.2 The SOS response and pathogen survival within macrophages

A hallmark of a number of bacterial infectious diseases is the ability of the pathogen to replicate within macrophages where they are assaulted by various killing mechanisms, including ROS and NOS, that damage DNA. 

Salmonella enterica: S. enterica, the causative agent of gastroenteritis, initially invades host cells by triggering actin rearrangements. The bacteria are taken up by a vacuole, which Salmonella remodels by injecting effectors to stall phagolysosomal maturation. Following translocation through intestinal epithelial cells, Salmonella can replicate within macrophages (Vazquez-Torres et al., 2000). 

Salmonella enzymatically destroys oxidative radicals produced by macrophages or interferes with localization of the enzymes involved in their production (Vazquez-Torres et al., 2000). A transcriptomic analysis of Salmonella gene expression following macrophage infection revealed a specific, moderate-level induction of the SOS system that allows DNA repair but also bacterial replication (Eriksson et al., 2003). Survival within macrophages is associated with filamentation due to induction of the SOS system in response to oxidative radicals (Eriksson et al., 2003; Rosenberger and Finlay, 2002). 

Shigella flexneri and EHEC: S. flexneri is another facultative intracellular pathogen that provokes human bacillary dysentery. As for Salmonella, transcriptome analysis of the gene expression profile of S. flexneri during macrophage infection likewise showed moderate induction of the SOS response, most probably due to oxidative stress (Lucchini et al., 2005). 

An additional study investigating the interaction of EHEC and human macrophages showed upregulation of Shiga-like toxin genes in macrophages as well as involvement of Shigalike toxins in increased bacterial survival in macrophages (Poirier et al., 2008). 

Mycobacterium tuberculosis – a global pathogen provoking persistent infections: M. tuberculosis is the causative agent of tuberculosis and a highly successful pathogen capable of persisting in the host for years. Tuberculosis is a major global health problem, causing approximately 1.75 million deaths annually, with about one-third of the world’s population latently infected. M. tuberculosis resides in macrophages where it is continually assaulted by ROS and RNS capable of damaging its genome. Macrophages in the lungs of people with tuberculosis lesions have been found to express the iNOS (Nicholson et al., 1996). A crucial step during infection is the ability of M. tuberculosis to mount an efficient DNA damage response. In M. tuberculosis, two mechanisms of DNA damage repair have been identified: one RecA–LexAdependent response, and a second RecA–LexA-independent response (Dos Vultos et al., 2009). In vitro, following engulfment into human-derived macrophages, M. tuberculosis has been shown to transform into filamentous bacteria (Chauhan et al., 2006) indicative of the SOS response. Nevertheless, in M. tuberculosis, only a small group of inducible DNA damage repair genes – namely, lexA, ruvA, ruvB, and dinE2 – are regulated solely by LexA, whereas expression of most of the remaining inducible repair genes is independent of recA. Additionally, recA, radA, ruvC, and ssb seem to be regulated by both recA-dependent and independent mechanisms. It has been speculated that the different mechanisms could be responding to different stimuli (Dos Vultos et al., 2009). Nevertheless, the SOS-regulated dnaE2, encoding the error-prone subunit of DNA polymerase III, has been shown to be required for persistence during infection and for development of antibiotic resistance (Boshoff et al., 2003). Interestingly, a recent study employing chromatin immunoprecipitation combined with high-throughput sequencing (ChIP-seq) identified several novel LexAbinding sites, including one positively regulated by LexA and two linked to potential small RNAs (Smollett et al., 2012). 

Listeria monocytogenes: The SOS response has been shown to be significant for survival of L. monocytogenes, a foodborne pathogen and the causative agent of listeriosis that is associated with meningitis, encephalitis, and spontaneous abortions (Vazquez-Boland et al., 2001). Activation of the SOS response has been demonstrated upon growth in macrophages (Chatterjee et al., 2006) and in vivo during infection in mouse organs (Camejo et al., 2009). Furthermore, RecA was shown to contribute to survival of L. monocytogenes upon exposure to acid and bile, conditions that resemble those in the gastrointestinal tract and during invasion of intestinal cells (van der Veen and Abee, 2011a). 

Burkholderia pseudomallei: B. pseudomallei is the etiological agent of melioidosis and is endemic in southeast Asia, particularly northeast Thailand and northern Australia. Melioidosis can be manifested as an asymptomatic pulmonary infiltration, acute pulmonary infection, and acute septicemic infection. In areas where it is endemic, B. pseudomallei is a common cause of opportunistic infections. B. pseudomallei is known to infect various cell lines and survives phagocytosis by alveolar macrophages (Jones et al., 1996). Furthermore, in a mouse model of melioidosis, the recA gene was shown to be essential for pathogenesis of B. pseudomallei (Cuccui et al., 2007). 

## 9.1.2.3 Opportunistic pathogens and the SOS response

Pseudomonas aeruginosa – evasion of killing by neutrophils and macrophages: P. aeruginosa is an opportunistic pathogen that causes diverse infections, local and systemic, including life-threatening lung infections in patients with cystic fibrosis (Lyczak et al., 2002). P. aeruginosa produces several types of virulence factors, such as adhesins, toxic proteins, enzymes, alginate, and a T3SS (Hauser, 2009). 

Studies of the P. aeruginosa SOS response have revealed a regulon composed of 15 genes, including recA, lexA, as well as others involved in DNA repair and induced mutation (Cirz et al., 2006). In P. aeruginosa upon DNA-damaging treatment, the activated RecA∗ protein induces autocatalytic cleavage of LexA and two LexA-like Ser–Lys dyad transcription regulators, PtrR and PAO960. The latter seems to regulate six genes with as-yetunknown functions. 

The SOS system plays a significant role in virulence of P. aeruginosa via regulation of the T3SS that injects effector proteins, ExoS, and ExoU into host cells. These effectors provide P. aeruginosa strains with the ability to evade killing by neutrophils and macrophages (Hauser, 2009; Sun et al., 2012) and are therefore crucial for bacterial survival and replication within the host. The SOS-controlled PtrR protein regulates the 

T3SS via repression of ptrB, the inhibitor of the T3SS. Recently, studies employing a mouse acute pneumonia model have shown that ROS produced by neutrophils induced expression of ptrR to achieve a stable level of the PtrR protein, repressing the ptrB gene to allow increased expression of the T3SS genes. PtrR has also been shown to negatively regulate expression of its own gene (Sun et al., 2014). 

Clostridium difficile: C. difficile causes a spectrum of diseases, from mild diarrhea to pseudomembranous colitis characterized by severe ulceration of the colon. It is a leading cause of nosocomial diarrhea in hospitals and long-term healthcare facilities, and infections are associated with prior antibiotic treatment. The incidence, severity, and mortality due to C. difficile infection have increased markedly since the 2000s. Strains that cause pseudomembranous colitis produce two large toxins, toxin A (TcdA) and toxin B (TcdB), that glucosylate target G proteins, Rho, Rac, and Cdc42 and induce release of chemokines from intestinal epithelial cells, cell rounding, apoptosis, or necrosis, leading to inflammation and intestinal damage (Farrell and La Mont, 2000). 

Studies have shown that sublethal concentrations of antibiotics increase toxin levels (Gerber et al., 2008) as well as tcdA gene expression (Aldape et al., 2013). 

A recent study has identified 16 LexA-binding sites in the C. difficile genome. Binding of LexA was demonstrated for core SOS genes (recA, lexA, uvrBA, and ruvCA) as well as to the tcdA operator (Walter et al., 2014). Interestingly, this study shows that in C. difficile, two housekeeping genes, namely rplR (50S ribosomal protein) and rpoB for the β subunit of RNA polymerase, as well as genes involved in sporulation and antibiotic resistance (vancomycin response regulator) are also part of the LexA regulon. Nevertheless, due to differences in LexA– operator affinities, their expression is most probably fine-tuned by LexA independent of significant recA induction. 

## 9.1.3 Membrane vesicle formation

Both Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria produce membrane-derived vesicles. Gram-negative bacteria form membrane vesicles (MVs) when the outer membrane bulges and pinches off, encapsulating periplasmic material. MVs have been found to be involved in host–microbe interactions, including delivery of virulence factors and quorum-sensing signals (see Section 21) (Deatherage and Cookson, 2012). MVs have also been found to harbor DNA (Kolling and Matthews, 1999). Inclusion into MVs provides protection against proteolytic degradation, enhances the efficiency of long-distance delivery, and enables coordinated secretion with other bacterial effectors. Membrane vesicles may be produced in response to stress, including a stress response to antibiotics (Manning and Kuehn, 2011). In Shigella dysenteriae, activation of the SOS response has been shown to induce Shiga toxin–associated MV production (Dutta et al., 2004). Further MV purified from EHEC 

O157:H7 has been found to contain Shiga-like toxins (Kolling and Matthews, 1999). 

In P. aeruginosa, activation of the SOS response has also been found to be involved in MV formation. P. aeruginosa is characterized by a flexible metabolism that upon oxygen depletion switches to denitrification, the utilization of N-oxides as alternative electron acceptors (Arai, 2011). In P. aeruginosa, the SOS response has been shown to induce MV formation under denitrifying conditions. Furthermore, MV are involved in pathogenesis as they have been shown to deliver multiple virulence factors, including alkaline phosphotase, hemolytic phospholipase C, and the Cif toxin, directly into the host cell cytoplasm (Bomberger et al., 2009). SOS-stimulated vesiculation has been shown to contribute to cytotoxicity (Maredia et al., 2012). 

## 9.1.4 The SOS response promotes inter- and intraspecies competition

In the natural environment, bacteria compete for scarce nutrients by interference or inhibition. To this end, they employ antimicrobial products such as antibiotics, bacteriocins, and low-molecular-weight toxic compounds like $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ . A wellknown case of clinically significant interspecies competition is the displacement of Staphylococcus aureus by Streptococcus pneumonia in the nasopharynx. The basis of the interference is the production of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ by S. pneumoniae, which is bactericidal to S. aureus (Regev-Yochay et al., 2006). The $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ produced by S. pneumoniae kills lysogenic S. aureus indirectly, via induction of the SOS response and prophage activation (Selva et al., 2009). 

The normal mammalian gut lumen is dominated by strictly anaerobic bacteria that keep the density of facultative anaerobes low. However, intestinal inflammation triggered by the gut immune system or due to pathogen infection, such as Salmonella spp. or pathogenic E. coli strains, provokes dysbiosis, suppressing anaerobes and inciting Enterobacteriaceae overgrowth (Stecher et al., 2007). Within such blooms, extremely high conjugation frequencies are achieved (Stecher et al., 2012) that could transiently induce the SOS response throughout the bacterial population. Under such conditions, strains of the same and closely related species, at high titers, compete for limited resources. Infiltrating neutrophils in the gut lumen produce iron-depleting agents as well as ROS and RNS that induce the SOS response. Activation of the SOS response induces synthesis of enterobacterial bacteriocins, termed colicins. Bacteriocins are narrow-spectrum antibiotics that are active against bacterial cells. It was recently shown that, in the inflamed mouse gut, production of a pore-forming colicin, colicin Ib, conferred to a pathogenic strain a competitive advantage over E. coli strains (Nedialkova et al., 2014). The SOS Salmonella typhimurium response is thus involved in regulating bacterial population dynamics, including interactions between pathogenic and commensal strains and species. 

## 9.1.5 DNA transfer and recombination among pathogens

Whereas transferred ssDNA induces the SOS response, the latter promotes DNA transfer and recombination. Thus, activation of the SOS response induces a number of pathogen-associated bacteriophages such as the Shiga-like toxin encoding prophage in EHEC O157:H7 (Zhang et al., 2000), the V. cholerae filamentous bacteriophage CTXΦ encoding the cholera toxin (Quinones et al., 2005), and the prophages and co-resident pathogenicity islands of S. aureus (Ubeda et al., 2005; see Chapter 2.10). Induction of the SOS response also activates the transfer and integration of the V. cholerae SXT (Beaber et al., 2004), an integrating conjugative element encoding resistance to several antibiotics and heavy metals (Hochhut et al., 2001). Transfer of SXT is induced upon SOS-induced cleavage of the SetR repressor (Beaber et al., 2004).

Biofilms are structured microbial communities in which bacteria adhere to a biotic or abiotic surface. Microbial cells growing in biofilms are characterized by increased resistance and tolerance to antibiotics, disinfectants, host immune responses, as well as increased genetic diversity. The SOS response has been shown to play a key role in pathogen-associated biofilm formation (van der Veen and Abee, 2010; see Section 22).

S. aureus is a significant opportunist provoking nosocomial and community-acquired infections, including endocarditis, osteomyelitis, and toxic shock syndrome. Staphylococcal infections also develop on indwelling medical devices as S. aureus readily colonizes implant surfaces to develop a biofilm. In addition to numerous virulence factors, S. aureus isolates produce alternative biofilm matrices, including surface proteins such as fibronectin-binding proteins FnBPA and FnBPB (O’Neill et al., 2008). FnBPs have been found to play a significant role in S. aureus invasion of mammalian cells (Sinha et al., 2000) and in adherence to various host extracellular matrix components such as fibronectin, fibrinogen, and elastin (Roche et al., 2004; Wann et al., 2000). It has been shown that LexA is a repressor of fnbB (Bisognano et al., 2004) and that activation of the SOS response enhances biofilm formation (Vergara-Irigaray et al., 2009). Thus, induction of the SOS response by antibiotics such as fluoroquinolones or host defense mechanisms could enhance invasion and the ability of S. aureus isolates to produce biofilms on abiotic surfaces.

Replication-inhibiting antibiotics induce biofilm formation in various bacterial species (Gotoh et al., 2010; Hammer and Bassler, 2003; Kaplan et al., 2011). P. aeruginosa forms biofilms in wounds and in the lungs of patients with cystic fibrosis. Exposure of P. aeruginosa to subinhibitory concentrations of norfloxacin, a fluoroquinolone that targets DNA gyrase, activating the SOS response, has been shown to induce biofilm formation (Linares et al., 2006). Furthermore, treatment of P. aeruginosa with agents that inhibit DNA replication stimulated biofilm formation (Gotoh et al., 2010).

Blocking SOS activation could assist in the control of significant bacterial pathogens.

# RNAP secondary-channel interactors in Escherichia coli: makers and breakers of genome stability

Priya Sivaramakrishnan and Christophe Herman 

Department of Molecular and Human Genetics, Baylor College of Medicine, Houston, Texas, USA 

## 9.2.1 Introduction

## 9.2.1.1 Transcription: source and surveillance of genome stability

Transcription is a fundamental metabolic process and an important step in gene regulation. Additionally, it is also a major event during the coordination of cellular responses to various endogenous and exogenous stresses. RNA polymerase (RNAP), the molecular machine that directs DNA-dependent RNA synthesis, is charged with the important task of adding nucleotides to the nascent RNA chain with high accuracy and speed. This undertaking is made more cumbersome by several other processes that occur on the same DNA template, such as DNA replication and repair, which impede the progress of RNAP. While transcribing, RNAP can run into lesions or damaged DNA. Unable to proceed across such a barrier, RNAP stalls. Early studies in Escherichia coli implicated such a stalled RNAP as a detector of DNA damage, which then mobilizes proteins that repair the lesion (Hanawalt and Spivak, 2008). Transcription is considered to be a monitoring system eliciting the rapid repair of lesions that would have gone unrecognized in the absence of RNAP, thus aiding in the overall protection of the genome. However, the act of transcription imposes topological changes on the DNA template and can also physically block important cellular processes such as DNA replication instigating genomic instability (Nudler, 2012). Transcription factors that bind RNAP directly have profound effects on modulating transcription during encounters with replication as well as lesions. This chapter focuses on a class of auxiliary transcription factors that interact with a specialized region of the RNAP called the secondary channel and their impact on the maintenance of genome stability. 

## 9.2.1.2 The transcription cycle

In E. coli, the core RNAP enzyme is made up of five subunits: β, β′ , αI, αII, and ω (Figure 9.2.1a). The process of 

RNA synthesis has three main stages: initiation, elongation, and termination. Synthesis begins with the RNAP holoenzyme, which has an additional σ subunit to facilitate promoter recognition, searching for an appropriate promoter sequence. Binding to the promoter results in the formation of the closed complex. This is followed by promoter melting and DNA unwinding that expose template DNA to be copied and allow for the transition to the open complex. The first complementary nucleotide then binds, initiating transcription. The active center of RNAP (Figure 9.2.1 a,b) then catalyzes the formation of a phosphodiester bond: attachment of a nucleoside monophosphate to the 3′ OH of the nascent RNA chain and the release of pyrophosphate. Two magnesium ions are essential for polymerization; one is permanently held in the enzyme, whereas the second is coordinated by the incoming nucleotide (Nudler, 2009). The active site possesses a domain known as the trigger loop, which is also essential for bond formation. The initiation complex goes through several rounds of synthesis of short RNAs (9–11 nucleotides in length) while still bound to the promoter, a process termed abortive initiation. This forces the RNAP to restart synthesis until one of the complexes escapes the promoter, which is typically coupled with the dissociation of the σ subunit. RNAP now enters the elongation phase (Figure 9.2.2a). The core RNAP (without the sigma factor) bound to the DNA template incorporating nucleotides into the nascent RNA is referred to as the ternary elongation complex (EC) (Borukhov and Nudler, 2008). The EC moves along the template DNA, carrying out RNA chain elongation at the rate of ≅50 nucleotides per second. Nucleotides are presumed to reach the active site through the secondary channel, an opening formed by the β and β′ subunits of RNAP (Figure 9.2.1a,b). Destabilization of the EC via multiple signals (RNA hairpins, Rho factor, or Mfd helicase) is the precursor to transcription termination and release of the nascent RNA transcript (Brennan et al., 1987; Park et al., 2002).

## 9.2.1.3 Backtracking or arrest of RNAP

Although, once formed, an EC is highly processive, the path of an elongating RNAP is riddled with obstacles including protein roadblocks and DNA sequences that cause the enzyme to pause. One particular type of pause called RNAP backtracking is instigated by DNA sequences that destabilize the RNA–DNA hybrid (Nudler et al., 1997), physical protein roadblocks, or nucleotide deprivation (Toulme´ et al., 2000). These conditions induce the backward translocation of RNAP along the DNA in the direction opposite to transcription. During this process, the transcription bubble also slides back and the 3′ end of the nascent transcript is extruded into the secondary channel of RNAP (Figure 9.2.2b) (Komissarova and Kashlev, 1997). Even though such an RNAP is inactive and cannot continue elongation due to misplacement of the 3′ OH of the nascent RNA, it is highly stable. An RNAP existing in this conformation is referred to as a backtracked RNAP (Figure 9.2.2b) (Nudler, 2012). In vitro studies suggest that, under specific conditions, RNAP possesses an intrinsic activity for endonucleolytic cleavage of the transcript near the 3′ end, releasing a fragment containing the extruded 3′ OH (Orlova et al., 1995). The cleaved portion then diffuses out of the polymerase (Figure 9.2.2c). This generates a new 3′ OH end of RNA that is realigned with the active site. Since the polymerase maintains register with the DNA during the entire cycle of backtracking and cleavage, transcription elongation can resume in the presence of nucleotides (Figure 9.2.2c). In vivo, cleavage of RNA in backtracked complexes needs to be stimulated by additional factors (Toulme´ et al., 2000). In E. coli, the proteins GreA and GreB promote transcript cleavage, thereby reducing transcription elongation arrest. 

## 9.2.1.4 Gre factors

GreA was initially identified as a high copy suppressor of the temperature sensitivity of an RNAP β subunit mutation (Sparkowski and Das, 1990), followed by the chance discovery of the protein’s function in transcription elongation. Borukhov et al. (1992) noticed that purified RNAP as well as crude cell lysates, but not RNAP reconstituted from each subunit purified separately, were able to cleave the 3′ terminal dinucleotide from the nascent RNA in an arrested EC. This cleavage activity was ascribed to a contaminant in the RNAP preparation, which was revealed by sequencing to be GreA (Borukhov et al., 1992). Shortly afterward, the same group noticed another protein also capable of transcript cleavage bearing homology to GreA, which they named GreB. Both GreA and GreB are capable of stimulating the endonucleolytic cleavage of nascent RNA in backtracked RNAP complexes (Figure 9.2.2b,c). Examination of the in vitro cleavage activity of the two proteins exposed some differences in their anti-backtracking abilities. GreA was only able to prevent arrest – GreA did not cleave RNA when added after a backtracked RNAP was generated on the template DNA. GreB, in contrast, was able to revive RNAP that had undergone backtracking. Furthermore, GreA stimulated the hydrolysis of di- and tri-nucleotides, while GreB yielded larger fragments up to 18 nucleotides in length (Borukhov et al., 1993). Another distinction between GreA and GreB is their cellular abundance as determined by Western blots: GreA concentration is four times as much as GreB during the log phase, but this disparity is reduced in the stationary phase (Rutherford et al., 2007). The crystal structure of E. coli GreA has been solved (Stebbins et al., 1995) as well as cryo-electron images of GreB bound to RNAP (Opalka et al., 2003). The proteins are made up of two domains: a C-terminal globular domain consisting of a single α-helix and a five-strand β-sheet, and an N-terminal domain constituted by an antiparallel α-helical coiled-coil dimer (Figure 9.2.3) (Stebbins et al., 1995). The C-terminal domain is thought to make contacts with the surface of RNAP that forms the rim of the secondary channel, while the coiled-coil domain inserts into the secondary channel of the enzyme. Mutational analysis of the coiled-coil domain identified two conserved acidic residues at the tip of this domain to be functionally required for transcript cleavage (Figure 9.2.3) (Laptenko et al., 2003). These two residues chelate a magnesium ion that enables catalysis during the cleavage reaction (Sosunova et al., 2003). Complete loss of function mutations in GreA or GreB separately do not affect normal growth of cells, but a double mutation impacts survival at higher temperatures. How these factors appear to prevent conflict between transcription and important DNA metabolic processes provides a potential explanation for the thermosenstivity seen in the absence of GreA and GreB. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/6c2e57f4-f177-4731-acc4-f560c6f82e69/0a889f871a04e885ccbbf1fc8d94d757414baaa3d0e193e3d92f0ec2fd2003f5.jpg)



Figure 9.2.2 RNAP backtracking and cleavage. Template DNA is shown in black, and nascent RNA in red. (a) During elongation, the active site catalyzes the formation of phosphodiester bonds to synthesize the nascent RNA chain. The 3′ OH of the terminal nucleotide of the nascent RNA chain is found within the active site. (b) During RNAP backtracking, the enzyme translocates along the DNA in the opposite direction, threading the nascent RNA through the secondary channel of the enzyme. An internal portion of the RNA chain now occupies the active site, precluding the addition of NTPs and causing elongation arrest. (c) Gre factors stimulate cleavage of RNA located in the secondary channel of a backtracked RNAP. This generates a new terminal 3′ OH in correspondence with the active site. Transcription elongation can resume in the presence of NTPs (Komissarova and Kashlev, 1997; Shaevitz et al., 2003).


## 9.2.1.5 DksA and ppGpp

The E. coli stringent response is an orchestration of gene regulation changes to overcome the limitation of any charged transfer RNA (tRNA) species that restricts protein synthesis. Guanosine tetraphosphate (ppGpp) was an early player credited with transcriptional regulation during the stringent response (Potrykus and Cashel, 2008; see Section 7). Discrepancies between the magnitude of ppGpp control in vitro and in vivo were resolved by uncovering its cofactor, DksA (Perederina et al., 2004; see Chapter 6.3). Together, ppGpp and DksA control transcription initiation during the stringent response by destabilizing open complexes at ribosomal RNA promoters, redistributing RNAP to be bound by stress-specific σ factors, and stimulating transcription initiation of amino acid synthesis genes. The crystal structure of DksA bears striking similarity to GreA/B with a globular domain and coiled-coil domain (Figure 9.2.3), but DksA possesses a third structural element, a C-terminal α helix that is proposed to aid in RNAP–DksA binding (Perederina et al., 2004). The DksA–RNAP interaction was mapped by protein–protein crosslinking and footprinting. Subsequent modeling revealed that DksA also binds in the secondary channel of RNAP. The tip of the coiled-coil domain (Figure 9.2.3) may interact with the trigger loop part of the RNAP active center (Lennon et al., 2012). A ppGpp binding site on RNAP was also recently located – the interaction occurs at the interface between the ω and β′ subunits (Ross et al., 2013). Since this site is positioned away from the secondary channel, DksA and ppGpp appear to not bind each other even though they act as cofactors in modulating RNAP during transcription initiation. Moreover, current developments in the field indicate a ppGppindependent aspect of DksA action during transcription elongation (Tehranchi et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2014).

Figure 9.2.3 Structure of DksA, GreA, and GreB. The three transcription factors are structurally similar with a globular domain (orange) and a coiled-coil domain (purple) (Perederina et al., 2004; Stebbins et al., 1995). Two acidic residues at the tip of GreA/B’s coiled-coil domain are essential for the chelation of magnesium during the cleavage reaction in backtracked RNAP complexes (Laptenko et al., 2003). The residue at the tip of DksA interacts with the trigger loop of RNAP, but no function has been ascribed to it yet (Lennon et al., 2012). DksA also has an additional C-terminal alpha helix and a Zinc ion (pink sphere) coordinated by four cysteine residues (green).


Since the Gre factors and DksA bind within the secondary channel and the proteins share structural similarity (Figure 9.2.3), it is possible that they compete with each other for RNAP binding. In vivo, the absence of DksA increases the interaction between RNAP and GreA/B (Aaberg et al., 2008). However, mutations in specific RNAP residues can abolish DksA binding to RNAP without affecting Gre factor interaction with the polymerase (Satory et al., 2013). It has also been shown that GreA/B and DksA respond to different conformations of RNAP, increasing the binding of one or the other factor depending on cellular requirements (Furman et al., 2013). Importantly, DksA is incapable of transcript cleavage, and the way in which DksA potentiates its effects is still under investigation. The Gre factors can compensate for lack of DksA under some conditions, but not others (Rutherford et al., 2007). Furthermore, there are a number of examples where the Gre factors operate synergistically with DksA but several situations in which they are antagonistic (Tehranchi et al., 2010; Vinella et al., 2012). The secondary channel is an important control point for transcription regulation, affecting growth and response to stress. However, a whole additional realm of RNAP modulation by factors that bind the secondary channel exists in order to avoid encounters with other cellular processes that occur simultaneously on the DNA template such as replication and repair. Studies on how these factors contribute to conflict control have unearthed interesting conundrums that we attempt to describe and discuss in this chapter. 

## 9.2.2 Replication–transcription collisions in E. coli

During rapid bacterial proliferation, there is an imperative need for quick and accurate DNA copying alongside efficient gene expression in order to grow, divide, and deliver genetic information to new daughter cells. Even though a recent study suggests the spatial compartmentalization of transcription and replication into separate chromosomal territories (Cagliero et al., 2014), this analysis was focused on ribosomal RNA (rrn) operons, and evidence from early studies (Merrikh et al., 2012, and references within; Rudolph et al., 2007) and those described in this chapter indicates that the concurrent engagement of the DNA template by ECs and replisomes leads to collisions between these processes. Hence, E. coli has evolved multiple replication–transcription conflict avoidance mechanisms (Figure 9.2.4) as well as ways to resolve conflicts when they do arise. These strategies need to be adjusted to suit variable nutrient conditions and environmental perturbations. Furthermore, the orientation in which a replication fork runs into ongoing transcription significantly alters the factors required and the outcome of the collision. Transcription of genes on the leading strand relative to DNA replication provokes co-directional encounters, whereas expression of genes encoded on the lagging strands leads to head-on collisions. Co-directional conflicts between transcription and replication machineries translocating in the same direction but on opposite strands are inevitable since the replisome travels approximately 20 times faster than RNAP (Brewer, 1988). In E. coli, 55% of all genes, and 70% of essential genes, are encoded on the leading strand (Rocha, 2004). This orientation bias led to the conclusion that co-directional collisions are less calamitous compared to those that are headon. However, recent evidence from E. coli (Dutta et al., 2011) and Bacillus subtilis (Merrikh et al., 2011) demonstrates the critical ramifications of collisions between RNAP and replication forks traveling in the same direction. In vitro experiments show that replication terminates following an encounter with a co-directionally oriented E. coli RNAP. But once RNAP is removed, replication can perform a template switch, proceeding to use the nascent RNA as a primer to continue DNA synthesis. This has been suggested as one probable reason for the disjointedness of leading strand replication in vivo (Pomerantz and O’Donnell, 2008). Thus, regardless of replication conflict directionality, high levels of transcription have detrimental repercussions. The most drastic consequence is blocking replication fork progression, which threatens genome stability and ultimately cell survival. An RNAP complex that is in the initiation, elongation, or termination stage can potentially obstruct the path of replication. But stalled or backtracked ECs form extremely stable complexes with the template DNA, making them a common and formidable barrier to traversing replication forks. A majority of known conflict avoidance pathways hence function to either avert RNAP stalling or rescue those that have been backtracked (Figure 9.2.4). Secondary channel interactors have been identified as vital contributors to preventing conflicts between transcription and the replisome by attenuating levels of RNAP backtracking. In this section, we outline how conflict prevention mechanisms including the Gre factors and DksA act in conjunction to reduce the impact of collisions between ECs and replication. 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/6c2e57f4-f177-4731-acc4-f560c6f82e69/8466b192ee8411305c7091d1c39a5f2f50e297b4fb07c9a0d823a6e75919afcc.jpg)



Figure 9.2.4 Mechanisms that act in concert to prevent replication–transcription conflicts. A major pathway of conflict avoidance centers on preventing RNAP backtracking or rescuing backtracked RNAP complexes. DNA is shown in black, nascent RNA is red, and RNAP molecules are dark blue. (a) Multiple initiation events at strong promoters result in cooperation between RNAPs; hence, trailing ECs can push the ones ahead forward (Epshtein and Nudler, 2003). (b) The coupling of translation with transcription in E. coli allows ribosomes (green) translating behind ECs to promote elongation and reduce backtracking (Proshkin et al., 2010). (c) DksA prevents backtracking by an unknown mechanism, and the Gre factors help revive backtracked complexes via transcript cleavage.


## 9.2.2.1 Conflict avoidance mechanisms

Intuitively, the easiest way to prevent transcription from interfering with chromosome copying is to dislodge RNAP complexes, plowing a clear track for the replicative machinery. In vitro, a halted EC composed of an E. coli RNAP on a DNA template, opposed to replication in the head-on direction, stalled the approaching fork. However, the RNAP was shown to be dislodged by the replisome, which then continued with DNA synthesis (Pomerantz and O’Donnell, 2010). This ability of the replisome to displace ECs has not been corroborated in vivo, where multiple rounds of initiation from the same promoter can cause an array of RNAPs to build behind a single stalled EC, a barrier likely insurmountable by a single replication fork. The Rep, UvrD, and DinG helicases act in concert to remove ECs and allow replicative synthesis to proceed through tracts of intense transcription (Boubakri et al., 2010). The transcription– repair coupling factor, Mfd, uses its DNA translocase activity to collapse the transcription bubble and push RNAP off the DNA in the direction of RNA synthesis, effectively terminating transcription. If nucleotides are present, however, Mfd can reverse backtracking by forward translocation of the RNAP, which can then resume transcription elongation (Roberts and Park, 2004). GreA and GreB also function to revive backtracked RNAP, reducing clashes with the replisome (Figure 9.2.4) (Dutta et al., 2011). Rho, a factor that promotes transcription termination, along with two RNAP auxiliary proteins NusA and NusG, can remove inactive RNAP complexes resulting in early cessation of transcription, precluding its encounter with replication (Washburn and Gottesman, 2011). Inhibiting the formation of backtracked RNAPs is another efficient conflict aversion method. In highly transcribed genes, multiple rounds of transcription initiation enable trailing RNAP molecules to push complexes ahead of them, onward (Epshtein and Nudler, 2003). The coupling between transcription and translation in E. coli allows ribosomes traveling behind RNAPs to act analogously to mitigate backtracking (Figure 9.2.4) (Proshkin et al., 2010). Folding of nascent RNA to form secondary structures also offers protection against backtracking (Zhang et al., 2014). 

## 9.2.2.2 ppGpp and RNAP mutants (rpo∗)

McGlynn and Lloyd discovered a surprising relationship between ppGpp, DNA repair, and DNA replication (McGlynn and Lloyd, 2000). In E. coli, strains lacking the Holliday junction resolvase RuvABC (ruv mutants) have compromised ability to repair broken replication forks. It was shown that ppGpp could suppress the survival deficit of UV-irradiated ruv cells. A set of RNAP mutants were then isolated that also rescued the viability of UV-treated ruv mutants. These were classified as one subset of stringent RNAP mutants or $r p o ^ { * }$ , as they mimicked the action of ppGpp. This rescue depended on proteins required to process a regressed replication fork as well as replication restart proteins. It was thus concluded that RNAP complexes stalled at UV-induced lesions cause replication fork stalling and regression. Both $r p o ^ { * }$ and ppGpp were proposed to destabilize open complexes at promoters damaged by UV irradiation or elongating ECs stalled at lesions in the coding region, prompting RNAP dissociation and reducing replication fork encounters (McGlynn and Lloyd, 2000). Further characterization of $r p o ^ { * }$ mutants established that the amino acids that were substituted are mostly positioned around the path that the DNA follows through RNAP. This suggests that inactivation of these residues eliminates interactions critical for binding of the enzyme to the template DNA. RNAP that is inactive or backtracked at a lesion may thus dissociate more easily due to weak DNA–RNAP interactions in the $r p o ^ { * }$ mutants (Trautinger and Lloyd, 2002). The same group later utilized in vitro transcription assays performed on UV-irradiated DNA templates, with wild-type RNAP transcribing from the bacteriophage lambda promoter cro, to show that UV-induced lesions were capable of blocking transcription. Stalled arrays of RNAP complexes built up on the irradiated template that could be visualized by atomic force microscopy. However, the presence of ppGpp, or the use of some of the $r p o ^ { * }$ mutants instead of wild-type RNAP, reduced the formation of RNAP arrays, suggesting that both ppGpp and $r p o ^ { * }$ destabilized stalled or backtracked ECs formed at UV-induced lesions (Trautinger et al., 2005). A nonstringent mutation in RNAP that is also thought to reduce replication–transcription conflicts by destabilization of the EC has been shown to rescue the temperature sensitivity produced as a result of inactivating both GreA and GreB (Baharoglu et al., 2010). This suggests that high temperatures may increase replication fork collision with backtracked RNAP. Although it has been argued that some $r p o ^ { * }$ mutants do not impact EC stability (Dutta et al., 2011), these early studies provide a link between curtailing the buildup of backtracked ECs and reducing replication–transcription conflicts. 

## 9.2.2.3 Secondary channel interactors and conflicts

Co-directional conflicts with spontaneously backtracked RNAP complexes have been shown to result in genome instability by generating double-strand DNA breaks (DSBs) (Dutta et al., 2011; see Chapter 2.14). The absence of the anti-backtracking factors GreA, GreB, or Rho-dependent transcription termination leads to DSB formation on a plasmid engineered with a ColE1 replication origin and the lambda pL promoter. These breaks occur when a replisome encounters backtracked RNAP molecules originating from the promoter exclusively in the codirectional orientation. In addition to the engineered plasmid, breaks were also generated on the E. coli chromosome when either GreA or GreB was removed while simultaneously slowing down ribosomes translating behind RNAP. DSB formation triggered the DNA damage (SOS) response and required homologous recombination in order to be repaired. The authors (Dutta et al., 2011) propose that replication stalling upon a codirectional confrontation with a backtracked RNAP and a replication fork creates an extended R-loop between the nascent transcript and template DNA: the R-loop provides an RNA template to prime DNA synthesis, and the template switch to RNA leaves a single-strand gap. The gap is converted to a DSB upon the arrival of a second replication fork. Other than the breaks formed by fork collapse during conflict (Rudolph et al., 2007), this R-loopmediated mechanism suggests an alternate source of DSBs. To determine if transcription initiation is also an impediment to replication, Mirkin et al. constructed a mutant promoter that resulted in ineffective promoter clearance, trapping RNAP in a stable initiation complex (Mirkin et al., 2006). A plasmid containing the promoter, pBR322 replication origin, and transcription terminators from the rrnB operon was transformed into cells. 2D gels were used to map the location of replisome stalling. Transcription from the mutant promoter in the head-on orientation, and to a very minor extent co-directionally, caused replication stalling exclusively in the promoter region. Interestingly, the co-directional encounter resulted in fork stalling at the terminator that was exacerbated by loss of GreA/B, suggesting that backtracking at transcription terminators may be problematic for replication fork movement. This study illustrates that inactive RNAP at any step during the transcription cycle may provoke collisions with DNA replication (Mirkin et al., 2006). 

The action of DksA in conflict aversion is different from the Gre factors, and the exact mechanism by which this RNAP modulator exerts its effect on transcription elongation is currently unknown. Tehranchi et al. were the first to identify a role for DksA during elongation (Tehranchi et al., 2010). Using microarrays to examine genome-wide replication stalling, they found that during transcription elongation, depletion of amino acids in combination with loss of DksA function induced replication arrest, which in turn triggered the SOS response. It was determined that DksA was counteracting RNAP stalling, and this was independent of ppGpp. Loss of GreA and GreB together had a similar phenotype, causing almost complete replication disruption upon starvation. A DksA homolog encoded on conjugative plasmids, TraR, was found to compensate for DksA when overexpressed. This study unraveled a novel means to reduce transcription-associated replication interruptions utilizing RNAP modulators that bind the secondary channel under starvation (Tehranchi et al., 2010). More recently, it has been found that ribosome deceleration, which accompanies amino acid starvation, causes transcription–translation uncoupling elevating the requirement for anti-backtracking factors such as DksA and Gre (Zhang et al., 2014). A common theme that emerges from these studies is that ribosomes serve as a link between environmental conditions and the essential cellular processes of replication and transcription. DksA and GreA/B cooperate synergistically with the ribosomes to regulate RNAP under conditions of stress in order to prevent conflict and allow for productive replication. However, the functions of DksA and the Gre factors are not completely overlapping – loss of all three exacerbates conflict between replication and transcription (Tehranchi et al., 2010). The elucidation of the mechanism through which DksA controls RNAP during conflicts will aid in understanding which aspects of modulation are performed by each factor individually. 

## 9.2.3 Conflicts between transcription and DNA repair

The discovery, by Mellon and Hanawalt, that UV-induced lesions in the transcribed DNA strand were discriminatorily repaired at a faster rate than ones in the nontranscribed strand allowed for the hypothesis that RNAP encountering this lesion could operate as a beacon for repair (Mellon and Hanawalt, 1989). This phenomenon, now called transcriptioncoupled repair (TCR), is initiated when the EC confronts a helix-distorting lesion, rendering RNAP stalled and the lesion obscured by the arrested complex (Selby and Sancar, 1994). Mfd dislodges the RNAP and also recruits repair proteins to excise the offending lesion and ligate the DNA (Figure 9.2.5a) (Park et al., 2002). An alternative Mfd-independent TCR pathway has been recently characterized involving the helicase UvrD and the transcription factor NusA (Figure 9.2.5b) (Cohen et al., 2010; Epshtein et al., 2014). While attempting to elucidate the exact role of UvrD in preventing replication–transcription conflicts, Gwynn et al. found a conserved domain of UvrD that interacts directly with RNAP (Gwynn et al., 2013). This binding was confirmed in a study by Epshtein et al. (2014). They found that UvrD was associated with RNAP with the same abundance as several well-described transcription factors. Furthermore, they used UV-irradiated cells harboring a plasmidencoded lacZ to track repair zones by primer extension. These experiments showed that UV lesions impeded RNAP progression, causing backtracking that was mediated by UvrD. Interestingly, UV adducts were repaired faster in the absence of GreA and GreB. The model from this study proposes that UvrD pulls

Figure 9.2.5 Pathways of transcription-coupled DNA repair in E. coli. (a) When RNAP (dark blue) encounters a lesion in the DNA (yellow star), transcription is stalled and the damage cannot be repaired due to physical obstruction by the RNAP. The transcription–repair coupling factor Mfd (green) can dislodge RNAP from the DNA by forward translocation (green arrow). Transcription is thus terminated. Mfd then recruits repair factors such as UvrA (purple) and UvrB (light blue) that begin the repair process (Hanawalt and Spivak, 2008). (b) In an alternate pathway, UvrD (pink) is associated with RNAP and dimerizes to promote RNAP backtracking (pink arrow) when a lesion (yellow star) is present on the template DNA. This allows repair factors access to the lesion. This process is assisted by NusA (light green). GreA/B act antagonistically to rescue backtracking (black arrow). UvrD is then also thought to recruit the repair factors UvrA and UvrB (purple and light blue, respectively) (Epshtein et al., 2014).


RNAP backward at UV lesions. UvrD then also recruits repair factors to the lesion that is no longer obstructed by the EC (Figure 9.2.5b) (Epshtein et al., 2014). By stimulating cleavage and restart of backtracked RNAP, the Gre factors act in opposition to TCR, suggesting a negative role for these factors in repair and the maintenance of genome stability. In the absence of UvrD, the thermosensitivity of the GreA–GreB double mutant is rescued (Epshtein et al., 2014). It is thus possible that high temperatures create conditions (similar to damage by UV irradiation) that induce RNAP backtracking. The opposing effects of UvrD and the Gre factors on backtracked RNAP may be then brought into play. The contribution of DksA to TCR is currently not well understood. Complete-loss-of-function DksA mutants are sensitive to mitomycin C and UV radiation, both of which induce damage that elicits TCR (Trautinger et al., 2005). Since DksA is thought to prevent RNAP backtracking, it is possible that there is a greater buildup of backtracked RNAP complexes at mitomycin C–induced or UV-induced lesions in the absence of DksA. Interestingly, some rpo∗ mutants as well as removal of GreA can rescue the sensitivity to these agents in the absence of DksA (Trautinger et al., 2005). The rescue by $r p o ^ { * }$ can be explained by the fact that this mutant destabilizes backtracked RNAPs, the levels of which are greater in the absence of DksA. The effect of inactivating GreA, however, still remains a mystery. DksA has also been implicated in the repair of DSBs. Complete-loss-of-function DksA mutants are mildly sensitive to ionizing radiation, a potent inducer of DSBs. However, DksA loss combined with the absence of an SOS-inducible DSB repair protein (RecN) rendered cells hypersensitive to breaks generated by both exogenous and endogenous damaging agents. The high levels of DNA breakage in the double mutant was rescued by one of the rpo∗ mutations (rpoB∗35), reiterating the concept that stalled or backtracked RNAP complexes impede repair just as they retard replication fork progression (Meddows et al., 2005). 

## 9.2.4 Conflicting roles for Gre factors in modulating conflicts?

The current conceptual idea of transcription collisions with DNA-centric processes not only depicts the Gre proteins as guardians of the genome due to the prevention of replication– transcript conflicts but also shows them as factors that prevent repair, hence propagating DNA instability. One key aspect in reconciling this paradox may be the importance of RNA fidelity. By promoting elongation, GreA/B increase the number of full-length transcripts and hence maintain transcription fidelity. Backtracking after nucleotide misincorporation followed by cleavage and removal of the incorrect nucleotide by the Gre factors, allowing for replacement with the appropriate base, also contributes to improving RNA fidelity (Erie et al., 1993). Cells lacking both GreA and GreB have increased transcription errors that result in heritable phenotypic consequences (Gordon et al., 2009). Unlike the most commonly occurring Mfd pathway for TCR, UvrD pushes RNAP backward without causing transcription termination. Hence, once the lesion is removed, RNAP can continue elongation and manufacture a completed transcript (Epshtein et al., 2014). Although the Mfd helicase and Rho factor terminate transcription when RNAP encounters replication, the anti-backtracking factors push RNAP forward, aiding in productive elongation. An efficient solution to an encounter between a replication fork and ongoing transcription that maintains DNA integrity would be the dissociation of the RNAP by the replisome. This does not appear to happen in vivo, suggesting that the cell tries to keep the EC active. Whilst we have become accustomed to the sequence hypothesis, postulating that RNA is a mere transient intermediate in the information transfer process (Crick, 1970), the identification of new roles for RNAP modulators in coordinating cellular processes to protect RNA indicates that preserving transcriptome fidelity is also essential for survival.
