# How a large gene network couples mutagenic DNA break repair to stress in Escherichia coli

Elizabeth Rogers, P.J. Hastings, Mar´ıa Angelica Bravo N ´ u´ nez, and Susan M. Rosenberg ˜ 

Department of Molecular and Human Genetics, Baylor College of Medicine, Houston, Texas, USA 

## 9.3.1 Introduction

Historically, mutations that drive evolution were thought to occur gradually and randomly within a population (Mayr, 1982). An alternate hypothesis of punctuated equilibrium (Eldredge and Gould, 1972) imagined populations that remain relatively static over time until a selective pressure was applied, and then change rapidly. Although Eldredge and Gould thought in geological time from the macroscopic fossil record, and not in terms of molecular mechanisms, mechanisms of mutagenesis, or bacterial or cell evolution, we now see much evidence supporting their concept at these more molecular levels. In times of plenty, mutation rates are low and DNA is replicated with high fidelity. Under times of stress, stresses such as starvation (Al Mamun et al., 2012), hypoxia, changes in pH or osmolarity, and exposure to antibiotics (Gutierrez et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2011) or antifungal drugs (Forche et al., 2011) can cause increased mutagenesis in various bacteria, in human cancer cells (Bindra et al., 2007), and in yeast (Shor et al. 2013; and reviewed by Rosenberg et al., 2012). Mutation pathways that are upregulated by stress responses promote mutagenesis and the ability to evolve specifically when cells or organisms are poorly adapted to their environment, potentially accelerating evolution. Modeling indicates that stress-inducible mutagenesis in bacterial populations is a powerful evolution accelerator, selectable based on its evolutionpromoting property (Ram and Hadany, 2012, 2014). Here, we focus on the discovery of a large gene network that promotes mutagenic DNA break repair (MBR) in Escherichia coli. We see that the identities and functions of the genes in it cement the conclusion that orchestrating mutagenesis to occur during times of stress is a very important regulatory and perhaps evolutionary strategy for E. coli and, by implication, probably to cells and organisms generally. 

## 9.3.2 The mutagenic break repair mechanism: three stress responses are required

Three known stress responses are required for MBR in E. coli (Figure 9.3.1): the SOS DNA damage response (George et al., 1974; Janion, 2008; McKenzie et al., 2000; see Chapter 9.1), the RpoS general stress response (Battesti et al., 2011; Lombardo et al., 2004; Storvik and Foster, 2010; see Chapter 2.4), and the RpoE membrane stress response (Ades, 2008; Gibson et al., 2010; see Section 18). Their roles in MBR are illustrated in Figure 9.3.1. 

## 9.3.2.1 The SOS DNA damage response

The SOS response is induced by single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) that signals DNA damage. RecA bound to ssDNA acts as a coprotease for LexA, a transcriptional repressor. LexA represses about 40 genes (Courcelle et al., 2001). Once LexA is cleaved, these promoters are de-repressed, and transcription of SOS genes occurs or is increased from basal levels. The only protein of the SOS response required at induced levels for indels (from one to a few bp insertions or deletions) generated by MBR in a lac reporter gene is the error-prone DNA polymerase, DinB (DNA polymerase (Pol) IV). DinB is upregulated 10-fold during an SOS response and generates ∼85% of indels in MBR (Galhardo et al., 2009; McKenzie et al., 2001). MBR-generated base substitutions and some indels additionally require or partially require DNA Pol V (Petrosino et al., 2009; Shee et al., 2011), and because Pol V is produced only during an SOS response, SOS induction of Pol V is presumably also required for base substitutions made by MBR. Similarly, the SulA inhibitor of cell division is synthesized only during an SOS response, and it is partially required for MBR (McKenzie et al., 2000). 

![image](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2026-06-13/6c2e57f4-f177-4731-acc4-f560c6f82e69/689305fb6fe05f47747ff6246b1b0136cc4812ac23e53ad6cc0f9de04f683cac.jpg)



Figure 9.3.1 Roles of stress responses in, and the SOS/RpoS-controlled switch to, mutagenic break repair (MBR). MBR is coupled to stress via at least three stress responses. (a) The $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { E } }$ envelope stress response contributes to formation of spontaneous double-strand breaks (DSBs) at some genomic locations (Gibson et al., 2010). DSBs are repaired by homologous recombination (HR) in a high-fidelity process using replicative DNA polymerase (Pol) III (Motamedi et al., 1999) unless the SOS and RpoS/σS general stress responses are activated simultaneously. (b) DSBs induce the SOS DNA-damage response. SOS induction causes 10-fold transcriptional upregulation of the DinB error-prone polymerase, SOS upregulation of which is required for MBR (Galhardo et al., 2009), and allows expression of Pol V, another error-prone DNA Pol partially required for some MBR (base substitutions and some indels) (reviewed by Rosenberg et al., 2012), and SulA, an inhibitor of cell division also partially required for MBR (McKenzie et al., 2000). (c) However, even with 10 times more DinB, repair remains high fidelity unless the general stress response is also activated. The general stress response is activated by starvation, antibiotics, and many other stressors. RpoS transcriptionally upregulates – and, indirectly, downregulates – hundreds of genes, and it licenses the use of lower fidelity DNA Pols I, II, V, and DinB in DSB repair by as-yet-unknown means.


## 9.3.2.2 The general stress response

The general stress response is also required for MBR. RpoS or $\sigma ^ { \mathrm { S } }$ is a sigma factor (transcriptional activator) that regulates the expression of over 500 genes in E. coli (Ito et al., 2008). $\mathrm { R p o S } / \sigma ^ { \mathrm { S } }$ is induced in the stationary phase, in response to starvation, by acid shock, osmotic shock, cold shock, and oxidative stresses (Battesti et al., 2011). The RpoS response activates the switch to MBR under stress, in that repair of DSBs is nonmutagenic in unstressed cells, using high-fidelity DNA Pol III (Motamedi et al., 1999), but switches to a mutagenic mode using DinB and other low-fidelity DNA polymerases under the control of RpoS. The switch to MBR occurs either during stress that activates RpoS expression or in unstressed cells if RpoS is artificially upregulated (Ponder et al., 2005; Shee et al., 2011). RpoS upregulates DinB about two-fold (Layton and Foster, 2003), but this is unlikely to be its main contribution to MBR in that RpoS is also required for the DNA Pol II– and Pol V–dependent components of MBR (Frisch et al., 2010; Shee et al., 2011) as well as the Pol I–dependent component of MBR that results in genome rearrangements (Lombardo et al., 2004; Slack et al., 2006). Induction of the general stress response licenses the use of all of the lower fidelity DNA polymerases in MBR by as-yet-unknown means. 

## 9.3.2.3 The membrane stress response

The RpoE membrane stress response is induced in response to misfolded membrane proteins that often occur when cells are exposed to high temperatures. The RpoE role in MBR is upstream of formation of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) in that providing a DSB (via an engineered restriction enzyme and site) near a mutation-reporter gene substitutes for RpoE (Gibson et al., 2010), whereas it does not substitute for DSB downstream effectors like DSB repair proteins, DinB, and RpoS (Figure 9.3.1). Spontaneous DSB formation is a key step in MBR. 

## 9.3.3 The mutagenic break repair mechanism: three events are required

MBR requires three events (Rosenberg et al., 2012): (i) a DSB and its repair by homologous recombination; (ii) activation of the SOS response, which upregulates DinB; and (iii) activation of the RpoS response, which licenses the use of error-prone DNA polymerases in the DSB repair replisome. 

## 9.3.3.1 DSBs and repair

MBR strongly requires RecBCD, a DSB-end-specific repair enzyme (Harris et al., 1994) and is blocked by production of a phage-encoded DSB-end-specific binding protein, both results demonstrate (Wimberly et al., 2013 Nature communications) its DSB dependence. When cells are artificially given a DSB by cleavage of the DNA near a mutation reporter gene with the restriction endonuclease I-SceI, mutagenesis increases up to 100-fold (Gibson et al., 2010; Ponder et al., 2005; Shee et al., 2011) and the mutations fall near the DSB site (Ponder et al., 2005; Shee et al., 2012). When a lac gene in an F’ conjugative plasmid is used as the mutation-reporter gene, most nearby DSBs arise through the action of the F-specific TraI endonuclease (Ponder et al., 2005; Wimberly et al., 2013), the action of RpoE (Gibson et al., 2010), and RNA–DNA hybrids (Wimberly et al., 2013). Key recombination proteins RecA recombinase, RecBCD exonuclease, and RuvABC Hollidayjunction resolvasome are required for MBR (Bull et al., 2001; Foster et al., 1996; Harris et al., 1994, 1996; Shee et al., 2011). However, even when cells have both a DSB and an SOS response, repair is not mutagenic unless the RpoS response is also upregulated, either in response to stress or artificially in unstressed cells (Ponder et al., 2005; Shee et al., 2011). Thus, the RpoS response, not stress itself, causes the switch to mutagenic repair. As mentioned above, RpoS directly and indirectly up- and down-regulates the transcription of over 500 genes. It is not known which of these genes accounts for the important role of RpoS in MBR. 

## 9.3.4 A large gene network supports mutagenic break repair

In ∼20 years of testing candidate genes, our lab and others discovered fewer than 20 proteins required for MBR. To make a more comprehensive picture, we (Al Mamun et al., 2012) performed a genetic screen to identify new candidate genes that promote MBR. Transposon-mutagenized cells were screened for mutants deficient in MBR using a colony-color assay for reversion of a lac frameshift allele in an F’ conjugative plasmid (Figure 9.3.2). To avoid transposition into the F’ plasmid (a hotspot for transposon hops), the cells were mutagenized in the absence of the F’, which was introduced by conjugation subsequently. Individual colonies were spotted onto minimal medium with a small amount of glycerol (to allow colony formation) and abundant P-gal (a lactose analog). After the glycerol is consumed, the cells starve. The P-gal can be consumed only in cells with a lac frameshift reversion, which occurs usually by −1 bp deletions (Foster and Trimarchi, 1994; Rosenberg et al., 1994). When this happens, X-gal in the plates turns the small growing Lac+ papillae blue (Figure 9.3.2). 

The MBR-proficient parental strain forms ∼20–30 blue papillae per colony during a 5–10-day incubation period. Colonies with fewer papillae were candidates for MBR-defective mutants, and were identified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and sequencing. 

Null alleles of each non-essential candidate gene identified were validated in quantitative Lac MBR assays, as were the (nonnull) transposon hops into essential genes. A representative sample of genes was also confirmed in two additional MBR assays, both in chromosomes of plasmid-free cells: one for frameshift reversions in a tetracycline gene, and the other for base substitutions in a gyrase gene causing resistance to nalidixic acid, both stimulated by I-SceI enzyme-generated DSBs near the reporter genes. MBR is not specific to plasmids or one particular assay, and it causes base substitutions as well as frameshift mutations. Candidate mutants confirmed by these quantitative assays were used in a series of experiments designed to elucidate the role of each gene in MBR. 

Many well-known molecular mechanisms of nucleic-acid biology, such as DNA replication and transcription, are defined by fewer than 20 proteins acting on a few nucleic-acid substrates. Prior to the transposon screen, the MBR network was a similar size (17 genes). The screen revealed a very large network of 93 genes that promote stress-induced MBR. The diverse and initially perplexing network includes varied functional classes of genes from DNA repair to metabolism, with electron transfer being the largest single gene class at 20 genes (Table 9.3.1).

This list contains the 93-gene network of Al Mamun et al. (2012) plus an additional four genes identified by Wimberly et al. (2013): mfd and the genes encoding RNA polymerase, which are rpoA, rpoB, and rpoC. Superscripts S, E, and SOS indicate that mutations in these genes decrease σS activity, σE activity, and spontaneous SOS induction, respectively. For RecA and RecBCD, these are needed in MBR not only for SOS induction but also for DSB repair. 


A directed genetics approach elucidated the MBR-promoting roles of over half of the genes in the network by testing for upstream roles in activation of each of the three MBR-promoting stress responses: RpoS, RpoE, and SOS. These secondary assays reveal a method for taking a large, seemingly disparate group of genes and binning them into useful functional categories within an existing mechanism. Most proteins in the network are indirect effectors involved in sensing and responding to stress (changing intracellular and environmental conditions). 

Each network gene was tested to see whether it was required for activation of the general stress response, using a fluorescent transcriptional reporter for induction of the RpoS response and flow cytometry. We made and used a yiaG–yfp fusion of the RpoS-upregulated yiaG promoter driving the yellowfluorescent-protein gene and examined each mutant by flow cytometry for the ability to activate this promoter during carbon starvation. A full one-third of the 93 genes in the network were found to act upstream of RpoS with this assay. That figure includes the electron transfer genes – the largest class identified in the primary screen as MBR deficient. We showed that a representative subset of the electron transfer proteins, though needed for MBR, is not needed if RpoS is artificially upregulated, indicating that these genes promote MBR by upregulation of RpoS activity and become superfluous if RpoS is supplied otherwise. 

Epistasis analyses of these mutants with a ΔrpoS mutation confirmed this conclusion. 

The identities of the electron-transfer proteins upstream of RpoS activation suggested a hypothesis for how starvation stress is sensed, leading to RpoS activation – a puzzle previously. The network reveals that specific energy sources, malate and succinate, perhaps derived from recycling cellular components, signal through part of the electron transfer chain, the oxidized ubiquinone pool, to prevent ArcB autophosphorylation. This is proposed to allow de-repression of ArcA and upregulation of RpoS. Thus, the model predicts that metabolism of malate and succinate under starvation conditions increases the availability of ubiquinone, which signals through ArcB and ArcA to increase levels of RpoS and switch DSB repair from accurate to mutagenic. Whether this model is correct (i.e., how RpoS is activated by carbon starvation) remains to be tested. Given that RpoS promotes the critical switch to MBR by licensing the use of errorprone DNA polymerases in repair (Figure 9.3.1), this proposed chain of events is thus the proposed mechanism by which mutagenesis is coupled directly to the stress of starvation, coupling the ability to evolve to the environment. 

Each gene in the network was also tested for roles in activating the SOS and RpoE responses, with the goal of elucidating the role of each component. Sensitivity to ultraviolet light and expression from a specific SOS promoter were used to identify genes upstream of the SOS response. Sensitivity to sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS)–EDTA identified candidate genes upstream of the RpoE membrane stress response. Ultimately, more than 50% (50 of 93) of the genes were shown to function in MBR by sensing stress and transducing signals that activate the stress-response regulators (Figure 9.3.3), which are critical hubs in the network. 

## 9.3.5 Functional systems biology for deconvoluting large networks

The ability to classify a majority of genes from a transposon screen into functional roles serves as a model for deconvoluting large gene networks, a frequently challenging or impossible goal. The approach used here was to first identify a functional network in which each gene is truly required for the process (MBR); and, second, use the known molecular mechanism to design hypothesis-testing secondary screens for gene functions at each of several separable steps in the mechanism. This is a powerful approach that can be generally useful for many different gene networks in biological processes. 

## 9.3.6 Understanding gene functions in large networks clarifies biological functions

The precise role in stress-induced MBR of the membrane stress response regulator RpoE, and thus of the large network segment that acts upstream of (in activation of) RpoE (33 genes),

is not yet understood. RpoE is required for DSB formation in the pathway leading to stress-induced mutagenesis by an asyet-unknown mechanism (Gibson et al., 2010). That a stress response regulates the availability of a precursor to MBR suggests that stress-induced MBR is not a simple aberration of DNA metabolism under stress, but is, rather, a complex coordinated process: The membrane stress response instigates DSB formation at some genomic loci; the SOS DNA-damage response makes more error-prone DNA polymerases available, and the general stress response tilts polymerase competition in favor of error-prone polymerases. The allocation of more than half the network genes to stress-response-activating roles demonstrates that promoting mutagenesis specifically during stress, when cells are maladapted to their environment, is important to E. coli. This is a strategy that accelerates evolution. Recent modeling further implies that stress-inducible mutagenesis can evolve selected on this basis – as an evolutionary engine (Ram and Hadany, 2012, 2014). 

## 9.3.7 General and medical importance

Stress-induced mutagenesis mechanisms including MBR may promote survival by allowing some cells to overcome the stress by mutating (Galhardo et al., 2007; Rosenberg et al., 2012). This applies not only for starvation stress (discussed here) but also in response to antibiotics, antifungal drugs, and hypoxia in cancer cells. Many of the genes required for stress-induced MBR are also required for mutagenesis in response to antibiotics, including the general stress response sigma factor RpoS, many SOS genes like RecA and RecB, and the error-prone DNA polymerase DinB (Cirz et al., 2005; Gutierrez et al., 2013). Other bacteria including Bacillus subtilis (Robleto et al., 2007) and Pseudomonas putida (Kasak et al., 1997) also induce mutation under starvation stress, dependently on stress responses and DinB. Stress-induced mutagenesis occurs in yeast (Babudri et al., 2001; Halas et al., 2002, 2009; Hall, 1992; Heidenreich et al., 2003; Shor et al., 2013; Steele and Jinks-Robertson, 1992), and in human diseases like heart disease and cancer (Bindra et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2014; Scanlon and Glazer, 2014; Siggens et al., 2012). Thus, stress-inducible mutagenesis is widespread in biology, using different mechanisms in different organisms but with stress response regulation as a recurring theme. 

The existence and widespread occurrence of stress-induced mutagenesis have profound implications for evolution and society. The E. coli stress responses that turn up mutation in response to antibiotics may be similar to pathways in human cancer cells that respond to chemotherapy drugs to become resistant. The widespread and similar mechanisms of stressinduced mutagenesis that span from bacteria and yeast to humans suggest new ways to combat phenomena like antibiotic resistance and chemotherapy resistance (Rosenberg and Queitsch, 2014). The identification of key regulators that could be targeted with drugs to prevent MBR suggests potential “antievolutionary” therapies to block the ability of cells to evolve antibiotic or chemotherapy resistance and possibly to block the ability of tumors to progress and pathogens to out-evolve our immune systems (Al Mamun et al., 2012; Frisch et al., 2010; Rosenberg and Queitsch, 2014). Because the overwhelming majority of MBR network genes regulate mutagenesis, upstream regulatory pathways converging on critical, targetable hubs may be general to many large gene networks. Using the approach of functional systems biology could potentially reveal drug targets in many biological processes.

Discovery of large networks, including function-specific gene networks, has limited usefulness in itself. Frequently, the functions of only small parts of networks are deconvoluted, and the remainder go unexplained. In the MBR network, we developed a functional-systems biology strategy and protocols for binning network genes into useful subsets, which can then be analyzed further. Moreover, the mere binning both demonstrated a profound biological conclusion – that control of mutagenesis by stress responses is important, occupying most of the network – and generated new hypotheses for specific mechanisms underlying some old biological problems.

## 9.4.1 Introduction

Repair of double-strand DNA breaks (DSBs) is critical to all living organisms. Scission of the phosphodiester backbone of both DNA strands is lethal if not repaired because such loss of linear chromosome integrity compromises chromosome replication and thereby prevents genome duplication. In contrast to some other types of DNA lesions, which can be bypassed by damage-tolerant DNA polymerases, there is no known mechanism for the replication or transcription machinery to bypass a DSB, mandating their repair before replication or transcription can proceed. As such, multiple systems have evolved to repair DSBs in species from bacteria to humans (Daley et al., 2005; Dillingham and Kowalczykowski, 2008; Lieber, 2010; Shuman and Glickman, 2007; Symington and Gautier, 2011; Yeeles and Dillingham, 2010). Since the 2000s, mycobacterial DNA repair systems in general, and mycobacterial DSB repair systems in particular, have received increasing attention. It has become clear that mycobacterial DSB repair differs substantially from the standard model of prokaryotic DSB repair derived from work in the Escherichia coli system. Most prominent among these differences is the existence of two additional DSB repair pathways that are not present in E. coli, and previously thought not to exist in bacteria: nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ) and single-strand annealing (SSA) (see Figure 9.4.1). Multiple other novel features of mycobacterial DSB repair have also been elucidated, making mycobacteria a new model system for the study of prokaryotic DSB repair. As now conceptualized, mycobacterial DSB repair actually most resembles DSB repair in budding yeast rather than in other prokaryotes (Table 9.4.1). In addition to its emerging place as a model system, studies of mycobacterial DNA repair also are of great importance for understanding mechanisms of mutagenesis and genome diversification in Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the ultimate cause of antimicrobial resistance in M. tuberculosis (Ford et al., 2013). In addition to the information and references contained in this chapter, we point the reader to several excellent reviews of mycobacterial 

DNA repair and mutagenesis recently published in the literature (Gorna et al., 2010; Kurthkoti and Varshney, 2012; Warner et al., 2013). 

Although DSBs are induced experimentally by ionizing radiation (IR) or clastogenic chemicals such as bleomycin, the doses of IR used in laboratory experiments are not often encountered in nature. The major sources of physiologic DSBs that arise in vivo are likely to be (i) DNA replication across a single strand nick, (ii) oxidative damage, (iii) desiccation, and potentially (iv) ribonucleotides incorporated into DNA (Hiller et al., 2012; Reijns et al., 2012). The frequency and number of DSBs that arise in a mycobacterial cell are difficult to estimate, and in particular it is difficult to know the frequency and character of DNA lesions that M. tuberculosis experiences within its human host. We will review the three pathways of DSB repair in mycobacteria with emphasis on recent genetic studies. 

## 9.4.2 Homologous recombination (HR)

HR is a universally distributed mechanism of DSB repair throughout all domains of life. From bacterial to human cells, HR proceeds through a common set of biochemical transactions that share common themes (see Figure 9.4.1). By definition, homology-directed repair of a DSB requires an unbroken homologous chromosome to direct repair, and therefore must occur after chromosome replication has occurred. The DNA structure ultimately used for homology search and strand invasion into the homologous duplex is a 3′ single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) coated with a strand invasion protein, RecA in bacteria. Therefore, the initiating step in HR is recognition of the break by proteins that initiate resection to generate this 3′ single-stranded substrate. In E. coli, this resection is accomplished by the RecBCD enzyme complex (Dillingham and Kowalczykowski, 2008; Wigley, 2013). RecBCD resects doublestranded DNA from the DSB until it encounters a Chi site, an 8 bp recognition sequence distributed throughout the E. coli chromosome. Upon encountering Chi, RecBCD converts to a single-stranded $5 ^ { \prime }$ to $3 ^ { \prime }$ exonuclease, thereby generating $\texttt { a } 3 ^ { \prime }$ ssDNA that is coated by the SSB protein. Exchange of SSB for RecA to form the RecA nucleoprotein filament is facilitated by RecBCD (Dillingham and Kowalczykowski, 2008). 


Pathways of mycobacterial DSB repair

## 9.4.2.1 End resection in mycobacterial recombination

Mycobacteria encode orthologs of RecBCD, but the role of this enzyme complex in mycobacterial recombination differs substantially from that in E. coli. Mycobacterium smegmatis lacking RecBCD is not sensitive to a variety of clastogens (Gupta et al., 2011; Stephanou et al., 2007), which is inconsistent with a dominant role in homologous recombination as M. smegmatis lacking recA is highly sensitized to these same clastogens (Gupta et al., 2011; Stephanou et al., 2007). A natural hypothesis of redundancy between resection nucleases arose when mycobacteria were found to have a novel heterodimeric helicase-nuclease that was named AdnAB (Sinha et al., 2009b), which is similar to the AddAB enzyme complex of Bacillus subtilis (Yeeles and Dillingham, 2010). This enzyme complex resects doublestranded DNA in vitro and has helicase activity (Sinha et al., 2009b), suggesting it may participate in DSB resection. In contrast to the RecBCD null strain, M. smegmatis lacking AdnAB is sensitive to ionizing radiation, although not to the level of the ΔrecA strain. A ΔrecBCD ΔadnAB strain was identical to the ΔadnAB strain in clastogen sensitivity, a finding inconsistent with redundancy between these two enzyme complexes (Gupta et al., 2011). Although these studies provided some insight into the epistatic relationships between recBCD and adnAB, clastogen sensitivity assays invariably involve multiple types of DNA damage and therefore do not specifically interrogate the function of a particular factor in the repair of specific DNA lesions.

Clarification of the roles of mycobacterial AdnAB and RecBCD in recombination came from studies using a chromosomal reporter system in which a single chromosomal break is induced by the homing endonuclease I-SceI. In this system, two 18 bp recognition sites for I-SceI were placed into a defective lacZ allele with a downstream lacZ donor segment. A key feature of this system is that one of the two I-SceI sites is inverted such that I-SceI cleavage at both sites creates a DSB with incompatible ends. This break cannot be directly ligated by NHEJ without end modification. This configuration seeks to minimize repeated cycles of I-SceI cutting and resealing that can occur with a single I-SceI site and obscure conclusions about the frequency of each repair pathway. Chromosomal breakage is induced by transformation of an I-SceI encoding plasmid. Three repair outcomes are possible in this system, all of which can be distinguished by scoring the surviving colonies on X-gal and kanamycin-containing media (Gupta et al., 2011): NHEJ, HR, and SSA (Figure 9.4.1). When this assay is performed in strains lacking putative repair factors, the role of each can be deduced by examining the repair outcomes in this genetic background. 

When repair outcomes were assayed using the I-SceI system in strains lacking recBCD, adnAB, or both, surprising findings emerged. First, RecBCD was not required for homologous recombination in mycobacteria, as the percentage of HR outcomes in the I-SceI system was actually increased above that of wild-type in ΔrecBCD M. smegmatis (Gupta et al., 2011). Deletion of adnAB resulted in an approximately 50% decrement in HR outcomes, supporting a role for adnAB in DSB resection in vivo. Notably, some residual HR events, which were all recA dependent, were preserved in the ΔrecBCD ΔadnAB strain, indicating an additional pathway of DSB resection that is yet to be defined (Gupta et al., 2011). Additional conclusions about the function of RecBCD in mycobacteria were gleaned from these experiments, which are discussed in Section 9.4.4 about the SSA pathway. 

## 9.4.2.2 Mediator function in mycobacterial recombination

After resection of the DSB to create the 3′ single-stranded tail, the single strand is coated by the single-strand binding protein SSB. SSB has a very high affinity to ssDNA, and therefore loading of RecA onto the 3′ single strand requires exchange of SSB for RecA to create the RecA nucleoprotein filament, which is the agent of homology search and strand invasion. This exchange reaction is facilitated by a mediator complex, a function that is conserved in all domains of life. In E. coli, the mediator function is supplied by RecBCD, which has a RecA loading function. An additional mediator function is supplied by the RecFOR complex, which is evident in E. coli when RecBCD is inactivated, but is a more prominent mediator in wild-type B. subtilis cells (Fernandez´ et al., 1999; Lenhart et al., 2014). In yeast, the major mediator is Rad52, which participates in Rad51 loading, and in human cells BRCA2 is the primary mediator (Table 9.4.1). 

Until recently, the mediator function in mycobacteria was not investigated in depth. The finding that RecBCD in mycobacteria is not required for RecA-dependent HR would seem to exclude a mediator function for RecBCD. AdnAB, as a resection nuclease in mycobacterial HR, is a candidate for the RecA loading function, analogous to the mediator function of RecBCD in E. coli, but this function has not yet been demonstrated. A recent publication examined the function of the RecO protein in mycobacteria. RecO is a widely conserved bacterial protein that is the central component of the RecFOR complex (Gupta et al., 2013). M. smegmatis lacking recO was found to be viable but highly sensitive to a variety of clastogens, including ionizing radiation. Importantly, the ΔrecO strain was nearly as sensitive as the ΔrecA strain and more sensitive than the ΔadnAB strain, suggesting a major role for the RecFOR system in mycobacterial recombination (Gupta et al., 2013). 

The phenotype of the M. smegmatis ΔrecO strain in the I-SceI recombination system confirmed a major role in HR. HR events in the ΔrecO strain were significantly reduced compared to the wild-type strain, although some residual HR was present (Gupta et al., 2013). Examination of the ΔrecO ΔadnAB strain in this assay revealed a complete lack of HR events, indicating that RecO and AdnAB define two parallel pathways that lead to RecA-dependent recombination in mycobacteria. 

We have recently completed a genetic analysis of the recF and recR genes in mycobacterial recombination (Gupta et al., 2015). M. smegmatis lacking recR is severely sensitized to all clastogens tested, including UV and IR. However, M. smegmatis ΔrecF displays an intermediate clastogen sensitivity phenotype that is more severe than the ΔadnAB strain but not as severe as either ΔrecO or ΔrecR. The I-SceI assay provided substantial and surprising insight into the function of RecR. Loss of RecR abolished all homologous recombination in M. smegmatis, whereas loss of recF resulted in partial impairment of HR to a degree similar to loss of recO or adnAB (Gupta et al., 2015). This finding indicates that RecR is required for all HR in mycobacteria, including those HR events initiated by AdnAB, and establishes RecR as a central mediator of mycobacterial recombination. 

## 9.4.2.3 Other recombination factors

Unfortunately, the focus of this chapter on genetic studies of DSB repair does not permit full discussion of extensive studies that have been performed on recombination proteins from Mycobacterium and the regulation of their expression. These include the biochemical features of RecA (Datta et al., 2003; Ganesh and Muniyappa, 2003; Patil et al., 2011; Reddy et al., 2001), the regulation of the DNA damage response in mycobacteria (Brooks et al., 2001; Davis et al., 2002; Dawson et al., 2010; Rand et al., 2003; Yang et al., 2012), and studies on Holliday junction resolvases (Khanduja and Muniyappa, 2012; Khanduja et al., 2009; Prabu et al., 2006; Thakur et al., 2013). We point the reader to these references for in-depth discussion of these important topics. 

## 9.4.3 NHEJ in bacteria

## 9.4.3.1 Historical perspective

The standard model of prokaryotic double-stranded DNA break repair was derived from seminal studies in E. coli that defined, over many decades, the molecular requirements for homologous recombination. These studies established the primacy of RecA as the dominant strand exchange protein in bacterial recombination. However, the existence of alternative DSB repair pathways in E. coli was not documented, and such pathways were presumed not to exist. This situation is in stark contrast to the plethora of DSB repair pathways that have been intensely studied in eukaryotic cells and that include HR, NHEJ, and SSA (Figure 9.4.1). As genomic sequencing of broad bacterial phyla revealed new prokaryotic protein families, bioinformatic analysis of these genomes revealed clues to a greater diversity of DSB repair pathways than had been deduced from studies in E. coli. Foremost among these observations was the finding that some bacterial genomes, including M. tuberculosis and M. smegmatis, encoded apparent orthologs of the Ku protein (Aravind and Koonin, 2001). In eukaryal organisms, the Ku70– Ku80 heterodimer binds DNA ends and acts as an organizing hub for NHEJ. The existence of Ku in bacteria suggested the existence of an NHEJ pathway. Tantalizing additional bioinformatic observations identified adenosine triphosphate (ATP)- dependent DNA ligases, sometimes in close genomic proximity to the gene encoding Ku, in these bacteria. The conserved bacterial DNA ligase, LigA (Nandakumar et al., 2007), is a nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD)-dependent enzyme, whereas eukaryotic ligases, such as DNA ligase IV (which mediates NHEJ), are ATP dependent. 

## 9.4.3.2 In vivo evidence for a bacterial NHEJ pathway

Early biochemical studies of the putative NHEJ proteins, M. tuberculosis LigD and Ku, demonstrated that these proteins can cooperate to seal DNA ends in vitro (Della et al., 2004; Weller et al., 2002). Definitive evidence for the existence of an NHEJ pathway in vivo initially came from studies using transformation of linear plasmids into M. tuberculosis and M. smegmatis and mutant strains lacking the genes encoding LigD and Ku. In contrast to E. coli, M. tuberculosis and M. smegmatis can recircularize linear plasmid DNA with either blunt or cohesive ends. For 5′ and blunt-ended linear plasmids, this recircularization is reduced by approximately 500-fold in strains with null mutations in Ku or LigD (Aniukwu et al., 2008; Gong et al., 2004, 2005), indicating an active NHEJ pathway that depends on Ku and LigD, which physically interact. The linear plasmid transformation assay is useful for interrogating NHEJ, but because the DNA sequence flanking the plasmid DSB does not have homology to the chromosome, HR-mediated repair is not possible. Therefore, the plasmid assay does not interrogate the relative frequency of NHEJ when alternative repair pathways are possible. Additional evidence for the existence and characteristics of the mycobacterial NHEJ pathway came from the I-SceI system. In wild-type cells carrying the I-SceI recombination substrate in which all repair outcomes are possible, NHEJ-mediated repair constitutes 20% of the repair outcomes (Gupta et al., 2011). These NHEJ events are abolished in strains lacking Ku or LigD, and loss of NHEJ leads to a compensatory increase in HR (Gupta et al., 2011). 

As noted here, NHEJ in bacteria was first demonstrated using linear plasmid transformation and homing endonuclease– induced DSBs. In yeast and human cells, NHEJ is critical for DSB repair when a chromosomal homolog is not available to provide a template for strand invasion (Lieber, 2010). By analogy, NHEJ in bacteria should be critical for clastogen resistance in the stationary phase or other states in which chromosome replication has ceased and/or the cell is monochromosomal. Spores of B. subtilis are monochromosomal and nonreplicating, and thereby provide a physiologic state in which NHEJ should be important for genomic integrity. Accordingly, Ku-deficient B. subtilis spores are highly sensitive to dry heat or hydrogen peroxide (in an α–β SASP mutant background) (Wang et al., 2006). Similarly, Ku- or LigD-deficient M. smegmatis in the late stationary phase is sensitive to ionizing radiation, a sensitivity that is not observed in log phase cells or in stationary phase cells grown in rich media (Stephanou et al., 2007). Additional studies have also shown that NHEJ protects stationary phase mycobacteria from desiccation (Pitcher et al., 2007). 

In summary, M. tuberculosis and M. smegmatis encode a pathway of NHEJ that repairs DSBs in late-stationary phase cells and is dependent upon Ku and Ligase D. These experiments indicated that these two proteins, Ku and LigD, perform many (although not all, as discussed further here) of the repair functions of NHEJ. In contrast, eukaryotic NHEJ has multiple additional proteins that participate in end-remodeling during NHEJ, including polymerases and nucleases that remodel the broken ends into ligatable termini (Lieber, 2010). In the mycobacterial NHEJ system, some of these end-remodeling functions are supplied by autonomous enzymatic activities encoded within the LigD protein. 

## 9.4.3.3 Biochemical functions of the LigD proteins and their role in NHEJ in vivo

The LigD protein from M. smegmatis and M. tuberculosis has three identifiable enzymatic domains: polymerase (POL), phosphoesterase (PE), and ligase (Lig). Detailed biochemical, structural, and genetic studies have elucidated the NHEJ functions of each of these domains. 

LigD–Lig: The LigD–Lig domain is an ATP-dependent DNA ligase with a classic three-step ligation mechanism (Akey et al., 2006; Gong et al., 2004). As noted above, deletion of the ligD gene from M. tuberculosis or M. smegmatis reduces the efficiency of NHEJ for both plasmid and chromosomal substrates. Surprisingly, ablation of the LigD–Lig active site in vivo (through replacement of the active site lysine with alanine) did not phenocopy the severe NHEJ defect observed in the ΔligD strain (Akey et al., 2006; Aniukwu et al., 2008). NHEJ efficiency was substantially preserved, although these LigD–Lig-independent NHEJ events were low fidelity (Aniukwu et al., 2008). This result indicated that another DNA ligase can supply strand-sealing activity when LigD–Lig is inactivated, and further studies indicated that this activity is supplied by Ligase C1 (Aniukwu et al., 2008; Bhattarai et al., 2014). 

LigD–POL: A remarkable feature of mycobacterial NHEJ is the frequent addition of templated and nontemplated nucleotides to the repaired ends (Aniukwu et al., 2008; Gong et al., 2005). These end modifications imply the participation of a polymerase in mycobacterial NHEJ. The POL domain of LigD is a primase-like polymerase that can add both templated and nontemplated nucleotides to DNA in vitro (Gong et al., 2005; Pitcher et al., 2005; Zhu et al., 2006). LigD– POL is also proficient at adding ribonucleotides, a property it shares with polymerases that participate in eukaryotic NHEJ (Bebenek et al., 2005). Ablation of the LigD–POL domain activity by mutation of the di-aspartate metalbinding site abolishes mutagenic NHEJ at blunt ends during plasmid NHEJ, but has relatively little effect on the templated fill-in events observed at resealed 5′ overhang plasmid termini (Aniukwu et al., 2008; Gong et al., 2005; Zhu et al., 2006). The necessity of the LigD protein for NHEJ, which is independent of its ligase activity, is supplied by the POL domain, which, in addition to catalyzing NHEJ additions, also appears to play a structural role in the NHEJ complex (Aniukwu et al., 2008; Brissett et al., 2007). 

LigD–PE: The LigD–PE domain is the third enzymatic module of the LigD protein that participates in end remodeling. The PE domain from Pseudomonas LigD has been most extensively characterized in vitro. LigD–PE is the founding member of a novel 3′ end-healing enzyme family present in bacteria, archaea, and fungi. PE resects the ribonucleotide tract on a RNA–DNA hybrid until a single ribonucleotide with a 3′ OH group remains (Li et al., 2011; Sinha et al., 2009a; Zhu and Shuman, 2005; Zhu et al., 2012). This ribonucleotide terminated strand is the preferred substrate for the LigD ligase, indicating that the PE and POL domains may cooperate to produce a ribonucleotide terminated DNA strand that is the ultimate substrate for LigD ligase activity. The role of the PE domain in NHEJ in vivo is less well understood as it does not participate in the efficiency or fidelity of plasmid NHEJ (Aniukwu et al., 2008). 

## 9.4.3.4 Additional potential NHEJ factors

Several additional factors have been identified in mycobacteria that may participate in NHEJ. As noted in Section 9.4.3.3, the LigD–POL domain is a primase-like polymerase that is the direct catalyst of nontemplated mutagenic NHEJ in vivo. The persistence of templated fill-in events when LigD–POL activity is inactivated indicated the participation of additional polymerases in mycobacterial NHEJ. Prime candidates for this activity are the PolD1 and PolD2 enzymes. PolD1 and PolD2 are freestanding LigD–POL-like enzymes without the Lig and PE domains contained in the LigD polypeptide. PolD1 and PolD2 have similar biochemical activities to LigD–POL, including a preference for ribonucleotide addition over deoxyribonucleotides, and both templated and nontemplated polymerase activities (Zhu et al., 2012). Despite the suspicion that PolD1 and PolD2 participate in NHEJ based on their activities and genomic proximity (in the case of PolD1) to the backup NHEJ ligase LigC, ablation of PolD1 and PolD2 in vivo did not affect the NHEJ fidelity of 5′ overhangs, even when LigD–POL was inactivated (Zhu et al., 2012). However, the loss of PolD1 and PolD2 in combination did confer sensitivity to ionizing radiation in late-stationary phase cells when LigD–POL is inactivated, clearly implicating these polymerases in NHEJ-mediated repair of DSBs (Bhattarai et al., 2014). These results indicate that a suite of LigD–POL-like polymerases participates in NHEJ, but there are additional polymerases that can act in the NHEJ pathway to fill in 5′ overhang DSBs. 

Experiments seeking mycobacterial proteins interacting with Ku identified UvrD1 as a Ku-interacting protein (Sinha et al., 2007). Ku stimulates UvrD1 helicase activity in vitro, and ablation of UvrD1 sensitizes M. smegmatis to ionizing radiation in all growth phases (Sinha et al., 2007), but deletion of UvrD1 does not impair NHEJ-mediated resealing of linear plasmids. The exact function of the Ku–UvrD1 interaction in mycobacterial DSB repair remains to be elucidated. Additional efforts to identify Ku-interacting proteins identified the protein encoded by 

MSmeg 5175, which has homology to NAD-dependent deacetylases of the Sir2 family. Deletion of MSmeg 5175 in M. smegmatis reduced NHEJ efficiency and conferred sensitivity to IR, although not to the degree of the M. smegmatis Δku strain (Li et al., 2011). 

## 9.4.4 SSA pathway

Single-strand annealing is a mechanism of DSB repair that occurs when the DSB is flanked by direct repeats. Bidirectional single-strand resection from the break reveals complementary single strands that can anneal. Subsequent flap removal, fill-in synthesis, and ligation result in repair of the break with a deletion and single remaining repeat (Figure 9.4.1). SSA has been described in yeast and is independent of the eukaryal strand exchange protein Rad51, but it is dependent on the Rad52 protein (Ivanov et al., 1996). However, SSA was not described as a DSB repair pathway in bacteria. Use of the I-SceI recombination system described in this chapter allowed detection of recombination events consistent with an SSA mechanism of repair. Specifically, approximately 15% of repair events at an I-SceI-induced DSB resulted in a deletion of the intervening DNA between two lacZ repeats. Importantly, these repair events were independent of RecA, consistent with an SSA mechanism of repair (Gupta et al., 2011). Surprisingly, although deletion of RecBCD did not reduce HR events (see above), SSA events were abolished in a RecBCD-null strain (Gupta et al., 2011). In conjunction with the lack of any clastogen sensitivity of the ΔrecBCD strain, this finding strongly indicated that RecBCD in mycobacteria has a function distinct from its well-established role as a resection nuclease and RecA mediator in the E. coli HR pathway. 

Inactivation of adnAB resulted in a 50% reduction in the net SSA frequency in M. smegmatis compared to the wild-type strain, possibly indicating that AdnAB may play a secondary role in end resection in the SSA pathway (Gupta et al., 2011). However, the complete absence of SSA in the ΔrecBCD strain indicates that AdnAB cannot replace the function of RecBCD in SSA. 

Additional studies with M. smegmatis strains lacking components of the RecFOR complex indicated a substantial role for these proteins in the mycobacterial SSA pathway. A deletion mutant of M. smegmatis lacking RecO was severely compromised in executing SSA compared to wild-type cells (Gupta et al., 2013). Consistent with this involvement in the SSA pathway, purified RecO protein displayed a zinc-dependent DNAbinding activity and accelerated the annealing of ssDNA (Gupta et al., 2013). Surprisingly, recent data from our studies indicate that not only RecO is required for the SSA mechanism, but also RecF and RecR (Gupta et al., 2015). Neither M. smegmatis ΔrecF nor ΔrecR could execute repair of an I-SceI-induced DSB by SSA, indicating that all members of the RecFOR pathway are required for the SSA mechanism. 

As a pathway that repairs DSBs that arise between repeats, the SSA pathway may have particular relevance to M. tuberculosis genome evolution. The M. tuberculosis chromosome contains repetitive DNA in the form of PE, PPE, and PGRS elements, which account for a substantial fraction of the M. tuberculosis chromosome. DSBs that may arise within these regions are prime candidates to be repaired by the SSA pathway (or NHEJ, for that matter), but problematic for repair by HR because of difficulty in finding the appropriate homologous sequence for RecA-dependent strand invasion. Whether SSA-mediated repair would preferentially operate within repetitive regions of the mycobacterial chromosome remains to be tested, but it is potentially relevant that studies of M. tuberculosis genome variation have found that PE, PPE, and PGRS genes do contain sequence polymorphisms that could be consistent with either SSA- or NHEJ-mediated repair (McEvoy et al., 2009, 2012; Talarico et al., 2005), and studies of instability of direct and inverted repeats in mycobacteria have implicated these pathways (Wojcik et al., 2012). 

## 9.4.5 Role of DNA repair in M. tuberculosis pathogenesis

It is clear that the products of the mammalian immune system can damage DNA through base damage, sugar damage, or phosphodiester strand breakage. It is also clear that several bacterial pathogens rely on DNA repair systems to resist the clastogenic environment of the host, including Helicobacter pylori, Salmonella enterica, and Neisseria meningitidis. However, despite the strong suspicion that M. tuberculosis uses DNA repair pathways to survive in vivo, demonstration of the importance of repair pathways in animal models of infection has been difficult. As has been suggested (Warner et al., 2013), the lack of dramatic pathogenesis phenotypes of some DNA repair mutant strains may reflect redundancy among repair mechanisms, or the relatively gross nature of colony-forming unit (CFU) assays to detect significant changes in bacterial chromosome structure that may occur independently of net bacterial survival. Nevertheless, some important findings have implicated specific DNA repair pathways in M. tuberculosis pathogenesis and in vivo mutagenesis. 

Several studies have examined the role of nucleotide excision repair (NER) in M. tuberculosis pathogenesis. After its identification as a factor conferring resistance to nitric oxide (Darwin and Nathan, 2005), an M. tuberculosis ΔuvrB strain was tested in the mouse model of infection and found to be mildly attenuated by CFU and time-to-death assays (Darwin and Nathan, 2005). The attenuation phenotype of the ΔuvrB strain was reversed in phox–iNOS −/− mice, indicating that the NER system does defend against host immune pressure in vivo. A recent study examined the role of the UvrD1 helicase in M. tuberculosis pathogenesis (Houghton et al., 2012). UvrD is a component of the NER machinery and in this function removes the incised oligonucleotide after strand cleavage by UvrABC. However, UvrD also has additional functions in recombination, and in mycobacteria there are two UvrD-like proteins, UvrD1 and UvrD2. As noted in this chapter, UvrD1 interacts directly with Ku, whereas UvrD2 is essential (Sinha et al., 2008; Williams et al., 2011), although this essential function is not supplied by its helicase activity (Williams et al., 2011). The Davis group examined ΔuvrA, ΔuvrD1, and ΔuvrA ΔuvrD1 strains in the mouse model of infection. The ΔuvrA strain was mildly attenuated, comparable to previously reported findings with the ΔuvrB strain. The ΔuvrD1 strain was attenuated by ∼1.5 logs at 50 days post infection and by ∼3 logs at 150 days. Dramatically and somewhat surprisingly, the ΔuvrA ΔuvrD1 strain was more attenuated than either single mutant and barely replicated in mice, a phenotype that was complemented by uvrD1 (Houghton et al., 2012). The attenuation phenotype of this double mutant is the most dramatic attenuation phenotype reported for a DNA repair–deficient strain of M. tuberculosis and clearly indicates the value in combining mutations from distinct repair pathways (in this case, presumably reflecting the inactivation of NER through loss of uvrA and the non-NER functions of UvrD1). 

Another dramatic example of the effect of a DNA repair pathway on M. tuberculosis infection and in vivo mutagenesis came from the examination of the dnaE2 mutant by the Mizrahi group. Inactivation of DnaE2 conferred attenuation to M. tuberculosis in mice as measured by CFU and time-to-death analyses (Boshoff et al., 2003). In addition, the ΔdnaE2 strain failed to evolve resistance to rifampin, providing a clear example that an error-prone repair pathway is essential to the evolution of drug resistance in vivo (Boshoff et al., 2003).

Pitcher RS, Tonkin LM, Green AJ, Doherty AJ. 2005. Domain structure of a NHEJ DNA repair ligase from Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Journal of Molecular Biology 351(3): 531–544. 



Despite the substantial advances in understanding the pathways of double-strand DNA break repair in mycobacteria, including the discovery of the NHEJ and SSA pathways as detailed in this chapter, the role of DSB repair in M. tuberculosis pathogenesis has been difficult to document. Early studies tested a BCG strain lacking recA and found no attenuation in either BALB/c mice or nude mice with intravenous infection (Sander et al., 2003). As noted, mycobacteria elaborate three pathways of DSB repair: HR, NHEJ, and SSA (Figure 9.4.1). Two of these pathways, NHEJ and SSA, do not require a replicated chromosome to direct repair and therefore may be relevant to stages of M. tuberculosis infection during which replication has ceased. In addition, the presence of three repair pathways may suggest redundancy that would mask the phenotypes of M. tuberculosis strains lacking a single DSB repair pathway. Extensive experimentation in the Glickman lab has examined the pathogenesis phenotypes of M. tuberculosis Δku, ΔrecA, and Δku ΔrecA in multiple mouse models of infection, including C57Bl/6 and C3HeB–FeJ mice (Harper et al., 2012), and in guinea pigs. Surprisingly, these experiments did not demonstrate any change in bacterial load of any of these mutant strains, in any of the animal models, compared to wild-type M. tuberculosis (Heaton et al., 2014). These surprising findings fail to document a role for DSB repair in M. tuberculosis pathogenesis. The lack of phenotype of NHEJ-deficient strains in the mouse model could be attributed to the lack of true growth arrest or latency in these models (Gill et al., 2009), although the lack of phenotype of the recA/ku double mutant cannot be explained by ongoing replication. The possibility exists that the murine immune response to M. tuberculosis is not capable of inflicting DSB-inducing genotoxic stress on the M. tuberculosis chromosome. The lack of phenotype of these DSB repair–deficient strains fits with other studies that show a similar lack of phenotype for DNA repair– deficient strains (Kana et al., 2010) and, as has been suggested by others, may reflect the relative gross measure of bacterial load as an outcome (Warner et al., 2013). More granular data about the role of individual repair pathways in pathogenesis may come from examination of chromosomal mutagenesis and rearrangements by next-generation sequencing of DNA repair pathway mutant strains passaged through animal models (Ford et al., 2011).

## Adaptation to oxidative stress

# Peroxide-sensing transcriptional regulators in bacteria

## James M. Dubbs1 and Skorn Mongkolsuk1–4

1Laboratory of Biotechnology, Chulabhorn Research Institute, Lak Si, Bangkok, Thailand 

2Center of Emerging Bacterial Infections, Faculty of Science, Mahidol University, Bangkok, Thailand 

3Department of Biotechnology, Faculty of Science, Mahidol University, Bangkok, Thailand 

4Center of Excellence for Environmental Health, Toxicology and Management of Chemicals, Bangkok, Thailand 

## 10.1.1 Introduction

Every choice in life comes with a cost. This is no less true for the evolution-driven choice to adopt an aerobic lifestyle. Oxygen is a very good electron acceptor, and aerobic organisms take advantage of this by using $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ as a terminal electron acceptor for respiratory electron transport. The cost of choosing this lifestyle is derived from the fact that $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ can also accept electrons from reduced cofactors of cellular redox enzymes, such as flavins, to form reactive oxygen species (ROS) (Imlay, 2003). These aberrant $\mathrm { e ^ { - } }$ transfers to $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ generate either superoxide anion $( \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ^ { \bullet - } )$ or hydrogen peroxide $\left( \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } \right)$ depending on whether one or two electrons are transferred, respectively (Imlay, 2003). $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ can also be formed as a normal byproduct of enzymatic activity (Ravindra Kumar and Imlay, 2013). 

The danger posed by ROS lies in their ability to cause oxidative damage to proteins, DNA, and lipids (Imlay, 2003). Both $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ^ { \bullet - }$ and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ can oxidize exposed iron–sulfur clusters (Imlay, 2008), and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ is known to oxidize ferrous iron $( \mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + } )$ in proteins containing mononuclear iron centers (Sobota and Imlay, 2011). Oxidative damage to iron-containing proteins inactivates the target enzyme and results in the release of ferric iron $( \mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + } )$ , which is quickly converted to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ in the reducing environment of the intracellular space (Imlay, 2003). This release of free $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ is an important aspect of oxidative stress in that $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ can reduce $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ to generate hydroxyl radical (∙ OH) via the Fenton reaction: 

$$
\mathrm{Fe} ^ {2 +} + \mathrm{H} _ {2} \mathrm{O} _ {2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Fe} ^ {3 +} + \cdot \mathrm{OH} + \mathrm{OH} ^ {-} (\text {   Fenton   reaction   })
$$

∙ OH is an extremely potent oxidant that reacts with cellular macromolecules, particularly DNA, at nearly diffusion-limited rates (Imlay, 2003). Therefore, oxidative damage to susceptible iron-containing proteins serves to make a bad situation worse by increasing the potential for further ∙ OH-mediated damage. $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ^ { \bullet - } , \mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ , and ∙ OH are all capable of causing a variety of oxidative lesions in proteins, DNA, and lipids (Imlay, 2003). Some of these reactions can result in the formation of organic peroxides that can cause further damage to cellular constituents (Imlay, 2003; Semchyshyn et al., 2005). 

Significant ROS exposure also originates from external sources. Host defense responses are a good example of this. Macrophages produce copious amounts of ROS and RNS (reactive nitrogen species) in response to infection (Robinson, 2009), and an analogous defense response in plants includes the production of organic peroxides (Lamb and Dixon, 1997). Similarly, some microorganisms excrete ROS in order to kill their competitors (He et al., 2010). Exposure to redox cycling compounds, such as quinones and the herbicide paraquat, can mediate the transfer of electrons from cellular donors to $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ to generate $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ^ { \bullet - }$ (Cohen and d’Arcy Doherty, 1987). 

By necessity, bacteria produce basal levels of ROS-scavenging enzymes to prevent accumulation of endogenous $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ^ { \bullet - }$ and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ to toxic levels (Seaver and Imlay, 2001a). These include superoxide dismutases that catalyze the dismutation of ${ \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } } ^ { \bullet - }$ to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and catalases that convert $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ to $\mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ (Imlay, 2008). A variety of peroxides, including organic peroxides, serve as substrates for peroxiredoxins. This class of peroxidases functions to reduce $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and organic peroxides (ROOH) to either $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ or $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O }$ and the corresponding alcohol (ROH) via the peroxide-mediated oxidation of cysteine thiols. The oxidized catalytic cysteines are subsequently reduced using cellular electron donors to regenerate the active enzyme (Dubbs and Mongkolsuk, 2007; Poole, 2005; Seaver and Imlay, 2001a). 

When ROS exposure exceeds safe limits, bacteria have the ability to mount an inducible response to further increase expression of ROS detoxification enzymes and activate additional protective systems that repair oxidative damage, protect vulnerable enzymes from inactivation, and control the levels of free $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ (Pomposiello and Demple, 2002). For example, oxidative stress increases the demand for reducing equivalents leading to the induction of metabolic pathways to increase the reductant supply (Giro et al., 2006). The expression of iron-binding proteins, like Dps, is often induced to reduce intracellular levels of free Fe to prevent production of ∙ OH via the Fenton reaction (Calhoun and Kwon, 2011). In order to protect enzymes that contain vulnerable Fe-containing centers from oxidation, the uptake of $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ is often increased (Faulkner and Helmann, 2011). Manganese is able to replace $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ at some active sites, rendering them resistant to oxidation (Imlay, 2008; Sobota and Imlay, 2011). In some cases, Fe-containing enzymes are replaced with analogs that do not require Fe (Liochev and Fridovich, 1992). 

Not surprisingly, the coordinated regulation of gene expression during the bacterial oxidative stress response is a complex task that is often under the control of regulators that can directly sense the levels of specific ROS and activate, repress, or de-repress target gene transcription. This chapter attempts to give the reader a basic understanding of the mechanisms of oxidant sensing and transcriptional regulation by OxyR, PerR, and OhrR. These three well-studied peroxide responsive regulators have the ability to distinguish between ROOH and $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ (Dubbs and Mongkolsuk, 2012). Two different mechanisms for peroxide sensing have evolved in these regulators that involve either the oxidation of cysteine residues (OxyR and OhrR) or the $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ - catalyzed oxidation of histidine residues (PerR). In both cases, oxidation of the regulator changes its DNA-binding properties. 

## 10.1.2 OxyR

OxyR is a LysR-type transcriptional regulator that is generally found in Gram-negative bacteria but also occurs in a few Grampositive bacteria (Hahn et al., 2002; Morikawa et al., 2006). Like other regulators of the LysR-family, OxyR contains a conserved N-terminal helix-turn-helix DNA-binding domain, a central coinducer recognition and response domain that senses the regulatory signal, and a C-terminal domain that functions in multimerization and activation (Kona and Brinck, 2006; Kullik et al., 1995a,b; Maddocks and Oyston, 2008; Schell, 1993; Wang et al., 2006). LysR-family regulators tend to regulate transcription in response to the binding of a small-molecule ligand (Maddocks and Oyston, 2008; Schell, 1993). OxyR differs somewhat in that the signal it responds to involves direct oxidation of the protein (Antelmann and Helmann, 2011; Dubbs and Mongkolsuk, 2012). Under aerobic conditions, Escherichia coli OxyR functions as a global regulator of the peroxide stress response that maintains intracellular $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ levels within safe limits (Seaver and Imlay, 2001a). It also plays a role in the cellular response to thiol depletion (Aslund et al., 1999) and can sense and respond to RNS (reactive nitrogen species) under anaerobic conditions (Seth et al., 2012). It should be noted at this point that while 

OxyR functions as an activator of the peroxide stress response in E. coli (Christman et al., 1989), this is not the case in all bacteria. OxyR functions as a repressor of the peroxide stress response in a number of cases (Jiang et al., 2014; Kim and Holmes, 2012; Seib et al., 2007; Teramoto et al., 2013; Tseng et al., 2003) and can function as either a positive or negative transcriptional regulator in both its oxidized and reduced forms (Heo et al., 2010; Ieva et al., 2008; Zeller et al., 2007). 

So far, the OxyR regulon of E. coli is known to be composed of about 30 genes, including those involved in $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ detoxification (katE, ahpCF), heme biosynthesis (hemH), reductant supply (grxA, gor, trxC), thiol–disulfide isomerization (dsbG), Fe–S center repair (sufA-E, sufS), iron binding (yaaA, dps), repression of iron import systems (fur), and manganese import (mntH) (Kehres et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 1999, 2001b). OxyR also upregulates the expression of OxyS, a small regulatory RNA that integrates peroxide stress with general stress pathways (Gonzalez-Flecha and Demple, 1999; Zhang et al., 1998). 

The OxyR regulons of other organisms all include genes involved in ROS detoxification (Harrison et al., 2007; Ochsner et al., 2000; Seib et al., 2007; Sund et al., 2008; Wei et al., 2012). They also reveal a significant amount of organism-specific variation as well as illustrate the truly global nature of this regulator. One genome-wide study in Pseudomonas aeruginosa that augmented transcriptome analyses with results from chromatin immunoprecipitation coupled to tilling arrays (ChiP–chip) to identify OxyR-binding sites provides one of the more complete pictures of an OxyR regulon (Wei et al., 2012). It was found that $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ exposure caused extensive remodeling of the cell’s metabolism. OxyR induced the expression of oxidative stress defense genes while repressing the expression of genes encoding products involved in translation (ribosomal proteins, transfer RNA (tRNA), and tRNA synthetases) and aerobic and anaerobic respiration (ubiquinol oxidase and cytochrome c), indicating that OxyR actively slows or stalls growth to allow the cell time to adapt and repair before growth resumes. The response also included the induction of a gene involved in cell wall synthesis (lpxC), possibly related to thickening of the outer membrane. OxyR was also found to control several regulatory RNAs (Wei et al., 2012). 

E. coli OxyR is the most extensively studied and best understood of the OxyR orthologs. It is active as a tetramer, and oxidation of the protein affects its binding to a conserved sequence motif (5′ -ATAGntnnnanCTATnnnnnnnATAGntnnnanCTAT-3′ ) in the promoter and operator regions of target genes (Kullik et al., 1995a; Toledano et al., 1994; Zheng et al., 1998, 2001a) that is somewhat conserved in other bacteria (Wei et al., 2012). The oxidized (OxyRox) and reduced $( { \mathrm { O x y R } } ^ { \mathrm { r e d } } )$ forms of OxyR are known to adopt different conformational states that affect DNA binding to target promoters (Choi et al., 2001). One example of this is the OxyR-mediated regulation of the oxyS promoter of E. coli shown in Figure 10.1.1. OxyS transcription is highly induced by $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ,$ and OxyR binds to the oxyS promoter-operator under both oxidized and reduced conditions. In the absence of oxidative stress, $\mathrm { O x y R ^ { r e d } }$ binds to a sequence that extends beyond the consensus binding sequence and makes contacts with two pairs of major grooves separated by one helical turn that induces a bend in the DNA (Toledano et al., 1994). Upon oxidation OxyRox shifts its DNA contacts to four successive major grooves corresponding to the consensus DNA-binding motif (Toledano et al., 1994). This results in a reduction in the DNA-binding footprint as well as a change in promoter conformation due to the relaxation of the DNA bend (Toledano et al., 1994). Transcription activation is accomplished through direct interaction between OxyRox and the alpha-CTD domain of RNA polymerase (Storz et al., 1990; Tao et al., 1995). This redox-dependent shift in DNA contacts is not observed in all target promoters, and regulation of these is likely due to oxidation state-dependent changes in DNA-binding affinity (Storz et al., 1990; Tartaglia et al., 1992; Toledano et al., 1994).
