Figure 10.1.1 OxyR-mediated activation of the oxyS promoter in response to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and the reductive recycling of oxidized disulfide-containing OxyR via glutathione (GSH) and the glutaredoxin (GrxA)–glutathione reductase (Gor) system. Adapted from Dubbs and Mongkolsuk (2012).


Very little is known about OxyR-associated accessory factors or interacting regulatory partners. There is, however, good evidence implicating RecG as an accessory factor in the OxyRdependent induction of some genes in Pseudomonas putida (Yeom et al., 2012). In vivo studies using the trxB promoter have shown that a palindromic region overlapping the OxyR consensus binding site forms a cruciform structure that has to be resolved by RecG before an OxyR tetramer could bind. In other target promoters, the cruciform structure did not overlap the OxyR-binding site, suggesting an alternate role for RecG, possibly affecting promoter conformation. RecG is encoded in the same operon as OxyR in P. putida as well as several other organisms (Loprasert et al., 2002; Yeom et al., 2012), indicating that this regulatory scheme is likely not unique to P. putida. 

OxyR senses the level of intracellular $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ through the direct oxidation of a conserved “sensing” cysteine residue. In E. coli, the concentration of intracellular $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ is approximately 20 nM during normal aerobic growth (Seaver and Imlay, 2001b), while growth inhibition occurs at around 2 mM $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ (Gonzalez-Flecha and Demple, 1997). Under normal growth conditions, in which the intracellular $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ concentration is ∼20 nm, OxyR remains in the reduced form (Zheng et al., 1998) and becomes oxidized when the $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ level reaches about 100 nM, thereby insuring that the induction of defensive systems occurs well before toxic $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ levels are reached (Gonzalez-Flecha and Demple, 1997). As peroxide-scavenging enzymes bring $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ levels back to normal, a regulatory feedback system is necessary to reduce $\mathrm { O x y R ^ { o x } }$ and shut down the defense response. In E. coli, reduction of $\mathrm { O x y R } ^ { \mathrm { o x } }$ is achieved through the slow action of glutaredoxin 1 using reduced glutathione as the electron donor, as shown in Figure 10.1.1. Reduced glutathione is in turn regenerated via glutathione reductase using electrons supplied by NADH (Aslund et al., 1999; Tao, 1999; Zheng et al., 1998). The genes encoding glutaredoxin 1 (grxA) and glutathione reductase (gor) are both part of the OxyR regulon (Zheng et al., 2001b). This type of feedback regulatory system is likely a common feature of OxyR regulation in other organisms, although the reduction system can vary. For example, P. aeruginosa utilizes a thioredoxin–thioredoxin reductase system to recycle OxyRox, which is also part of the OxyR regulon (Wei et al., 2012). In addition, it has also been shown that P. aeruginosa OxyRox can also be reduced by the thiol disulfide reductase, DsbM, in vitro. Physiological relevance is suggested by the facts that inactivation of dsbM results in activation of genes in the OxyR regulon and that DsbM and OxyR have been shown to physically interact in a yeast two-hybrid assay (Li et al., 2014). 

E. coli OxyR is currently the best characterized in terms of the mechanism of oxidant sensing. This protein is termed a 2-Cys OxyR because it contains a “sensing” cysteine residue (C199) and a second cysteine residue (C208) that is also involved in $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ sensing. $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ -mediated activation of E. coli OxyR is a twostep process that results in the formation of an intramolecular disulfide bond between C199 and C208 (see Figure 10.1.1) (Choi et al., 2001). C199 is solvent accessible and lies in a hydrophilic pocket where the sulfhydyl group exists as a thiolate ion due to its proximity to the positively charged side group of R266. This interaction is important since amino acid changes that enhance or reduce stabilization of the C199 thiolate ion affect the sensitivity of OxyR to peroxide (Choi et al., 2001). C199 is readily oxidized by $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ to form a cysteine sulfenic acid (C199- SOH) that quickly undergoes a condensation reaction with C208 to form an intramolecular disulfide bond. In the reduced form, the SH groups of C199 and C208 are separated by a large distance (17 angstroms). Repositioning of these residues allows for disulfide bond formation and coincides with a structural rearrangement within the regulatory domain (residues 80 to 305) of the monomer that induces a conformational shift between the subunits of the tetramer (Choi et al., 2001). Disulfide bond formation serves to stabilize OxyR in this oxidized conformation (Choi et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2004), which changes the DNA-binding properties of the protein, as well as promote interactions with RNA polymerase, as mentioned previously (Storz et al., 1990; Tao et al., 1995). 

E. coli OxyR is also capable of sensing other types of oxidants via a mechanism that involves oxidative modification of C199 alone. Initial indications of this were revealed in a study by Kim et al. (2002). It was found that the OxyRs in which C199 was hydroxylated (C199-SOH), S-nitrosylated (C199-SNO), and Sglutathionylated (C199-S-S-G) were able to activate transcription of target promoters in vitro and that activation could be reversed in the presence of the reductant, dithiothreitol. Differences in the CD spectra of DNA–OxyR complexes of the different modified forms indicated that each adopted a different conformation. This led to the formulation of a “molecular code hypothesis” predicting that modification of C199 alone was sufficient to activate OxyR and that the different modifications led to the differential regulation of distinct sets of genes in the OxyR regulon (Kim et al., 2002). Further support for this idea came from the observation that C199 could also undergo thioesterification (C199-S-COO-R) with avicins, a group of plantderived terpenoids, which resulted in activation of the expression of OxyR target genes both in vitro and in vivo (Haridas et al., 2005). Final confirmation came with the demonstration that OxyR undergoes S-nitrosylation at C199 during anaerobic respiratory growth on nitrate, resulting in the activation of a set of genes that was distinct from those induced by $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and included nitrosative stress-protective genes (Seth et al., 2012; see Section 17). It is therefore clear that E. coli OxyR, and likely others, can regulate distinct sets of genes in response to oxidation and subsequent disulfide bond formation as well as other types of oxidative modifications to C199. 

It is becoming apparent that there is a good bit of functional diversity between OxyR orthologs in other bacteria compared to E. coli. A good example of this in found in the 2-Cys OxyR of the anaerobe, Porphyromonas gingivalis (see Chapter 17.3). In this organism, a number of oxidative stress defense genes (ahpC, ahpF, dps, sod, ftn, and trx) are constitutively activated by $\mathrm { O x y R } _ { \mathrm { P G } }$ and show either only modest induction in the presence of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ or none at all (Diaz et al., 2006; Ohara et al., 2006; Wu et al., 2008). Comparisons of the crystal structures of the oxidized and reduced forms of both $\mathrm { O x y R } _ { \mathrm { P G } }$ and $\mathrm { O x y R } _ { \mathrm { E C } }$ showed that oxidation of $\mathrm { O x y R } _ { \mathrm { P G } }$ resulted in less pronounced conformational changes in the regulatory domain of the monomer, resulting in a dimer structure that is very similar to that seen in the reduced (i.e., activated) form. It was suggested that this is due to a single Arg residue insertion at position 215 relative to the $\mathrm { O x y R } _ { \mathrm { E C } }$ sequence. Comparisons with the OxyR from Neisseria meningitidis, another organism that shows a different regulatory pattern than $\mathrm { O x y R } _ { \mathrm { E C } }$ (Ieva et al., 2008), identified a five-amino-acid residue insertion at position 215, which has led to the proposal that insertions of variable length within this region are indicative of OxyRs with different regulatory functions from those of $\mathrm { \Delta O x y R _ { E C } }$ (Svintradze et al., 2013). 

There is also an example of an OxyR that may utilize an additional cysteine residue for oxidant sensing. Free thiol labeling in extracts of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ -exposed P. aeruginosa strains, containing either $\mathrm { O x y R } _ { \mathrm { P A } }$ wild-type or C199/C208 single and double mutants, detected several oxidized forms of the protein in addition to the one corresponding to disulfide bond formation between C199 and C208 (Bae and Cho, 2012). The resulting suggestion that additional cysteine residue(s) are involved in $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ sensing by P. aeruginosa OxyR has been supported by mutagenesis results indicating that C296 is necessary for $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ resistance. C296 has so far only been found in several Pseudomonas species, as well as a small group within the betaproteobacteria (Bae and Cho, 2012). 

Finally, a new class of 1-Cys OxyR has been identified in Deinococcus radiodurans. This organism carries two OxyR orthologs designated DrOxyR and $\mathrm { D r O x y R } _ { 2 }$ that share 31 and 28% identity with E. coli OxyR, respectively (Chen et al., 2008; Yin et al., 2010). Both are noteworthy in that they constitute a class of 1-Cys OxyRs that contain only the sensing cysteine residue. The sensing cysteines in both proteins are essential for function, and free thiol labeling studies indicate that oxidant sensing by both regulators involves the formation of a sulfenic acid at the sensing cysteine. However, neither was able to complement an E. coli OxyR mutant, indicating significant functional differences. The deduced amino acid sequences of both DrOxyR and $\mathrm { D r O x y R } _ { 2 }$ retain residues that, in E. coli OxyR, are known to be involved in DNA binding (R4, L32 S33, and R50), activation (D142 and R273), and multimerization (A233) (Kullik et al., 1995a; Wang et al., 2006). Residues in the E. coli protein predicted to play a role in stabilizing the thiolate ion at C199 (R266) and disulfide bond formation between C199 and C208 (H198, R201, and T238) (Kona and Brinck, 2006; Kullik et al., 1995b) are absent. DrOxyR and $\mathrm { D r O x y R } _ { 2 }$ are both required to maintain wild-type levels of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ resistance, with a droxyR– droxyR double mutant having greater sensitivity to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ than the single mutants (Yin et al., 2010). The reason why $D .$ radiodurans maintains two OxyRs remains a mystery. The only other case of multiple OxyRs that has been studied is in Vibrio vulnificus, which contains two 2-Cys OxyRs (OxyR1 and OxyR2) that differ in their sensitivity to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ and activate different oxidative stress defense genes (Kim et al., 2014). 

## 10.1.3 PerR

PerR is a small, dimeric, metal-binding repressor of the Fur family that functions as a global regulator that senses $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ (Dubbs and Mongkolsuk, 2012) and the nitrosylating agent, nitrous oxide (NO; see Section 17) (Moore et al., 2004). PerR is found primarily in Gram-positive bacteria, but it can occur in 

Gram-negative bacteria (Li et al., 2004; Morikawa et al., 2006; Rea et al., 2005; van Vliet et al., 1999). PerR’s role is somewhat analogous to that of OxyR (Mongkolsuk and Helmann, 2002), although it is sometimes found along with OxyR (Hahn et al., 2000, 2002; Tseng et al., 2003; Wu et al., 2006). 

The PerR regulon of Bacillus subtilis includes perR, as well as genes involved in oxidative stress defense (katA, ahpCF, and mrgA) (Bsat et al., 1998; Chen et al., 1995), metal homeostasis (zosA, fur, and hemAXCDBL) (Chen et al., 1995; Fuangthong et al., 2002; Gaballa and Helmann, 2002), and surfactant production (srfA) (Hayashi et al., 2005). Similar classes of genes are regulated by PerR homologs in other organisms (Hahn et al., 2000; Horsburgh et al., 2001; Mukhopadhyay et al., 2007; Rea et al., 2005). One notable exception to this is PerR in Streptococcus pyogenes that does not appear to regulate any catalases, peroxidases, or the iron-binding protein, MgrA (Brenot et al., 2005, 2007; Grifantini et al., 2011). 

In most cases, PerR acts as a repressor that binds to a conserved “per box” sequence (Fuangthong and Helmann, 2003). Binding sites generally overlap part of the target gene promoter or are immediately downstream from it (Hahn et al., 2000; Herbig and Helmann, 2001). PerR can also act as a positive regulator. In the two cases of positive regulation that have been examined, PerR binding occurs at distant upstream sites, but the exact mechanism of activation is not known (Brenot et al., 2005; Hayashi et al., 2005). 

The functional unit of B. subtilis PerR is a homodimer, and its crystal structure (Jacquamet et al., 2009) is shown in Figure 10.1.2a. Each monomer is composed of a dimerization domain connected by a linker region to an N-terminal DNA-binding domain containing a helix-turn-helix motif and contains two metal-binding sites. One site, which is located in the dimerization domain, binds a $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ molecule that is coordinated by four cysteine residues (C96, C99, C136, and C139) (Traore´ et $a l . _ { \cdot }$ , 2006). Coordination of $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ at this site plays a structural role that is required for PerR function, but is not thought to be involved in peroxide sensing due to the fact that the coordinating cysteines are highly resistant to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ -mediated oxidation (Lee and Helmann, 2006a; Traore´ et al., 2006). 

A second “regulatory” metal-binding site is located between the DNA-binding and dimerization domains. The regulatory site binds either an $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ or $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ (Herbig and Helmann, 2001). Coordination of either metal at this site locks the PerR dimer in a caliper-like conformation that holds the DNA-binding domains in an orientation that allows them to interact with DNA (Figure 10.1.2a) (Jaquamet et al., 2009). 

Peroxide sensing occurs at the regulatory site of the ironcontaining form of the protein, $\mathrm { P e r R : } Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + } { : } \mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ . Metal bound at the regulatory site is coordinated by three histidine (H37, H91, and H93) and two aspartate (D104 and D85) residues, as shown in Figure 10.1.2c. These residues are positioned to form a four-sided pyramid with His 93 at the apex and alternating aspartate and histidine residues at the corners of the base (Jaquamet et al., 2009). The metal $( \mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + } \ \mathrm { o r } \ \mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + } )$ bound at the regulatory site is solvent accessible via an opening that is lined with hydrophilic residues that confer the $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ specificity of the protein (Jaquamet et al., 2009). $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ that diffuses into the regulatory site can then undergo Fenton chemistry with bound $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ to yield $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 3 + }$ and hydroxyl radical (OH∙ ) (see Figure 10.1.2a). $\mathrm { O H ^ { \bullet } }$ is highly reactive and quickly oxidizes one of the coordinating histidines that form the base of the pyramid to 2-oxo-His, showing a preference for His37 (Lee and Helmann, 2006b; Traore´ et al., 2009). This process results in the loss of Fe at the regulatory site and the destabilization of the DNA-binding domain of the oxidized monomer, leading to the release of bound PerR from the target gene promoter. The dramatic effect of the loss of bound metal at the regulatory site of PerR can be seen in Figure 10.1.2b, in which the DNA-binding domains and dimerization domains of the oxidized dimer are coplanar. This splayed conformation is seen in the crystal structures of both demetalated nonoxidized apo- $\mathrm { \cdot P e r R : } Z \mathrm { n } ^ { \dot { 2 } + }$ and oxidized $\mathrm { P e r R { : } Z n ^ { 2 + } { : } F e ^ { 2 + } }$ (Jaquamet et al., 2009; Traore´ et al., 2006, 2009). It is thought that oxidized PerR is not able to be recycled, as is the case for $\mathrm { O x y R ^ { \mathrm { o x } } }$ , given that there is no known physiological system to repair 2-oxo-histidine (Lee and Helmann, 2006b). 

The physiological role of $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ in PerR function is not completely understood. Competition between $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ and $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ for binding at the regulatory site is physiologically relevant since alteration in the concentrations of Fe and Mn in the culture media changes the relative sensitivity of genes in the PerR regulon to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ induction (Chen et al., 1995; Faulkner et al., 2012; Lee and Helmann, 2006b). Moreover $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ , not $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ , appears to function as the co-repressor for some target genes (Fuangthong et al., 2002). One common feature of the bacterial oxidative stress response is to increase the intracellular $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ concentration during oxidative stress (Faulkner and Helmann, 2011). $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ is then able to replace iron at some metal-binding sites and thereby protect iron-containing proteins from oxidative damage (Imlay, 2014; Sobota and Imlay, 2011). $\mathrm { P e r } { : } Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + } { : } \mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ is ${ \mathrm { > } } 1 0 ^ { 4 } { \mathrm { - } } { \mathrm { f o l d } }$ more resistant to $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ -mediated oxidation than $\mathrm { P e r R { : } Z n ^ { 2 + } { : } F e ^ { 2 + } }$ , whereas $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ binds to the regulatory site with a much higher affinity than $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ (Lee and Helmann, 2006ba,b). It has been proposed that one possible role for $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ binding is to protect the PerR pool from oxidative inactivation while still allowing for PerR-mediated de-repression of target genes in response to $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ released due to oxidative damage (Lee and Helmann, 2006b). Thus, PerR senses the relative intracellular concentrations of Fe and Mn as well as the level of $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 }$ . 

Similar to OxyR, PerR has the ability to sense nitrosylating agents such as nitrous oxide (NO) during growth under aerobic and anaerobic conditions (Moore et al., 2004; see Chapter 17.3). It is likely that NO sensing is performed by $\mathrm { P e r R : Z n ^ { 2 + } : F e ^ { 2 + } }$ since anaerobic growth in the presence of $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ reduced NOinduced expression of PerR regulon genes, whereas high iron levels increased expression. The mechanism of NO-mediated inactivation of PerR is not known but is thought to be due to nitrosylation of bound $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ (Moore et al., 2004).

The crystal structure of one PerR ortholog, shown in Figure 10.1.3, differs markedly from the dimeric PerR from B. subtilis $( { \mathrm { P e r R } } _ { \mathrm { B s } } )$ . Reduced PerR of S. pyogenes $( { \mathrm { P e r R } } _ { \mathrm { S p } } )$ has a domain structure that is similar to that of the B. subtilis protein $( { \mathrm { P e r R } } _ { \mathrm { B s } } )$ (i.e., a dimerization domain, an interdomain linker region, and an N-terminal DNA-binding domain); however, the crystal structure of the PerRSp dimer takes on a splayed conformation similar to the demetalated form of $\mathrm { P e r R } _ { \mathrm { B s } }$ (Lin et al., 2014; Makthal et al., 2013). Per $\mathrm { R } _ { \mathrm { S p } }$ contains both a structural $Z \mathrm { n } ^ { 2 + }$ -binding site as well as a regulatory site that can coordinate either $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ or $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ . The $\mathrm { M n } ^ { 2 + }$ -containing form is resistant to oxidation by $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { O } _ { 2 } ,$ while $\mathrm { F e } ^ { 2 + }$ bound at the regulatory site is required for peroxide-mediated inactivation of PerR (Makthal et al., 2013). Metal coordination at the regulatory site is also different from that in ${ \mathrm { P e r R } } _ { \mathrm { B S } } .$ Metal bound at the $\mathrm { P e r R } _ { \mathrm { S p } }$ regulatory site is coordinated by five histidines (H4, H6, H19, H97, and H99) and one asparagine residue (N15), as shown in Figure 10.1.3b. H44 of $\mathrm { P e r R } _ { \mathrm { S p } } ,$ which is equivalent to H37 in $\mathrm { P e r R } _ { \mathrm { B s } } ,$ is involved in interdomain interactions and does not participate in peroxide sensing at the regulatory site (Makthal et al., 2013). Single-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) studies suggest that $\mathrm { P e r R } _ { \mathrm { S p } }$ adopts a tetrameric structure in solution that is made up of two dimers in a head-to-tail association (Lin et al., 2014). DNA binding to a target containing two Per boxes appears to involve the wrapping of the DNA around the tetramer with protein–DNA contacts at two sites. DNA binding at each site was predicted to involve two DNA-binding helices, one from each dimer (Lin et al., 2014). 

## 10.1.4 OhrR

OhrR is a dimeric transcriptional repressor that occurs in both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria (Antelmann and Helmann, 2011; Panmanee et al., 2006) and senses both organic peroxides and NaOCl (Chi et al., 2011). OhrR belongs to the MarR family of transcriptional regulators (Perez-Rueda et al., 2004) and can be found along with OxyR (Panmanee et al., 2002), PerR (Fuangthong et al., 2001), or both (Oh et al., 2007). The initial examples of OhrR were found to regulate themselves along with a gene encoding an organic peroxide-specific peroxiredoxin (ohr) (Chuchue et al., 2006; Fuangthong et al., 2001; Mongkolsuk et al., 2002; Oh et al., 2007), but OhrR has recently been demonstrated to also regulate toxinogenesis in B. subtilis (Clair et al., 2013).
